title: Japanese N1
description: The fifth step in Japanese, from N2 to JLPT N1. Grammar lessons cover time and sequence (が早いか, や否や, なり, そばから, を皮切りに, をもって), concession (といえども, たりとも, ものを, であれ, はおろか, ないまでも), reasons, purpose and basis (ばこそ, んがため, べく, とあれば, をよそに, に即して, いかんによらず), feelings and judgements (を禁じ得ない, てやまない, にたえない, に足る, 極まりない, を余儀なくされる, まじき), scope and likeness (ならでは, に至っては, ずくめ, まみれ, めく, きらいがある, ごとき, なりに, たる) and the literary and academic written language, with long editorials, essays, literary prose and academic texts in every lesson and exam practice at the end. About 4,000 new words build on the 6,000 from the earlier courses for about 10,000 in all, learned through typed vocabulary reviews with pitch accent, conjugation drills and sentence building; about 960 new kanji (about 2,000 in all, nearly every jōyō kanji in common use) are learned through notecards, tracing and inside words, with furigana you can turn off. Requires Japanese N2.
author: Erudior

lessons.title: No sooner than: が早いか, や否や, なり, そばから
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Welcome to N1, the last step of the series. You finished N2 able to argue, concede, give reasons
and read editorials of 500 to 800 characters. N1 is the level of newspapers, essays, literature
and lectures read and heard as they are, without simplification. The grammar you'll meet is
mostly **[[written style]]**: patterns that a native speaker reads every day but rarely says in
conversation, each with narrow rules about what can come before it, who can be the subject and
what may follow.

What changes in this course:

- **Kanji: 32 a lesson.** The course adds 960 kanji to the 1,039 you know, for 1,999 in all,
  nearly every kanji in everyday use. They come in three or four groups per lesson, each a table
  you trace and a set of notecards. Many of them spell words you already know in kana: {誰|だれ},
  {頃|ころ}, {玄関|げんかん}, {挨拶|あいさつ} and {椅子|いす} all take their kanji in this lesson.
- **About 130 words a lesson**, for about 10,000 words by the end of the course.
- **Readings of 1,000 to 1,400 characters** in every lesson (longer in lessons 26 to 28): editorials,
  essays, critiques, literary prose, academic texts, letters and notices.
- **The test.** The JLPT N1 has two timed parts: language knowledge (vocabulary and grammar)
  together with reading, then listening. It gives three scored sections: vocabulary and grammar,
  reading, and listening. Lesson 30 describes the test in detail; the questions in every lesson
  follow its question types.

This lesson's grammar is about time, and about speed: four ways to say that one thing happened the
instant another did. You know two of them already in their everyday form, N3's 〜たとたん and
N2's 〜たかと{思|おも}うと. The four new ones belong to writing and narrative, and each has its own
shade. The theme is everyday life: the people around you, the home, greetings and the words of
the local news, most of which you've been writing in kana until now.

## Writing at N1: kanji or kana

Every word in this course is written with kanji when **all** of its **[[kanji]]** are on the course
list (the N5 to N2 kanji and the 960 of this course), and in kana otherwise. That rule now reaches
almost every word you know: {誰|だれ}, {僕|ぼく}, {傘|かさ}, {鍵|かぎ}, {玄関|げんかん}, {挨拶|あいさつ},
{叱|しか}る, {匂|にお}い, {暇|ひま}, {隣|となり}, {詳|くわ}しい, {大丈夫|だいじょうぶ}. Their vocabulary cards from
earlier courses still show kana; in lessons, examples and questions they now appear in kanji.
**[[Furigana]]** stay on every kanji, and you can switch them off.

Some words stay in kana even though their kanji are listed. These are the course's rules (and,
for most of them, the newspapers'):

| Stays in kana | Examples |
|---|---|
| auxiliary verbs after て | 〜ている, 〜てある, 〜ておく, 〜てみる, 〜てしまう, 〜ていく, 〜てくる, 〜てもらう, 〜てほしい |
| formal nouns and grammar words | こと, もの, ところ, とき, ため, はず, わけ, つもり, よう, まま, うち, ほど, おかげ, おそれ, ゆえ |
| basic verbs and adjectives | ある, いる, する, なる, できる, いい / よい |
| keigo verbs | いたす, いただく, まいる, おる, もうす, ください |
| honorific prefixes | お〜, ご〜 (御 only in fixed words: {御社|おんしゃ}, {御中|おんちゅう}, {御礼|おんれい}) |
| adverbs and conjunctions newspapers write in kana | ついに, しばらく, いずれ, もっとも, ほとんど, なお, ただし, むしろ, まさに, あえて, ちなみに, かつ |

And some are written in kanji: {既|すで}に, {僅|わず}か, {殊|こと}に, {徐々|じょじょ}に, {再|ふたた}び,
{直|ただ}ちに, {必|かなら}ずしも, {専|もっぱ}ら, {甚|はなは}だ. The formal conjunctions {及|およ}び,
{並|なら}びに, {又|また}は and {若|も}しくは take kanji in written texts but stay in kana (および,
または) in casual lines. Lesson 27 and 28 come back to them.

**N1 grammar patterns** follow a decision of this course, shown in each lesson's title and in the
module 1 reference sheet: kanji for や{否|いな}や, を{皮切|かわき}りに, を{限|かぎ}りに, を{境|さかい}に,
を{経|へ}て, {矢先|やさき}に, {折|おり}から, に{至|いた}る, に{即|そく}して, を{踏|ふ}まえて and a few
others; kana for が{早|はや}いか (with 早 in kanji), なり, そばから, かたわら, がてら, かたがた, ところを,
にあって, なくして, なしに, ずじまい, までだ and most of the rest. The reference sheet
(Time and sequence) lists them all.

A few spellings to know from the start:

- {付|つ}ける for attach, add or apply; つける for switching on; {漬|つ}ける (lesson 4) for pickling.
- {辞|や}める for quitting a job; やめる for stopping an action.
- The noun {後|あと} (after, later); the adverb あと (more, left).
- {頃|ころ} as a noun ({子供|こども}の{頃|ころ}, その{頃|ころ}); 〜ごろ in kana after a time ({三時|さんじ}ごろ).
- {叱|しか}る is printed with the common form 叱 in this course. The official form in the jōyō
  table is 𠮟, which many fonts lack; the tracing pad accepts both. Lessons 15 and 25 have two
  more pairs of this kind.
- Established mixed spellings stay mixed: ひな{祭|まつ}り, {夫婦|ふうふ}げんか.

## The moment A, B: 〜が{早|はや}いか

〜が{早|はや}いか joins the dictionary form of a verb (sometimes the た form). Literally "whether A
was early": A and B are so close together that you can hardly say which came first. It's the
grammar of **[[immediacy]]**, and it lives in writing and in storytelling.

{電車|でんしゃ}のドアが{開|ひら}くが{早|はや}いか、{乗客|じょうきゃく}がホームに{飛|と}び{出|だ}した。 — The instant the train doors opened, passengers streamed out onto the platform.
{彼|かれ}は{受話器|じゅわき}を{置|お}くが{早|はや}いか、{部屋|へや}を{出|で}ていった。 — No sooner had he put down the phone than he left the room.
{子供|こども}たちは{弁当|べんとう}を{食|た}べ{終|お}わるが{早|はや}いか、{外|そと}へ{遊|あそ}びに{行|い}った。 — The moment the children had finished their lunch, they went out to play.
{記事|きじ}が{出|で}るが{早|はや}いか、{抗議|こうぎ}の{電話|でんわ}が{殺到|さっとう}した。 — The moment the article came out, the phone was flooded with complaints.

The rules:

- **B is a real event, usually past**, and usually a quick action: someone runs off, a crowd
  rushes in. The sentence reports what happened, often with a little surprise at the speed.
- **No will, no requests in B**: not a plan, an order or an invitation. ×{家|いえ}に{着|つ}くが{早|はや}いか、
  {電話|でんわ}してください is ungrammatical; say {家|いえ}に{着|つ}いたらすぐ{電話|でんわ}してください.
- **Mostly about other people.** The speaker can be the subject in a narrative of their own past
  ({私|わたし}は{家|いえ}に{着|つ}くが{早|はや}いか、ベッドに{倒|たお}れ{込|こ}んだ), but it isn't used for present
  habits or plans.
- A and B may have the same subject or different ones.

## As soon as (written): 〜や{否|いな}や, 〜や

〜や{否|いな}や joins the dictionary form, and so does the shorter 〜や. {否|いな} means "no", so the
pattern once meant "whether it happened or not": before anyone could tell, B had followed.

{開店|かいてん}のベルが{鳴|な}るや{否|いな}や、{客|きゃく}が{店内|てんない}になだれ{込|こ}んだ。 — The moment the opening bell rang, the customers surged into the shop.
{彼女|かのじょ}は{合格|ごうかく}の{知|し}らせを{聞|き}くや{否|いな}や、{母親|ははおや}に{電話|でんわ}をかけた。 — As soon as she heard she had passed, she phoned her mother.
{新製品|しんせいひん}は{発売|はつばい}されるや、たちまち{売|う}り{切|き}れた。 — The new product sold out as soon as it was released.

や{否|いな}や and が{早|はや}いか are close, and in many sentences either works. The differences are
tendencies, not hard rules:

- や{否|いな}や is the more literary of the two and the commoner one in newspapers;
  が{早|はや}いか stresses the speed itself, often with a hint of haste.
- Both need a past B that's a fact, and neither takes the speaker's will in B.
- Both are rare in conversation. In speech, use 〜たとたん or 〜たらすぐ.

## As soon as, then (unexpectedly): 〜なり

〜なり joins the dictionary form. It says that someone did A and at once did B, and B is usually
something the listener wouldn't expect: a sudden action or reaction.

{父|ちち}は{家|いえ}に{帰|かえ}るなり、{何|なに}も{言|い}わずに{部屋|へや}にこもった。 — The moment he got home, my father shut himself in his room without a word.
{彼女|かのじょ}は{手紙|てがみ}を{読|よ}むなり、{泣|な}き{出|だ}した。 — She had no sooner read the letter than she burst into tears.
{店|みせ}に{入|はい}ってくるなり、その{客|きゃく}は{大声|おおごえ}で{文句|もんく}を{言|い}い{始|はじ}めた。 — No sooner had the customer walked in than they started complaining loudly.

なり is stricter than the others:

- **The same subject** does A and B. ×{私|わたし}が{帰|かえ}るなり、{犬|いぬ}が{飛|と}びついてきた mixes two
  subjects; say {私|わたし}が{帰|かえ}るとすぐ or {帰|かえ}ったとたん. With one subject it's fine:
  {犬|いぬ}は{私|わたし}の{顔|かお}を{見|み}るなり{飛|と}びついてきた.
- **Not normally the speaker.** なり describes someone else's surprising behaviour. Your own
  actions go with 〜たとたん or 〜てすぐ.
- **B is a past fact**, never a request, plan or order.
- It's at home in written narrative and also heard in adult speech when telling a story
  ({彼|かれ}、{来|く}るなり{怒|おこ}り{出|だ}してさ).

You'll also meet the た form + なり in literature: {出|で}かけたなり{帰|かえ}ってこない ("went out and has
never come back"). That's a different use (A happens and nothing follows); this course only asks
you to recognize it.

## No sooner done than undone: 〜そばから

〜そばから joins the dictionary form or the た form. そば is "right beside": B comes right next to A,
and undoes it, and the whole thing keeps happening. The tone is weary or complaining.

{片付|かたづ}けるそばから、{子供|こども}たちが{散|ち}らかす。 — No sooner have I tidied up than the children make a mess again.
{習|なら}ったそばから{忘|わす}れてしまう。 — I forget things as soon as I've learned them.
{雪|ゆき}かきをするそばから、また{雪|ゆき}が{積|つ}もっていく。 — As fast as we clear the snow, more piles up.
{給料|きゅうりょう}が{入|はい}るそばから、{支払|しはら}いで{消|き}えていく。 — My pay disappears into bills the moment it comes in.

- **Repeated actions**, not a single event: it describes a pattern, often in the present tense.
- **B cancels or spoils A**: tidying and mess, learning and forgetting, earning and spending.
- A and B may have different subjects ({片付|かたづ}ける is the speaker; {散|ち}らかす the children).
- Common in speech as well as writing.

## Review: 〜たとたん and 〜たかと{思|おも}うと

> 〜たとたん(に) (N3): "just as, the moment": {立|た}ち{上|あ}がったとたん、めまいがした. B is
> unexpected and outside anyone's control; everyday speech and writing.
>
> 〜たかと{思|おも}うと / 〜たかと{思|おも}ったら (N2, lesson 3): "one moment A, the next B": a sudden
> change, often to something contrasting: {泣|な}いたかと{思|おも}うと、もう{笑|わら}っている. Used of
> others, not of the speaker's own actions.

## Six ways to say "as soon as"

| Pattern | Joins | What B is | Subjects | Register |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 〜たとたん (N3) | た form | unexpected, uncontrolled; past | same or different | speech and writing |
| 〜たかと{思|おも}うと (N2) | た form | a sudden change, often a contrast | others, not the speaker | speech and writing |
| 〜が{早|はや}いか | dictionary form | a quick action; past fact; no will | same or different | written, narrative |
| 〜や{否|いな}や / 〜や | dictionary form | a reaction or result; past fact; no will | same or different | written, newspapers |
| 〜なり | dictionary form | a surprising action; past fact | same, usually not the speaker | narrative; storytelling speech |
| 〜そばから | dictionary / た form | undoes A, again and again | same or different | speech and writing |

One sentence where only one fits: {教|おし}えたそばから{忘|わす}れる (taught it, and it's gone again,
every time) needs そばから, because the others describe a single event. And one where そばから
can't go: {彼|かれ}は{部屋|へや}に{入|はい}るなり{窓|まど}を{開|あ}けた is a single, surprising action by one
person, so なり, が{早|はや}いか or や{否|いな}や, but not そばから.

## Everyday life in kanji

This lesson's words are the people, places and objects of ordinary life that earlier courses
wrote in kana, and the news words that go with them.

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| people and address | {隣人|りんじん}, {両隣|りょうどなり}, {隣近所|となりきんじょ}, {住人|じゅうにん}, {家主|やぬし}, {居候|いそうろう}, {令嬢|れいじょう}, お{嬢|じょう}さん, {叔父|おじ}, {叔母|おば}, {老婆|ろうば}, {坊|ぼう}や, {坊|ぼっ}ちゃん, {赤|あか}ん{坊|ぼう}, {玄人|くろうと}, {僕|ぼく}ら |
| the home | {扉|とびら}, {戸棚|とだな}, {枕|まくら}, {枕元|まくらもと}, {鍵穴|かぎあな}, {風呂場|ふろば}, {玄関先|げんかんさき}, {勝手口|かってぐち}, {客間|きゃくま}, {茶|ちゃ}の{間|ま}, {書斎|しょさい}, {障子|しょうじ}, {引|ひ}き{戸|ど}, {網戸|あみど}, {敷居|しきい}, {表札|ひょうさつ}, {呼|よ}び{鈴|りん}, {間取|まど}り, {屋根裏|やねうら} |
| daily objects | {日傘|ひがさ}, {折|お}り{畳|たた}み{傘|がさ}, {傘立|かさた}て, {手帳|てちょう}, {通帳|つうちょう}, {洗剤|せんざい}, {掛|か}け{布団|ぶとん}, {敷|し}き{布団|ぶとん}, インターホン, オートロック |
| greetings and manners | {会釈|えしゃく}, {一礼|いちれい}, {挨拶状|あいさつじょう}, {挨拶回|あいさつまわ}り, {手土産|てみやげ}, お{邪魔|じゃま}, お{構|かま}いなく, {恐縮|きょうしゅく}, {恐|おそ}れ{入|い}る, {世間話|せけんばなし} |
| time | {近頃|ちかごろ}, {日頃|ひごろ}, {頃合|ころあ}い, {年頃|としごろ}, {余暇|よか}, {休暇|きゅうか}, {往年|おうねん}, {往々|おうおう}にして |
| the local news | {近隣|きんりん}, {隣接|りんせつ}する, {復興|ふっこう}, {立|た}ち{往生|おうじょう}, {某|ぼう}, {某所|ぼうしょ}, {不詳|ふしょう}, {刑務所|けいむしょ}, {実刑|じっけい}, {死刑|しけい}, {刑法|けいほう}, {宮内庁|くないちょう} |

Notes:

- {叔父|おじ} and {叔母|おば} are a **[[special reading]]**: two kanji read as one native word, おじ, not
  piece by piece. Readings of this kind, where the kanji give the meaning but not the sound, are
  also called **[[jukujikun]]**. You know some already ({今日|きょう}, {大人|おとな}, {眼鏡|めがね}); this
  course teaches about twenty more, one or two at a time. {玄人|くろうと} (an old hand, a professional)
  is this lesson's other one. In speech you say {叔父|おじ}さん, {叔母|おば}さん (N5's words, now in
  kanji when they mean a parent's younger brother or sister); a parent's older siblings are
  written {伯父|おじ} and {伯母|おば} (lesson 7).
- {某|ぼう} is the written "a certain": {某|ぼう}{大手|おおて}{企業|きぎょう} (a certain major company),
  {都内|とない}{某所|ぼうしょ} (somewhere in Tokyo). News uses it when a name is withheld.
- {近頃|ちかごろ} is a little old-fashioned and often comes with a comment: {近頃|ちかごろ}の{若|わか}い{人|ひと}は…
  N5's {最近|さいきん} is neutral.
- お{構|かま}いなく and {恐|おそ}れ{入|い}ります are a guest's words: the first declines a host's offer
  ("please don't go to any trouble"), the second thanks or apologizes before a request.
- {扉|とびら} is the written word for a hinged door; N5's ドア is the everyday one, and N3's {戸|と} is
  the traditional, often sliding, door.

## Kanji

Thirty-two kanji in four groups: people and how we address them, the home, greetings and time,
and the words of the local news.

### People and forms of address

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 誰 | who | — | だれ | 15 | {誰|だれ}しも, {誰一人|だれひとり}, {誰|だれ} (carried), {誰|だれ}か (carried) |
| 僕 | I (men and boys); servant | ボク | — | 14 | {僕|ぼく}ら, {公僕|こうぼく}, {僕|ぼく} (carried) |
| 俺 | I (rough, male) | — | おれ | 10 | {俺|おれ} (carried) |
| 嬢 | young lady, daughter | ジョウ | — | 16 | {令嬢|れいじょう}, お{嬢|じょう}さん |
| 叔 | a parent's younger sibling | シュク | — | 8 | {叔父|おじ}, {叔母|おば} |
| 婆 | old woman | バ | — | 11 | {老婆|ろうば} |
| 坊 | boy; priest's lodging | ボウ, ボッ | — | 7 | {坊|ぼう}や, {坊|ぼっ}ちゃん, {坊主|ぼうず}, {寝坊|ねぼう} (carried) |
| 某 | a certain (unnamed) | ボウ | — | 9 | {某|ぼう}, {某所|ぼうしょ} |

- 誰 has no on'yomi in the jōyō table: it's always だれ. {誰|だれ}しも (anyone at all) and
  {誰一人|だれひとり}〜ない (not a single person) are its written uses.
- 僕 (I) also means "servant": {公僕|こうぼく}, a servant of the people.
- 嬢 has the "woman" radical 女 beside a shape it shares with 譲 (yield, lesson 7) and 醸 (brew,
  lesson 4): the left side tells them apart (女, 言, 酉).
- 叔 gives the younger siblings of a parent; lesson 7's 伯 gives the older ones.
- 坊 is read ボッ before ちゃん: {坊|ぼっ}ちゃん.

```trace
誰僕俺嬢叔婆坊某
```

### The home

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 鍵 | key | ケン | かぎ | 17 | {鍵穴|かぎあな}, {鍵盤|けんばん}, {鍵|かぎ} (carried), {合|あ}い{鍵|かぎ} (carried) |
| 枕 | pillow | — | まくら | 8 | {枕|まくら}, {枕元|まくらもと} |
| 扉 | door (hinged) | ヒ | とびら | 12 | {扉|とびら} |
| 棚 | shelf | — | たな | 12 | {戸棚|とだな}, {棚上|たなあ}げ, {棚|たな} (carried), {本棚|ほんだな} (carried) |
| 呂 | (sound ロ, in 風呂) | ロ | — | 7 | {風呂場|ふろば}, {風呂上|ふろあ}がり, お{風呂|ふろ} (carried), {風呂敷|ふろしき} (carried) |
| 玄 | dark, deep; entrance | ゲン | — | 5 | {玄人|くろうと}, {玄米|げんまい}, {玄関先|げんかんさき}, {玄関|げんかん} (carried) |
| 椅 | chair | イ | — | 12 | {椅子|いす} (carried), {車椅子|くるまいす} (carried) |
| 帳 | notebook; curtain | チョウ | — | 11 | {手帳|てちょう}, {通帳|つうちょう}, {帳消|ちょうけ}し |
| 傘 | umbrella | サン | かさ | 12 | {日傘|ひがさ}, {雨傘|あまがさ}, {傘立|かさた}て, {傘|かさ} (carried) |

- 鍵 is read かぎ alone and ケン in {鍵盤|けんばん} (piano keys). The metal radical 金 is on the left, as
  in 鍋 (lesson 4).
- 棚 and 枕 have no on'yomi in the jōyō table; 呂 appears almost only in {風呂|ふろ}.
- 椅 appears only in {椅子|いす} and {車椅子|くるまいす}, both carried words now in kanji.
- 帳 has the cloth radical 巾: it once meant a curtain, then the cloth-bound book: {手帳|てちょう},

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

It's five years since I moved into a flat in the city, but I can't clearly picture the faces of
the people on either side of me. On the day I moved in I took a small gift round to say hello, but
all I got was "Oh, thanks for coming" over the intercom; the door never opened. These days, I'm
told, many people don't do the moving-in greeting at all. No one, I suppose, wants other people
peering into their lives.

In the morning, if I share the lift with someone, we each stare silently at our phone screens.
The moment the doors open, everyone hurries out. We see each other's faces every day but hardly
ever exchange a word. To be honest, I had never once found that lonely. Without the bother of
neighbourly ties, city life is easy.

The country town where I grew up was different. At my grandmother's house, nobody locked the
front door, and the neighbours would come in by the kitchen door and stay chatting in the family
room. The moment the neighbourhood notices arrived, my grandmother would take them next door and
not come back for an hour. In summer someone would leave vegetables from their field at our
door, and in winter my grandmother's pickles went back in return. When I got home from school, the woman next door would call out as
soon as she saw me, "Welcome home! You're early today."

Of course, that kind of neighbourliness had its irritations. Everything that went on in your house
was known up and down the street, and my mother often grumbled, "No sooner have I cleaned than
the neighbours' children come in with their muddy feet." News travelled fast, too. When a family's
son got into university, the whole town knew before he even got home. In return, if someone fell ill, a neighbour would
bring round meals without being asked.

City life freed me from all that. But in exchange for freedom, something was lost. Last winter, an
elderly person living on my floor collapsed at home and was taken away by ambulance. The one who
noticed something was wrong was the newspaper delivery person: three days' papers had piled up in
the letterbox. Living just a few metres away, I had known nothing. I remember hearing the ambulance siren, but
it never occurred to me that it was for someone on my floor.

Since then I've made a point of bowing first when I meet people in the corridor. Often enough I
get nothing back, but that's fine. I don't want to go back to country-style neighbourliness, and
there's no need to be close friends with your neighbours. A simple "good morning" is enough. But
knowing each other's faces may turn out, when it counts, to be a small key that saves someone.

## Common mistakes

- ×{駅|えき}に{着|つ}くが{早|はや}いか、{電話|でんわ}してね. が{早|はや}いか, や{否|いな}や and なり report what
  happened; they can't introduce a request or a plan. Use 〜たらすぐ.
- ×{私|わたし}が{帰|かえ}るなり、{母|はは}が{怒|おこ}った. なり needs one subject for both actions:
  {母|はは}は{私|わたし}の{顔|かお}を{見|み}るなり{怒|おこ}った.
- そばから for a single event: {一度|いちど}{片付|かたづ}けたそばから、{客|きゃく}が{来|き}た isn't used that way. そばから describes
  something that keeps happening and undoes the first action; for one event use 〜たとたん.
- ×{聞|き}いたや{否|いな}や. や{否|いな}や and が{早|はや}いか join the dictionary form, even for past
  events: {聞|き}くや{否|いな}や.
- Using や{否|いな}や in chat. It's correct but sounds like a novel. In speech, 〜たとたん or 〜たらすぐ.
- Reading {叔父|おじ} kanji by kanji. The two kanji are one word, おじ (a rare formal reading,
  しゅくふ, exists in dictionaries).

## Key points

- Written style: most N1 grammar lives in writing, with strict rules on what precedes, the subject
  and what follows.
- 〜が{早|はや}いか (dictionary form): the instant A, B; a quick action, a past fact; written and narrative.
- 〜や{否|いな}や / 〜や (dictionary form): as soon as; a past fact, often a reaction; literary, newspapers.
- 〜なり (dictionary form): as soon as, then something surprising; same subject, usually not the
  speaker; past.
- 〜そばから (dictionary / た form): no sooner done than undone, again and again; a complaint.
- None of the four takes a request, order or plan in B. In speech: 〜たとたん, 〜たらすぐ.
- Kanji: 32 new; {誰|だれ}, {頃|ころ}, {傘|かさ}, {鍵|かぎ}, {玄関|げんかん}, {挨拶|あいさつ}, {椅子|いす},
  {叱|しか}る and many more carried words now take kanji. Special readings: {叔父|おじ}, {叔母|おば},
  {玄人|くろうと}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Starting and ending: を皮切りに, をもって, を限りに, を境に
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 1 was about the instant one thing follows another. This lesson is about points on a time
line: where a series starts, the formal moment something ends, the last time before a change you
decide on, the turning point after which everything is different, and the stages something passes
through. All five patterns are built on を + a noun or verb, and all are written or formal:

{東京|とうきょう}{公演|こうえん}を{皮切|かわき}りに、{全国|ぜんこく}ツアーが{始|はじ}まる。 — Starting with the Tokyo performance, a nationwide tour begins.
{本日|ほんじつ}をもって{閉店|へいてん}いたします。 — We close our doors as of today.
{今日|きょう}を{限|かぎ}りに、たばこはやめる。 — From today on, I'm giving up smoking.
あの{日|ひ}を{境|さかい}に、{彼|かれ}は{変|か}わった。 — From that day on, he changed.
{審議|しんぎ}を{経|へ}て、{法案|ほうあん}は{可決|かけつ}された。 — After deliberation, the bill was passed.

The theme is nature: trees and flowers through the seasons, animals, birds and insects, the
weather and the sky. Many of the words were in kana until now ({桜|さくら}, {雷|かみなり}, {嵐|あらし},
{霧|きり}, {虹|にじ}, {猿|さる}); the rest are the words of weather reports, nature columns and seasonal
letters.

## Starting with: 〜を{皮切|かわき}りに

N + を{皮切|かわき}りに (also を{皮切|かわき}りにして, を{皮切|かわき}りとして): "with A as the first, and then
others followed". {皮切|かわき}り is the first cut, the start. A is the first in a series of similar
events, and B says how the series spread or continued.

{新作|しんさく}{映画|えいが}は、{東京|とうきょう}を{皮切|かわき}りに{全国|ぜんこく}で{公開|こうかい}される。 — The new film opens in Tokyo first and then nationwide.
{一人|ひとり}の{発言|はつげん}を{皮切|かわき}りに、{次々|つぎつぎ}と{反対|はんたい}の{声|こえ}が{上|あ}がった。 — One person spoke up, and then one objection after another followed.
{桜|さくら}の{開花|かいか}は、{九州|きゅうしゅう}などを{皮切|かわき}りに{北|きた}へと{進|すす}んでいく。 — The cherries open first in places such as Kyushu and then further and further north.

- **B is a spreading series**: 〜で{次々|つぎつぎ}と, {各地|かくち}で, 〜へと{広|ひろ}がる. A single following
  event doesn't fit: {朝食|ちょうしょく}を{皮切|かわき}りに{会社|かいしゃ}へ{行|い}った isn't said.
- Usually neutral or positive (tours, sales, a run of wins, a wave of opinions); in the news also
  for a run of incidents.
- Written and formal speech (news, announcements, business).

## As of (a formal end or start): 〜をもって

N + をもって marks the date or moment when something formal ends or begins. It's the language of
notices, announcements and official letters.

{当店|とうてん}は、{三月|さんがつ}{末日|まつじつ}をもって{閉店|へいてん}いたします。 — This shop will close as of the end of March.
これをもちまして、{本日|ほんじつ}の{会|かい}を{終了|しゅうりょう}いたします。 — With this, we bring today's meeting to a close.
{十二月|じゅうにがつ}{一日|ついたち}をもって、{新|あたら}しい{規則|きそく}が{適用|てきよう}される。 — The new rules apply from 1 December.

- **Very formal**: これをもちまして (with this, we conclude) is the polite form in speeches.
- The subject is usually an organization: shops, companies, events, rules.
- をもって has a second sense, "by means of, with" ({書面|しょめん}をもって{通知|つうち}する: to notify
  in writing). Lesson 12 teaches it; N2 lesson 13 met it.

## From this point on, no more: 〜を{限|かぎ}りに

N + を{限|かぎ}りに: "with A as the last time": after A, something stops for good. A is a time word
({今日|きょう}, {今回|こんかい}, {今年|ことし}, {本日|ほんじつ}).

{今日|きょう}を{限|かぎ}りに、お{酒|さけ}はやめることにした。 — I've decided today will be my last drink.
{彼女|かのじょ}は{今季|こんき}を{限|かぎ}りに{引退|いんたい}する。 — She will retire at the end of this season.
{本日|ほんじつ}を{限|かぎ}りに、この{路線|ろせん}の{運行|うんこう}を{終了|しゅうりょう}いたします。 — Today is the last day of service on this line.

- It looks forward: B is what stops after A, often a decision (〜ことにした, 〜する).
- をもって and を{限|かぎ}りに overlap in notices ({本日|ほんじつ}をもって / {本日|ほんじつ}を{限|かぎ}りに{閉店|へいてん}). を{限|かぎ}りに
  stresses "this is the last time"; をもって is the neutral formal date.
- {声|こえ}を{限|かぎ}りに{叫|さけ}ぶ (to shout at the top of one's voice) is a fixed phrase with another
  sense, "to the limit". Recognize it.

## With A as the turning point: 〜を{境|さかい}に

N + を{境|さかい}に (also を{境|さかい}にして, を{境|さかい}として): "from A on, things were different". A is an
event or a date that divides before and after; B is a change.

{事故|じこ}を{境|さかい}に、{父|ちち}はお{酒|さけ}をやめた。 — After the accident, my father stopped drinking.
{十月|じゅうがつ}に{入|はい}ったのを{境|さかい}に、{急|きゅう}に{寒|さむ}くなった。 — Once October came, it suddenly got cold.
{転職|てんしょく}を{境|さかい}にして、{生活|せいかつ}のリズムががらりと{変|か}わった。 — Changing jobs completely changed the rhythm of my life.

- **B is a change**: 〜ようになった, 〜なくなった, {変|か}わった, {急|きゅう}に〜.
- A verb clause takes の: {入|はい}ったのを{境|さかい}に.
- Neutral to formal; heard in speech too.
- {境|さかい} is also a plain noun, a boundary ({県|けん}の{境|さかい}): the pattern is "taking A as the boundary".

## Via, after going through: 〜を{経|へ}て

N + を{経|へ}て: "via a place" or "after going through a stage". {経|へ}る (to pass through) is a
written verb; its て form is {経|へ}て.

この{飛行機|ひこうき}は、ソウルを{経|へ}てシドニーへ{向|む}かう。 — This plane flies to Sydney via Seoul.
{長|なが}い{議論|ぎろん}を{経|へ}て、{計画|けいかく}はようやく{承認|しょうにん}された。 — After a long debate, the plan was finally approved.
{彼|かれ}は{営業|えいぎょう}{部長|ぶちょう}を{経|へ}て{社長|しゃちょう}に{就任|しゅうにん}した。 — He became president after a spell as head of sales.

- With places, it's the route; with processes, stages ({審査|しんさ}を{経|へ}て, {試行錯誤|しこうさくご}を{経|へ}て); with
  posts, a career.
- Written and formal; in speech 〜を{通|とお}って or 〜の{後|あと}で.
- Don't read 経 as けい here: {経|へ}る / {経|へ}て. (経 is けい in {経験|けいけん}, {経済|けいざい}.)

## Review: 〜{以来|いらい} and 〜てからというもの

> 〜て{以来|いらい} / N + {以来|いらい} (N2, lesson 8): "ever since": {卒業|そつぎょう}して{以来|いらい}、{一度|いちど}も
> {会|あ}っていない. 〜てからというもの (N2, lesson 8) adds a strong feeling that life changed:
> {犬|いぬ}を{飼|か}い{始|はじ}めてからというもの、{毎朝|まいあさ}{散歩|さんぽ}するようになった. Both describe a
> state that has lasted since A; を{境|さかい}に points at the moment of change itself.

## Five points on the time line

| Pattern | A is | B is | Register | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| を{皮切|かわき}りに | the first of a series | the series spreading | written, news | {大阪|おおさか}を{皮切|かわき}りに{各地|かくち}で{開催|かいさい} |
| をもって | a formal date or moment | an end or a start | very formal, notices | {本日|ほんじつ}をもって{終了|しゅうりょう} |
| を{限|かぎ}りに | the last time | something that stops for good | formal; decisions | {今日|きょう}を{限|かぎ}りにやめる |
| を{境|さかい}に | a turning point | a change, before vs after | neutral to formal | {事故|じこ}を{境|さかい}に{変|か}わった |
| を{経|へ}て | a place, stage or post passed through | the destination or result | written, formal | {審議|しんぎ}を{経|へ}て{決定|けってい} |

Where only one works: {彼|かれ}の{引退|いんたい}{試合|じあい}を{皮切|かわき}りに… needs a series after it; for
"from his retirement match on, the team changed", it's を{境|さかい}に. And for a shop's notice, both
{本日|ほんじつ}をもって and {本日|ほんじつ}を{限|かぎ}りに work, but a personal resolution is を{限|かぎ}りに only:
{今日|きょう}を{限|かぎ}りに{夜更|よふ}かしはやめる ({今日|きょう}をもって isn't used for this: it sounds like a company notice).

## Nature and the seasons

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| cherry and plum | {桜前線|さくらぜんせん}, {夜桜|よざくら}, {葉桜|はざくら}, {八重桜|やえざくら}, {桜吹雪|さくらふぶき}, {花冷|はなび}え, {見頃|みごろ}, {満開|まんかい}, {梅|うめ}, {梅干|うめぼ}し, {松竹梅|しょうちくばい} |
| trees and plants | {松|まつ}, {松林|まつばやし}, {杉|すぎ}, {杉花粉|すぎかふん}, {柳|やなぎ}, {樹木|じゅもく}, {街路樹|がいろじゅ}, {樹齢|じゅれい}, {広葉樹|こうようじゅ}, {針葉樹|しんようじゅ}, {芝生|しばふ}, {草木|くさき}, {落葉|らくよう} |
| flowers | {菊|きく}, {菜|な}の{花|はな}, {朝顔|あさがお}, {彼岸花|ひがんばな}, {藤|ふじ} |
| rice and growth | {稲|いね}, {稲穂|いなほ}, {稲刈|いねか}り, {穂|ほ}, {芽|め}, {新芽|しんめ}, {芽生|めば}える, {芽吹|めぶ}く, {発芽|はつが}, {苗|なえ}, {苗木|なえぎ} |
| weather | {濃霧|のうむ}, {霧雨|きりさめ}, {霜|しも}, {初霜|はつしも}, {霜柱|しもばしら}, {雷雨|らいう}, {落雷|らくらい}, {稲妻|いなずま}, {稲光|いなびかり}, {砂嵐|すなあらし}, {露|つゆ}, {朝露|あさつゆ}, {結露|けつろ}, {黄砂|こうさ}, {寒暖差|かんだんさ}, {季節風|きせつふう}, {春一番|はるいちばん}, {小春日和|こはるびより}, {梅雨前線|ばいうぜんせん}, {梅雨明|つゆあ}け |
| the sky | {晴|は}れ{間|ま}, {曇|くも}り{空|ぞら}, {夕焼|ゆうや}け, {朝焼|あさや}け, {夕暮|ゆうぐ}れ, {夜明|よあ}け, {三日月|みかづき} |
| insects | {蚊|か}, {蚊取|かと}り{線香|せんこう}, {蜂|はち}, {蜜蜂|みつばち}, {芋虫|いもむし}, {毛虫|けむし} |
| animals and birds | {蛇|へび}, {亀|かめ}, {鶴|つる}, {虎|とら}, {鯨|くじら}, {獣|けもの}, {猛獣|もうじゅう}, {鳥獣|ちょうじゅう}, {子羊|こひつじ}, {野鳥|やちょう}, {渡|わた}り{鳥|どり}, {巣|す}, {巣立|すだ}つ, {羽|はね}, {羽|は}ばたく, さえずる, {冬眠|とうみん}, {天敵|てんてき}, {生態系|せいたいけい} |

Notes:

- {芝生|しばふ} is a **[[special reading]]** (生 read ふ), and {梅雨|つゆ}, N5's つゆ, is another: the kanji
  give the meaning, not the sound. In weather news and in compounds, 梅雨 is read ばいう:
  {梅雨前線|ばいうぜんせん}. {梅雨明|つゆあ}け and {梅雨入|つゆい}り keep つゆ.
- {露|つゆ} (dew) sounds the same as {梅雨|つゆ}; context tells them apart. {露|ろ} also means "expose":
  {露骨|ろこつ} (blatant), {暴露|ばくろ} (exposure), {露天風呂|ろてんぶろ} (N3's ろてんぶろ).
- Several animals sound like other words: {蚊|か} and the particle か, {蜂|はち} and {八|はち}, {巣|す} and
  lesson 4's {酢|す} (vinegar), {鶴|つる} and lesson 3's {釣|つ}る (to fish). The accent sometimes helps:
  {鶴|つる:1} (crane) and {釣|つ}る (to fish, flat); {蜂|はち:0} (bee) and {八|はち:2} (eight).
- {小春日和|こはるびより} is a warm day in late autumn, not in spring: {小春|こはる} is an old name for the
  tenth lunar month. Letter writers use it in November.
- {羽目|はめ} (an awkward position) has nothing to do with feathers in today's use: 〜{羽目|はめ}になる
  (end up having to), {羽目|はめ}を{外|はず}す (go overboard, let one's hair down).

## Kanji

Thirty-two kanji: trees and flowers, growth and the weather, insects and small creatures, and
birds and beasts.

### Trees, flowers and the rice plant

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 桜 | cherry | オウ | さくら | 10 | {桜前線|さくらぜんせん}, {夜桜|よざくら}, {八重桜|やえざくら}, {桜|さくら} (carried) |
| 梅 | plum (ume) | バイ | うめ | 10 | {梅|うめ}, {梅干|うめぼ}し, {梅雨前線|ばいうぜんせん}, {梅雨|つゆ} (carried) |
| 菊 | chrysanthemum | キク | — | 11 | {菊|きく} |
| 松 | pine | ショウ | まつ | 8 | {松|まつ}, {松林|まつばやし}, {門松|かどまつ}, {松竹梅|しょうちくばい} |
| 杉 | Japanese cedar | — | すぎ | 7 | {杉|すぎ}, {杉花粉|すぎかふん} |
| 柳 | willow | リュウ | やなぎ | 9 | {柳|やなぎ} |
| 樹 | tree | ジュ | — | 16 | {樹木|じゅもく}, {街路樹|がいろじゅ}, {樹齢|じゅれい}, {樹立|じゅりつ} |
| 芝 | lawn grass | — | しば | 6 | {芝生|しばふ}, {芝|しば}, {芝居|しばい} |
| 稲 | rice plant | トウ | いね, いな | 14 | {稲|いね}, {稲妻|いなずま}, {稲穂|いなほ}, {稲作|いなさく} (carried) |

- 桜, 梅, 松, 杉, 柳, 樹 and 芝 all have a plant radical: 木 on the left for trees, 艹 on top for
  grasses (芝, and 菊 too).
- 梅 is うめ alone and バイ in {梅雨前線|ばいうぜんせん}; N5's {梅雨|つゆ} is a special reading.
- 稲 is いね alone but いな before some words: {稲妻|いなずま}, {稲穂|いなほ}, {稲作|いなさく}.
- 杉 has no on'yomi in the jōyō table; 樹 has no kun'yomi.

```trace
桜梅菊松杉柳樹芝稲
```

### Growth, the seasons and the weather

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 穂 | ear of grain | スイ | ほ | 15 | {穂|ほ}, {稲穂|いなほ} |
| 芽 | bud, sprout | ガ | め | 8 | {芽|め}, {新芽|しんめ}, {発芽|はつが}, {芽生|めば}える |
| 苗 | seedling | ビョウ | なえ, なわ | 8 | {苗|なえ}, {苗木|なえぎ} |
| 節 | season; joint, knot | セツ, セチ | ふし | 13 | {節|ふし}, {節目|ふしめ}, {季節|きせつ} (carried), {節約|せつやく} (carried) |
| 霧 | fog, mist | ム | きり | 19 | {濃霧|のうむ}, {霧雨|きりさめ}, {霧|きり} (carried) |
| 霜 | frost | ソウ | しも | 17 | {霜|しも}, {初霜|はつしも}, {霜柱|しもばしら} |
| 露 | dew; expose | ロ, ロウ | つゆ | 21 | {露|つゆ}, {露骨|ろこつ}, {暴露|ばくろ}, {露天風呂|ろてんぶろ} (carried) |
| 雷 | thunder | ライ | かみなり | 13 | {雷雨|らいう}, {落雷|らくらい}, {雷鳴|らいめい}, {雷|かみなり} (carried) |
| 嵐 | storm | — | あらし | 12 | {砂嵐|すなあらし}, {嵐|あらし} (carried) |
| 虹 | rainbow | — | にじ | 9 | {虹|にじ} (carried) |

- 霧, 霜, 露 and 雷 carry the rain radical 雨 on top: weather words. 雪 and 雲 do too.
- 嵐 is 山 over 風: a mountain wind, a storm. 虹 has the insect radical 虫, said to come from an old Chinese idea of
  the rainbow as a dragon-like creature.
- 節 is セツ in {季節|きせつ} and {節約|せつやく} and ふし on its own (a joint, a knot; a tune). Its
  bamboo radical ⺮ points to the joints of a bamboo stem.
- 芽 (bud) and 苗 (seedling) both have 艹: 芽 has 牙 (fang, lesson 30) below, 苗 has 田 (field).

```trace
穂芽苗節霧霜露雷嵐虹
```

### Insects, snakes and creatures of the water

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 蚊 | mosquito | — | か | 10 | {蚊|か}, {蚊取|かと}り{線香|せんこう} |
| 蜂 | bee, wasp | ホウ | はち | 13 | {蜂|はち}, {蜜蜂|みつばち}, {蜂蜜|はちみつ} |
| 蛍 | firefly | ケイ | ほたる | 11 | {蛍光灯|けいこうとう}, {蛍|ほたる} (carried) |
| 巣 | nest | ソウ | す | 11 | {巣|す}, {巣立|すだ}つ, {古巣|ふるす}, {巣箱|すばこ} |
| 蛇 | snake | ジャ, ダ | へび | 11 | {蛇|へび}, {蛇口|じゃぐち}, {蛇足|だそく} |
| 鯨 | whale | ゲイ | くじら | 19 | {鯨|くじら}, {捕鯨|ほげい} |

- 蚊, 蜂, 蛍 and 蛇 have the insect radical 虫 (it covers snakes too). 蛍's on'yomi ケイ gives
  {蛍光灯|けいこうとう} (fluorescent light).
- 蛇 is へび alone, ジャ in {蛇口|じゃぐち} (a tap: the "snake's mouth"), ダ in {蛇足|だそく}.
- 鯨 has the fish radical 魚, though a whale isn't a fish; 京 on the right is a sound element (ケイ, ゲイ).
- 巣 is a nest in a tree (木) with birds (the three strokes on top).

```trace
蚊蜂蛍巣蛇鯨
```

### Birds and beasts

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 鶴 | crane | — | つる | 21 | {鶴|つる}, {千羽鶴|せんばづる} |
| 亀 | turtle | キ | かめ | 11 | {亀|かめ} |
| 猿 | monkey | エン | さる | 13 | {猿|さる}まね, {猿|さる} (carried) |
| 虎 | tiger | コ | とら | 8 | {虎|とら} |
| 獣 | beast | ジュウ | けもの | 16 | {獣|けもの}, {猛獣|もうじゅう}, {怪獣|かいじゅう}, {獣医|じゅうい} (carried) |
| 羊 | sheep | ヨウ | ひつじ | 6 | {羊毛|ようもう}, {子羊|こひつじ}, {羊|ひつじ} (carried) |
| 羽 | feather, wing | ウ | は, はね | 6 | {羽|はね}, {羽毛|うもう}, {羽|は}ばたく, {羽目|はめ} |

- 鶴 and 亀 go together: {鶴|つる}は{千年|せんねん}、{亀|かめ}は{万年|まんねん} (the crane lives a thousand
  years, the turtle ten thousand), a saying of long life and good luck.
- 鶴 has 21 strokes; with 露 (also 21) and 躍 (lesson 3, 21) it's the most complex kanji in this
  module.
- 羽 is はね (feather, wing), the counter 〜{羽|わ} for birds, and ば in {千羽鶴|せんばづる}.
- 猿 has the animal radical 犭, as do 狩 and 猟 (lesson 3).

```trace
鶴亀猿虎獣羊羽
```

### Words you can now write in kanji

Carried words: {桜|さくら}, {梅雨|つゆ}, {雷|かみなり}, {嵐|あらし}, {虹|にじ}, {霧|きり}, {猿|さる}, {羊|ひつじ},
{蛍|ほたる} (N2's ホタル), {季節|きせつ}, {節約|せつやく}, {節分|せつぶん}, {獣医|じゅうい}, {稲作|いなさく},
{露天風呂|ろてんぶろ}.

Special readings of this lesson: {芝生|しばふ}, and the spelling {梅雨|つゆ} of N5's つゆ.

## Dialogue: the last nature corner

A radio programme's seasonal corner. The announcer, Satō, talks to the weather forecaster
Morita on the corner's last broadcast. (Formal speech on air; surnames, as on radio.)

```dialogue
# The last broadcast
さとう: {毎週|まいしゅう}お{送|おく}りしてきた「{季節|きせつ}のたより」ですが、{今日|きょう}をもって{最終回|さいしゅうかい}となります。{森田|もりた}さん、よろしくお{願|ねが}いします。
= Our weekly "Letters from the Seasons" comes to an end with today's broadcast. Morita, welcome.
もりた: よろしくお{願|ねが}いします。{四年間|よねんかん}、あっという{間|ま}でしたね。
= Thank you. Four years: it went in a flash.

= Yes. Starting with Hokkaido, it's been recorded one place after another in Tōhoku and the hills of Kantō.

= Until last week we had a run of warm days, though.
もりた: はい、{月曜|げつよう}の{雨|あめ}を{境|さかい}に{季節風|きせつふう}が{吹|ふ}き{始|はじ}めて、{一気|いっき}に{冬|ふゆ}らしくなりました。{寒暖差|かんだんさ}が{大|おお}きいので、{体調|たいちょう}には{十分|じゅうぶん}お{気|き}をつけください。
```

All five patterns are here: をもって (the programme's formal last broadcast), を{皮切|かわき}りに (a series
of frost reports), を{境|さかい}に (the change after Monday's rain), を{限|かぎ}りに (the last time before a
change of life) and を{経|へ}て (a stage passed through). {最終回|さいしゅうかい} = the last episode;
{便|たよ}り = news, a letter; {山沿|やまぞ}い = along the mountains. {離|はな}れられる is an honorific
(the れる / られる form). {故郷|こきょう} is lesson 7's word.

## Reading: when the cherries bloom

A newspaper column (だ / である style) on the cherry blossom front and the changing seasons.

> {毎年|まいとし}{三月|さんがつ}になると、テレビの{天気予報|てんきよほう}に{桜前線|さくらぜんせん}の{地図|ちず}が{登場|とうじょう}する。{南|みなみ}の{地方|ちほう}を{皮切|かわき}りに、{桜|さくら}の{開花|かいか}は{一日|いちにち}に{数十|すうじゅっ}キロの{速|はや}さで{北|きた}へと{進|すす}み、{五月|ごがつ}ごろには{北海道|ほっかいどう}に{達|たっ}する。{天気予報|てんきよほう}の{最後|さいご}に「{東京|とうきょう}の{桜|さくら}は{来週|らいしゅう}{見頃|みごろ}を{迎|むか}えるでしょう」と{告|つ}げられると、{会社|かいしゃ}では{花見|はなみ}の{相談|そうだん}が{始|はじ}まる。{開花|かいか}{予想|よそう}の{日付|ひづけ}が{一日|いちにち}ずれただけで、{旅行|りょこう}の{予定|よてい}を{変|か}える{人|ひと}さえいる。{日本人|にほんじん}ほど{一|ひと}つの{花|はな}の{咲|さ}く{日|ひ}を{気|き}にかける{国民|こくみん}は、{世界|せかい}でも{珍|めずら}しいのではないか。

> {季節|きせつ}の{便|たよ}りを{運|はこ}んでくるのは、{桜|さくら}だけではない。{春|はる}には{渡|わた}り{鳥|どり}が{北|きた}へ{帰|かえ}り、{軒先|のきさき}にはつばめが{巣|す}を{作|つく}る。{田|た}んぼに{水|みず}が{張|は}られたのを{境|さかい}に、{夜|よる}はかえるの{声|こえ}でにぎやかになる。{夏|なつ}の{川辺|かわべ}には{蛍|ほたる}が{飛|と}び、{秋|あき}には{稲穂|いなほ}が{頭|あたま}を{垂|た}れ、{虫|むし}の{声|こえ}が{庭|にわ}を{満|み}たす。そして{冬|ふゆ}の{朝|あさ}、{霜柱|しもばしら}を{踏|ふ}む{音|おと}に、{季節|きせつ}が{一巡|いちじゅん}したことを{知|し}るのである。{虫|むし}や{鳥|とり}や{獣|けもの}たちは、{暦|こよみ}を{持|も}たずに{季節|きせつ}を{知|し}っている。

> {季節|きせつ}の{変化|へんか}を{感|かん}じ{取|と}る{力|ちから}は、{桜|さくら}に{限|かぎ}らない。{古|ふる}くから{日本|にほん}の{手紙|てがみ}は{時節|じせつ}の{挨拶|あいさつ}で{始|はじ}まり、{俳句|はいく}には{季節|きせつ}を{表|あらわ}す{言葉|ことば}が{欠|か}かせない。{初霜|はつしも}、{小春日和|こはるびより}、{花冷|はなび}え。どれも、{自然|しぜん}の{小|ちい}さな{変化|へんか}に{目|め}を{留|と}めてきた{人々|ひとびと}の{言葉|ことば}だ。{長|なが}い{時間|じかん}を{経|へ}て{磨|みが}かれたこれらの{言葉|ことば}は、{季節|きせつ}を{感|かん}じるための{道具|どうぐ}でもあった。

> {気候|きこう}が{変|か}われば、こうした{言葉|ことば}の{中|なか}には{実感|じっかん}を{失|うしな}うものも{出|で}てくるだろう。だが、{言葉|ことば}そのものを{今日|きょう}を{限|かぎ}りに{捨|す}てる{必要|ひつよう}はない。{夏|なつ}の{暑|あつ}さがいつまでも{続|つづ}く{年|とし}にこそ、{窓|まど}の{外|そと}の{小|ちい}さな{秋|あき}を{探|さが}してみたい。{夕暮|ゆうぐ}れの{空|そら}の{色|いろ}、{夜明|よあ}けの{冷|つめ}たい{空気|くうき}、{夜露|よつゆ}にぬれた{草|くさ}の{匂|にお}い。{季節|きせつ}は{大|おお}きな{出来事|できごと}としてではなく、そうした{小|ちい}さな{変化|へんか}の{積|つ}み{重|かさ}ねとしてやってくる。{季節|きせつ}は、{気|き}づこうとする{人|ひと}の{前|まえ}にだけ{姿|すがた}を{現|あらわ}すのかもしれない。

{標本木|ひょうほんぼく} = sample tree (the tree a weather station watches); {場所取|ばしょと}り = saving a
spot; {揺|ゆ}らぐ = to waver (lesson 23's word); {実感|じっかん} = a real feeling (of something).

1. How is the "opening" of the cherries in an area decided?
2. What happens as soon as the opening is announced?
3. Why can a warm winter delay the blossoms in some areas, according to the column?
4. What does the writer suggest doing in years when summer heat lasts and lasts?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. By a particular tree the weather station watches, the 「{標本木|ひょうほんぼく}」: when five or six
   flowers or more have opened on it, the opening is announced for that area.
2. The moment it's announced ({発表|はっぴょう}されるや{否|いな}や), sheets appear in the parks to save
   places, and at night the parks fill with people enjoying the blossoms.
3. Because cherry buds only begin preparing for spring after going through the winter cold
   ({寒|さむ}さを{経|へ}て); if the winter is too warm, the flowers may "wake up" later.
4. Not to throw away the seasonal words, and to look for small signs of autumn outside the
   window: the seasons may show themselves only to people who try to notice them.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Every March, the map of the cherry blossom front appears in the television weather forecasts.
Starting in the south, the opening of the cherries moves north at a speed of several tens of
kilometres a day and reaches Hokkaido around May. When the forecast ends with "The cherries in
Tokyo should be at their best next week," offices start planning their blossom-viewing parties. Some people even change their travel plans
because the forecast date has shifted by a single day. Few nations in the world, surely, care as
much as the Japanese do about the day one particular flower opens.

What decides the opening is a tree called the "sample tree" that the weather station uses for
its observations. When five or six flowers or more have opened on this tree, the "opening" for that area is
announced. The moment it's announced, sheets to save places line the parks, and at night they
fill with people enjoying the cherries in the dark. After full bloom comes the shower of falling
petals, and then the trees in leaf. Year after year, people have been moved in the same way by
these few short days.

The cherries aren't the only messengers of the seasons. In spring the migratory birds fly back
north and swallows build nests under the eaves. Once the paddies have been flooded, the nights
are loud with frogs. In summer fireflies dance along the rivers; in autumn the ears of rice hang
their heads and the gardens fill with the sound of insects. And on a winter morning, the crunch
of frost needles underfoot tells us the seasons have come full circle. Insects, birds and beasts
know the seasons without a calendar.

Yet that "same every year" is starting to waver. The records show that the opening tends to come
earlier than in the past. At the same time, it's said that in some areas a winter that's too warm
actually delays the flowers' waking, because cherry buds only begin to prepare for spring after
going through the winter cold. Cold, too, is something the flowers need in order to bloom. The complexity of nature lies in the
fact that it isn't as simple as "warmer means earlier".

The ability to sense the changing seasons isn't limited to the cherry. Japanese letters have long
begun with a greeting on the time of year, and haiku can't do without words for the seasons.
First frost, a warm late-autumn day, a cold snap in blossom time: all of them are the words of
people who have paid attention to small changes in nature. Polished over a long time, these words
were also tools for feeling the seasons.

If the climate changes, some of these words will lose their meaning in real life. But there's no
need to throw the words themselves away from this day on. It's precisely in years when the summer
heat goes on and on that I want to look for a small sign of autumn outside my window: the colour of the evening sky,
the cold air at dawn, the smell of grass wet with night dew. The seasons don't arrive as big
events but as an accumulation of such small changes. Perhaps the
seasons show themselves only to those who try to notice them.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{東京|とうきょう}を{皮切|かわき}りに、{全国|ぜんこく}で{公開|こうかい}される。
= It opens in Tokyo first and then all over the country.
{本日|ほんじつ}をもって{閉店|へいてん}いたします。
= We are closing as of today.
{今日|きょう}を{限|かぎ}りに、たばこはやめます。
= From today on, I'm giving up smoking.
あの{雨|あめ}を{境|さかい}に、{急|きゅう}に{寒|さむ}くなった。
= After that rain it suddenly turned cold.
{長|なが}い{議論|ぎろん}を{経|へ}て、{計画|けいかく}が{決|き}まった。
= After a long debate, the plan was decided.
```

## Common mistakes

- を{皮切|かわき}りに for one next step: {朝食|ちょうしょく}を{皮切|かわき}りに{家|いえ}を{出|で}た isn't said. It needs a series of similar
  events after A, not one next step.
- ×{入学|にゅうがく}したを{境|さかい}に. A verb clause takes の before を: {入学|にゅうがく}したのを{境|さかい}に.
- Reading {経|へ}て as けいて. The verb is {経|へ}る, so {経|へ}て.
- をもって in a personal resolution: {今日|きょう}をもってダイエットを{始|はじ}める isn't used; it sounds like an official
  notice. Say {今日|きょう}から, or を{限|かぎ}りに for something you stop.
- Confusing を{境|さかい}に with 〜{以来|いらい}. を{境|さかい}に stresses the dividing moment and the change;
  {以来|いらい} stresses the state that has continued since.
- Reading {小春日和|こはるびより} as a spring day. It's late autumn.

## Key points

- N + を{皮切|かわき}りに: starting with A, a series spreads; news and formal speech.
- N + をもって: as of (a formal end or start); これをもちまして in speeches. (12: "by means of".)
- N + を{限|かぎ}りに: with A as the last time; something stops for good. {声|こえ}を{限|かぎ}りに = at the top
  of one's voice.
- N + を{境|さかい}に (verb + のを{境|さかい}に): with A as the turning point; B is a change.
- N + を{経|へ}て: via (a place); after going through (a stage, a post). {経|へ}る, not けい.
- Kanji: 32 new; {桜|さくら}, {雷|かみなり}, {嵐|あらし}, {霧|きり}, {虹|にじ}, {猿|さる}, {季節|きせつ} now in
  kanji. Special readings: {芝生|しばふ}, {梅雨|つゆ}.

lessons.title: Alongside: かたわら, がてら, かたがた
topics: ついでに and つつ
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lessons 1 and 2 put events in order. This lesson puts two activities side by side: a hobby kept
up beside a career, a walk that is also an errand, a visit that is both thanks and a report. Each
of the three patterns fits a different time span and register:

{彼女|かのじょ}は{会社|かいしゃ}に{勤|つと}めるかたわら、{小説|しょうせつ}を{書|か}いている。 — Besides working for a company, she writes novels.
{散歩|さんぽ}がてら、{駅前|えきまえ}の{本屋|ほんや}に{寄|よ}った。 — I took a walk and dropped into the bookshop by the station on the way.
お{礼|れい}かたがた、ご{報告|ほうこく}に{伺|うかが}いました。 — I've come both to thank you and to report to you.

You know the everyday ways to say this: N3's ついでに and N2's 〜つつ (lesson 9). This lesson adds
the three that writing and formal speech prefer, and a table to choose between all five. The
theme is sport, games and pastimes: martial arts, go and shogi, fishing and hunting, traditional
instruments played for pleasure, training and competing.

## Alongside one's main work: 〜かたわら

N + の / dictionary form + かたわら: "while A (one's main occupation), also B". {傍|かたわ}ら means
"beside" (its kanji is lesson 18's; the pattern is written in kana). A is what someone mainly does,
usually their job or studies; B is a second activity kept up beside it, over months or years.

{父|ちち}は{教師|きょうし}の{仕事|しごと}のかたわら、{地元|じもと}の{子供|こども}たちに{剣道|けんどう}を{教|おし}えている。 — Besides his work as a teacher, my father teaches kendo to local children.
{彼|かれ}は{大学|だいがく}で{研究|けんきゅう}するかたわら、プロの{棋士|きし}としても{活躍|かつやく}している。 — Alongside his research at university, he's also doing well as a professional go player.
{祖母|そぼ}は{店|みせ}を{営|いとな}むかたわら、{四十年|よんじゅうねん}{琴|こと}を{続|つづ}けてきた。 — Besides running the shop, my grandmother has played the koto for forty years.

- **Long-term**, not a single moment: テレビを{見|み}るかたわら{食事|しょくじ}をした isn't said. For two things
  at once, use 〜ながら.
- **A is the main activity**, B the extra. The order matters: {仕事|しごと}のかたわら{作曲|さっきょく}する
  makes composing the side activity.
- **Written** and formal speech (profiles, introductions, news). In conversation:
  {仕事|しごと}をしながら / {仕事|しごと}の{合間|あいま}に.
- Mostly about other people, in the third person.
- The plain noun かたわら ("the side, beside") also exists: {道|みち}のかたわらに{咲|さ}く{花|はな}.

## Doing two things on one outing: 〜がてら

ます stem / action noun + がてら: "while doing A, I also did B" (or "A, and B along the way"). One
trip serves two ends. A is often {散歩|さんぽ}, {買|か}い{物|もの}, {見物|けんぶつ}, {運動|うんどう} or a
visit; B is usually a movement verb: {行|い}く, {寄|よ}る, {歩|ある}く, {回|まわ}る.

{運動|うんどう}がてら、{駅|えき}まで{歩|ある}いて{行|い}った。 — I walked to the station, partly for the exercise.
{桜|さくら}を{見|み}がてら、{川沿|かわぞ}いを{散歩|さんぽ}した。 — We walked along the river, looking at the cherry blossoms as we went.
{釣|つ}りがてら、{海辺|うみべ}の{温泉|おんせん}に{泊|と}まってきた。 — I went fishing and stayed at a seaside hot spring while I was at it.
{近|ちか}くまで{来|き}たので、ご{挨拶|あいさつ}がてら{寄|よ}らせていただきました。 — I was in the area, so I thought I'd drop in to say hello.

- **B is usually a movement**: going somewhere, walking, dropping in. Two activities at a desk
  don't take がてら.
- Both are the speaker's own plans, often: がてら is common for the speaker, unlike かたわら.
- **Casual to neutral**, also in polite speech (ご{挨拶|あいさつ}がてら). Not for business letters,
  where かたがた is used.
- A can't be a long occupation: {会社|かいしゃ}{勤|づと}めがてら{小説|しょうせつ}を{書|か}く doesn't work (that's かたわら).

## Two purposes, formally: 〜かたがた

N + かたがた: "both A and B": one visit, letter or call that serves two purposes. The nouns are a
small set of formal ones: お{礼|れい}, ご{挨拶|あいさつ}, お{見舞|みま}い, ご{報告|ほうこく}, おわび (its kanji is off the list),
{散歩|さんぽ} (old-fashioned).

{先日|せんじつ}のお{礼|れい}かたがた、{一言|ひとこと}ご{挨拶|あいさつ}{申|もう}し{上|あ}げます。 — I write to thank you for the other day and to send my greetings.
お{見舞|みま}いかたがた、{近況|きんきょう}をお{知|し}らせいたします。 — I write to ask after your health and to let you know my news.
{転勤|てんきん}のご{報告|ほうこく}かたがた、ご{挨拶|あいさつ}に{伺|うかが}いました。 — I've come to tell you of my transfer and to pay my respects.

- **Business letters, formal visits and speeches.** It sounds out of place in casual talk.
- Usually followed by a humble verb: {伺|うかが}う, {申|もう}し{上|あ}げる, お{知|し}らせする.
- Module 6's sheet on formal letters lists it with the other letter phrases.

## Review: ついでに and 〜つつ

> ついでに (N3): "while you're at it": something done because the chance is there.
> {郵便局|ゆうびんきょく}に{行|い}くなら、ついでにこの{手紙|てがみ}も{出|だ}してきて. Everyday speech; B is the
> incidental one. 〜のついでに joins a noun: {買|か}い{物|もの}のついでに.
>
> 〜つつ (N2, lesson 9): ます stem + つつ: "while" (two actions at the same time, written):
> {景色|けしき}を{楽|たの}しみつつ{歩|ある}く. Also 〜つつも, "although" ({分|わ}かっていつつも).

And one to recognize, taught in lesson 7: 〜ながらに / 〜ながらの joins a few fixed nouns and stems
for "in the state of": {涙|なみだ}ながらに{語|かた}る (tell it in tears), {生|う}まれながらの{才能|さいのう} (an
inborn gift).

## Five ways to do two things

| Pattern | Joins | Time span | Which is the main action | Register |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 〜かたわら | N + の / dictionary form | long-term: work and a side activity | A (the job) | written, profiles |
| 〜がてら | ます stem / action noun | one outing | both; B is a movement | casual to polite speech |
| 〜かたがた | formal noun (お{礼|れい}, ご{挨拶|あいさつ}) | one visit, letter or call | two purposes of equal weight | business letters, formal visits |
| ついでに (N3) | (のついでに) | one occasion | A; B is incidental | everyday |
| 〜つつ (N2) | ます stem | the same moment | B is the main verb | written |

Where only one fits: {銀行員|ぎんこういん}として{働|はたら}くかたわら{絵|え}を{描|か}く (a career and a side
activity: かたわら); {公園|こうえん}を{散歩|さんぽ}がてら{図書館|としょかん}に{寄|よ}る (one outing: がてら); お{礼|れい}かたがた
ご{報告|ほうこく}{申|もう}し{上|あ}げます (a letter: かたがた).

## Dialogue: at the community centre

Sakura has joined a go class at the community centre. After the class she talks to Mitsuo, who
has taught there for years since retiring. (Polite speech from Sakura, plain from Mitsuo.)

```dialogue
# After the go class
さくら: {今日|きょう}もありがとうございました。やっぱり{先生|せんせい}の{布石|ふせき}はきれいですね。
= Thank you for today. Your opening moves really are beautiful.
みつお: いやいや、{長|なが}くやってるだけだよ。さくらさんは{上達|じょうたつ}が{早|はや}いね。
= Oh, no, I've just been at it a long time. You're improving fast.
さくら: {家|いえ}でもネットで{打|う}ってるんです。{先生|せんせい}は、{昔|むかし}から{囲碁|いご}をなさっていたんですか。
= I play online at home too. Have you played go for a long time?
みつお: {会社|かいしゃ}{勤|づと}めのかたわら、{四十年|よんじゅうねん}ぐらいかな。{本当|ほんとう}は{棋士|きし}になりたかったんだけどね。
= Alongside my office job, about forty years, I suppose. I really wanted to be a professional, you know.
さくら: そうなんですか。じゃあ、ここで{教|おし}えるようになったのは{定年|ていねん}{後|ご}ですか。
= Really? So you started teaching here after you retired?
みつお: うん。{散歩|さんぽ}がてら、ここを{見|み}に{来|き}たら、{先生|せんせい}がいないって{言|い}われてね。
= Yes. I came to have a look while I was out for a walk, and they told me they had no teacher.
さくら: それで{引|ひ}き{受|う}けてくださったんですね。
= And so you kindly took it on.
みつお: そういうこと。さくらさんは、どうして{囲碁|いご}を{始|はじ}めたの？
= That's it. And why did you start playing go?
さくら: {父|ちち}の{影響|えいきょう}です。{父|ちち}は{釣|つ}りが{趣味|しゅみ}で、{雨|あめ}で{行|い}けない{日|ひ}は{家|いえ}で{碁盤|ごばん}に{向|む}かっていました。
= My father's influence. His hobby was fishing, and on rainy days when he couldn't go, he sat at the go board at home.
みつお: いいお{父|とう}さんだね。{今度|こんど}、お{父|とう}さんとも{手合|てあ}わせしてみたいな。
= Sounds like a good dad. I'd like to play him one day.
さくら: {父|ちち}に{伝|つた}えます。きっと{喜|よろこ}びます。あ、{来月|らいげつ}の{大会|たいかい}、{私|わたし}も{出|で}てみようと{思|おも}うんです。
= I'll tell him. He'll be thrilled. Oh, I'm thinking of entering next month's tournament too.
みつお: いいね。{腕試|うでだめ}しのつもりで、{気楽|きらく}に{挑|いど}んでごらん。
= Good idea. Treat it as a test of your skill and go into it relaxed.
さくら: はい。{勝|か}ち{負|ま}けより、{楽|たの}しむことを{大事|だいじ}にします。
= I will. I'll focus on enjoying it rather than on winning or losing.
みつお: それが{一番|いちばん}。じゃ、{次|つぎ}の{稽古|けいこ}で{作戦|さくせん}を{考|かんが}えよう。
= That's the best way. Right, let's work out a plan at the next session.
さくら: よろしくお{願|ねが}いします。{来週|らいしゅう}は、お{礼|れい}かたがた{父|ちち}の{作|つく}った{干|ほ}し{柿|がき}をお{持|も}ちしますね。
= Thank you. Next week I'll bring some of my father's dried persimmons, as a thank-you too.
```

かたわら describes the man's long life beside his job, がてら his single walk, and Sakura's last
line uses かたがた half-jokingly, as a formal touch (in a letter it would be quite natural).
{上達|じょうたつ} = progress, getting better; {定年|ていねん} = retirement age; {作戦|さくせん} = a plan of
attack; {干|ほ}し{柿|がき} is lesson 4's word.

> {中川|なかがわ}：{高校|こうこう}{一年|いちねん}の{春|はる}です。{部活動|ぶかつどう}の{見学|けんがく}で{弓道場|きゅうどうじょう}に{入|はい}った{瞬間|しゅんかん}、{空気|くうき}が{違|ちが}うと{感|かん}じました。{誰|だれ}も{話|はな}さず、{矢|や}が{的|まと}に{当|あ}たる{音|おと}だけが{響|ひび}いていたんです。{見学|けんがく}を{終|お}えたその{足|あし}で、{入部届|にゅうぶとどけ}を{出|だ}しに{行|い}ったのを{覚|おぼ}えています。

>

> {中川|なかがわ}：あります。{病棟|びょうとう}では、{急|きゅう}な{呼|よ}び{出|だ}しや{予想外|よそうがい}のことが{次々|つぎつぎ}に{起|お}こります。そういうとき、{弓|ゆみ}を{引|ひ}く{前|まえ}のように{一度|いちど}{深|ふか}く{息|いき}を{吸|す}うと、{慌|あわ}てずに{済|す}むんです。{逆|ぎゃく}に、{患者|かんじゃ}さんの{痛|いた}みに{向|む}き{合|あ}う{毎日|まいにち}が、{道場|どうじょう}での{集中力|しゅうちゅうりょく}を{鍛|きた}えてくれているのかもしれません。

> {中川|なかがわ}：はい。{三年前|さんねんまえ}から、{月|つき}に{二回|にかい}、{市|し}の{教室|きょうしつ}で{教|おし}えています。{最初|さいしょ}は{的|まと}に{当|あ}てたくて{弓|ゆみ}を{引|ひ}くそばから{姿勢|しせい}が{崩|くず}れていた{子|こ}が、{半年|はんとし}もすると{見違|みちが}えるように{落|お}ち{着|つ}くんです。その{変化|へんか}を{見|み}るのが、{今|いま}の{一番|いちばん}の{楽|たの}しみです。

> ―{最後|さいご}に、{読者|どくしゃ}の{皆|みな}さんに{一言|ひとこと}お{願|ねが}いします。
>
> {中川|なかがわ}：{趣味|しゅみ}は、{生活|せいかつ}に{余裕|よゆう}ができてから{始|はじ}めるものだと{思|おも}われがちです。でも、{忙|いそが}しいからこそ、{自分|じぶん}に{戻|もど}れる{時間|じかん}が{必要|ひつよう}なのだと{思|おも}います。{道場|どうじょう}はいつでも{見学|けんがく}できますので、お{散歩|さんぽ}がてら、ぜひ{気軽|きがる}にのぞいてみてください。{弓|ゆみ}に{触|さわ}ったことのない{方|かた}も、もちろん{大歓迎|だいかんげい}です。

{入部届|にゅうぶとどけ} = an application to join a club; {両立|りょうりつ} = doing both successfully; {夜勤|やきん}
= night shift; かんぺき = perfection (its second kanji is off the list);
{病棟|びょうとう} = a hospital ward (lesson 29's word); {見違|みちが}える = to be hardly recognizable.

1. What made Nakagawa decide to take up Japanese archery?
2. How does Nakagawa fit practice around shift work?
3. According to Nakagawa, what matters most in training, and what does missing the target show?
4. How do archery and nursing help each other?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. On a club visit in the first year of high school, the silent atmosphere of the hall, where only
   the sound of arrows hitting the target could be heard. Nakagawa went straight from the
   visit to hand in the application (その{足|あし}で: "on the same feet", straight away).
2. On days off, Nakagawa drops in at a local hall while out for a walk (がてら) and shoots for an
   hour or so; in busy periods, sometimes just checks posture at home, without aiming for
   perfection.
3. Correct posture and a calm mind, more than hitting the target; a miss shows how unsettled one's
   mind is.
4. Taking one deep breath, as before drawing the bow, keeps Nakagawa calm in emergencies on the
   ward; and facing patients' pain every day may be training the concentration Nakagawa uses in the
   hall.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Today we talk to Nakagawa, who has practised Japanese archery for more than thirty years alongside
working as a nurse. Tell us how you first came across archery.

Nakagawa: It was the spring of my first year of high school. When I went to look round the
archery hall during the club visits, I felt the air was different the moment I walked in. No one
spoke; there was only the sound of arrows striking the target. I remember going straight from the
visit to hand in my application to join.

Isn't it hard to combine work and practice?

Nakagawa: My job involves night shifts, so it's hard to go to the hall on fixed days. So on my
days off I drop in at a hall near home while I'm out for a walk and shoot for an hour, even if
that's all. Sometimes, after a night shift, I shoot a single arrow in the empty hall in the
morning and go home. In busy times there are days when I just check my posture at home. Perhaps the secret
of keeping going is not to look for perfection.

Where does the appeal of archery lie?

Nakagawa: Perhaps in the fact that winning and losing aren't clear-cut. In competitions, of course,
you compete on the number of hits, but what's valued in practice is correct posture and a calm
mind rather than hitting the target. It isn't a martial art where you fight an opponent; you face
yourself. The times you miss are when you see most clearly how unsettled your mind is.

Isn't it hard to get all the equipment together?

Nakagawa: Bows and arrows aren't cheap, but while you're a beginner you can borrow the hall's. I
used borrowed ones for my first three years too. I got my own bow when I passed first dan. I still
use it, and every time I look after it I remember how I felt then.

Does it help you in your work?

Nakagawa: It does. On the ward, sudden calls and the unexpected come one after another. At times
like that, if I take one deep breath, as before drawing the bow, I don't panic. And the other way
round, days spent facing patients' pain may be training my concentration in the hall.

I hear you've recently been teaching children too.

Nakagawa: Yes. For three years now I've taught twice a month at a city class. Children who at
first are so eager to hit the target that their posture falls apart every time they draw become
remarkably calm after six months or so. Watching that change is my greatest pleasure now.

Finally, a word for our readers, please.

Nakagawa: People tend to think a hobby is something you take up once you have time to spare. But I
think it's precisely because we're busy that we need time to return to ourselves. You can look
round the hall at any time, so please do drop in, perhaps while you're out for a walk. People who have never touched a bow
are, of course, very welcome.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{彼女|かのじょ}は{会社|かいしゃ}に{勤|つと}めるかたわら、{小説|しょうせつ}を{書|か}いている。
= Besides working for a company, she writes novels.
{散歩|さんぽ}がてら、{本屋|ほんや}に{寄|よ}ってきた。
= I dropped into the bookshop while I was out for a walk.
お{礼|れい}かたがた、ご{挨拶|あいさつ}に{伺|うかが}いました。
= I've come to thank you and to pay my respects.
{王手|おうて}をかけた。
= We're one win away.
```

## Common mistakes

- かたわら for two things at the same moment: {音楽|おんがく}を{聞|き}くかたわら{勉強|べんきょう}する isn't said. かたわら is a
  long-term side activity; for "while" use 〜ながら.
- ×{散歩|さんぽ}のがてら. がてら joins the noun directly: {散歩|さんぽ}がてら, or a ます stem: {見|み}がてら.
- かたがた with ordinary nouns: {買|か}い{物|もの}かたがた isn't used. かたがた takes a few formal nouns (お{礼|れい},
  ご{挨拶|あいさつ}, お{見舞|みま}い, ご{報告|ほうこく}); for an errand, がてら or ついでに.
- Reading {相撲|すもう} or {稽古|けいこ} kanji by kanji. {相撲|すもう} is a special reading; {稽古|けいこ} is
  one word.
- ×{蹴|け}ます. {蹴|け}る is group 1: {蹴|け}ります, {蹴|け}って.

## Key points

- N + の / dictionary form + かたわら: besides one's main work, also B, over a long time; written;
  usually third person.
- ます stem / action noun + がてら: on one outing, A and B; B is usually movement; casual to polite.
- N + かたがた: one visit or letter, two purposes; formal nouns (お{礼|れい}, ご{挨拶|あいさつ}); business letters.
- ついでに (incidental, everyday) and 〜つつ (same moment, written) are the earlier ways.
- Kanji: 32 new; {相撲|すもう}, {将棋|しょうぎ}, {趣味|しゅみ}, {釣|つ}り, {挑戦|ちょうせん}, {興奮|こうふん} now in
  kanji.

lessons.title: At the very moment: やさきに, 折から, ところを, にあって
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson's four patterns all point at a moment or a situation and say what happened in it:
the instant before a plan was carried out, the season a letter is written in, the moment someone
was caught, and the circumstances someone lives through.

{出|で}かけようとした{矢先|やさき}に、{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}り{出|だ}した。 — Just as I was about to go out, it started to rain.
{寒|さむ}さ{厳|きび}しき{折|おり}から、お{体|からだ}を{大切|たいせつ}になさってください。 — In this bitterly cold season, please take good care of yourself.
お{忙|いそが}しいところを、ありがとうございました。 — Thank you for your time when you're so busy.
この{不況|ふきょう}にあって、{売|う}り{上|あ}げを{伸|の}ばす{店|みせ}もある。 — Even in this recession, some shops are increasing their sales.

You'll also review two patterns for "during": N2's 〜{際|さい} and N3's 〜{最中|さいちゅう}. The theme is
food, cooking and drink: ways of cooking, the pantry, fermentation, fruit, alcohol and tableware.

## Just as (and then something went wrong): 〜{矢先|やさき}に

〜た{矢先|やさき}に / 〜ようとした{矢先|やさき}に (also 〜ようとしていた{矢先|やさき}に): "just as A (had
happened or was about to happen), B". {矢先|やさき} is the tip of an arrow: the very point of
action. B is almost always unwelcome and unexpected.

{店|みせ}を{改装|かいそう}しようとした{矢先|やさき}に、{店主|てんしゅ}が{病気|びょうき}で{倒|たお}れた。 — Just as they were about to renovate the shop, the owner fell ill.
{夕飯|ゆうはん}の{支度|したく}を{始|はじ}めた{矢先|やさき}に、{停電|ていでん}になった。 — I'd just started getting dinner ready when the power went off.
{禁酒|きんしゅ}を{誓|ちか}った{矢先|やさき}に、{忘年会|ぼうねんかい}の{誘|さそ}いが{来|き}た。 — I'd only just sworn off alcohol when an invitation to a year-end party arrived.

- **B is bad news**, or at least an unwelcome surprise. {家|いえ}を{出|で}ようとした{矢先|やさき}に、{虹|にじ}が{出|で}た
  isn't used unless the rainbow is somehow a problem.
- B is a past event: something that happened, not a plan or a request.
- The subject can be the speaker. It's at home in writing and in adult speech, especially when
  telling someone about bad luck.
- Compare N3's 〜ところに / 〜ところへ (just when, B arrives): {出|で}かけようとしたところに{電話|でんわ}が
  {鳴|な}った is neutral; {矢先|やさき}に stresses that B spoiled a plan.

## At this time of year: 〜{折|おり}から

〜{折|おり}から has two uses, both formal.

**1. In letters**: "at this time when…". It closes a letter with a wish for the reader's health and
names the season. Adjectives often take their classical attributive -き form here: {寒|さむ}さ{厳|きび}しき,
{暑|あつ}さ{厳|きび}しき.

{寒|さむ}さ{厳|きび}しき{折|おり}から、くれぐれもご{自愛|じあい}ください。 — In this bitterly cold season, please take the greatest care of yourself.
{天候|てんこう}{不順|ふじゅん}の{折|おり}から、どうぞお{体|からだ}を{大切|たいせつ}に。 — With the weather so unsettled, please look after yourself.
ご{多忙|たぼう}の{折|おり}から{恐縮|きょうしゅく}ですが、ご{出席|しゅっせき}いただければ{幸|さいわ}いです。 — We realize how busy you are, but we would be delighted if you could attend.

**2. In news and narrative**: N + {折|おり}からの + N, "the … going on at the time": the weather or
circumstances that made things worse.

{火|ひ}は{折|おり}からの{強風|きょうふう}にあおられ、{隣家|りんか}に{燃|も}え{移|うつ}った。 — Fanned by the strong wind blowing at the time, the fire spread to the house next door.

- N2's lesson 6 met {折|おり} as "occasion" (〜の{折|おり}に, お{越|こ}しの{折|おり}には). {折|おり}から adds the
  sense "since it is now such a time".
- Lesson 29's sheet of letter phrases collects the seasonal openings and closings.

## Just when (sorry to trouble you; caught in the act): 〜ところを

〜ところを joins the plain form (dictionary, ている or adjective) and an expression of thanks or
apology, or a verb of seeing, catching or helping. ところ is the moment someone is in.

**Thanks and apologies** (polite speech and letters):

お{忙|いそが}しいところを、お{越|こ}しいただきありがとうございます。 — Thank you for coming when you're so busy.
お{休|やす}みのところを{申|もう}し{訳|わけ}ありません。 — I'm sorry to disturb you on your day off.
お{食事|しょくじ}{中|ちゅう}のところを{失礼|しつれい}いたします。 — Excuse me for interrupting your meal.

**Caught or helped at that moment**: B is a verb such as {見|み}つかる, {見|み}られる, {捕|つか}まえる,
{助|たす}ける, {起|お}こす, {呼|よ}び{止|と}める. The first part is what someone was doing.

{冷蔵庫|れいぞうこ}のケーキをつまみ{食|ぐ}いしているところを、{母|はは}に{見|み}つかった。 — My mother caught me sneaking a bite of the cake in the fridge.
{男|おとこ}は{店|みせ}から{逃|に}げるところを、{警察官|けいさつかん}に{取|と}り{押|お}さえられた。 — The man was seized by a police officer as he tried to run from the shop.
{溺|おぼ}れかけているところを、{通|とお}りかかった{人|ひと}に{助|たす}けられた。 — I was rescued by a passer-by just as I was starting to drown.

- を is the object marker: the moment itself is what is seen, caught or interrupted.
- Not the same as 〜ところに / 〜ところへ (B arrives at that moment) or 〜ところで (at that point).
- In thanks and apologies, {忙|いそが}しいところ is often said without を in speech.

## In (a time, place or situation): 〜にあって

N + にあって / にあっては / にあっても: "in, being in". A is a time, a place or a position, often a
difficult one; the sentence says how someone behaves there. Written and formal speech.

この{厳|きび}しい{不況|ふきょう}にあって、{地元|じもと}の{酒蔵|さかぐら}は{売|う}り{上|あ}げを{伸|の}ばしている。 — Even in this severe recession, the local brewery is increasing its sales.
{異国|いこく}にあっても、{彼|かれ}は{毎朝|まいあさ}みそ{汁|しる}を{作|つく}り{続|つづ}けた。 — Even in a foreign country, he went on making miso soup every morning.
{飽食|ほうしょく}の{時代|じだい}にあっては、{食|た}べ{物|もの}を{大切|たいせつ}にする{心|こころ}が{失|うしな}われがちだ。 — In an age of plenty, respect for food tends to be lost.
{責任|せきにん}ある{立場|たちば}にあって、そのような{発言|はつげん}は{許|ゆる}されない。 — For someone in a responsible position, such a remark is unacceptable.

- にあっては: in that situation (often "it's different there"); にあっても: even in it.
- Usually a special or severe situation ({非常時|ひじょうじ}, {戦時下|せんじか}, {不況|ふきょう}) or a high
  position; not ordinary places ({台所|だいどころ}にあって{料理|りょうり}する isn't said).
- Close to N2's 〜において (in, at), which is neutral; にあって adds "being in that situation".

## Review: 〜{際|さい} and 〜{最中|さいちゅう}

> 〜{際|さい}(に) / の{際|さい}は (N2, lesson 6): "when" (formal): お{帰|かえ}りの{際|さい}は、お{忘|わす}れ{物|もの}の
> ないようご{注意|ちゅうい}ください. Used for routine occasions in notices and staff speech.
>
> 〜ている{最中|さいちゅう}に / N の{最中|さいちゅう}に (N3): "in the middle of", usually with an
> interruption: {食事|しょくじ}の{最中|さいちゅう}に{地震|じしん}があった.

## Five ways to point at a moment

| Pattern | Joins | Meaning | B | Register |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 〜{矢先|やさき}に | た form / ようとした | just as (a plan) | an unwelcome surprise | writing, adult speech |
| 〜{折|おり}から | N の / adjective (〜き) | at this time when… (letters); the … going on then (news) | a wish for health; a worsening | letters, news |
| 〜ところを | plain form | just when (someone was busy, or doing something) | thanks, apology; caught, helped | polite speech; narrative |
| 〜にあって | N | in (a severe situation or high position) | how someone behaves | written, formal |
| 〜{最中|さいちゅう}に (N3) | ている / N の | in the middle of | an interruption | everyday |

Where only one fits: in a letter's last line, {暑|あつ}さ{厳|きび}しき{折|おり}から, not {矢先|やさき}に;
for "I was found eating the cake", ところを{見|み}つかった, not {最中|さいちゅう}に (which would need
{食|た}べている{最中|さいちゅう}に{母|はは}が{来|き}た, with the mother as subject).

## Food and drink

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|

## Dialogue: a brewery visit

Ono, a guide at a small sake brewery, shows Lee, a visitor from Seoul, round the storehouse.
(Formal speech from the guide; polite from the visitor.)

```dialogue

= It's huge. The grains of rice look very small.
```

Two kinds of ところを open the visit, as they do in real life: お{足元|あしもと}の{悪|わる}いところを (thanks for
coming in bad weather) and お{忙|いそが}しいところを. {矢先|やさき}に tells of bad luck, and にあっても sets a
hopeful fact against hard times. {仕込|しこ}み = the brewing (preparing the mash); {削|けず}る = to
shave, polish (lesson 19's word); しぼる = to press (its kanji is off the list); {肝|きも}を{冷|ひ}やす = to get a scare (lesson 5);
{復旧|ふっきゅう} = restoration of service; {試飲|しいん} = a tasting; {甘酒|あまざけ} = a sweet drink made
from fermented rice (N2's word).

> {振|ふ}り{返|かえ}りますと、{思|おも}い{出|だ}すのは{皆様|みなさま}のお{顔|かお}ばかりです。{雪|ゆき}の{夜|よる}、{閉店|へいてん}{間際|まぎわ}に{駆|か}け{込|こ}んでこられ、{熱|あつ}い{鍋焼|なべや}きうどんを{召|め}し{上|あ}がって「これで{生|い}き{返|かえ}った」と{笑|わら}われたお{客様|きゃくさま}。{受験|じゅけん}の{朝|あさ}、ご{家族|かぞく}そろって{縁起|えんぎ}を{担|かつ}ぎにいらした{皆様|みなさま}。しょうゆの{香|かお}りの{汁|しる}を{一滴|いってき}も{残|のこ}さず{飲|の}み{干|ほ}してくださったお{子|こ}さんの{笑顔|えがお}。{部活|ぶかつ}{帰|がえ}りに{毎日|まいにち}のように{寄|よ}ってくれた{高校生|こうこうせい}たちが、{今|いま}ではご{自分|じぶん}のお{子|こ}さんを{連|つ}れて{来|き}てくださいます。{食|た}べ{物|もの}があふれる{飽食|ほうしょく}の{時代|じだい}にあって、{一杯|いっぱい}のうどんをこれほど{大切|たいせつ}に{味|あじ}わってくださる{方々|かたがた}に{支|ささ}えられてきたことは、{店|みせ}にとって{何|なに}よりの{幸|しあわ}せでございました。
>
> また、{長年|ながねん}にわたり{材料|ざいりょう}を{届|とど}けてくださった{製粉所|せいふんじょ}の{皆様|みなさま}、{毎朝|まいあさ}{煮干|にぼ}しと{昆布|こんぶ}を{運|はこ}んでくださった{乾物屋|かんぶつや}さんにも、この{場|ば}を{借|か}りて{御礼|おんれい}{申|もう}し{上|あ}げます。
>
> なお、{当店|とうてん}のだしの{作|つく}り{方|かた}は、{近所|きんじょ}の{料理|りょうり}{教室|きょうしつ}で{来春|らいしゅん}から{教|おし}えることになりました。{店|みせ}はなくなりましても、{味|あじ}は{町|まち}のどこかで{生|い}き{続|つづ}けてくれればと{願|ねが}っております。
>
> {閉店|へいてん}までの{日々|ひび}は、{普段|ふだん}どおり{営業|えいぎょう}いたします。お{忙|いそが}しいところを{恐縮|きょうしゅく}ではございますが、お{時間|じかん}がございましたら、ぜひもう{一度|いちど}お{立|た}ち{寄|よ}りください。{最後|さいご}の{日|ひ}には、ささやかながら、{祖父|そふ}の{代|だい}から{変|か}わらない{煮物|にもの}を{一品|いっぴん}お{付|つ}けいたします。
>
> {最後|さいご}になりましたが、{寒|さむ}さ{厳|きび}しき{折|おり}から、{皆様|みなさま}どうぞご{自愛|じあい}くださいますよう、お{祈|いの}り{申|もう}し{上|あ}げます。{本当|ほんとう}に{長|なが}い{間|あいだ}、ありがとうございました。　{敬具|けいぐ}

{拝啓|はいけい} / {敬具|けいぐ} = the formal opening and closing of a letter; {存|ぞん}じます = I think
(humble); {屋台|やたい} = a street stall; {口癖|くちぐせ} = a favourite saying (lesson 24's word); {総出|そうで} = everyone together; ご{愛顧|あいこ} = your custom (patronage); {調理場|ちょうりば} = a commercial kitchen; {間際|まぎわ} = just
before; {縁起|えんぎ}を{担|かつ}ぐ = to do something for luck; {乾物屋|かんぶつや}
= a shop selling dried foods; {来春|らいしゅん} = next spring.

1. Why is the shop closing?
2. Why didn't the owner keep the shop going with machines?
3. Which customers does the owner remember? Give two.
4. How will the shop's taste "live on"?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Just as they were about to renovate the old kitchen ({改装|かいそう}しようとした{矢先|やさき}に), the owner
   hurt their back and can no longer stand for long hours.
2. Making the noodles by hand every morning was the shop's greatest pride, so the owner chose to
   close rather than rely on machines.
3. Any two: a customer who rushed in on a snowy night just before closing, ate hot noodles and
   laughed that it had brought them back to life; families who came on the morning of entrance
   exams for luck; a child who drank every drop of the soup.
4. The owner will teach how to make the shop's stock at a local cookery school from next spring.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Dear customers,

The season of cold winter winds has come. I trust you are all keeping well.

I am writing, rather suddenly, to let you know that our shop will close at the end of this month.
Seventy years have passed since my grandfather opened the shop in this town, and I thank you from
the bottom of my heart for your custom over three generations.

The little business my grandfather started with a street stall moved to its present site in my
father's day. My father used to say, almost as a catchphrase, "Make a soup that silences the
customer from the very first sip." Every New Year's Eve, people wanting their year-end noodles
queued outside, and the whole family would keep boiling noodles until late into the night.

Last autumn, just as we were about to renovate our old kitchen, I, the owner, hurt my back and
can no longer stand for long hours. The doctor has told me not to overdo things for a while.
There was talk of my son taking over the shop, but he has his own path to follow. Kneading the flour and making the noodles by hand every
morning was this shop's greatest pride, so rather than rely on machines, I have chosen to close.

Looking back, all I can think of is your faces. The customer who rushed in on a snowy night just
before closing time, ate a hot pot of noodles and laughed, "That's brought me back to life." The
families who came together on the morning of an entrance exam, for luck. The smiles of the
children who drank every last drop of the soy-scented soup. The high-school students who dropped
in almost every day on their way home from club practice now come with children of their own. In an age of plenty, when food is
everywhere, being supported by people who savour a single bowl of noodles so dearly has been the
greatest happiness this shop could know.

I would also like to take this opportunity to thank the people at the flour mill who delivered our
ingredients for so many years, and the dried-goods shop that brought us dried sardines and kelp
every morning.

I should add that I will be teaching how we make our stock at a cookery school in the neighbourhood
from next spring. Though the shop will be gone, I hope its taste will live on somewhere in the town.

Until we close, we will be open as usual. I know how busy you are, but if you have the time, please
do drop in once more. On our last day, as a small token, we will add one of the simmered dishes
that have not changed since my grandfather's time.

Last of all, in this bitterly cold season, I pray that you will all take good care of yourselves.
Thank you, truly, for all these years.

Yours sincerely

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{出|で}かけようとした{矢先|やさき}に、{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}り{出|だ}した。
= Just as I was about to go out, it started to rain.
お{忙|いそが}しいところを、ありがとうございます。
= Thank you for your time when you're so busy.
{寒|さむ}さ{厳|きび}しき{折|おり}から、ご{自愛|じあい}ください。
= In this bitterly cold season, please look after yourself.
この{不況|ふきょう}にあって、{売|う}り{上|あ}げを{伸|の}ばしている。
= Even in this recession, sales are growing.
{箸|はし}、{橋|はし}、{端|はし}。
= Chopsticks, bridge, edge.
```

## Common mistakes

- {矢先|やさき}に with good news: {諦|あきら}めかけた{矢先|やさき}に、{合格|ごうかく}の{知|し}らせが{来|き}た isn't used. The pattern
  expects B to spoil a plan; for a happy surprise, 〜たところに or 〜たとたん.
- ×{寒|さむ}さが{厳|きび}しい{折|おり}からに. {折|おり}から ends the clause itself; it isn't followed by に.
- Confusing ところを and ところに: {寝|ね}ているところを{起|お}こされた (I was woken: the moment is the
  object) but {寝|ね}ているところに{電話|でんわ}が{来|き}た (a call came at that moment).
- にあって for an ordinary place: {教室|きょうしつ}にあって{勉強|べんきょう}する isn't said. Use で; にあって is for a
  situation or position.
- ×{飽|あ}きります. {飽|あ}きる is group 2: {飽|あ}きます, {飽|あ}きて.

## Key points

- 〜た{矢先|やさき}に / 〜ようとした{矢先|やさき}に: just as (a plan), something unwelcome happened.
- 〜{折|おり}から: letters, "at this time when…" ({寒|さむ}さ{厳|きび}しき{折|おり}から, ご{自愛|じあい}ください); news,
  N + {折|おり}からの N "the … at the time".
- 〜ところを: thanks and apologies (お{忙|いそが}しいところを); the moment someone is caught, seen or helped.
- N + にあって / にあっては / にあっても: in (a severe situation or high position); written.
- Review: 〜{際|さい} (formal "when"), 〜{最中|さいちゅう}に (in the middle of).
- Kanji: 32 new; {鍋|なべ}, {箸|はし}, {缶|かん}, {瓶|びん}, {砂糖|さとう}, {豚|ぶた}, {煮|に}る, {炊|た}く, {沸|わ}く,
  {腐|くさ}る now in kanji.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Without and left undone: なくしては, なしに, ずじまい, までだ
topics: っぱなし and ないことには
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 1 ends with things that are missing: the one thing without which nothing works, an action
done without a step it should have had, a plan that was never carried out, and the plain "then
I'll just…" of someone who has run out of options.

{健康|けんこう}なくしては、{仕事|しごと}も{趣味|しゅみ}も{楽|たの}しめない。 — Without your health, you can enjoy neither work nor hobbies.
{彼|かれ}は{予約|よやく}なしに{病院|びょういん}を{訪|おとず}れた。 — He went to the hospital without an appointment.
{忙|いそが}しくて、{結局|けっきょく}{検査|けんさ}を{受|う}けずじまいだった。 — I was so busy that in the end I never had the check-up.
{薬|くすり}が{効|き}かないなら、{手術|しゅじゅつ}するまでだ。 — If the medicine doesn't work, then we'll just have to operate.

Two patterns you know join them in a review: N3's 〜っぱなし (left as it is) and N2's
〜ないことには (unless). The theme is the body, illness and medicine: the body parts still in kana
until now, the organs, conditions and immunity, pregnancy and sleep, and medicines.

## Without A, B is impossible: N + なくして(は)

N + なくして(は)〜ない: "without A, B can't happen". A is something essential (effort, support,
understanding, love, a sacrifice); B is negative: 〜ない, 〜{得|え}ない, {難|むずか}しい, あり{得|え}ない.

{患者|かんじゃ}の{協力|きょうりょく}なくして、{治療|ちりょう}の{成功|せいこう}はあり{得|え}ない。 — Without the patient's cooperation, successful treatment is impossible.
{早期|そうき}{発見|はっけん}なくしては、この{病気|びょうき}の{治癒|ちゆ}は{望|のぞ}めない。 — Without early detection, there's no hope of curing this disease.
{家族|かぞく}の{支|ささ}えなくして、{今|いま}の{私|わたし}はなかった。 — Without my family's support, I wouldn't be where I am today.

- **Written** and formal speech (speeches, editorials, thanks). In conversation: 〜がなければ /
  〜なしでは.
- B is always "can't, won't, impossible"; なくしては can't introduce a positive result.
- 〜なくしては{語|かた}れない (you can't talk about A without B) is a common set phrase:
  {彼|かれ}の{存在|そんざい}なくしては、この{町|まち}の{歴史|れきし}は{語|かた}れない.
- A verb takes こと: {努力|どりょく}することなくしては (rare and very written).

## Without (doing): N + なしに, 〜ことなしに

N + なしに (also なしで, なしには) and dictionary form + ことなしに: "without", the written
equivalent of 〜ずに / 〜ないで. B can be anything: what happened without A.

{彼|かれ}は{断|ことわ}りなしに{会議|かいぎ}を{欠席|けっせき}した。 — He missed the meeting without a word.
この{薬|くすり}は{処方|しょほう}なしには{買|か}えない。 — You can't buy this medicine without a prescription.
{彼女|かのじょ}は{一日|いちにち}も{休|やす}むことなしに{練習|れんしゅう}を{続|つづ}けた。 — She kept practising without missing a single day.
{誰|だれ}にも{知|し}られることなしに、{計画|けいかく}は{進|すす}められた。 — The plan went ahead without anyone knowing.

- なしに / なしで: なしで is everyday ({予約|よやく}なしで{入|はい}れる); なしに is more written.
- なしに vs なくして: なしに simply says A was absent; なくして says B is impossible without A.
  {予約|よやく}なしに{来|き}た (they came without booking) can't take なくして.
- 〜ことなしに is written; in speech, 〜ずに / 〜ないで.
- Common nouns: {断|ことわ}り, {予約|よやく}, {許可|きょか}, {連絡|れんらく}, {休|やす}み, {理由|りゆう}: {断|ことわ}りなしに, {休|やす}みなしに.

## Ended up never doing it: 〜ずじまい

ない stem + ずじまい(だ / で / に): "ended up not doing (something one meant to)". Usually past and
regretful: the chance has gone. する → せずじまい.

{旅行|りょこう}{中|ちゅう}、{雨|あめ}で{結局|けっきょく}{富士山|ふじさん}は{見|み}ずじまいだった。 — It rained all through the trip, and in the end we never saw Mount Fuji.
{気|き}になっていた{検査|けんさ}を、{今年|ことし}も{受|う}けずじまいになってしまった。 — Another year has gone by without my having that check-up I've been worrying about.
{退院|たいいん}の{日|ひ}、{看護師|かんごし}さんにお{礼|れい}を{言|い}わずじまいだった。 — On the day I left hospital, I never got to thank the nurses.
{父|ちち}とは、{最後|さいご}まで{本音|ほんね}で{話|はな}せずじまいだった。 — Right to the end, I never managed to talk to my father honestly.

- **Past or final**: ずじまいだった / ずじまいで{終|お}わった / ずじまいになった. ×{明日|あした}は{行|い}かずじまいだ.
- **Something meant or expected**: you wanted to, should have, or might have. {一度|いちど}も{転|ころ}ばずじまいだった
  sounds odd: nobody means to fall.
- じまい comes from しまう (to finish, put away): the matter "ended" without it.
- Neutral: speech and writing.

## Then I'll just…; it's only that…: 〜までだ, 〜までのことだ

〜までだ (also 〜までのことだ) has two uses.

**1. Dictionary form + までだ: "then I'll just (do it); there's nothing else for it."** A resolute
decision when the obvious way is closed, often after a condition (なら, ても, たら).

{最終|さいしゅう}バスに{乗|の}り{遅|おく}れたら、{歩|ある}いて{帰|かえ}るまでだ。 — If I miss the last bus, I'll just walk home.
{反対|はんたい}されても、{自分|じぶん}で{決|き}めた{道|みち}を{行|い}くまでのことだ。 — Even if they're against it, I'll simply go the way I've chosen.
{薬|くすり}で{治|なお}らないなら、{手術|しゅじゅつ}を{受|う}けるまでです。 — If medicine won't cure it, then I'll have the operation, that's all.

**2. た form + までだ: "I only did it because…; it's no more than that."** It plays down what
someone did: modesty, or a cool justification.

{当然|とうぜん}のことをしたまでです。 — I only did what anyone would have done.
{気|き}になったから{聞|き}いてみたまでで、{深|ふか}い{意味|いみ}はない。 — I only asked because I was curious; there's nothing more to it.
{規則|きそく}に{従|したが}ったまでのことで、{個人的|こじんてき}な{感情|かんじょう}はありません。 — I simply followed the rules; there's nothing personal in it.

- Use 1 is the speaker's will (or someone determined): 〜するまでだ. Use 2 looks back at a past
  act.
- Both are firm and a little formal, at home in speech among adults and in writing.
- Don't confuse with N5's 〜まで (until) or N2's 〜までもない (there's no need to, lesson 19's
  review): {言|い}うまでもない.

## Review: 〜っぱなし and 〜ないことには

> 〜っぱなし (N3, lesson 27): ます stem + っぱなし, "left as it is" (often carelessly), or "all the
> time": {電気|でんき}をつけっぱなしにする, {一日中|いちにちじゅう}{立|た}ちっぱなしだった.
>
> 〜ないことには (N2, lesson 19): "unless A, B can't happen": {診察|しんさつ}を{受|う}けないことには、
> {原因|げんいん}は{分|わ}からない. It's the everyday cousin of なくしては: both put a condition before an
> impossibility, but ないことには joins verbs and adjectives, なくしては nouns.

## Without, undone, and nothing else for it

| Pattern | Joins | Meaning | What follows | Register |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| なくして(は) | N | without A (essential) | can't, impossible | written, formal |
| なしに / なしで / ことなしに | N / dictionary form + こと | without (doing) A | anything | なしに, ことなしに written; なしで everyday |
| ずじまい | ない stem (せず) | ended up never doing | past, regret | neutral |
| までだ (1) | dictionary form | then I'll just | a decision | firm; speech and writing |
| までだ (2) | た form | I only did | playing it down | modest or cool |
| ないことには (N2) | ない form | unless | can't | everyday |
| っぱなし (N3) | ます stem | left as it is | (state) | everyday |

Where only one fits: {彼|かれ}は{挨拶|あいさつ}なしに{帰|かえ}った (he left without saying goodbye: a plain
fact, so なしに, not なくして). {努力|どりょく}なくして{成功|せいこう}なし (no success without effort: B is
impossible, so なくして). And for a plan that never happened, {行|い}かずじまいだった, not
{行|い}かないことにはだった.

## The body and medicine

|---|---|
