lessons.title: In order to: んがため, べく, べくもない, をもって
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 11 was about why; this lesson is about what for. A **[[purpose clause]]** says what an action
is meant to achieve: in everyday Japanese 〜ために and 〜ように. Written Japanese has
two more, both built on classical forms, and both much stronger in tone:

{勝|か}たんがため、{選手|せんしゅ}たちは{厳|きび}しい{練習|れんしゅう}に{耐|た}えた。 — Determined to win, the players endured gruelling training.
{原因|げんいん}を{究明|きゅうめい}すべく、{調査|ちょうさ}{委員会|いいんかい}が{設置|せっち}された。 — An investigative committee was set up in order to establish the cause.

It also adds a negative relative of べく, 〜べくもない ("there's no way to"), and the "means"
sense of 〜をもって ("with, by means of"), whose "as of" sense you met in lesson 2.

The theme is the economy and finance: markets and shares, debt and lending, currency and
exchange, supply and demand, earning and rewards, saving and spending. Earlier courses gave you the
household words ({給料|きゅうりょう}, {物価|ぶっか}, {景気|けいき}, {投資|とうし}); this lesson's kanji let you write
{稼|かせ}ぐ, {需要|じゅよう}, {貧乏|びんぼう} and {小銭|こぜに}, and add the words of the business pages.

## In order to (at all costs): 〜んがため(に)

〜んがため joins the ない stem (the form before ない) with ん, the classical "will", and がため,
an old way of saying ために. It means "in order to", with a strong sense of determination: the
subject is set on the goal and may pay a price for it.

| Verb | ない form | + んがため |
|---|---|---|
| {勝|か}つ | {勝|か}たない | {勝|か}たんがため |
| {生|い}きる | {生|い}きない | {生|い}きんがため |
| {見|み}る | {見|み}ない | {見|み}んがため |
| {知|し}る | {知|し}らない | {知|し}らんがため |
| する | (しない) | せんがため (not ×しんがため) |
| {来|く}る | (こない) | こんがため (rare) |

{生|い}きんがために、{男|おとこ}は{盗|ぬす}みを{働|はたら}いた。 — Just to stay alive, the man turned to theft.
{勝|か}たんがため、{選手|せんしゅ}たちは{厳|きび}しい{練習|れんしゅう}に{耐|た}えた。 — Determined to win, the players endured gruelling training.
{利益|りえき}を{上|あ}げんがための{値上|ねあ}げだと{批判|ひはん}された。 — The price rise was criticized as being purely to make a profit.
{会社|かいしゃ}を{存続|そんぞく}させんがため、{社長|しゃちょう}は{私財|しざい}まで{投|とう}じた。 — To keep the company alive, the president even put in their own money.

Points to remember:

- Very written, and dramatic. It belongs in literary prose, history, editorials and speeches.
  Use it for an aim pursued seriously, often at a cost or by questionable means; for everyday
  purposes it sounds like a parody: {電車|でんしゃ}に{間|ま}に{合|あ}わんがため{走|はし}った is a joke.
- The subject's own will. The goal is something the subject sets out to achieve, as with
  ために. It doesn't take potentials or states ({上手|じょうず}になるように is ように's job).
- Before a noun: 〜んがための N. With に or without: {勝|か}たんがため(に).
- It isn't a drill form. The ん is the classical auxiliary む (lesson 5h2), and lesson 26 comes back
  to it.

## In order to (written): 〜べく

〜べく is the classical べし (should, must) in a form that joins clauses. After the dictionary
form it means "in order to, with the aim of": the second half is an action taken toward the goal.

| Verb | + べく |
|---|---|
| {解決|かいけつ}する | {解決|かいけつ}すべく / {解決|かいけつ}するべく |
| {応|こた}える | {応|こた}えるべく |
| {確|たし}かめる | {確|たし}かめるべく |

{原因|げんいん}を{究明|きゅうめい}すべく、{調査|ちょうさ}{委員会|いいんかい}が{設置|せっち}された。 — An investigative committee was set up to establish the cause.
{期待|きたい}に{応|こた}えるべく、{全力|ぜんりょく}を{尽|つ}くします。 — I will do everything I can to live up to your expectations.
{父|ちち}は{借金|しゃっきん}を{返|かえ}すべく、{昼|ひる}も{夜|よる}も{働|はたら}いた。 — My father worked day and night to pay back the debt.
{販路|はんろ}を{広|ひろ}げるべく、{海外|かいがい}に{支店|してん}を{設|もう}けた。 — The company opened a branch abroad to widen its sales channels.

Points to remember:

- する becomes すべく (the classical form, commoner in writing) or するべく; both are used.
- The second half is a deliberate action, in a statement. ×{合格|ごうかく}すべく、{勉強|べんきょう}
  しなさい and ×〜すべく、{来|き}てください are not used: べく doesn't lead to an order or a request.
  Use ために there.
- Register: written and formal speech (announcements, speeches, business). Less dramatic than
  んがため: a news report says {再建|さいけん}を{図|はか}るべく, not {再建|さいけん}を{図|はか}らんがため.
- 〜べく is related to N3's べきだ and lesson 20's べからず; all come from べし.

## There's no way to: 〜べくもない

〜べくもない after the dictionary form means "there's no way to, it's out of the question". It
goes with a small set of verbs, and it often sounds resigned.

{当時|とうじ}の{私|わたし}には、{父|ちち}の{苦労|くろう}など{知|し}るべくもなかった。 — At the time, I had no way of knowing what my father was going through.
{今|いま}の{給料|きゅうりょう}では、{都心|としん}に{家|いえ}を{買|か}うなど{望|のぞ}むべくもない。 — On my present salary, buying a house in central Tokyo is out of the question.
{名人|めいじん}の{技|わざ}とは{比|くら}べるべくもない。 — It can't begin to compare with the master's skill.
{彼|かれ}の{誠実|せいじつ}さは{疑|うたが}うべくもない。 — His sincerity is beyond doubt.

Notes:

- The usual verbs: {知|し}る, {望|のぞ}む, {比|くら}べる (also the older {比|くら}ぶべくもない), {疑|うたが}う,
  {求|もと}める. With other verbs it sounds made up.
- {望|のぞ}むべくもない is very common in business and economic writing: {高|こう}{成長|せいちょう}は
  {望|のぞ}むべくもない (rapid growth is out of the question).
- Don't confuse it with 〜べきではない (one shouldn't, N3): べくもない is about possibility, not duty.

## By means of, with: 〜をもって, 〜をもってすれば, 〜をもってしても

Lesson 2 taught 〜をもって as "as of" ({本日|ほんじつ}をもって{閉店|へいてん}). Its other sense is "by
means of, with": a formal を{使|つか}って or で, for means, methods and qualities.

{結果|けっか}は{書面|しょめん}をもってお{知|し}らせいたします。 — We will notify you of the result in writing.
{彼|かれ}の{実力|じつりょく}をもってすれば、{優勝|ゆうしょう}も{夢|ゆめ}ではない。 — With his ability, even winning the title isn't a dream.
{最新|さいしん}の{技術|ぎじゅつ}をもってしても、{地震|じしん}の{予知|よち}は{難|むずか}しい。 — Even with the latest technology, predicting earthquakes is difficult.
{身|み}をもって{知|し}った。 — I learned it from bitter personal experience.
{以上|いじょう}をもちまして、{本日|ほんじつ}の{説明会|せつめいかい}を{終了|しゅうりょう}いたします。 — With that, we bring today's briefing to a close.

| Form | Meaning | Second half |
|---|---|---|
| N をもって | by means of N (formal で) | an official act: notifying, deciding, showing |
| N をもってすれば | if you use N (an ability, a resource) | something becomes possible |
| N をもってしても | even with N | still impossible or difficult |
| {身|み}をもって | in one's own person | {知|し}る, {示|しめ}す, {体験|たいけん}する |

Notes:

- With をもってすれば and をもってしても, N is usually a strength: {実力|じつりょく}, {技術|ぎじゅつ}, {資金力|しきんりょく}.
- をもちまして is the polite form in speeches and announcements.
- This course writes をもって in kana (the newspaper style for the pattern); {持|も}つ "to hold"
  keeps its kanji.

## Review: 〜ために, 〜ように

> 〜ために: a purpose the subject can bring about by will; the same subject in both halves:
> {家|いえ}を{買|か}うために{貯金|ちょきん}している.
>
> 〜ように: a hoped-for state, often with potentials, negatives and non-volitional verbs:
> {誰|だれ}でも{読|よ}めるように、{大|おお}きな{字|じ}で{書|か}いた.

## Which "in order to"?

| Pattern | Before it | Tone | Can the second half be a request? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 〜ために | dictionary form, N の | neutral | yes |
| 〜ように | dictionary or ない form, potential | neutral | yes |
| 〜べく | dictionary form (する → すべく) | written, formal | no |
| 〜んがため(に) | ない stem + ん (する → せん) | very written, dramatic, determined | no |
| N をもって(すれば) | noun (a means or ability) | formal | (means, not purpose) |

{家族|かぞく}を{養|やしな}うために{働|はたら}く。 — I work to support my family. (neutral)
{家族|かぞく}を{養|やしな}うべく、{遠|とお}い{町|まち}へ{出稼|でかせ}ぎに{出|で}た。 — To support the family, they went to work in a distant town. (written)
{家族|かぞく}を{養|やしな}わんがため、{危険|きけん}な{仕事|しごと}も{引|ひ}き{受|う}けた。 — Determined to support the family, they took on even dangerous work. (dramatic)

## The economy and finance

## Dialogue: asking for a loan

A small factory's president, Yamamoto, meets Inoue, a loan officer at a bank. (Business keigo;
surnames.)

```dialogue
# Asking for a loan
いのうえ: {本日|ほんじつ}はお{忙|いそが}しいところ、ありがとうございます。{設備|せつび}{投資|とうし}のための{融資|ゆうし}のご{相談|そうだん}と{伺|うかが}っております。
= Thank you for coming in today when you're so busy. I understand you'd like to discuss a loan for new equipment.
やまもと: ええ。{取引先|とりひきさき}から{大口|おおぐち}の{注文|ちゅうもん}をいただきまして、それに{応|こた}えるべく、{生産|せいさん}ラインを{一本|いっぽん}{増|ふ}やしたいと{考|かんが}えているんです。
= Yes. A client has given us a large order, and to meet it we'd like to add another production line.
いのうえ: {事業|じぎょう}{計画書|けいかくしょ}を{拝見|はいけん}しましたが、{設備費|せつびひ}はおよそ{三千万円|さんぜんまんえん}とのことですね。
= I've looked at your business plan: the equipment comes to about thirty million yen, I believe.
やまもと: はい。{自己|じこ}{資金|しきん}で{一千万円|いっせんまんえん}、{残|のこ}りの{二千万円|にせんまんえん}をお{借|か}りできればと{思|おも}いまして。
= Yes. Ten million from our own funds, and we were hoping to borrow the remaining twenty million.
いのうえ: {承知|しょうち}いたしました。{正直|しょうじき}に{申|もう}し{上|あ}げますと、{原材料|げんざいりょう}の{高騰|こうとう}で、{製造業|せいぞうぎょう}の{皆様|みなさま}は{厳|きび}しい{状況|じょうきょう}にあると{伺|うかが}っております。{返済|へんさい}の{見通|みとお}しをもう{少|すこ}し{詳|くわ}しくお{聞|き}かせいただけますか。

やまもと: {注文|ちゅうもん}は{三年|さんねん}{契約|けいやく}ですので、その{売|う}り{上|あ}げで{五年|ごねん}{以内|いない}には{返済|へんさい}できる{見込|みこ}みです。
= The order is on a three-year contract, so we expect to repay within five years from those sales.
いのうえ: {三年|さんねん}{後|ご}はいかがでしょう。
= And after the three years?
やまもと: そこなんです。{一社|いっしゃ}に{頼|たよ}り{切|き}っては、{先方|せんぽう}の{都合|つごう}ひとつで{経営|けいえい}が{傾|かたむ}きかねません。ですから、{新|あたら}しいラインで{培|つちか}った{技術|ぎじゅつ}をもって、ほかの{分野|ぶんや}にも{販路|はんろ}を{広|ひろ}げたいと{考|かんが}えております。
= That's the thing. If we depend entirely on one company, the business could founder on that client's whim alone. So we want to use the skills we build up on the new line to open up sales in other fields too.
いのうえ: なるほど。{御社|おんしゃ}の{加工|かこう}{技術|ぎじゅつ}をもってすれば、{十分|じゅうぶん}{可能性|かのうせい}はあると{存|ぞん}じます。
= I see. With your company's machining skills, I think there's every possibility of that.
やまもと: ありがとうございます。{父|ちち}の{代|だい}から、{生|い}き{残|のこ}らんがために、{技術|ぎじゅつ}だけは{磨|みが}いてきましたから。
= Thank you. Since my father's day we've kept honing our skills, if nothing else, determined to survive.
いのうえ: 「{生|い}き{残|のこ}らんがため」とは、{重|おも}みのあるお{言葉|ことば}ですね。
= "Determined to survive": those are weighty words.
やまもと: いや、{大|おお}げさでした。ただ、{昔|むかし}のような{好景気|こうけいき}は{望|のぞ}むべくもありませんから、{自分|じぶん}たちの{力|ちから}で{道|みち}を{開|ひら}くしかないんです。
= Oh, I exaggerated. But there's no hope of the boom times of the past, so we have no choice but to make our own way.
いのうえ: おっしゃる{通|とお}りです。では、{担保|たんぽ}の{件|けん}も{含|ふく}めて、{審査|しんさ}に{必要|ひつよう}な{書類|しょるい}をご{用意|ようい}いただけますでしょうか。
= Quite so. Then could you prepare the documents we need for the review, including those on collateral?
やまもと: {決算書|けっさんしょ}は{三期分|さんきぶん}あればよろしいですか。
= Will three years' financial statements be enough?
いのうえ: はい、{三期分|さんきぶん}で{結構|けっこう}です。{審査|しんさ}の{結果|けっか}は、{二週間|にしゅうかん}ほどで{書面|しょめん}をもってお{知|し}らせいたします。
= Yes, three years is fine. We'll let you know the result of the review in writing in about two weeks.
やまもと: よろしくお{願|ねが}いいたします。
```

{大口|おおぐち} = large (of an order or a customer); {頼|たよ}り{切|き}る = to rely entirely on;
{傾|かたむ}く (N2: to lean) is also "to decline", of a business; {販路|はんろ} = sales channels, a
market; {培|つちか}う (to cultivate, build up) is lesson 9's word; {御社|おんしゃ} = your company (spoken,
polite); {決算書|けっさんしょ} = financial statements. Yamamoto's べく and んがため are the written purpose
patterns used in speech for weight, and Inoue picks up the dramatic one; をもって appears in both
senses ("with our skills", "in writing").

## Reading: keeping money in town

A newspaper column with a claim and a counter-view (である style).

> 「{買|か}い{物|もの}は{地元|じもと}で」。そう{呼|よ}びかけるポスターが、ある{地方都市|ちほうとし}の{商店街|しょうてんがい}のあちこちに{貼|は}られている。この{町|まち}では{数年前|すうねんまえ}から、{市内|しない}の{店|みせ}でしか{使|つか}えない{地域通貨|ちいきつうか}が{発行|はっこう}されている。{一万円|いちまんえん}で{一万一千円分|いちまんいっせんえんぶん}の{買|か}い{物|もの}ができる{仕組|しく}みで、{上乗|うわの}せ{分|ぶん}は{市|し}が{負担|ふたん}している。
>
> {背景|はいけい}にあるのは、{町|まち}のお{金|かね}が{外|そと}へ{流|なが}れ{出|だ}していくことへの{危機感|ききかん}だ。{郊外|こうがい}の{大型店|おおがたてん}やインターネット{通販|つうはん}で{使|つか}われたお{金|かね}は、その{多|おお}くが{地域|ちいき}の{外|そと}の{企業|きぎょう}の{利益|りえき}となる。{人口|じんこう}が{減|へ}り{続|つづ}ける{町|まち}にとって、このお{金|かね}の{流出|りゅうしゅつ}は{死活問題|しかつもんだい}である。{地元|じもと}の{店|みせ}で{使|つか}われれば{店主|てんしゅ}の{収入|しゅうにゅう}となり、その{店主|てんしゅ}がまた{近所|きんじょ}で{買|か}い{物|もの}をする。{市|し}の{担当者|たんとうしゃ}は「お{金|かね}を{地域|ちいき}の{中|なか}で{循環|じゅんかん}させるべく{始|はじ}めた{取|と}り{組|く}みです」と{語|かた}る。
>
> {効果|こうか}は{確|たし}かに{表|あらわ}れている。{発行|はっこう}{初日|しょにち}には{購入|こうにゅう}を{求|もと}める{市民|しみん}の{列|れつ}ができ、{閉店|へいてん}を{考|かんが}えていた{青果店|せいかてん}が「おかげで{客足|きゃくあし}が{戻|もど}った」と{話|はな}すなど、{商店街|しょうてんがい}は{久|ひさ}しぶりに{潤|うるお}っている。{生|い}き{残|のこ}らんがため、{店主|てんしゅ}たちも{営業|えいぎょう}{時間|じかん}を{延|の}ばしたり{配達|はいたつ}を{始|はじ}めたりと、{工夫|くふう}を{重|かさ}ねている。{客|きゃく}を{呼|よ}び{戻|もど}すべく、{合同|ごうどう}で{朝市|あさいち}を{開|ひら}く{計画|けいかく}もあるそうだ。
>
> {商店街|しょうてんがい}の{組合|くみあい}で{理事長|りじちょう}を{務|つと}める{男性|だんせい}は、この{取|と}り{組|く}みに{特別|とくべつ}な{思|おも}いを{寄|よ}せる。{父親|ちちおや}の{代|だい}から{続|つづ}く{金物店|かなものてん}を{営|いとな}んできたが、{客|きゃく}の{減少|げんしょう}に{歯止|はど}めがかからず、{店|みせ}を{畳|たた}むことも{考|かんが}えたという。「{大型店|おおがたてん}が{悪|わる}いとは{思|おも}いません。ただ、{町|まち}から{店|みせ}が{消|き}えれば、{車|くるま}を{持|も}たないお{年寄|としよ}りは{日々|ひび}の{買|か}い{物|もの}にも{困|こま}ります。{地元|じもと}の{店|みせ}は{暮|く}らしを{支|ささ}える{基盤|きばん}なんです」。スマートフォンで{支払|しはら}える{電子版|でんしばん}も{加|くわ}わり、{若|わか}い{世代|せだい}の{利用|りよう}も{少|すこ}しずつ{増|ふ}えている。
>
> しかし、{手放|てばな}しで{喜|よろこ}べるわけではない。ある{経済学者|けいざいがくしゃ}は、{上乗|うわの}せ{分|ぶん}が{税金|ぜいきん}で{賄|まかな}われている{以上|いじょう}、{売|う}り{上|あ}げの{伸|の}びの{一部|いちぶ}は{市民|しみん}{自身|じしん}のお{金|かね}で{生|う}み{出|だ}されたものにすぎないと{指摘|してき}する。{補助|ほじょ}がなくなれば{客|きゃく}も{離|はな}れていくのではないか、という{懸念|けねん}も{根強|ねづよ}い。{発行|はっこう}や{換金|かんきん}にかかる{事務|じむ}の{費用|ひよう}も{小|ちい}さくない。{品|しな}ぞろえや{価格|かかく}では、{大型店|おおがたてん}とは{比|くら}べるべくもないのが{実情|じつじょう}だ。
>
> では、{地域通貨|ちいきつうか}は{一時|いちじ}しのぎの{策|さく}にすぎないのか。{私|わたし}はそうは{思|おも}わない。{店主|てんしゅ}と{客|きゃく}が{顔|かお}を{合|あ}わせ、{言葉|ことば}を{交|か}わす{機会|きかい}が{増|ふ}えたことは、{数字|すうじ}には{表|あらわ}れない{財産|ざいさん}である。もちろん、{地域通貨|ちいきつうか}をもってすれば{町|まち}の{衰退|すいたい}を{止|と}められるというほど、{話|はなし}は{単純|たんじゅん}ではない。どんな{制度|せいど}をもってしても、{人|ひと}がどこで{買|か}い{物|もの}をするかまで{決|き}めることはできないのだ。{大切|たいせつ}なのは、{補助|ほじょ}が{続|つづ}くうちに、{客|きゃく}が「また{来|き}たい」と{思|おも}う{店|みせ}をどれだけ{育|そだ}てられるかであろう。{地域通貨|ちいきつうか}は、そのための{時間|じかん}を{稼|かせ}ぐ{手段|しゅだん}と{考|かんが}えるべきではないか。

{地域通貨|ちいきつうか} = a local currency (vouchers valid only in one area); {上乗|うわの}せ = an extra amount
added on top; {危機感|ききかん} = a sense of crisis; {青果店|せいかてん} = a greengrocer's; {客足|きゃくあし} = the
flow of customers; {手放|てばな}しで = unreservedly; {根強|ねづよ}い = deep-rooted; {品|しな}ぞろえ = the
range of goods (its second kanji is off the list); {一時|いちじ}しのぎ = a stopgap; {理事長|りじちょう} = the chair (of an association); {金物店|かなものてん} = a
hardware shop; {歯止|はど}めがかからない = there's no stopping it; {換金|かんきん} = cashing in; {死活問題|しかつもんだい} = a matter of life and death. {賄|まかな}う is lesson
11's word; {懸念|けねん} (concern) lesson 16's; {衰退|すいたい} (decline) lesson 18's.

1. Why did the town start issuing its local currency?
2. What two effects does the third paragraph describe?
3. What does the economist point out, and what other worry is there?
4. What does the writer think matters most?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Because of a sense of crisis that the town's money flows out: money spent at big out-of-town
   stores or online mostly becomes profit for companies outside the area. The aim is to make money
   circulate inside the community ({循環|じゅんかん}させるべく).
2. The shopping street is prospering again (queues on the first day; a greengrocer that had
   thought of closing has its customers back), and shopkeepers, determined to survive, are making
   their own efforts (longer hours, deliveries).
3. Since the extra amount is paid from taxes, part of the rise in sales is only produced with the
   residents' own money. Others worry that customers will leave once the subsidy ends; and on range
   and price the local shops can't begin to compare with the big stores.
4. How many shops customers will want to come back to can be built up while the subsidy lasts. The
   new chances for shopkeepers and customers to meet and talk are also a valuable asset that
   figures don't show.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

"Shop locally." Posters with that appeal are up all over the shopping street of a regional city.
For several years this town has issued a local currency that can only be used in shops within the
city. Under the scheme, ten thousand yen buys eleven thousand yen's worth of shopping, and the city
pays the extra.

Behind it is a sense of crisis about the town's money flowing out. Most of the money spent at big
out-of-town stores or through online shopping becomes profit for companies outside the area. For a town whose population keeps shrinking, this
outflow of money is a matter of life and death. If it
is spent at local shops, it becomes the shopkeepers' income, and they in turn shop nearby. "It's a
scheme we started to get money circulating within the community," says the official in charge.

The effects are certainly showing. On the first day of issue there was a queue of residents
wanting to buy, and a greengrocer that had been thinking of closing says, "Thanks to this, the
customers have come back." The shopping street is prospering for the first time in years.
Determined to survive, the shopkeepers too are making efforts, extending their opening hours and
starting deliveries. They are even said to be planning a joint morning market to bring customers
back.

The man who chairs the shopping street's association has special feelings about the scheme. He
has run the hardware shop his father started, but customer numbers kept falling and he says he even
thought of closing. "I don't think the big stores are bad. But if the shops disappear from the town,
elderly people without cars will struggle even with their daily shopping. Local shops are the
foundation that supports people's lives." With an electronic version that can be paid with a
smartphone added, use by younger people is gradually growing too.

But this is not cause for unreserved celebration. One economist points out that since the extra
amount is paid for by taxes, part of the increase in sales has merely been produced with the
residents' own money. There is also a deep-rooted worry that customers will drift away once the
subsidy ends. The administrative costs of issuing the vouchers and cashing them in are not small
either. The truth is that on range and price, the local shops cannot begin to compare with
the big stores.

Is the local currency, then, no more than a stopgap? I don't think so. The increase in chances
for shopkeepers and customers to meet face to face and talk is an asset that doesn't show in the
figures. Of course, it isn't so simple that a local currency can stop the town's decline. No
system, however good, can decide where people do their shopping. What matters is how many shops
customers want to come back to can be nurtured while the subsidy lasts. Shouldn't we see the local currency as a way of buying
time for that?

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{期待|きたい}に{応|こた}えるべく、{全力|ぜんりょく}を{尽|つ}くします。
= I'll do my utmost to live up to your expectations.
{生|い}き{残|のこ}らんがため、{技術|ぎじゅつ}を{磨|みが}いてきた。
= Determined to survive, we've kept honing our skills.
そんなことは{知|し}るべくもなかった。
= There was no way I could have known that.
{結果|けっか}は{書面|しょめん}をもってお{知|し}らせいたします。
= We will inform you of the result in writing.
{円安|えんやす}で、{輸入品|ゆにゅうひん}の{価格|かかく}が{高騰|こうとう}している。
= With the weak yen, the prices of imported goods are soaring.
```

## Common mistakes

- ×しんがため. する becomes せんがため: {成功|せいこう}せんがため.
- ×{行|い}くんがため, ×{食|た}べるんがため. んがため joins the ない stem: {行|い}かんがため, {食|た}べんがため.
- べく before a request: ×{遅|おく}れないべく、{早|はや}めに{来|き}てください. Use ように or ために:
  {遅|おく}れないように. べく also follows the dictionary form, not the ない form.
- んがため for a small daily purpose: {牛乳|ぎゅうにゅう}を{買|か}わんがためコンビニに{行|い}った sounds like
  mock heroics. Use ために.
- べくもない with any verb: {行|い}くべくもない isn't used. It goes with {知|し}る, {望|のぞ}む, {比|くら}べる, {疑|うたが}う,
  {求|もと}める. For "can't go" say {行|い}けるはずもない.
- Mixing up the two をもって: {本日|ほんじつ}をもって is "as of today" (lesson 2); {書面|しょめん}をもって is
  "by means of a letter". A time word gives the first sense, a means the second.

## Key points

- Purpose clause: a clause that says what an action is for.
- 〜んがため(に) / 〜んがための (ない stem + ん; する → せん): in order to, at all costs; very
  written and dramatic.
- 〜べく (dictionary form; する → すべく / するべく): in order to; written; the second half is an
  action, never a request.
- 〜べくもない (知る, 望む, 比べる, 疑う): there's no way to; written; often resigned.
- N をもって (by means of), をもってすれば (with N, it's possible), をもってしても (even with N, it's
  not); "as of" is lesson 2's sense.
- New kanji: 株 債 融 幣 銭 款 為 託 租 賦 需 騰 衡 購 卸 剰 貢 献 獲 稼 酬 償 賠 蓄 恵 浪 循 潤 乏 縮 繁 盛.
  Write {稼|かせ}ぐ, {需要|じゅよう}, {小銭|こぜに}, {銭湯|せんとう}, {恵|めぐ}まれる, {貧乏|びんぼう}, {盛|も}り{上|あ}がる with
  kanji from now on; {為替|かわせ} is a special reading.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete

lessons.title: Given that: 手前, とあれば, ともなると, あっての
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Some reasons aren't causes at all: they are about the position you are in. Having promised, you
can't back out; if it's for your child, you'll do anything; once someone is a company president,
certain things come with the job; and some things only exist thanks to others. This lesson's four
patterns give these grounds:

{約束|やくそく}した{手前|てまえ}、{今|いま}さら{断|ことわ}れない。 — Having promised, I can't say no now.
{子|こ}どものためとあれば、どんな{苦労|くろう}もいとわない。 — If it's for my children, I'll spare no effort.
{社長|しゃちょう}ともなると、{自由|じゆう}な{時間|じかん}はほとんどない。 — Once you're a company president, you have hardly any free time.
{客|きゃく}あっての{商売|しょうばい}だ。 — There's no business without customers.

N2's 〜からには and 〜{以上|いじょう} ("now that") are close relatives; a review box comes below.

The theme is politics, government and diplomacy: the Diet and the cabinet, the imperial family,
parties and factions, treaties and alliances, local government. Earlier courses gave you the basics
({与党|よとう} and {野党|やとう}, {首相|しゅしょう}, {条約|じょうやく}, {議員|ぎいん}, {選挙区|せんきょく}); this lesson's kanji let you write
{内閣|ないかく}, {投票|とうひょう}, {天皇|てんのう} and {申請|しんせい}, and add the words of the political pages.

## Because of how it would look: 〜{手前|てまえ}

{手前|てまえ} is "the near side, in front of". As a grammar pattern it means "because of my position
in front of someone": having said or done something, or with certain people watching, you have to
keep face, so you can't do otherwise.

| Before {手前|てまえ} | Example |
|---|---|
| verb, plain form (usually past) | {約束|やくそく}した{手前|てまえ}, {大口|おおぐち}をたたいた{手前|てまえ} |
| noun + の | {子供|こども}の{手前|てまえ}, {部下|ぶか}の{手前|てまえ} |

{約束|やくそく}した{手前|てまえ}、{今|いま}さら{断|ことわ}れない。 — Having promised, I can't say no now.
「{必|かなら}ず{勝|か}つ」と{言|い}った{手前|てまえ}、{負|ま}けるわけにはいかない。 — Having said "we'll definitely win", we can't afford to lose.
{子供|こども}たちの{手前|てまえ}、{父親|ちちおや}が{泣|な}くわけにはいかなかった。 — In front of the children, their father couldn't let himself cry.
{選挙|せんきょ}で{公約|こうやく}に{掲|かか}げた{手前|てまえ}、{市長|しちょう}は{計画|けいかく}を{撤回|てっかい}できずにいる。 — Having made it a campaign pledge, the mayor can't withdraw the plan.

Points to remember:

- The second half is a constraint: 〜わけにはいかない, 〜ざるを{得|え}ない, 〜しかない, 〜できない,
  〜なければならない. The speaker is boxed in by what they did or by who is watching.
- It's about face, not logic. Compare N2's 〜{以上|いじょう}: {約束|やくそく}した{以上|いじょう}、{守|まも}るべきだ
  (since you promised, you should keep it: a principle). {約束|やくそく}した{手前|てまえ}、{守|まも}らざるを{得|え}ない
  (having promised, I'm stuck with it: my position).
- It's used in speech and writing, with a slightly self-conscious, rueful tone.
- {手前|てまえ} has other uses you'll meet: "just before" ({駅|えき}の{手前|てまえ}で{降|お}りる), and an old
  humble "I" in period drama; お{点前|てまえ} (also written お{手前|てまえ}) is the way of making tea in the tea
  ceremony.

## If it's for…: 〜とあれば

〜とあれば is a condition: "if it's (a case like this)", and the second half says that then the
speaker (or someone) will do something they wouldn't otherwise do, or must accept it.

| Before とあれば | Example |
|---|---|
| noun | {子|こ}どものためとあれば, {社長|しゃちょう}の{命令|めいれい}とあれば |
| plain form | {必要|ひつよう}とあれば, {彼|かれ}が{来|く}るとあれば |

{子|こ}どものためとあれば、どんな{苦労|くろう}もいとわない。 — If it's for my children, I'll spare no effort.
{会社|かいしゃ}の{命令|めいれい}とあれば、{従|したが}わざるを{得|え}ない。 — If it's an order from the company, I have no choice but to obey.
{必要|ひつよう}とあれば、{私|わたし}から{先方|せんぽう}に{説明|せつめい}いたします。 — If necessary, I'll explain to the other party myself.
{好|す}きな{作家|さっか}のサイン{会|かい}とあれば、{遠|とお}くても{行|い}きたい。 — If it's a signing by my favourite author, I want to go, however far.

Notes:

- The condition is a special reason that makes the effort worthwhile or unavoidable. The second
  half is often willingness (〜てもいい, いとわない, {何|なん}でもする) or acceptance (〜しかない).
- Formal, but at home in speech: {必要|ひつよう}とあれば is a common business phrase.
- Don't confuse it with lesson 11's 〜とあって (since it's a special occasion, a scene
  followed). とあって reports a fact; とあれば is a condition.

## When it comes to: 〜ともなると, 〜ともなれば

〜ともなると / 〜ともなれば follow a noun (or a dictionary-form verb) naming a higher level: a
position, an age, a season, a scale. The second half says what naturally comes with that level.

{社長|しゃちょう}ともなると、{自由|じゆう}な{時間|じかん}はほとんどない。 — Once you're a company president, you have hardly any free time.
{十二月|じゅうにがつ}ともなると、{街|まち}は{一気|いっき}ににぎやかになる。 — When it gets to December, the town suddenly livens up.
{大学生|だいがくせい}ともなれば、{自分|じぶん}のことは{自分|じぶん}で{決|き}めるべきだ。 — Once you're a university student, you should make your own decisions.
{国|くに}の{代表|だいひょう}として{発言|はつげん}するともなれば、{言葉|ことば}{一|ひと}つにも{責任|せきにん}が{伴|ともな}う。 — When it comes to speaking on behalf of the country, every word carries responsibility.

Restrictions:

- The noun is a stage reached, often one step up from the ordinary: {社長|しゃちょう}, {横綱|よこづな},
  {首相|しゅしょう}, {十二月|じゅうにがつ}, {百人|ひゃくにん}{規模|きぼ}. {学生|がくせい}ともなると for "if you're a
  student" sounds odd unless being a student is presented as a step up (a child about to become one).
- The second half is a general consequence, usually not a single past event or the speaker's own
  wish. ともなれば leans slightly to "if/when that happens", ともなると to "whenever it is so".
- Compare plain になると: {社長|しゃちょう}になると is "when someone becomes president"; ともなると adds
  "at a level as high as that".

## There's no B without A: N あっての N

N₁ あっての N₂ says that N₂ exists only thanks to N₁. It's an old construction (あって + の),
used today in fixed-sounding statements of gratitude and principle.

{客|きゃく}あっての{商売|しょうばい}だ。 — There's no business without customers.
{健康|けんこう}あっての{人生|じんせい}だから、{無理|むり}をしてはいけない。 — Life is nothing without health, so don't overdo things.
{国民|こくみん}あっての{政治|せいじ}であることを{忘|わす}れてはならない。 — We must not forget that politics exists for the people.
{今日|きょう}の{成功|せいこう}は、{皆様|みなさま}のご{支援|しえん}あってのことです。 — Today's success is thanks entirely to your support.

Notes:

- 〜あってのこと(だ) at the end of a sentence is common in speeches: "it's all thanks to".
- The nouns are usually short and weighty: {客|きゃく}, {命|いのち}, {健康|けんこう}, {信頼|しんらい}, {住民|じゅうみん}.

## Review: 〜からには, 〜{以上|いじょう} (N2)

> 〜からには and 〜{以上|いじょう}(は) (N2 lesson 11): "now that, since", and a duty or resolve
> follows: {引|ひ}き{受|う}けたからには、{最後|さいご}までやる. They state a principle that applies to
> anyone. 〜{手前|てまえ} is personal: it's about face. 〜とあれば is a condition, not a fact already
> settled.

## Comparing the patterns

| Pattern | What it gives | Second half | Register |
|---|---|---|---|
| 〜{手前|てまえ} | what I did or who's watching (face) | can't / must | speech and writing |
| 〜からには / 〜{以上|いじょう} | a settled fact | a duty, a resolve | speech and writing |
| 〜とあれば | a special case (condition) | willingness or acceptance | formal; business speech |
| 〜とあって (lesson 11) | a special case (fact) | an observed scene | news, narrative |

> 「はい。{役場|やくば}は{住民|じゅうみん}のためにあるものです。ところが{実際|じっさい}には{制度|せいど}が{複雑|ふくざつ}で、{住民|じゅうみん}が{気軽|きがる}に{相談|そうだん}に{来|こ}られない。そこで{月|つき}に{一度|いちど}、{私|わたし}が{各地区|かくちく}の{集会所|しゅうかいじょ}に{出向|でむ}いて、{直接|ちょくせつ}{話|はなし}を{聞|き}く{場|ば}を{設|もう}けることにしました。{先月|せんげつ}の{第一回|だいいっかい}には、{予想|よそう}を{上回|うわまわ}る{六十人|ろくじゅうにん}が{集|あつ}まってくれました。{役場|やくば}の{職員|しょくいん}にも、{窓口|まどぐち}で{待|ま}つのではなく{外|そと}に{出|で}ていくよう{求|もと}めています」
>
> ――{財政|ざいせい}は{厳|きび}しいと{聞|き}きます。
>
> 「ええ。{人口|じんこう}が{減|へ}り、{税収|ぜいしゅう}も{落|お}ち{込|こ}んでいます。{県|けん}や{国|くに}の{補助|ほじょ}を{求|もと}めて{何度|なんど}も{足|あし}を{運|はこ}んでいますが、{頼|たよ}ってばかりはいられません。{子育|こそだ}てや{医療|いりょう}のためとあれば、{他|ほか}の{事業|じぎょう}を{削|けず}ってでも{予算|よさん}を{確保|かくほ}するつもりです」
>
> ――{若|わか}い{世代|せだい}の{投票率|とうひょうりつ}の{低|ひく}さも{課題|かだい}です。
>
> 「そうですね。{今回|こんかい}の{選挙|せんきょ}でも、{二十代|にじゅうだい}の{投票率|とうひょうりつ}は{三割|さんわり}に{届|とど}きませんでした。でも、{関心|かんしん}がないわけではないと{思|おも}うんです。{自分|じぶん}の{一票|いっぴょう}で{何|なに}かが{変|か}わるという{実感|じっかん}がないから、{足|あし}が{向|む}かない。ですから、{高校生|こうこうせい}や{大学生|だいがくせい}に、{町|まち}の{予算|よさん}の{使|つか}い{道|みち}を{一緒|いっしょ}に{考|かんが}えてもらう{場|ば}を{作|つく}りたい。{若者|わかもの}の{意見|いけん}が{実際|じっさい}に{形|かたち}になれば、{次|つぎ}の{選挙|せんきょ}では{足|あし}を{運|はこ}んでくれるはずです」
>
> ――{議会|ぎかい}との{関係|かんけい}はいかがですか。
>
> 「{前|まえ}の{町長|ちょうちょう}を{支|ささ}えてきた{議員|ぎいん}も{多|おお}く、{最初|さいしょ}の{議会|ぎかい}は{紛糾|ふんきゅう}しました。でも、{対立|たいりつ}するばかりでは{何|なに}も{進|すす}みません。{町|まち}のためとあれば、{立場|たちば}の{違|ちが}いを{越|こ}えて{協力|きょうりょく}できるはずだと{信|しん}じています。{今|いま}は{月|つき}に{一度|いちど}、すべての{会派|かいは}の{代表|だいひょう}と{意見|いけん}を{交換|こうかん}する{場|ば}を{持|も}つようにしています」
>
> ――{最後|さいご}に、{町民|ちょうみん}へのメッセージをお{願|ねが}いします。
>
> 「{町|まち}の{将来|しょうらい}を{決|き}めるのは、{役場|やくば}ではなく{皆|みな}さんです。{不満|ふまん}も{提案|ていあん}も、{遠慮|えんりょ}なく{届|とど}けてください。{小|ちい}さな{声|こえ}でもかまいません。{皆|みな}さんの{声|こえ}あっての{町政|ちょうせい}ですから」

{破|やぶ}る = to defeat; {推|お}す = to recommend, back (a candidate); {手|て}を{挙|あ}げる = to put
oneself forward; {投|な}げ{出|だ}す = to give up, throw over; {町政|ちょうせい} = the running of a town;
{役場|やくば} = the town office; {出向|でむ}く = to go (to a place, in person); {足|あし}を{運|はこ}ぶ = to go
somewhere (repeatedly, to ask for something); {紛糾|ふんきゅう}する = to become tangled, (of a meeting)
to be thrown into confusion; {背中|せなか}を{押|お}す = to give someone the push to act; {会派|かいは} = a
group of members in an assembly.

1. Why did the mayor not give up after deciding to stand?
2. How has the mayor's life changed, and why must they be careful about what they say?
3. What has the mayor started doing to hear residents' views, and how did it go?
4. On what condition will the mayor cut other projects?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Having put themselves forward with the backing of young local people ({推|お}されて{手|て}を{挙|あ}げた
   {手前|てまえ}), the mayor couldn't drop out halfway: it was a matter of face toward those supporters.
2. Meetings and events from morning to night and hardly any days off. As the town's representative,
   every word carries weight: even a joke is all over town the next day.
3. Once a month the mayor goes to the meeting hall of each district to listen to people directly.
   At the first one, last month, sixty people came, more than expected.
4. If it's for child-rearing or healthcare ({子育|こそだ}てや{医療|いりょう}のためとあれば), the mayor will
   cut other projects to secure the budget.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Congratulations on taking office. You were elected at your first election, defeating the
incumbent.

"Thank you. To be honest, I hesitated a lot before deciding to stand. I was working for a company,
and my family were against it. But having put myself forward with the backing of the young people
here, I couldn't give up halfway. In the end, my family's words, "If you're going to do it, do it
properly", gave me the push I needed."

Once you're mayor, your life must have changed a great deal?

"It has. Meetings and events go on from morning to night, and I have hardly any days off. If I get dinner with my family
once a week, I'm doing well. When
you're the town's representative, a single word carries a different weight. Even something I mean
as a light joke has spread all over town by the next day."

In the campaign you called for "a town government that exists for its residents".

"Yes. The town office exists for the residents. But in reality the system is complicated, and
residents can't easily come in for advice. So I decided to go once a month to the meeting hall in
each district and set up a chance to hear people directly. At the first one last month, sixty
people came, more than we expected. I've also asked the town office staff to go out to people
instead of waiting at the counter."

We hear the town's finances are tight.

"Yes. The population is falling and so is tax revenue. I've been to the prefecture and the
national government many times to ask for subsidies, but we can't just rely on others. If it's for
child-rearing and healthcare, I intend to secure the budget even if it means cutting other
projects."

The low turnout among younger people is another challenge.

"It is. In this election, too, turnout among people in their twenties didn't reach thirty per
cent. But I don't think they aren't interested. They don't feel that their one vote changes
anything, so they don't go. That's why I want to create opportunities for high school and
university students to think with us about how the town's budget is spent. If young people's
opinions actually take shape, they'll surely come to vote at the next election."

How are relations with the council?

"Many councillors supported the previous mayor, and my first council session was in uproar. But
nothing moves forward if we only oppose each other. I believe that if it's for the town, we can
work together across our differences. Now I make a point of meeting the representatives of every
group on the council once a month to exchange views."

Finally, a message to the town's residents, please.

"It isn't the town office that decides the town's future; it's all of you. Please don't hesitate
to send us your complaints and proposals. Even a quiet voice is welcome. A town government exists through your voices."

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{約束|やくそく}した{手前|てまえ}、{行|い}かないわけにはいかない。
= Having promised, I can't not go.
{必要|ひつよう}とあれば、{私|わたし}からご{説明|せつめい}いたします。
= If necessary, I'll explain it myself.
{社長|しゃちょう}ともなると、{責任|せきにん}も{重|おも}い。
= When you're a company president, the responsibility is heavy too.
{客|きゃく}あっての{商売|しょうばい}です。
= There's no business without customers.
{法案|ほうあん}は{衆議院|しゅうぎいん}で{可決|かけつ}された。
= The bill was passed by the House of Representatives.
```

## Common mistakes

- 〜{手前|てまえ} with a pleasant result: {約束|やくそく}した{手前|てまえ}、{楽|たの}しく{過|す}ごした isn't how it's used.
  The second half is a constraint: {行|い}かないわけにはいかない.
- Mixing up とあれば and とあって: {連休|れんきゅう}とあれば、{道|みち}が{混|こ}んでいる sounds wrong for a
  fact you can see. Reporting a scene: {連休|れんきゅう}とあって. A condition for a decision:
  {会社|かいしゃ}のためとあれば.
- ともなると with an ordinary noun: {人|ひと}ともなると means nothing. The noun is a higher stage:
  {社長|しゃちょう}, {横綱|よこづな}, {年末|ねんまつ}, {百万人|ひゃくまんにん}.
- {客|きゃく}がある{商売|しょうばい} for "business that depends on customers": it doesn't say that. Use the set form:
  {客|きゃく}あっての{商売|しょうばい}.
- Reading 皇 always コウ: {天皇|てんのう} is てんのう.

## Key points

- 〜{手前|てまえ} (plain form, N の): because of how it would look (having said or done something, or in
  front of someone); a constraint follows.
- 〜とあれば (N, plain form): if it's (for) …; willingness or acceptance follows; formal.
- 〜ともなると / 〜ともなれば (N, dictionary form): when it comes to (a higher level); what
  naturally comes with it follows.
- N₁ あっての N₂: N₂ exists only thanks to N₁; 〜あってのことだ (it's all thanks to).
- New kanji: 閣 衆 憲 票 宰 閥 枢 迭 掌 陛 皇 后 妃 邦 韓 旗 揚 盟 擁 請 渉 諮 准 維 拒 是 施 措 圏 郡 轄 糾.
  Write {内閣|ないかく}, {投票|とうひょう}, {天皇|てんのう}, {韓国|かんこく}, {申請|しんせい}, {揚|あ}げ{物|もの} with kanji from
  now on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Paying no heed: をよそに, をものともせず, をかえりみず, にかこつけて
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson's patterns are about what someone does in spite of something, or by using it: they
ignore other people's worry, brave a danger, disregard their own safety, use something as an
excuse, or take advantage of a situation. Some of them praise, some criticize, and choosing the
right one shows how the writer judges the person.

{周囲|しゅうい}の{心配|しんぱい}をよそに、{彼|かれ}は{一人|ひとり}で{旅|たび}に{出|で}た。 — Ignoring the worries of those around him, he set off alone on a journey.
{大|おお}けがをものともせず、{選手|せんしゅ}は{最後|さいご}まで{走|はし}り{抜|ぬ}いた。 — Undaunted by a serious injury, the athlete ran to the finish.
{危険|きけん}を{顧|かえり}みず、{消防士|しょうぼうし}は{火|ひ}の{中|なか}へ{飛|と}び{込|こ}んだ。 — With no thought for the danger, the firefighter plunged into the fire.
{出張|しゅっちょう}にかこつけて、{温泉|おんせん}を{楽|たの}しんできた。 — Using the business trip as an excuse, I enjoyed the hot springs.
{親|おや}が{留守|るす}なのをいいことに、{夜|よる}{遅|おそ}くまでゲームをした。 — Taking advantage of my parents being out, I played games until late.

The theme is conflict, war and security: armies and weapons, attack and defence, invasion and
withdrawal, heroes and victims. Earlier courses gave you {戦争|せんそう}, {平和|へいわ}, {戦|たたか}う and N2's
{終戦|しゅうせん}; this lesson's kanji let you write {壊|こわ}す, {目撃者|もくげきしゃ} and {土砂崩|どしゃくず}れ, and add the
words of the international pages. The lesson describes, and doesn't take sides on any conflict.

## Ignoring (others' concern): 〜をよそに

よそ is "somewhere else, other people's". N をよそに is "treating N as if it had nothing to do with
one": going ahead while others worry, protest or expect something.

{親|おや}の{心配|しんぱい}をよそに、{息子|むすこ}は{大学|だいがく}をやめてしまった。 — Ignoring his parents' worries, the son dropped out of university.
{住民|じゅうみん}の{反対|はんたい}をよそに、{工事|こうじ}は{予定|よてい}どおり{始|はじ}められた。 — In spite of the residents' opposition, the work began as planned.
{周囲|しゅうい}の{期待|きたい}をよそに、{新人|しんじん}は{初戦|しょせん}で{敗|やぶ}れた。 — Contrary to everyone's expectations, the newcomer lost the first match.
{不況|ふきょう}をよそに、この{店|みせ}だけは{連日|れんじつ}にぎわっている。 — As if the recession had nothing to do with it, this shop alone is busy day after day.

Points to remember:

- N is other people's feeling or a situation around the subject: {心配|しんぱい}, {反対|はんたい},
  {期待|きたい}, {批判|ひはん}, {声|こえ}, {不安|ふあん}, {不況|ふきょう}, {騒|さわ}ぎ.
- The subject is usually someone else, and the writer observes: written and news style. With
  feelings it's usually critical (they didn't care); with a situation it can simply mark a contrast
  (the shop thrives regardless).
- Not for the speaker's own plans: {私|わたし}は{家族|かぞく}の{心配|しんぱい}をよそに{旅行|りょこう}する sounds as if
  you were describing yourself from outside.

## Undaunted by: 〜をものともせず(に)

N をものともせず is "not treating N as anything": overcoming a difficulty with courage. It's praise,
said of other people.

{大|おお}けがをものともせず、{選手|せんしゅ}は{最後|さいご}まで{走|はし}り{抜|ぬ}いた。 — Undaunted by a serious injury, the athlete ran to the finish.
{登山隊|とざんたい}は{吹雪|ふぶき}をものともせずに{頂上|ちょうじょう}を{目指|めざ}した。 — The climbing party pressed on toward the summit, undaunted by the blizzard.
{彼女|かのじょ}は{度重|たびかさ}なる{失敗|しっぱい}をものともせず、{研究|けんきゅう}を{続|つづ}けた。 — Undeterred by repeated failures, she kept up her research.

Points to remember:

- N is a hardship or a danger: {困難|こんなん}, {逆境|ぎゃっきょう}, けが, {悪天候|あくてんこう}, {反対|はんたい}.
- The second half is an achievement or a brave act, in the past or as a description.
- Not for oneself: {私|わたし}はけがをものともせず{走|はし}った sounds like boasting. It's the
  admiring voice of a reporter or a narrator.
- Compare をよそに: をよそに ignores other people's feelings (often critical); をものともせず
  overcomes a difficulty (admiring).

## With no regard for: 〜を{顧|かえり}みず

{顧|かえり}みる is "to look back on, to take into account". N を{顧|かえり}みず is "without taking N into
account": acting with no thought for a danger, for oneself, or for others.

{危険|きけん}を{顧|かえり}みず、{消防士|しょうぼうし}は{火|ひ}の{中|なか}へ{飛|と}び{込|こ}んだ。 — With no thought for the danger, the firefighter plunged into the fire.
{彼|かれ}は{自分|じぶん}の{身|み}の{危険|きけん}も{顧|かえり}みず、{溺|おぼ}れる{子供|こども}を{助|たす}けた。 — With no regard for his own safety, he saved the drowning child.
{家庭|かてい}を{顧|かえり}みず、{仕事|しごと}ばかりしていた{父|ちち}を、{私|わたし}は{長|なが}く{許|ゆる}せなかった。 — For a long time I couldn't forgive my father, who neglected his family and did nothing but work.
{周囲|しゅうい}の{迷惑|めいわく}も{顧|かえり}みず、{大声|おおごえ}で{電話|でんわ}をする{人|ひと}がいる。 — Some people talk loudly on the phone with no regard for the trouble they cause those around them.

Notes:

- Praise or blame depends on N. {危険|きけん}, {身|み}の{危険|きけん}, {我|わ}が{身|み}: brave. {家庭|かてい},
  {迷惑|めいわく}, {周囲|しゅうい}: selfish.
- ず is the written negative (N2's 〜ず); 〜を{顧|かえり}みずに also occurs. 〜も{顧|かえり}みず ("without
  even considering") is common.
- {顧|かえり}みる (to look back, take into account) and {省|かえり}みる (to reflect on oneself, with N2's
  省) are two spellings of かえりみる for different senses; this pattern uses {顧|かえり}みる.

## Using as a pretext: 〜にかこつけて

N にかこつけて is "making N an excuse": the stated reason is N, but the real purpose is something
else.

{出張|しゅっちょう}にかこつけて、{温泉|おんせん}を{楽|たの}しんできた。 — Using the business trip as an excuse, I enjoyed the hot springs.
{彼|かれ}は{体調不良|たいちょうふりょう}にかこつけて、{面倒|めんどう}な{会議|かいぎ}を{欠席|けっせき}した。 — He used feeling unwell as an excuse to skip the tiresome meeting.
{子供|こども}の{誕生日|たんじょうび}にかこつけて、{自分|じぶん}が{欲|ほ}しかったゲームを{買|か}った。 — I bought the game I'd wanted myself, using my child's birthday as a pretext.

Notes:

- Spoken and written, often critical or self-mocking.
- Written in kana: the dictionary verb かこつける is sometimes printed with lesson 12's 託, but that
  reading isn't jōyō.
- The second half is what the person really wanted to do.

## Taking advantage of: 〜をいいことに

〜をいいことに is "treating (a situation) as a good thing, and using it to do something one
shouldn't". It's always critical.

{親|おや}が{留守|るす}なのをいいことに、{夜|よる}{遅|おそ}くまでゲームをした。 — Taking advantage of my parents being out, I played games until late.
{上司|じょうし}が{何|なに}も{言|い}わないのをいいことに、{彼|かれ}は{毎日|まいにち}{遅刻|ちこく}してくる。 — Because the boss never says anything, he takes advantage and comes in late every day.
{相手|あいて}の{無知|むち}をいいことに、{高|たか}い{商品|しょうひん}を{売|う}りつけた。 — They exploited the customer's ignorance to push an expensive product on them.

Notes:

- A clause before it takes の: {留守|るす}なのをいいことに, {言|い}わないのをいいことに.
- The behaviour is selfish or unfair; the speaker disapproves (or admits their own guilt).

## Review: 〜にもかかわらず (N2)

> 〜にもかかわらず (N2 lesson 2): "in spite of", neutral and factual: {雨|あめ}にもかかわらず、{大勢|おおぜい}の
> {人|ひと}が{集|あつ}まった. It states a contrast without judging anyone. をよそに adds that someone
> ignored other people; をものともせず adds admiration.

## Which one?

| Pattern | N is | The writer… | Typical second half |
|---|---|---|---|
| 〜にもかかわらず | any fact | states a contrast | an unexpected result |
| 〜をよそに | others' feelings, a situation | notes indifference (often critical) | the action goes ahead |
| 〜をものともせず | a hardship, a danger | admires | an achievement |
| 〜を{顧|かえり}みず | a danger, oneself, others | praises or blames, by N | a bold or selfish act |
| 〜にかこつけて | an occasion used as excuse | sees through it | what was really wanted |
| 〜をいいことに | a convenient situation | disapproves | selfish behaviour |

The same storm, four ways:

{嵐|あらし}にもかかわらず、{試合|しあい}は{行|おこな}われた。 — Despite the storm, the match went ahead. (fact)
{周囲|しゅうい}の{心配|しんぱい}をよそに、{彼|かれ}は{嵐|あらし}の{海|うみ}へ{船|ふね}を{出|だ}した。 — Ignoring everyone's worries, he took the boat out into the stormy sea. (critical)
{嵐|あらし}をものともせず、{救助隊|きゅうじょたい}は{漁船|ぎょせん}に{近|ちか}づいた。 — Undaunted by the storm, the rescue team approached the fishing boat. (admiring)
{嵐|あらし}にかこつけて、{彼|かれ}は{仕事|しごと}を{休|やす}んだ。 — He used the storm as an excuse to take the day off. (seeing through it)

## Conflict, war and security

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| armies | {兵士|へいし}, {兵隊|へいたい}, {軍隊|ぐんたい}, {部隊|ぶたい}, {隊員|たいいん}, {自衛隊|じえいたい}, {元帥|げんすい}, {兵役|へいえき}, {徴兵|ちょうへい}, {軍事|ぐんじ}, {軍備|ぐんび}, {軍縮|ぐんしゅく} |
| weapons | {兵器|へいき}, {核|かく}, {核兵器|かくへいき}, {原爆|げんばく}, {弾丸|だんがん}, {爆弾|ばくだん}, {大砲|たいほう}, ミサイル, {戦車|せんしゃ}, {地雷|じらい}, {射程|しゃてい} |

abolition. にかこつけて and をいいことに are the critical, self-mocking patterns of the lesson, and
をよそに marks a reaction that ignores others.

> {戦地|せんち}から{届|とど}いた{手紙|てがみ}は{二通|につう}だけだった。どちらにも{自分|じぶん}のことはほとんど{書|か}かれておらず、「{母|かあ}さんは{無理|むり}をしていないか」「{妹|いもうと}はちゃんと{食|た}べているか」と、{家族|かぞく}を{気遣|きづか}う{言葉|ことば}ばかりが{並|なら}んでいた。{検閲|けんえつ}をおそれてのことだったのかもしれない、と{祖母|そぼ}は{言|い}った。
>
> {兄|あに}の{死|し}を{知|し}らせる{紙|かみ}が{届|とど}いたのは、{終戦|しゅうせん}の{翌年|よくとし}だった。{遺骨|いこつ}は{戻|もど}らず、{渡|わた}された{白|しろ}い{箱|はこ}の{中|なか}には、{小|ちい}さな{石|いし}が{一|ひと}つ{入|はい}っていただけだった。{母親|ははおや}はその{日|ひ}から、{兄|あに}の{名前|なまえ}を{口|くち}にしなくなった。
>
> 「{勲章|くんしょう}をもらったって、{兄|あに}は{帰|かえ}ってこない」。{祖母|そぼ}は{写真|しゃしん}を{見上|みあ}げたまま、{静|しず}かに{言|い}った。「{英雄|えいゆう}になるより、{生|い}きて{年|とし}を{取|と}ってほしかった。あの{時|とき}{助|たす}けた{兄弟|きょうだい}の{弟|おとうと}さんがね、{今|いま}でも{毎年|まいとし}、お{盆|ぼん}になると{線香|せんこう}をあげに{来|き}てくれるんだよ。{兄|あに}のことを{覚|おぼ}えていてくれる{人|ひと}がいる。それだけで、{私|わたし}は{救|すく}われるんだ」
>
> {帰|かえ}り{道|みち}、{私|わたし}は{夕焼|ゆうや}けの{空|そら}を{見上|みあ}げた。{写真|しゃしん}の{中|なか}の{大伯父|おおおじ}は、{今|いま}の{私|わたし}とほとんど{変|か}わらない{年|とし}だった。{家|いえ}に{着|つ}いたら、{今日|きょう}{聞|き}いた{話|はなし}を{忘|わす}れないうちに{書|か}き{留|と}めておこうと{思|おも}った。

{仏壇|ぶつだん} = a household Buddhist altar; {軍服|ぐんぷく} = military uniform; {大伯父|おおおじ} = a
great-uncle (lesson 7's 伯); ぼうくうごう = an air-raid shelter (its last kanji is off the list);
{制止|せいし} = an attempt to stop someone; {燃|も}え{盛|さか}る = to blaze; {火|ひ}の{粉|こ} = sparks; やけど
= a burn (often printed 火傷, a reading outside the jōyō table); {戦地|せんち} = the front; {遺骨|いこつ} = remains (ashes and bones); お{盆|ぼん} =
the summer festival of the dead (lesson 29's 盆); {線香|せんこう}をあげる = to offer incense; {検閲|けんえつ} = censorship; {気遣|きづか}う =
to worry about, look out for; {書|か}き{留|と}める = to write down. や{否|いな}や is
lesson 1's "as soon as".

1. Why does the grandmother shake her head when the narrator calls her brother a fine man?
2. What did her brother do on the night of the air raid, and how did his mother react?
3. What did the grandmother know that the neighbours didn't?
4. Who still visits every year, and why does it matter to the grandmother?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Because to her he was not a hero but "just a nineteen-year-old child" (ただの{十九|じゅうく}の{子供|こども}):
   she wishes he had lived and grown old rather than become a hero.
2. As soon as he learned that children had been left behind in a neighbour's house, he went back
   into the burning street, ignoring his mother's attempt to stop him (をよそに), and, undaunted by
   the falling sparks (をものともせず), carried two small brothers back about an hour later.
3. That the night before he left for the front, her brother had cried alone in the kitchen: the
   town's hero was a frightened young man.
4. The younger of the two brothers he rescued comes every year at Obon to offer incense. He lived
   because her brother saved him, and he still remembers.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

In the Buddhist altar at my grandmother's house stands an old photograph. A young man in uniform
is smiling a little shyly. The edges of the photo have long since faded. He was my grandmother's elder brother, which makes him my great-uncle.
I had been told that he was killed in the war at nineteen.

"He must have been a fine man," I said, and my grandmother shook her head. "Fine? He wasn't. He
was just a nineteen-year-old child."

My grandmother rarely talks about the war. When I was a child and asked her to tell me about it
for a school assignment, she said "I don't want to remember" and went off into the kitchen. But
today she picked up the photograph herself and slowly began to talk.

What she told me about was a summer night near the end of the war. The air-raid sirens wailed,
and the townspeople hurried to the shelters. My grandmother, fourteen at the time, ran too, pulled
along by her mother's hand. When she looked back, she said, the night sky had turned red. Somewhere a child was crying.

As soon as her brother heard that children had been left behind in a neighbour's house, he turned
back into the blazing street, ignoring his mother's attempts to stop him. It was about an hour
later that he came back, undaunted by the sparks raining down, carrying two small brothers. His
hair was singed and both his hands were covered in burns.

The next month, he was sent to the front. On the morning he left, the neighbours waved flags to
see him off. The young man who had saved children with no thought for the danger was the town's
hero. But my grandmother knew that the night before, he had cried alone in the kitchen.

Only two letters came from the front. Neither said much about himself; they were full
of words of concern for the family: "Is Mother overdoing things?" "Is my sister eating
properly?" Perhaps it was out of fear of the censors, my grandmother said.

The notice of his death arrived the year after the war ended. His remains never came back; in the
white box they were given there was nothing but a single small stone. From that day on, their mother never spoke his name.

"Getting a medal doesn't bring him back," my grandmother said quietly, still looking up at the
photograph. "I'd rather he had lived and grown old than become a hero. You know, the younger of
the two brothers he saved still comes every year at Obon to light incense for him. There's
someone who remembers my brother. That alone is a comfort to me."

On the way home I looked up at the sunset sky. My great-uncle in the photograph had been almost
the same age as I am now. I decided that when I got home I would write down what I had heard
today before I forgot it.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{周囲|しゅうい}の{反対|はんたい}をよそに、{計画|けいかく}は{進|すす}められた。
= The plan went ahead in spite of the opposition around it.
けがをものともせず、{最後|さいご}まで{戦|たたか}った。
= Undaunted by the injury, they fought to the end.
{危険|きけん}を{顧|かえり}みず、{子供|こども}を{助|たす}けた。
= With no thought for the danger, they saved the child.
{出張|しゅっちょう}にかこつけて、{観光|かんこう}してきた。
= I used the business trip as an excuse to go sightseeing.
{上司|じょうし}がいないのをいいことに、{早|はや}く{帰|かえ}った。
= Taking advantage of the boss being away, I went home early.
```

## Common mistakes

- をものともせず for oneself: {私|わたし}は{熱|ねつ}をものともせず{出社|しゅっしゃ}した sounds like boasting.
  Use it to admire someone else, or say {熱|ねつ}があったが、{出社|しゅっしゃ}した.
- をよそに for a neutral contrast with a fact: {雨|あめ}をよそに、{試合|しあい}は{中止|ちゅうし}にならなかった isn't said.
  For a plain "despite", use にもかかわらず. をよそに needs someone ignoring something.
- をいいことに for a good use of an opportunity: {休|やす}みをいいことに、{勉強|べんきょう}をがんばった isn't used. It
  is always critical; for a neutral "taking the opportunity" use 〜を{機|き}に or 〜を{利用|りよう}して.
- Forgetting の: ×{親|おや}がいないをいいことに. A clause takes の: いないのをいいことに.
- Writing かこつける or かえりみず in the wrong kanji. This course writes にかこつけて in kana and
  を{顧|かえり}みず with 顧 (lesson 19's kanji).

## Key points

- 〜をよそに (N: others' feelings, a situation): ignoring; written; often critical.
- 〜をものともせず (N: a hardship): undaunted by; admiring, of others; an achievement follows.
- 〜を{顧|かえり}みず (N: danger, oneself, others): with no regard for; praise or blame depends on N.
- 〜にかこつけて (N: an occasion): using as a pretext; critical or self-mocking.
- 〜をいいことに (N, clause + の): taking advantage of; always critical.
- New kanji: 兵 隊 帥 艦 砲 弾 射 核 翼 墜 撃 攻 衛 侵 征 抗 陣 敵 迫 鎖 遮 塞 撤 駆 戒 壊 崩 覇 威 勲 雄
  徴. Write {壊|こわ}す, {壊|こわ}れる, {弾|ひ}く, {注射|ちゅうしゃ}, {目撃者|もくげきしゃ}, {土砂崩|どしゃくず}れ with kanji
  from now on; {雪崩|なだれ} is a special reading.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: In line with: にそくして, にのっとって, をふまえて, いかんによらず
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last lesson of module 3 is about the basis of a decision: the facts, rules and traditions it
follows, what it takes into account, and what it depends on (or doesn't). These are the patterns
of courts, official reports, company rules and formal speeches:

{事実|じじつ}に{即|そく}して{判断|はんだん}する。 — to judge in line with the facts
{伝統|でんとう}にのっとって{式|しき}を{行|おこな}う。 — to hold the ceremony in accordance with tradition
{調査|ちょうさ}{結果|けっか}を{踏|ふ}まえて{対策|たいさく}を{考|かんが}える。 — to plan measures taking the survey results into account
{事態|じたい}の{重大|じゅうだい}さに{鑑|かんが}みて、{会議|かいぎ}を{延期|えんき}する。 — to postpone the meeting in view of the seriousness of the situation
{理由|りゆう}のいかんにかかわらず、{遅刻|ちこく}は{認|みと}めない。 — Lateness won't be accepted, whatever the reason.

Several of them say what one should follow: grammar books call such patterns **normative
expressions**. N2's 〜に{基|もと}づいて and 〜に{応|おう}じて come back in a review box.

The theme is law, courts and procedure: lawsuits and appeals, trials and judges, rules and their
interpretation, exemptions and penalties. N3 and N2 gave you the basics ({裁判|さいばん}, {判決|はんけつ}, {弁護士|べんごし},
{被告人|ひこくにん}, {有罪|ゆうざい}); this lesson's kanji let you write {証拠|しょうこ}, {根拠|こんきょ}, {解釈|かいしゃく} and
{免許|めんきょ}, and add the words of the legal pages. Lesson 11 had crime and the police; this lesson
picks up at the courtroom door.

## In line with (facts or rules): 〜に{即|そく}して, 〜に{即|そく}した

{即|そく}する is "to conform to, fit". N に{即|そく}して is "in line with N, based closely on N": the
facts, the actual situation, reality, an experience.

{裁判官|さいばんかん}は{証拠|しょうこ}に{即|そく}して{事実|じじつ}を{認定|にんてい}する。 — Judges establish the facts in line with the evidence.
{地域|ちいき}の{実情|じつじょう}に{即|そく}した{支援|しえん}が{求|もと}められている。 — Support suited to the actual situation in each area is needed.
{自分|じぶん}の{体験|たいけん}に{即|そく}して{話|はな}してください。 — Please speak from your own experience.
{時代|じだい}に{即|そく}した{制度|せいど}に{改|あらた}める{必要|ひつよう}がある。 — The system needs to be reformed to suit the times.

Notes:

- Before a noun: に{即|そく}した (に{即|そく}した{対策|たいさく}); in written style also に{即|そく}し、.
- Typical nouns: {事実|じじつ}, {実態|じったい}, {実情|じつじょう}, {現実|げんじつ}, {現状|げんじょう}, {状況|じょうきょう}, {時代|じだい}, {体験|たいけん}.
- With rules and laws you'll also see 〜に{則|そく}して, with N2's 則: {法律|ほうりつ}に{則|そく}して. It's the same
  word in a less common spelling, used for norms. This course writes 〜に{即|そく}して for facts and
  〜にのっとって for rules.
- {即|そく} is lesson 27's kanji; this pattern is written with it here, as newspapers do.

## In accordance with (a norm): 〜にのっとって

〜にのっとって is "following (a set norm)": a law, a rule, a tradition, a procedure, a precedent.
It's formal, and it often describes an official or ceremonial act.

{試合|しあい}はルールにのっとって{公正|こうせい}に{行|おこな}われた。 — The match was played fairly according to the rules.
{結婚式|けっこんしき}は{古式|こしき}にのっとって{執|と}り{行|おこな}われた。 — The wedding was held according to ancient custom.
{会社|かいしゃ}は{法律|ほうりつ}にのっとって{手続|てつづ}きを{進|すす}めている。 — The company is proceeding in accordance with the law.
{規定|きてい}にのっとった{処分|しょぶん}であり、{問題|もんだい}はない。 — The penalty was in line with the regulations, so there's no problem.

Notes:

- Kana: のっとる's kanji 則 has no jōyō kun'yomi.
- に{即|そく}して follows what *is* (facts); にのっとって follows what *should be done* (a norm).
  Compare N2's に{基|もと}づいて, which follows a basis of either kind: {調査|ちょうさ}に{基|もと}づく{報告|ほうこく},
  {法律|ほうりつ}に{基|もと}づく{処分|しょぶん}.
- Before a noun: にのっとった.

## Taking into account: 〜を{踏|ふ}まえて

{踏|ふ}まえる is "to plant one's feet on". N を{踏|ふ}まえて is "on the basis of, taking N into
account": results, a discussion, experience, past mistakes, a situation. It's one of the most used
patterns in meetings, reports and policy writing.

{前回|ぜんかい}の{反省|はんせい}を{踏|ふ}まえて、{今回|こんかい}は{準備|じゅんび}に{時間|じかん}をかけた。 — Taking last time's lessons on board, we spent more time preparing this time.
{調査|ちょうさ}{結果|けっか}を{踏|ふ}まえ、{具体的|ぐたいてき}な{対策|たいさく}を{検討|けんとう}する。 — We will consider concrete measures in the light of the survey results.
{皆様|みなさま}のご{意見|いけん}を{踏|ふ}まえた{上|うえ}で、{最終|さいしゅう}{案|あん}をまとめます。 — We'll draw up the final plan after taking your opinions into account.

Notes:

- 〜を{踏|ふ}まえ、 (written), 〜を{踏|ふ}まえた + noun, 〜を{踏|ふ}まえた{上|うえ}で (after taking … into account).
- N is something already known or done; the second half builds on it.
- {踏|ふ}まえる is a group 2 verb and also a vocabulary item in this lesson.

## In view of: 〜に{鑑|かんが}みて, 〜に{鑑|かんが}み

{鑑|かんが}みる is "to consider in the light of (a precedent or a mirror)". N に{鑑|かんが}みて is "in view
of, considering": the voice of official notices, rulings and corporate statements.

{事態|じたい}の{重大|じゅうだい}さに{鑑|かんが}み、{会議|かいぎ}を{延期|えんき}いたします。 — In view of the gravity of the situation, the meeting will be postponed.
{昨今|さっこん}の{状況|じょうきょう}に{鑑|かんが}みて、{今年|ことし}の{祭|まつ}りは{中止|ちゅうし}とする。 — In the light of the recent situation, this year's festival is cancelled.
{過去|かこ}の{例|れい}に{鑑|かんが}みても、この{判断|はんだん}は{妥当|だとう}である。 — Even in the light of past cases, this decision is reasonable.

Notes:

- Very formal and written: announcements, documents, speeches.
- N is a situation that justifies a decision: {状況|じょうきょう}, {事態|じたい}, {重要性|じゅうようせい}, {経緯|けいい}.
- 鑑 is lesson 21's kanji (mirror; judge); {鑑|かんが}みる is its jōyō kun'yomi. 〜を{鑑|かんが}みて is
  heard too, but に is the standard form.

## Depending on, regardless of: 〜いかん

いかん (written 如何 in older texts: kana in this course) is "how something turns out, what it is".
After a noun (with or without の), it gives "depending on" and "regardless of".

| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| N(の)いかんで / いかんでは | depending on N | {結果|けっか}いかんで{進路|しんろ}を{決|き}める |
| N(の)いかんによって(は) | depending on N (it may even…) | {交渉|こうしょう}のいかんによっては{訴訟|そしょう}も |
| N(の)いかんにかかわらず | regardless of N | {理由|りゆう}のいかんにかかわらず |
| N(の)いかんによらず | regardless of N | {国籍|こくせき}のいかんによらず |
| N(の)いかんを{問|と}わず | regardless of N | {年齢|ねんれい}のいかんを{問|と}わず |

{試験|しけん}の{結果|けっか}いかんで、{来年|らいねん}の{進路|しんろ}が{決|き}まる。 — Next year's path depends on the results of the exam.
{交渉|こうしょう}のいかんによっては、{訴訟|そしょう}も{辞|じ}さない{構|かま}えだ。 — Depending on how the negotiations go, they're prepared to go to court.
{理由|りゆう}のいかんにかかわらず、{期限|きげん}を{過|す}ぎた{申請|しんせい}は{受|う}け{付|つ}けない。 — Applications after the deadline will not be accepted, whatever the reason.
{国籍|こくせき}のいかんを{問|と}わず、{誰|だれ}でも{応募|おうぼ}できる。 — Anyone may apply, regardless of nationality.

Notes:

- いかん is very written; in speech 〜{次第|しだい}で (N2) and 〜に{関係|かんけい}なく say the same.
- The nouns are things that can turn out differently: {結果|けっか}, {理由|りゆう}, {対応|たいおう}, {成績|せいせき},
  {事情|じじょう}, {国籍|こくせき}, {年齢|ねんれい}.
- 〜いかんでは / 〜いかんによっては usually lead to a serious possibility: "it may come to…".
- 〜いかんによらず, 〜いかんにかかわらず and 〜いかんを{問|と}わず are close in meaning; を{問|と}わず is
  N2's word, without いかん: {年齢|ねんれい}を{問|と}わず.

## Review: 〜に{基|もと}づいて, 〜に{応|おう}じて (N2)

> 〜に{基|もと}づいて (N2 lesson 13): based on (data, a rule, an experience): {調査|ちょうさ}に{基|もと}づいて
> {判断|はんだん}する. It's the general "basis" word; に{即|そく}して stresses fitting the facts closely, and
> にのっとって following a norm.
>
> 〜に{応|おう}じて (N2 lesson 13): according to, in response to (something that varies):
> {収入|しゅうにゅう}に{応|おう}じて{税金|ぜいきん}が{変|か}わる. 〜いかんで is its very written relative.

## Choosing the pattern

| Pattern | N is | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| に{基|もと}づいて | data, a rule, a plan | the general "based on" |
| に{即|そく}して | facts, the actual situation | fitting the facts closely |
| にのっとって | a law, a rule, a tradition | following a norm, ceremonies |
| を{踏|ふ}まえて | results, discussion, lessons | building on what is known |
| に{鑑|かんが}みて | a situation, its gravity | justifying an official decision |
| N いかんで / によっては | something that can vary | depending on (seriously) |
| N いかんにかかわらず / によらず / を{問|と}わず | something that can vary | regardless of |

{過去|かこ}の{判例|はんれい}を{踏|ふ}まえ、{事実|じじつ}に{即|そく}して{判断|はんだん}した。 — The court decided on the facts, taking past precedents into account.
{判決|はんけつ}は{法|ほう}にのっとって{言|い}い{渡|わた}された。 — The sentence was handed down in accordance with the law.
{事件|じけん}の{重大|じゅうだい}さに{鑑|かんが}み、{審理|しんり}は{慎重|しんちょう}に{進|すす}められた。 — In view of the gravity of the case, the hearing proceeded with care.
{控訴|こうそ}するかどうかは、{判決|はんけつ}の{内容|ないよう}いかんで{決|き}める。 — Whether to appeal will be decided depending on what the judgment says.

## Law, courts and procedure

| Topic | Words |

Notes:

- Japan has three levels of court for most cases ({三審制|さんしんせい}): a district court ({地方|ちほう}
  {裁判所|さいばんしょ}, {地裁|ちさい}), a high court ({高等|こうとう}{裁判所|さいばんしょ}, {高裁|こうさい}) and the Supreme Court

  appeal to the Supreme Court a {上告|じょうこく}.
- {却下|きゃっか} is rejecting a suit or petition without examining its substance (it doesn't meet the
  conditions); {棄却|ききゃく} is rejecting it after examining it. Both are "dismissal" in English.
- {起訴|きそ} is the prosecutors charging a suspect (lesson 11's {送検|そうけん} comes first); {告訴|こくそ} is a
  victim's formal complaint; {提訴|ていそ} is filing a civil suit. {起訴|きそ} sounds like lesson 28's
  {基礎|きそ} (foundation).
- {執行猶予|しっこうゆうよ} is a suspended sentence: {拘禁刑|こうきんけい}{二年|にねん}、{執行猶予|しっこうゆうよ}{三年|さんねん} ({拘禁刑|こうきんけい},
  imprisonment, replaced {懲役|ちょうえき} and きんこ in June 2025).
- {陪審|ばいしん} (a jury) is the system of countries such as the US and Britain; Japan's lay-judge
  system ({裁判員|さいばんいん}{制度|せいど}) was N2's honors topic.
- {傍聴|ぼうちょう} is attending a trial as a member of the public; it sounds like lesson 20's
  {膨張|ぼうちょう} (expansion). {法曹|ほうそう} (the legal profession: judges, prosecutors and lawyers) sounds
  like N3's {放送|ほうそう}; {時効|じこう} like N2's {時候|じこう}; {求刑|きゅうけい} like N3's きゅうけい (a break);
  {刑法|けいほう} like N3's {警報|けいほう}.
- {免|まぬが}れる (to escape, be spared) is also read まぬかれる, the reading the jōyō table gives; both
  are heard, and まぬがれる is the commoner today.
- {差|さ}し{止|と}め is an injunction; {仮処分|かりしょぶん} a provisional disposition (an urgent court order).

## Dialogue: a legal consultation

Yano, who has moved out of a rented flat, consults Sakai, a lawyer. (Formal speech and keigo;
surnames.)

```dialogue
# A legal consultation
やの: {本日|ほんじつ}はお{時間|じかん}をいただき、ありがとうございます。
= Thank you for making time for me today.
さかい: いえ。{早速|さっそく}ですが、ご{相談|そうだん}の{内容|ないよう}をお{聞|き}かせください。
= Not at all. Shall we get straight to it? Please tell me what you'd like to consult me about.
やの: {実|じつ}は、{去年|きょねん}まで{住|す}んでいた{部屋|へや}の{敷金|しききん}が、ほとんど{返|かえ}ってこないんです。{大家|おおや}さんからは、{壁紙|かべがみ}の{張|は}り{替|か}え{代|だい}として{差|さ}し{引|ひ}くと{言|い}われまして。
= The thing is, I've had almost none of the deposit back on the flat I lived in until last year. The landlord says it's being deducted to pay for new wallpaper.
さかい: {契約書|けいやくしょ}と、{退去|たいきょ}のときの{写真|しゃしん}はお{持|も}ちですか。
= Do you have the contract and photos from when you moved out?
やの: はい、こちらです。
= Yes, here they are.

= Let me see… I see. Dirt and wear from ordinary living are generally held not to be the tenant's to pay for. From these photos, this looks as if it falls within that.
やの: では、{取|と}り{戻|もど}せる{可能性|かのうせい}はありますか。
= So is there a chance I can get it back?
さかい: ええ。ただ、{契約書|けいやくしょ}に{特別|とくべつ}な{取|と}り{決|き}めがある{場合|ばあい}は、その{内容|ないよう}いかんによっては{結論|けつろん}が{変|か}わります。この{条項|じょうこう}を{詳|くわ}しく{確認|かくにん}させてください。
= Yes. But if the contract has special terms, the conclusion may change depending on what they say. Let me look at this clause carefully.
やの: お{願|ねが}いします。できれば{裁判|さいばん}にはしたくないのですが…。
= Please do. If possible, I'd rather not go to court…
さかい: もちろんです。まずはこれまでの{経緯|けいい}を{踏|ふ}まえて、{書面|しょめん}で{返還|へんかん}を{求|もと}めましょう。それでも{応|おう}じていただけない{場合|ばあい}は、{少額訴訟|しょうがくそしょう}という{手続|てつづ}きもあります。
= Of course. First, taking into account how things have gone so far, let's ask in writing for the money back. If they still won't agree, there's a procedure called the small-claims suit.
やの: {少額訴訟|しょうがくそしょう}、ですか。
= A small-claims suit?
さかい: {六十万円|ろくじゅうまんえん}{以下|いか}のお{金|かね}の{支払|しはら}いを{求|もと}めるときに{使|つか}える{手続|てつづ}きで、{原則|げんそく}として{一回|いっかい}の{期日|きじつ}で{審理|しんり}を{終|お}えます。
= It's a procedure for claiming payment of six hundred thousand yen or less, and as a rule the hearing is finished in a single session.
やの: それなら{気|き}が{楽|らく}です。
= That's a relief.
さかい: いずれにしても、{事実|じじつ}に{即|そく}して、{冷静|れいせい}に{話|はなし}を{進|すす}めましょう。{費用|ひよう}についても、{結果|けっか}のいかんにかかわらず、{最初|さいしょ}に{見通|みとお}しをご{説明|せつめい}しますので、ご{安心|あんしん}ください。
= In any case, let's proceed calmly and stick to the facts. As for the costs, I'll explain what to expect at the outset, whatever the outcome, so please don't worry.
```

{敷金|しききん} = a rental deposit (lesson 29's 敷); {張|は}り{替|か}え = replacing (wallpaper);
{差|さ}し{引|ひ}く = to deduct; {退去|たいきょ} = moving out; {取|と}り{決|き}め = an arrangement, term;
{経緯|けいい} (how things came about) is lesson 28's word; {返還|へんかん} (return) is lesson 27's word; {少額訴訟|しょうがくそしょう} =
a small-claims suit; {期日|きじつ} = a set date, a hearing session; {見通|みとお}し = an outlook. The rule
that ordinary wear isn't the tenant's to repair is in the Civil Code (Article 621, since the 2020
revision) and in the government's guidelines on restoring rented homes; Sakai still hedges it
(とされています), as a careful lawyer would, because a contract's special terms can matter.
