## Dialogue: after the children's cafeteria

Rina and Kenta volunteer at a children's cafeteria ({子|こ}ども{食堂|しょくどう}) run by their
neighbourhood. They're tidying up after dinner. (Casual speech.)

```dialogue
# Tidying up
りな: {今日|きょう}、{何人|なんにん}{来|き}たと{思|おも}う？{六十人|ろくじゅうにん}だって。
= Guess how many came today? Sixty.
けんた: {六十人|ろくじゅうにん}！{始|はじ}めた{頃|ころ}は{十人|じゅうにん}も{来|こ}なかったのに。こんなに{増|ふ}えるとはね。
= Sixty! When we started, not even ten came. Who'd have thought it would grow like this.
りな: それだけ{困|こま}ってる{家庭|かてい}が{多|おお}いってことだよね。{喜|よろこ}んでいいのかどうか。
= It just means that many families are struggling. I don't know if we should be happy about it.
けんた: そういえば、この{前|まえ}の{市|し}の{会議|かいぎ}、どうだった？
= Speaking of which, how did that city meeting go the other day?
りな: ひどかったよ。{議員|ぎいん}の{一人|ひとり}が「{貧困|ひんこん}は{自己責任|じこせきにん}だ」って。{子|こ}どもに{責任|せきにん}なんかあるわけないのに。
= Awful. One of the councillors said "poverty is personal responsibility". As if children could be responsible.
けんた: {無責任|むせきにん}{極|きわ}まりないね。{子|こ}どもの{前|まえ}で{言|い}えるのかな、それ。
= That's utterly irresponsible. I wonder if they could say that in front of the kids.
りな: {腹|はら}が{立|た}つといったらなかったよ。でも、{会議|かいぎ}のあと、{別|べつ}の{議員|ぎいん}が{見学|けんがく}に{来|き}たいって{声|こえ}をかけてくれたの。
= I can't tell you how angry I was. But after the meeting, another councillor came up and said they'd like to visit.
けんた: へえ、{一人|ひとり}でもわかってくれる{人|ひと}がいるのは{心強|こころづよ}いね。
= Huh, it's reassuring that at least one person gets it.
りな: うん。{来月|らいげつ}{来|く}るって。{市長|しちょう}に{報告|ほうこく}してくれるかもしれない。
= Yeah. Coming next month. Might even report to the mayor.
けんた: {市長|しちょう}が{来|き}たらどうする？「{光栄|こうえい}の{至|いた}りでございます」とか{言|い}う？
= What if the mayor comes? Will you say "It is the greatest honour"?
りな: {言|い}わないよ、そんな{大|おお}げさなこと。…でも{言|い}っちゃうかも。
= I won't say anything that over the top. …Though I might.
けんた: ところで、{冷蔵庫|れいぞうこ}、そろそろ{限界|げんかい}じゃない？{今日|きょう}も{扉|とびら}がちゃんと{閉|し}まらなかったよ。
= By the way, isn't the fridge about done for? The door wouldn't shut properly today either.
りな: {寄付|きふ}でもらったものだしね。{古|ふる}いのは{仕方|しかた}ないけど、{食中毒|しょくちゅうどく}が{出|で}たら{痛恨|つうこん}の{極|きわ}みだから、{募金|ぼきん}を{呼|よ}びかけようか。
= It was donated, after all. Being old can't be helped, but if there were food poisoning it would be the worst thing imaginable, so shall we ask for donations?
けんた: そうしよう。{来週|らいしゅう}{張|は}り{紙|がみ}を{作|つく}るよ。
= Let's. I'll make a poster next week.
```

{議員|ぎいん} = a councillor (member of an assembly); {心強|こころづよ}い = reassuring; {大|おお}げさ =
exaggerated; {張|は}り{紙|がみ} = a notice, poster. Kenta's 「{光栄|こうえい}の{至|いた}りでございます」 is a
joke: the formula belongs to ceremonies, which is why Rina calls it {大|おお}げさ. The speakers mix
registers on purpose: casual といったらなかった for Rina's anger, the written {無責任|むせきにん}{極|きわ}まりない
and {痛恨|つうこん}の{極|きわ}み for emphasis, as people do when they want to sound like a headline.

## Reading: an editorial on isolation

An editorial from a national newspaper ({社説|しゃせつ} style, である).

> {一人暮|ひとりぐ}らしの{高齢者|こうれいしゃ}が{自宅|じたく}で{亡|な}くなり、{何週間|なんしゅうかん}も{誰|だれ}にも{気|き}づかれない。そうした{孤独死|こどくし}の{報道|ほうどう}が、もはや{珍|めずら}しくなくなった。{隣|となり}の{部屋|へや}に{人|ひと}が{住|す}んでいながら、{異変|いへん}に{気|き}づく{者|もの}がいないとは、{何|なん}とも{痛|いた}ましい。{長寿|ちょうじゅ}を{誇|ほこ}ってきた{社会|しゃかい}の、もう{一|ひと}つの{顔|かお}である。
>
> {孤立|こりつ}は{高齢者|こうれいしゃ}だけの{問題|もんだい}ではない。{長期|ちょうき}の{引|ひ}きこもり、{家族|かぞく}の{介護|かいご}を{一人|ひとり}で{背負|せお}う{若者|わかもの}、{夜|よる}を{一人|ひとり}で{過|す}ごす{子|こ}どもたち。{形|かたち}は{違|ちが}っても、{困|こま}ったときに{頼|たよ}れる{相手|あいて}がいないという{点|てん}は{共通|きょうつう}している。{近所|きんじょ}{付|づ}き{合|あ}いが{薄|うす}れ、{家族|かぞく}の{形|かたち}が{変|か}わる{中|なか}で、{私|わたし}たちの{社会|しゃかい}のセーフティーネットには{確実|かくじつ}に{綻|ほころ}びが{生|しょう}じている。
>
> こうした{問題|もんだい}を「{自己責任|じこせきにん}」の{一言|ひとこと}で{片|かた}づける{声|こえ}も{根強|ねづよ}い。しかし、{病気|びょうき}や{失業|しつぎょう}、{家族|かぞく}との{死別|しべつ}は{誰|だれ}の{身|み}にも{起|お}こり{得|う}る。{困窮|こんきゅう}して{助|たす}けを{求|もと}めた{人|ひと}を、{努力|どりょく}が{足|た}りないと{突|つ}き{放|はな}すのは、{無責任|むせきにん}{極|きわ}まりない。{支援|しえん}を{受|う}けることを{恥|は}じる{空気|くうき}こそが、{人|ひと}を{孤立|こりつ}に{追|お}い{込|こ}んでいるのではないか。
>
> ある{自治体|じちたい}が{行|おこな}った{調査|ちょうさ}では、{生活|せいかつ}に{困|こま}っていながら{公的|こうてき}な{支援|しえん}を{受|う}けていない{人|ひと}の{半数|はんすう}{近|ちか}くが、その{理由|りゆう}として「{人|ひと}に{知|し}られたくない」「{迷惑|めいわく}をかけたくない」を{挙|あ}げたという。{制度|せいど}があっても、{使|つか}われなければ{意味|いみ}がない。{窓口|まどぐち}で{冷|つめ}たい{対応|たいおう}をされ、{二度|にど}と{相談|そうだん}に{行|い}かなくなったという{話|はなし}も{聞|き}く。{助|たす}けを{求|もと}めることをためらわせる{原因|げんいん}が{制度|せいど}の{側|がわ}にもあるとすれば、それは{行政|ぎょうせい}の{盲点|もうてん}と{言|い}わざるを{得|え}ない。{申請|しんせい}の{手続|てつづ}きを{簡単|かんたん}にし、{支援|しえん}を{待|ま}つのではなく{届|とど}けに{行|い}く{仕組|しく}みが{必要|ひつよう}だ。
>
> {希望|きぼう}もある。{全国|ぜんこく}に{広|ひろ}がった{子|こ}ども{食堂|しょくどう}の{多|おお}くは、{地域|ちいき}の{住民|じゅうみん}が{手弁当|てべんとう}で{始|はじ}めたものだ。{食事|しょくじ}を{出|だ}すだけでなく、{子|こ}どもや{高齢者|こうれいしゃ}が{顔|かお}を{合|あ}わせる{居場所|いばしょ}になっている。ある{子|こ}ども{食堂|しょくどう}では、{食事|しょくじ}のあとに{大学生|だいがくせい}のボランティアが{宿題|しゅくだい}を{見|み}ており、{家|いえ}に{帰|かえ}っても{一人|ひとり}だという{子|こ}どもたちが{遅|おそ}くまで{残|のこ}っていく。{料理|りょうり}を{手伝|てつだ}うのは、{近所|きんじょ}に{住|す}む{一人暮|ひとりぐ}らしの{高齢者|こうれいしゃ}たちだ。{支|ささ}える{側|がわ}と{支|ささ}えられる{側|がわ}が、ここでは{自然|しぜん}に{入|い}れ{替|か}わっている。{見守|みまも}り{活動|かつどう}に{奔走|ほんそう}する{民生委員|みんせいいいん}や、{新聞|しんぶん}がたまっていないか{気|き}を{配|くば}る{配達員|はいたついん}もいる。こうした{善意|ぜんい}の{担|にな}い{手|て}たちの{尽力|じんりょく}には、{頭|あたま}が{下|さ}がる。
>
> とはいえ、{善意|ぜんい}だけに{頼|たよ}るのには{限界|げんかい}がある。{担|にな}い{手|て}の{多|おお}くは{高齢|こうれい}で、{運営費|うんえいひ}は{寄付|きふ}と{持|も}ち{出|だ}しで{賄|まかな}われているのが{実情|じつじょう}だ。{行政|ぎょうせい}は{民間|みんかん}の{活動|かつどう}を{傍観|ぼうかん}するのではなく、{資金|しきん}や{情報|じょうほう}の{面|めん}で{支|ささ}えるべきである。{孤立|こりつ}を{防|ふせ}ぐのは、{特別|とくべつ}な{制度|せいど}よりも、{日々|ひび}の{小|ちい}さなつながりの{積|つ}み{重|かさ}ねだ。{誰|だれ}も{取|と}り{残|のこ}さない{社会|しゃかい}を{目指|めざ}すなら、そのつながりを{絶|た}やさない{仕組|しく}みを{今|いま}こそ{築|きず}かなければならない。

{異変|いへん} = something wrong, an unusual change; {痛|いた}ましい = heartbreaking; {背負|せお}う = to carry on
one's back; {薄|うす}れる = to fade; {死別|しべつ} = bereavement; {突|つ}き{放|はな}す = to rebuff;
{手弁当|てべんとう}で = at one's own expense, unpaid; {居場所|いばしょ} = a place where one belongs;
{見守|みまも}り = keeping an eye on (vulnerable people); {民生委員|みんせいいいん} = a local welfare
volunteer; {頭|あたま}が{下|さ}がる = to feel deep respect; {持|も}ち{出|だ}し = paying out of one's own pocket;
{賄|まかな}う = to cover (costs; 賄 is lesson 11's kanji); {絶|た}やす = to let die out.

1. What does the editorial call "another face" of a society that has prided itself on longevity?
2. Which groups besides the elderly does it say are isolated, and what do they have in common?
3. How does the writer respond to the "personal responsibility" argument?
4. What does the writer ask of the authorities, and why?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Elderly people dying alone at home and going unnoticed for weeks ({孤独死|こどくし}), even with
   neighbours next door.
2. People in long-term social withdrawal, young people caring for family members alone, and
   children spending their evenings alone. They have no one to turn to when they are in trouble.
3. Illness, job loss and bereavement can happen to anyone; rebuffing people who ask for help is
   utterly irresponsible ({無責任|むせきにん}{極|きわ}まりない), and an atmosphere that makes people
   ashamed of receiving support is itself what drives them into isolation.
4. Not to look on but to support the volunteers' work with money and information, because
   goodwill alone has limits: many of the volunteers are elderly and costs are covered by
   donations and their own money.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

An elderly person living alone dies at home and goes unnoticed by anyone for weeks. Reports of
such lonely deaths are no longer unusual. That people live in the next flat and yet no one notices
anything wrong is heartbreaking indeed. It is the other face of a society that has prided itself
on longevity.

Isolation is not a problem of the elderly alone. People withdrawn from society for years, young
people carrying the care of a family member on their own, children spending the evening alone:
the forms differ, but they share having no one to turn to in trouble. As ties between neighbours
fade and the shape of families changes, our society's safety net is certainly coming apart at the
seams.

Many voices still dismiss these problems with the words "personal responsibility". But illness,
unemployment and bereavement can happen to anyone. To rebuff people who have fallen into hardship
and asked for help, saying they haven't tried hard enough, is utterly irresponsible. Isn't it the
very atmosphere that makes people ashamed of receiving support that is driving them into
isolation?

In a survey by one local authority, nearly half of those who were struggling to get by but were
receiving no public support gave as their reason "I don't want people to know" or "I don't want to
be a burden". A system that exists but isn't used is meaningless. One also hears of people who
were treated coldly at the counter and never went back for advice. If the causes that make people
hesitate to ask for help lie partly with the system itself, that can only be called a blind spot
of the authorities. Applications must be made simpler, and support must go out to people rather
than wait for them to come.

There is hope too. Many of the children's cafeterias that have spread across the country were
started by local residents at their own expense. Besides serving meals, they have become places
where children and old people meet. At one, university volunteers help with homework after the
meal, and children who would be alone at home stay on until late. The cooking is done with the
help of elderly people who live alone nearby. Here, those who give support and those who receive
it change places naturally. There are welfare volunteers who run around keeping an eye on
people, and delivery staff who watch for newspapers piling up. The efforts of these bearers of
goodwill command deep respect.

Goodwill alone, however, has its limits. Many of those who carry this work are themselves elderly,
and the reality is that running costs are covered by donations and money out of their own
pockets. Rather than looking on at private efforts, the authorities should support them with
funding and information. What prevents isolation is not a special system so much as the
accumulation of small, everyday connections. If we aim for a society that leaves no one behind,
now is the time to build arrangements that keep those connections alive.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{失礼|しつれい}{極|きわ}まりない{態度|たいど}だ。
= That's outrageously rude behaviour.
{光栄|こうえい}の{至|いた}りです。
= It is the greatest honour.
{痛恨|つうこん}の{極|きわ}みです。
= It is a matter of the deepest regret.
こんなところで{会|あ}うとは。
= Fancy meeting you here!
{恥|は}ずかしいといったらなかった。
= I can't tell you how embarrassed I was.
```

## Common mistakes

- 〜{極|きわ}まりない after an い-adjective: ×{危|あぶ}ない{極|きわ}まりない. Use a な-adjective:
  {危険|きけん}{極|きわ}まりない.
- Using {極|きわ}まりない as praise: "extremely kind" is {大変|たいへん}{親切|しんせつ}だ or {親切|しんせつ}この
  うえない; {親切|しんせつ}{極|きわ}まりない isn't a compliment.
- Reading {極|きわ}まりない as "not extreme". It means "extremely", like {極|きわ}まる.
- 〜の{至|いた}り with any noun: {疲労|ひろう}の{至|いた}り isn't used. の{至|いた}り is a short fixed list ({光栄|こうえい},
  {感激|かんげき}, {恐縮|きょうしゅく}, {赤面|せきめん}, {若気|わかげ}); for states use の{極|きわ}み ({疲労|ひろう}の{極|きわ}み).
- 〜とは in casual talk with friends: it sounds bookish. Say 〜なんて.
- 〜といったらない in a formal report: it's emotional speech. In writing use {極|きわ}まりない or
  {非常|ひじょう}に.
- {食糧|しょくりょう} and {食料|しょくりょう} in writing: food aid is {食糧|しょくりょう}{援助|えんじょ}, but the groceries
  you buy are {食料品|しょくりょうひん}.

## Key points

- な-adjective + {極|きわ}まりない / {極|きわ}まる: extremely (rude, dangerous, irresponsible); written,
  critical. {感極|かんきわ}まって: overcome with emotion.
- N + の{至|いた}り: the utmost, fixed ({光栄|こうえい}の{至|いた}り, {恐縮|きょうしゅく}の{至|いた}り); {若気|わかげ}の{至|いた}り
  (youthful folly) in everyday speech.
- N + の{極|きわ}み: the height of ({痛恨|つうこん}の{極|きわ}み, ぜいたくの{極|きわ}み, {疲労|ひろう}の{極|きわ}み).
- Plain form + とは: to think that…! (surprise, indignation); casual 〜なんて.
- 〜といったらない (N2): indescribably, spoken; 〜{限|かぎ}りだ (N2): one's own feeling.
- New kanji: 飢 餓 窮 衰 朽 劣 寿 糧 虐 疎 孤 偏 排 抑 隷 奴 盲 溝 裂 陥 綻 挫 禍 葛 藤 尽 遇 壮 傍 奉 堪 奔.
  Write {寿命|じゅみょう}, {過疎|かそ}, {孤独|こどく}, {孤立|こりつ}, {偏見|へんけん} with kanji from now on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Forced to: をよぎなくされる, ないではすまない, ずにはすまない
topics: ないではすまない and ずにはすまない
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The judgements so far have been about feelings (16), worth (17) and extremes (18). This lesson is
about pressure from outside: things you are forced to do by circumstances, and things society
won't let you get away without doing.

{台風|たいふう}の{影響|えいきょう}で、{花火大会|はなびたいかい}は{中止|ちゅうし}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされた。 — Because of the typhoon, the fireworks display had to be cancelled.

{取引先|とりひきさき}に{迷惑|めいわく}をかけた{以上|いじょう}、{直接|ちょくせつ}{謝|あやま}りに{行|い}かないではすまない。 — Now that we've caused our client trouble, we can't get away without going to apologize in person.

The theme is work and organizations: management and staff, transfers and posts, deadlines and
progress, mergers and cuts, shops and customers, and business letters. N2 lessons 1 and 17 gave
you employment and management; this lesson adds the words of personnel notices, board meetings,
shop floors and letters, and its kanji let you write carried words like {上司|じょうし}, {同僚|どうりょう},
{締|し}め{切|き}り and {弊社|へいしゃ} at last.

## Forced by circumstances: 〜を{余儀|よぎ}なくされる

{余儀|よぎ}ない is "unavoidable, leaving no other way" ({余儀|よぎ}ない{事情|じじょう}, unavoidable
circumstances). 〜を{余儀|よぎ}なくされる (literally "be made to have no other way than") follows a
noun, usually a する noun, and says that circumstances forced it:

| Noun | 〜を{余儀|よぎ}なくされる |
|---|---|
| {中止|ちゅうし} (cancellation) | {中止|ちゅうし}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされた |
| {延期|えんき} (postponement) | {延期|えんき}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされる |
| {撤退|てったい} (withdrawal) | {撤退|てったい}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされた |
| {閉店|へいてん}, {休業|きゅうぎょう} | {休業|きゅうぎょう}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされている |
| {避難生活|ひなんせいかつ} | {避難生活|ひなんせいかつ}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされている |

{原材料|げんざいりょう}の{高騰|こうとう}により、{多|おお}くの{店|みせ}が{値上|ねあ}げを{余儀|よぎ}なくされた。 — Because of soaring raw-material costs, many shops were forced to raise their prices.

{地震|じしん}から{一年|いちねん}が{過|す}ぎた{今|いま}も、{多|おお}くの{住民|じゅうみん}が{仮設住宅|かせつじゅうたく}での{生活|せいかつ}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされている。 — A year after the earthquake, many residents are still forced to live in temporary housing.

Points to remember:

- News and written style. In conversation: {中止|ちゅうし}になった, 〜しなければならなくなった,
  〜せざるを{得|え}なかった.
- The cause is outside the subject's control: weather, disasters, prices, an illness, a
  decision by someone else. It's typically marked with で, により or のため. The subject is the
  person or organization that suffered it, so it's never a choice: {自分|じぶん}の{意思|いし}で{退職|たいしょく}を
  {余儀|よぎ}なくされた is a contradiction.
- The noun is usually an action: {雨|あめ}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされた isn't said. For a state, add a noun
  ({生活|せいかつ}, {入院|にゅういん}).
- There's an adverb too: {余儀|よぎ}なく{撤退|てったい}した (withdrew because there was no other way).
  The pattern is written in kanji in this course: 余 and 儀 are both listed.

### Forcing it: 〜を{余儀|よぎ}なくさせる

The causative turns the cause into the subject: [cause] が [person or group] に [noun] を
{余儀|よぎ}なくさせる. It's rarer and still more written.

{記録的|きろくてき}な{大雪|おおゆき}が、{多|おお}くの{工場|こうじょう}に{操業停止|そうぎょうていし}を{余儀|よぎ}なくさせた。 — The record snowfall forced many factories to halt operations.

## You won't get away without: 〜ないではすまない, 〜ずにはすまない

These say that the situation, or other people, won't let the matter end without the action: "it
won't do not to, there's no way around it". The pressure is social or moral: an apology,
compensation, an explanation, a punishment.

| Form | Example |
|---|---|
| ない form + ではすまない | {謝|あやま}らないではすまない |
| ない stem + ずにはすまない | {謝|あやま}らずにはすまない |
| する → せずにはすまない | {弁償|べんしょう}せずにはすまない, {説明|せつめい}せずにはすまない |

{借|か}りた{本|ほん}を{汚|よご}してしまったのだから、{弁償|べんしょう}せずにはすまないだろう。 — I've stained the book I borrowed, so I'll have to pay for it.

ここまで{問題|もんだい}が{大|おお}きくなった{以上|いじょう}、{社長|しゃちょう}が{説明|せつめい}しないではすまない。 — Now that the problem has grown this big, the president can't avoid giving an explanation.

Notes:

- すまない is {済|す}まない (won't be settled): the matter won't be closed. The course writes the
  pattern in kana, like N2's ずにはいられない.
- 〜ずにはすまない is a little more written; 〜ないではすまない is common in speech too. Polite:
  〜ないではすみません.
- Noun + ではすまない is related: "won't end with just": {謝罪|しゃざい}だけではすまない (an apology alone
  won't settle it), {笑|わら}い{話|ばなし}ではすまない (it's no laughing matter). The passive
  〜ではすまされない is "can't be excused as": {知|し}らなかったではすまされない (ignorance is no
  excuse).
- Compare 〜ないわけにはいかない (N3), which is the speaker's own sense of duty ({行|い}かないわけには
  いかない, I can't not go), and lesson 16's 〜ずにはおかない (something will inevitably cause a
  reaction; a person will see it done).

## Review: 〜ざるを{得|え}ない, 〜までもない

> N2 lesson 17: ない stem + ざるを{得|え}ない (する → せざるを{得|え}ない), "have no choice but to", against
> one's wishes, usually with a reason: {人手|ひとで}が{足|た}りないので、{残業|ざんぎょう}せざるを{得|え}ない. It's the
> speaker's reluctant decision; 〜を{余儀|よぎ}なくされる is the same situation reported from outside.
>
> N2 lesson 19: dictionary form + までもない, "there's no need to (it's obvious)":
> {言|い}うまでもなく、{健康|けんこう}が{一番|いちばん}{大切|たいせつ}だ.

## How strong is the pressure?

Obligation and necessity from N3 to N1, roughly by where the pressure comes from. Speakers don't
draw the lines in exactly the same place.

| Pattern | Where the pressure comes from | Register |
|---|---|---|
| 〜なければならない (N4) | neutral necessity | both |
| 〜べきだ (N3) | the speaker's judgement of what is right | both |
| 〜ないわけにはいかない (N3) | one's own sense of duty or social sense | both |
| 〜ほかない / 〜しかない (N2) | no other option left | both |
| 〜ざるを{得|え}ない (N2) | circumstances, against one's wishes | formal; also common in speech |
| 〜ないではすまない / 〜ずにはすまない | others or society won't let it pass | both / written |
| 〜を{余儀|よぎ}なくされる | outside forces (weather, prices, decisions) | news, written |
| 〜てしかるべきだ (lesson 20) | what would be fitting and proper | formal |

## Dialogue: a delay before the opening

A department meeting at a retail company. Nakamura is the department head; Ono and Takeda are on
the team opening a new shop. (Business Japanese; surnames, as in a workplace.)

```dialogue
# The new shop
なかむら: では、{来月|らいげつ}{開店|かいてん}の{新店舗|しんてんぽ}について、{進捗|しんちょく}を{報告|ほうこく}してください。
= Right, please report on progress with the new shop opening next month.
おの: はい。{内装|ないそう}{工事|こうじ}はほぼ{予定|よてい}どおりですが、{一点|いってん}{問題|もんだい}がございます。{先週|せんしゅう}の{台風|たいふう}で{港|みなと}が{閉鎖|へいさ}され、{海外|かいがい}から{届|とど}く{予定|よてい}だった{陳列棚|ちんれつだな}の{到着|とうちゃく}が{遅|おく}れております。
= Yes. The interior work is almost on schedule, but there's one problem. Last week's typhoon closed the port, and the display shelves due from abroad are delayed.
なかむら: どのくらい{遅|おく}れそう？
= How late are they likely to be?
おの: {業者|ぎょうしゃ}によりますと、{搬入|はんにゅう}は{早|はや}くても{開店|かいてん}の{前日|ぜんじつ}になるとのことです。
= According to the supplier, they'll be brought in the day before the opening at the earliest.
たけだ: それでは{陳列|ちんれつ}が{間|ま}に{合|あ}いませんね。{開店|かいてん}の{延期|えんき}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされるかもしれません。
= Then we won't have time to set out the goods. We may be forced to postpone the opening.
なかむら: {延期|えんき}は{避|さ}けたい。{開店|かいてん}セールの{広告|こうこく}も、もう{出|だ}してしまったからね。
= I want to avoid a postponement. We've already put out the adverts for the opening sale.
たけだ: でしたら、{当面|とうめん}は{本店|ほんてん}の{棚|たな}を{一部|いちぶ}{運|はこ}んで、{代用|だいよう}してはいかがでしょうか。
= In that case, how about moving some of the head shop's shelves over for now as a stopgap?
おの: {本店|ほんてん}は{来月|らいげつ}が{繁忙期|はんぼうき}ですから、{棚|たな}を{減|へ}らすのは{難|むずか}しいかと…。
= Next month is the head shop's busy season, so I think it would be hard to take shelves away from it…
なかむら: {倉庫|そうこ}に{古|ふる}い{棚|たな}があったはずだ。{少|すこ}し{手入|てい}れすれば{使|つか}えるだろう。{運搬|うんぱん}の{手配|てはい}を{小野|おの}さんにお{願|ねが}いできるかな。
= There should be some old shelves in the warehouse. With a bit of work they'll be usable. Could I ask you to arrange the transport, Ono?
おの: かしこまりました。{今日中|きょうじゅう}にトラックを{手配|てはい}いたします。
= Certainly. I'll arrange a truck today.
たけだ: ただ、{広告|こうこく}に{載|の}せた{新商品|しんしょうひん}の{一部|いちぶ}も、{同|おな}じ{船|ふね}に{積|つ}まれておりまして…。
= However, some of the new products in the advert are on the same ship…
なかむら: それは{困|こま}ったな。お{客様|きゃくさま}にきちんと{説明|せつめい}しないではすまないだろう。
= That's a problem. We can't get away without explaining it properly to customers.
たけだ: はい。ホームページと{店頭|てんとう}で、おわびのお{知|し}らせを{出|だ}すことにします。
= Yes. We'll put up a notice of apology on the website and in the shop.
なかむら: {先方|せんぽう}の{社長|しゃちょう}にも、{私|わたし}から{一度|いちど}{連絡|れんらく}を{入|い}れておこう。{誰|だれ}のせいでもないが、{黙|だま}っているわけにはいかない。
= I'll get in touch with the supplier's president myself too. It's nobody's fault, but I can't just say nothing.
おの: よろしくお{願|ねが}いいたします。
= Thank you, we'd appreciate that.
```

{内装|ないそう} = interior fittings; {当面|とうめん} = for the time being; {代用|だいよう} = using as a
substitute; {店頭|てんとう} = the shop front; {先方|せんぽう} = the other party; おわび = an apology (its kanji
is off the list). Takeda reports the risk from outside (を{余儀|よぎ}なくされる), Nakamura states what
customers are owed (ないではすまない) and his own duty (わけにはいかない).

> ――{創業|そうぎょう}{百五十年|ひゃくごじゅうねん}の{老舗|しにせ}を{継|つ}がれて{十年|じゅうねん}になります。この{十年|じゅうねん}を{振|ふ}り{返|かえ}って、いかがですか。
>
> {正直|しょうじき}に{申|もう}し{上|あ}げて、{苦労|くろう}の{連続|れんぞく}でした。{継|つ}いで{三年目|さんねんめ}に、{駅前|えきまえ}の{再開発|さいかいはつ}で{本店|ほんてん}の{移転|いてん}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされました。{祖父|そふ}の{代|だい}から{同|おな}じ{場所|ばしょ}で{商売|しょうばい}をしてきましたから、{常連|じょうれん}のお{客様|きゃくさま}が{新|あたら}しい{店|みせ}まで{来|き}てくださるか、{不安|ふあん}でたまりませんでした。{移転先|いてんさき}は{駅|えき}から{歩|ある}いて{十五分|じゅうごふん}もかかる{住宅街|じゅうたくがい}で、{近所|きんじょ}の{方|かた}にさえ{店|みせ}の{名前|なまえ}を{知|し}られていなかったんです。
>
> ――{実際|じっさい}、{客足|きゃくあし}はどうでしたか。
>
> {最初|さいしょ}の{一年|いちねん}は、{売|う}り{上|あ}げが{三割|さんわり}{近|ちか}く{落|お}ちました。{職人|しょくにん}の{給料|きゅうりょう}を{下|さ}げるわけにはいきませんから、{私|わたし}の{報酬|ほうしゅう}を{削|けず}り、{経費|けいひ}も{一|ひと}つ{一|ひと}つ{見直|みなお}しました。それでも{足|た}りず、{支店|してん}を{一|ひと}つ{閉|と}じざるを{得|え}ませんでした。{長年|ながねん}{勤|つと}めてくれた{店長|てんちょう}には、{自分|じぶん}の{口|くち}から{説明|せつめい}しないではすまないと{思|おも}い、{何度|なんど}も{話|はな}し{合|あ}いました。{今|いま}は{本店|ほんてん}で{若|わか}い{職人|しょくにん}の{指導|しどう}にあたってくれています。
>
> ――{転機|てんき}になったのは{何|なん}でしょう。
>
> {若|わか}い{職人|しょくにん}の{提案|ていあん}です。お{客様|きゃくさま}が{季節|きせつ}の{和菓子|わがし}を{作|つく}る{教室|きょうしつ}を{開|ひら}いてはどうか、と。{最初|さいしょ}は{反対|はんたい}しました。{技|わざ}は{店|みせ}の{中|なか}で{守|まも}るもので、{外|そと}に{見|み}せるものではないと{思|おも}い{込|こ}んでいたんです。でも、{彼|かれ}は{企画書|きかくしょ}を{何度|なんど}も{書|か}き{直|なお}して、{粘|ねば}り{強|づよ}く{説得|せっとく}してきました。{試|ため}しに{一度|いちど}だけやってみたら、{予約|よやく}がすぐに{埋|う}まって{驚|おどろ}きました。
>
> ――{教室|きょうしつ}は{今|いま}も{続|つづ}いていますね。
>
> はい、{月|つき}に{四回|よんかい}{開|ひら}いています。{参加|さんか}された{方|かた}がお{店|みせ}のお{客様|きゃくさま}になり、{今度|こんど}はご{友人|ゆうじん}を{連|つ}れて{来|き}てくださる。{作|つく}る{手間|てま}を{知|し}っていただくと、{値段|ねだん}の{意味|いみ}もわかっていただけるようです。おかげさまで、{去年|きょねん}ようやく{移転前|いてんまえ}の{売|う}り{上|あ}げを{超|こ}えることができました。
>
> ――{後継者|こうけいしゃ}の{育成|いくせい}についてはいかがですか。
>
> {職人|しょくにん}の{世界|せかい}は、{昔|むかし}から「{見|み}て{覚|おぼ}えろ」でした。{私|わたし}も{父|ちち}から{手取|てと}り{足取|あしと}り{教|おし}わった{覚|おぼ}えはありません。でも、{今|いま}の{若|わか}い{人|ひと}にそれを{求|もと}めても{続|つづ}きません。そこで、{作業|さぎょう}の{手順|てじゅん}を{一|ひと}つ{一|ひと}つ{書|か}き{出|だ}し、{誰|だれ}が{見|み}てもわかるようにしました。{勘|かん}に{頼|たよ}っていた{部分|ぶぶん}を{言葉|ことば}にするのは{簡単|かんたん}ではありませんでしたが、おかげで{新人|しんじん}が{一人前|いちにんまえ}になるまでの{期間|きかん}が{半分|はんぶん}になりました。{教|おし}える{側|がわ}にとっても、{自分|じぶん}の{仕事|しごと}を{見直|みなお}すいいきっかけになったようです。
>
> ――{老舗|しにせ}を{守|まも}るうえで、{大切|たいせつ}にしていることは{何|なん}ですか。
>
> {変|か}えてはいけないものと、{変|か}えなければならないものを{見極|みきわ}めることでしょうか。{味|あじ}と{材料|ざいりょう}は{守|まも}る。でも、{売|う}り{方|かた}や{働|はたら}き{方|かた}は、{時代|じだい}に{合|あ}わせて{変|か}えていく。{伝統|でんとう}というのは、{変化|へんか}を{恐|おそ}れないことで{初|はじ}めて{続|つづ}いていくものだと{思|おも}います。

{継|つ}ぐ = to inherit, succeed to (a business); {再開発|さいかいはつ} = redevelopment; {移転|いてん} =
relocation; {転機|てんき} = a turning point; {和菓子|わがし} = Japanese confectionery; {企画書|きかくしょ} =
a written proposal; {見極|みきわ}める = to discern, judge clearly; {手取|てと}り{足取|あしと}り = step by step, holding someone's hand;
{一人前|いちにんまえ} = fully fledged.

1. What was the owner forced to do in the third year, and why?
2. What did the owner do to deal with the fall in sales, and what didn't the owner do?
3. Why did the owner first oppose the young craftsman's proposal, and what changed the owner's
   mind?
4. What does the owner say keeps a tradition alive?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. To move the main shop ({本店|ほんてん}の{移転|いてん}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされた), because of the redevelopment
   in front of the station.
2. Cut the owner's own pay, reviewed every expense and (having no choice) closed one branch. The
   owner didn't lower the craftsmen's wages ({下|さ}げるわけにはいきません), and explained the closure to
   the branch manager in person.
3. The owner believed skills were to be guarded inside the shop, not shown outside. The craftsman
   kept rewriting the proposal and persuading, and a single trial class filled up at once.
4. Telling apart what must not change (taste, ingredients) and what must (ways of selling and
   working): a tradition continues only by not fearing change.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

― It's ten years since you took over this 150-year-old shop. Looking back on those ten years, how
do they seem?

To be honest, it has been one hardship after another. In my third year, the redevelopment in front
of the station forced us to move the main shop. We'd been trading in the same place since my
grandfather's day, so I was terribly anxious about whether our regular customers would come to the
new shop. The new site was in a residential area fifteen minutes' walk from the station, where
even the neighbours didn't know the shop's name.

― And did the customers come?

In the first year, sales fell by nearly thirty per cent. I couldn't lower the craftsmen's pay, so
I cut my own and went through our expenses one by one. Even that wasn't enough, and we had no
choice but to close one branch. I felt I owed the manager who had worked for us for so many years
an explanation from my own mouth, and we talked it through many times. Now that manager is at the
main shop, training our young craftsmen.

― What was the turning point?

A proposal from a young craftsman: why not hold classes where customers make seasonal
confectionery? At first I was against it. I'd always assumed that our skills were to be guarded
inside the shop, not shown to the outside. But the craftsman rewrote the proposal again and again
and kept on persuading me. When we tried a single class, the places filled up at once, which
astonished me.

― The classes are still running, aren't they?

Yes, four times a month. People who come become customers of the shop, and then they bring their
friends. Once people know how much work goes into making them, they seem to understand the prices
too. Thanks to that, last year we finally exceeded our sales from before the move.

― What about training your successors?

In the craftsman's world it has always been "watch and learn". I don't remember my father ever
teaching me step by step either. But if you demand that of young people today, they won't stay.
So we wrote out the steps of the work one by one, so that anyone can follow them. Putting into
words what we'd done by feel wasn't easy, but thanks to it, the time it takes a newcomer to become
fully skilled has halved. It seems to have been a good chance for those who teach to rethink their
own work, too.

― What do you value most in keeping an old shop going?

Telling apart what mustn't change and what must, I suppose. We keep the taste and the
ingredients. But how we sell and how we work, we change with the times. I think a tradition is
something that goes on only when you aren't afraid of change.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{悪天候|あくてんこう}のため、{試合|しあい}は{中止|ちゅうし}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされました。
= Because of the bad weather, the match had to be called off.
これは{謝|あやま}らないではすまないね。
= We can't get away without apologizing for this.
{弊社|へいしゃ}の{担当者|たんとうしゃ}から、{改|あらた}めてご{連絡|れんらく}いたします。
= Our representative will contact you again.
{総務部|そうむぶ}{御中|おんちゅう}
= To the General Affairs Department (on an envelope)
{進捗|しんちょく}はいかがですか。
= How is it progressing?
```

## Common mistakes

- 〜を{余儀|よぎ}なくされる for one's own free choice: {留学|りゅうがく}したくて、{退職|たいしょく}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされた
  contradicts itself.
  The cause must be outside: {親|おや}の{介護|かいご}のため、{退職|たいしょく}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされた.
- Dropping を or the passive: ×{中止|ちゅうし}に{余儀|よぎ}なくされた, ×{中止|ちゅうし}を{余儀|よぎ}なくした (unless
  the subject is the cause: 〜を{余儀|よぎ}なくさせた).
- 〜を{余儀|よぎ}なくされる in casual speech with friends: it sounds like a news report. Say
  {中止|ちゅうし}になっちゃった.
- ×{弁償|べんしょう}しずにはすまない: する becomes せ before ず: {弁償|べんしょう}せずにはすまない.
- Confusing 〜ずにはすまない (others won't let it pass) with lesson 16's 〜ずにはおかない (it will
  inevitably cause; I'll see it done).
- Writing {御中|おんちゅう} and {様|さま} together, or {御中|おんちゅう} after a person's name.
- Using クレーム for a legal or insurance claim: that's {請求|せいきゅう}.

## Key points

- する noun + を{余儀|よぎ}なくされる: be forced (by outside circumstances) to; news and writing; the
  cause with で / により / のため. Causative: [cause] が 〜に〜を{余儀|よぎ}なくさせる.
- ない form + ではすまない / ない stem + ずにはすまない (する → せずにはすまない): one won't get away
  without (apologizing, paying, explaining); 〜ではすまない (won't end with just…).
- Review: 〜ざるを{得|え}ない (N2 17), 〜までもない (N2 19); obligation table from N4 to N1.
- New kanji: 幹 督 僚 司 遣 赴 遷 俸 締 揮 枠 勘 搬 捗 頓 舗 創 隆 併 兼 系 削 脱 粘 弊 御 宜 陳 顧 功 堅 彰. Write
  {上司|じょうし}, {同僚|どうりょう}, {締|し}め{切|き}り, {弊社|へいしゃ}, {小遣|こづか}い, {新幹線|しんかんせん} with kanji from
  now on; special reading {老舗|しにせ}.

the lesson.

lessons.title: Must not: まじき, べからず, べからざる, しかるべき
topics: べからず and べからざる
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 4 ends with the strongest judgements of all: what must not be done, what cannot be done
without, and what ought to have been done. The patterns come from classical Japanese (the
auxiliaries べし and まじ), and they survive in notices, editorials, official statements and
proverbs:

{教師|きょうし}にあるまじき{行為|こうい}だ。 — That is conduct unworthy of a teacher.

{関係者以外|かんけいしゃいがい}{立|た}ち{入|い}るべからず。 — No entry except for authorized persons.

{水|みず}は{生命|せいめい}に{欠|か}くべからざるものである。 — Water is indispensable to life.

{事故|じこ}の{原因|げんいん}について、{会社|かいしゃ}から{説明|せつめい}があってしかるべきだ。 — The company ought to have given an explanation of the cause of the accident.

The theme is science, technology and industry: elements and materials, metals and mining,
physics words (friction, expansion, pressure), microscopes and cells in the lab, cultivation, and
the ethics of research. N2 lesson 18 gave you science and space, and N2 lesson 9 industry; this
lesson's kanji write the materials themselves, and its grammar supplies the language of research
ethics: {研究者|けんきゅうしゃ}としてあるまじき{行為|こうい}, {科学|かがく}に{欠|か}くべからざる{信頼|しんらい}.

These are classical forms living on in modern Japanese: you need to understand and use them, but
they aren't conjugation-drill forms. Lesson 5h2 met the classical auxiliaries, and lesson 26 will
look at べし and ごとし in modern writing.

## Unworthy of: 〜まじき

まじき is the attributive (noun-modifying) form of the classical auxiliary まじ, the negative of
べし: "should not". In modern Japanese it survives almost only as

N + に / として + あるまじき + N ({行為|こうい}, {発言|はつげん}, {態度|たいど}…): conduct that a person in that position must
never commit.

{公務員|こうむいん}として、あるまじき{行為|こうい}である。 — It is conduct unworthy of a public servant.

{人|ひと}の{命|いのち}を{預|あず}かる{医師|いし}にあるまじき{発言|はつげん}だ。 — It is a remark unbecoming of a doctor, entrusted with people's lives.

A few other verbs take it in fixed phrases: {許|ゆる}すまじき (unforgivable), {言|い}うまじきこと
(something one must never say). With する it's するまじき or すまじき.

Points to remember:

- Written and very strong criticism. In editorials, official reprimands, and in speech when
  someone wants to sound grave. Polite: あるまじき{行為|こうい}です.
- It always comes before a noun: ×{教師|きょうし}にあるまじきだ. The noun is usually {行為|こうい},
  {発言|はつげん}, {態度|たいど} or こと.
- The person named is the one whose position makes the act unacceptable: a teacher, a doctor, a
  politician, a researcher.
- Compare 〜べきではない (N3): {教師|きょうし}は{体罰|たいばつ}をすべきではない (teachers should not use
  corporal punishment) is advice or a rule; {教師|きょうし}にあるまじき{行為|こうい} is a condemnation of
  something that has happened.

## Do not: 〜べからず

Dictionary form + べからず is a **[[prohibition]]**: "must not", the voice of old notices, rules and
maxims. する is するべからず or すべからず.

| Notice | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {芝生|しばふ}に{入|はい}るべからず | Keep off the grass |
| {関係者以外|かんけいしゃいがい}{立|た}ち{入|い}るべからず | No entry except for authorized persons |
| ここにごみを{捨|す}てるべからず | Do not dump rubbish here |
| {働|はたら}かざる{者|もの}{食|く}うべからず | Those who do not work shall not eat (a saying) |

{初心忘|しょしんわす}るべからず — Never forget the spirit of a beginner. (A saying traced to {世阿弥|ぜあみ}, the
noh master of lesson 10h2; its second kanji, 阿, is outside N1; {忘|わす}る is the classical form of {忘|わす}れる.)

- Today you'll see it on old-style signs, in school or club rules written for effect, and in
  sayings. A modern notice says 〜ないでください, 〜{禁止|きんし} or ご{遠慮|えんりょ}ください.
- It ends a sentence; for a noun-modifying form see べからざる below.
- Humorous use is common: {冷蔵庫|れいぞうこ}のケーキ、{食|た}べるべからず (on a note: hands off the cake).

## Indispensable, unpardonable: 〜べからざる

Dictionary form + べからざる + N is the attributive form: "that must not be…, that cannot be…".
It's written and formal, and nearly fixed to a few verbs:

| Phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {欠|か}くべからざる | indispensable (that must not be missing) |
| {許|ゆる}すべからざる | unpardonable |
| {侵|おか}すべからざる | inviolable |
| {言|い}うべからざる | that must not be spoken |

{信頼|しんらい}は、{医療|いりょう}に{欠|か}くべからざるものだ。 — Trust is indispensable to medicine.

{表現|ひょうげん}の{自由|じゆう}は、{民主主義|みんしゅしゅぎ}にとって{侵|おか}すべからざる{権利|けんり}である。 — Freedom of expression is an inviolable right for democracy.

{欠|か}くべからざる is by far the commonest; in speech, {欠|か}かせない or なくてはならない.

## Ought to, proper: 〜てしかるべきだ, しかるべき

しかるべき ("as it should be") has two uses.

1. て form + しかるべきだ: "ought to (and it hasn't happened)". It's formal criticism that
something proper is missing:

{被害者|ひがいしゃ}に{対|たい}して、{会社|かいしゃ}は{謝罪|しゃざい}してしかるべきだ。 — The company ought to apologize to the victims.

これだけの{成果|せいか}を{上|あ}げたのだから、もっと{評価|ひょうか}されてしかるべきだ。 — Having achieved so much, they deserve to be valued more highly.

2. しかるべき + N: "appropriate, proper".

{事実|じじつ}を{確認|かくにん}したうえで、しかるべき{措置|そち}を{取|と}ります。 — Once we have checked the facts, we will take appropriate measures.

この{件|けん}は、しかるべき{人|ひと}に{相談|そうだん}したほうがいい。 — You should consult the proper person about this.

- 〜てしかるべきだ is close to 〜べきだ, but says the speaker expected it as a matter of course and
  is dissatisfied that it hasn't happened. Common in editorials and complaints: 〜があってしかるべき
  だ, 〜されてしかるべきだ (passive).
- しかるべき{措置|そち} / {対応|たいおう} / {手続|てつづ}き are fixed in official statements and business letters.
- Written in kana: its old kanji spelling (然るべき) uses a reading that isn't jōyō.

## Review: 〜べきだ, 〜べきではない, 〜ものではない

> N3: dictionary form + べきだ (should; する → するべき / すべき), 〜べきではない (should not): the
> speaker's judgement of what is right. 〜べきだった is regret about the past.
>
> 〜ものではない (N3): what one normally shouldn't do, as a general rule or a reprimand: {人|ひと}の
> {悪口|わるぐち}を{言|い}うものではない (one mustn't speak ill of others). It's milder and more personal
> than まじき or べからず.

## From advice to condemnation

| Pattern | Says | Register |
|---|---|---|
| 〜ものではない (N3) | one doesn't (as a rule) | speech, advice |
| 〜べきではない (N3) | should not | both |
| 〜べからず | must not (a notice, a maxim) | signs, sayings |
| N にあるまじき N | unworthy of (a person in that role) | written, strong |
| 〜べからざる N | that must not / cannot be ({欠|か}く, {許|ゆる}す, {侵|おか}す) | written |
| 〜べきだ (N3) | should | both |
| 〜てしかるべきだ | ought to (and it hasn't happened) | formal |
| しかるべき N | proper, appropriate | formal, business |

## Words for science, technology and industry

| Area | Words |
|---|---|
| elements | {炭素|たんそ}, {酸素|さんそ}, {酸|さん}, {酸性|さんせい}, {酸化|さんか}, {酸味|さんみ} (lesson 4), {塩酸|えんさん}, {炭酸|たんさん}, {化合物|かごうぶつ}, {化学|かがく} |
| carbon and coal | {炭|すみ}, {木炭|もくたん}, {石炭|せきたん}, {炭鉱|たんこう} |
| metals | {金属|きんぞく}, {鉄鋼|てっこう}, {鋼|はがね}, {鉛|なまり}, {亜鉛|あえん}, {銅|どう}, {青銅|せいどう}, {合金|ごうきん}, {金塊|きんかい}, レアメタル |
| mining and making | {鉱物|こうぶつ}, {鉱山|こうざん}, {鉱石|こうせき}, {鋳造|ちゅうぞう}, {鋳物|いもの}, {鋳型|いがた}, {炉|ろ}, {溶鉱炉|ようこうろ}, {溶接|ようせつ}, {純度|じゅんど} |
| energy | {原子炉|げんしろ}, {臨界|りんかい}, {電流|でんりゅう}, {電圧|でんあつ}, {磁石|じしゃく}, {磁気|じき}, {磁場|じば}, {磁力|じりょく}, {電磁波|でんじは}, {半導体|はんどうたい} |
| states of matter | {結晶|けっしょう}, {液晶|えきしょう}, {水晶|すいしょう}, {凝縮|ぎょうしゅく}, {凝固|ぎょうこ}, {沸点|ふってん}, {融点|ゆうてん}, {塊|かたまり} |

Professor Inoue talks to Hayakawa, a graduate student who has just joined the laboratory.


> {情報|じょうほう}の{扱|あつか}いも{重要|じゅうよう}な{問題|もんだい}になりつつある。{医療|いりょう}や{遺伝子|いでんし}の{研究|けんきゅう}では、{個人|こじん}を{特定|とくてい}できる{情報|じょうほう}が{大量|たいりょう}に{集|あつ}められる。こうした{情報|じょうほう}が{外部|がいぶ}に{漏|も}れれば、{協力|きょうりょく}してくれた{人々|ひとびと}に{取|と}り{返|かえ}しのつかない{損害|そんがい}を{与|あた}えかねない。{研究者|けんきゅうしゃ}には、データを{集|あつ}める{段階|だんかい}から{保管|ほかん}、{廃棄|はいき}に{至|いた}るまで、しかるべき{管理|かんり}を{行|おこな}う{責任|せきにん}がある。{便利|べんり}だからといって{個人|こじん}のパソコンに{保存|ほぞん}したり、{許可|きょか}なく{共有|きょうゆう}したりすることは{許|ゆる}されない。
>

{完結|かんけつ} = being complete in itself; {営|いとな}み = an activity, undertaking; {基盤|きばん} = a foundation;
{後|あと}を{絶|た}たない = never to cease; {若手|わかて} = young (staff); {倫理観|りんりかん} = a sense of ethics;
{追試|ついし} = replication (repeating an experiment); {画期的|かっきてき} = epoch-making; {疑|うたが}ってかかる = to
approach with suspicion; {名前|なまえ}を{連|つら}ねる = to have one's name on a list; {苦痛|くつう} = pain,
suffering; {縛|しば}る = to bind; {携|たずさ}わる = to be engaged in (携 is lesson 6's kanji).

1. Why does the text call trust {欠|か}くべからざる for science?
2. What are the three kinds of research misconduct the text names?
3. What background is often pointed out for misconduct, and what does the writer conclude from it?
4. What does the text say about the responsibility of co-authors, and how does it end?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Because science works by researchers building on each other's reported results (other
   researchers plan experiments and companies develop products from them), so it depends on
   trusting others' reports.
2. Fabrication (ねつぞう: creating data that don't exist), falsification ({改|かい}ざん: altering data or
   images conveniently) and plagiarism ({盗用|とうよう}: using others' text or ideas without citing them).
3. Pressure for results (being judged by the number of papers, needing quick results for
   funding). Pressure doesn't excuse misconduct, but measures that rely only on individual ethics
   have limits.
4. Everyone whose name is on a joint paper ought to take responsibility for the data
   (〜{持|も}ってしかるべきだろう). It ends with a playful classical-style maxim: researchers must not
   forget that each decision keeps or breaks society's trust (〜を{忘|わす}れるべからず).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Scientific research is not something completed by one researcher alone. On the basis of results
one researcher publishes, another plans the next experiment and companies develop products. In
other words, science is an undertaking that stands on trust in other people's reports. In this
sense, trust can be called the indispensable foundation of science.

Research misconduct is generally divided into three kinds: "fabrication", creating data that do
not exist; "falsification", rewriting data or images to suit oneself; and "plagiarism", using
others' text or ideas without citing the source. It goes without saying that all of these are
conduct unworthy of a researcher.

Why, then, does misconduct never cease? The background often pointed out is the pressure for
results. Researchers are evaluated by their number of papers and must produce results in a short
time to obtain funding. In a questionnaire one university carried out among young researchers,
more than half of the respondents reportedly answered that they felt pressed to hurry their
results. Of course, pressure does not make misconduct permissible. But measures that rely only on
individual ethics have their limits.

Mechanisms for preventing misconduct include peer review, in which experts examine papers;
replication, in which third parties repeat the same experiment to confirm it; and the keeping of
lab notebooks and original data. A result whose reproducibility cannot be confirmed should be
approached with suspicion, however epoch-making it may look. In joint research, too, everyone
whose name appears on the paper ought surely to take responsibility for the data.

Ethical issues are not only about misconduct. In research involving people, the purpose and risks
must be fully explained to the test subjects and their consent obtained. In animal experiments
too, researchers are required to reduce the number of animals used and keep their suffering to a
minimum.

The handling of information is also becoming a serious issue. Medical and genetic research
gathers large amounts of information that can identify individuals. If it leaked, it could do
irreparable harm to the people who cooperated. Researchers are responsible for managing data
properly at every stage, from collection through storage to disposal. Saving it on a personal
computer for convenience, or sharing it without permission, is not acceptable.

Research ethics is not a collection of rules that bind researchers. It is a promise that lets
society go on trusting science. Once misconduct comes to light, trust wavers not just in that
researcher but in the whole field. Those engaged in research must not forget, as the saying might
go, that each of their decisions leads either to keeping that promise or to breaking it.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{医師|いし}にあるまじき{発言|はつげん}だ。
= That is a remark unworthy of a doctor.
{芝生|しばふ}に{入|はい}るべからず。
= Keep off the grass.
{健康|けんこう}は、{生活|せいかつ}に{欠|か}くべからざるものだ。
= Health is indispensable to life.
{説明|せつめい}があってしかるべきだ。
= There ought to have been an explanation.
しかるべき{措置|そち}を{取|と}ります。
= We will take appropriate measures.
```

## Common mistakes

- ×{教師|きょうし}にあるまじきだ: まじき must modify a noun: {教師|きょうし}にあるまじき{行為|こうい}だ.
- ×{教師|きょうし}があるまじき{行為|こうい}: the person takes に or として: {教師|きょうし}に / として
  あるまじき.
- Using べからず in a real modern notice: it sounds old or jokey. A public sign today says
  {立|た}ち{入|い}り{禁止|きんし} or お{入|はい}りにならないでください.
- ×{欠|か}くべからずもの: before a noun the form is べからざる: {欠|か}くべからざるもの.
- 〜てしかるべきだ for one's own plans: {明日|あした}{私|わたし}は{早|はや}く{起|お}きてしかるべきだ isn't said. It's a judgement
  about what others (or society) ought to do, usually with dissatisfaction.
- Reading しかるべき as "to scold": the verb {叱|しか}る (lesson 1's kanji) sounds similar, but
  しかるべき is "proper, appropriate".
- Writing {化学|かがく} for science in general: {科学|かがく} is science, {化学|かがく} chemistry.

## Key points

- **[[Prohibition]]** in classical style: dictionary form + べからず (notices, maxims: {立|た}ち{入|い}るべからず,
  {初心忘|しょしんわす}るべからず); する → するべからず / すべからず.
- N に / として + あるまじき + N: conduct unworthy of (a teacher, a doctor, a researcher); strong
  written criticism.
- Dictionary form + べからざる + N: {欠|か}くべからざる (indispensable), {許|ゆる}すべからざる, {侵|おか}すべからざる.
- て form + しかるべきだ: ought to (and it hasn't happened); しかるべき + N: proper, appropriate.
- These classical forms aren't conjugation-drill forms.
- New kanji: 炭 酸 鋼 鉛 銅 鉱 鋳 炉 晶 塊 凝 繊 紡 微 顕 殖 栽 軸 磁 滑 摩 擦 透 膨 斜 径 尺 坪 架 芯 汽 槽. Write
  {二酸化炭素|にさんかたんそ}, {酸|す}っぱい, {鉛筆|えんぴつ}, {滑|すべ}る with kanji from now on.

lessons.title: Akutagawa and "Rashomon"
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Japanese N2's honors lesson on {芥川|あくたがわ}{龍之介|りゅうのすけ} (1892–1927) told his life and retold
『くもの{糸|いと}』 ("The Spider's Thread"). This lesson reads the story that made his name, and
one of the most widely read short stories in Japanese: 『{羅生門|らしょうもん}』 ("Rashōmon"), a tale
of a servant, an old woman and a ruined gate, and of what people will do to survive. Japanese high
schools have long taught it in their literature classes, so most adult readers know it.

You'll read the story retold in this course's own modern Japanese, its one famous last line, how
that line came to be, and how a film of 1950 carried the gate's name around the world. The
discussion uses this module's judgements: what is {人|ひと}としてあるまじき, what one is
{余儀|よぎ}なくされる to do, and what one {堪|た}えない to watch.

The writer's name has three kanji outside N1 ({芥|あくた}, {龍|りゅう} and {之|の}); 羅 in the title is
lesson 28's kanji, and 生 and 門 are long familiar, so the title is written {羅生門|らしょうもん}. The
story was first published in 1915 and is in the public domain; apart from its last line, what
follows is this course's retelling, not Akutagawa's text.

## The story and where it came from

Akutagawa was a 23-year-old student of English literature at Tokyo Imperial University when
『{羅生門|らしょうもん}』 appeared in November 1915 in the magazine 『{帝国文学|ていこくぶんがく}』. He signed it with a pen
name, {柳川隆之介|やながわりゅうのすけ} (之 again off the list). It is usually said to have attracted little notice at first.

He took his material from 『{今昔物語集|こんじゃくものがたりしゅう}』, a large collection of tales compiled around
the twelfth century (the exact date is unknown). Two short tales were combined: one (volume 29,
tale 18) about a thief who climbs to the upper storey of the gate and finds an old woman pulling
hair from a dead body, and one (volume 31, tale 31) about a woman who sold cut and dried snake
to palace guards as fish. The medieval tales simply report; Akutagawa added the servant's wavering
thoughts and turned them into a question about human nature.

The gate itself was real. {羅城門|らじょうもん}, the spelling of its historical name, was the great south gate
of {平安京|へいあんきょう}, the capital founded in 794 on the site of today's Kyoto. In the story, years of
earthquakes, whirlwinds, fires and famine have left the city in ruins and the gate abandoned,
and unclaimed bodies are left on its upper floor.

## The story, retold

> {激|はげ}しい{雨|あめ}の{降|ふ}る{夕方|ゆうがた}、{羅生門|らしょうもん}の{下|した}に、{一人|ひとり}の{下人|げにん}がぼんやりと{座|すわ}っていた。ここ{数年|すうねん}、{京|きょう}の{都|みやこ}は{地震|じしん}や{火事|かじ}、ききんなどの{災|わざわ}いに{見舞|みま}われ、すっかり{荒|あ}れ{果|は}てていた。{門|もん}も{修理|しゅうり}されないまま{放|ほう}っておかれ、{日|ひ}が{暮|く}れると{誰|だれ}も{近|ちか}づかない。{引|ひ}き{取|と}り{手|て}のない{死体|したい}が{捨|す}てられる{場所|ばしょ}にさえなっていたのである。
>
> {下人|げにん}は{数日前|すうじつまえ}、{長年|ながねん}{仕|つか}えた{主人|しゅじん}から{暇|ひま}を{出|だ}されたばかりだった。{雨|あめ}がやんでも、{行|い}く{当|あ}てはない。このままでは{飢|う}え{死|じ}にを{待|ま}つしかない。{生|い}き{延|の}びるには{盗人|ぬすびと}になるほかない。{頭|あたま}ではそうわかっていても、{一歩|いっぽ}を{踏|ふ}み{出|だ}す{勇気|ゆうき}が、{下人|げにん}にはどうしても{出|で}なかった。
>
> {夜|よる}を{過|す}ごす{場所|ばしょ}を{探|さが}そうと、{下人|げにん}は{門|もん}の{上|うえ}の{階|かい}へはしごを{上|のぼ}った。そこには{死体|したい}がいくつも{転|ころ}がっていた。その{間|あいだ}に、{小|ちい}さな{明|あ}かりをともして、やせた{老婆|ろうば}が{一人|ひとり}うずくまっていた。{老婆|ろうば}は、{女|おんな}の{死体|したい}から{髪|かみ}の{毛|け}を{一本|いっぽん}ずつ{抜|ぬ}いていたのである。
>
> その{姿|すがた}を{見|み}たとたん、{下人|げにん}の{胸|むね}には、あらゆる{悪|あく}への{激|はげ}しい{憎|にく}しみが{燃|も}え{上|あ}がった。{盗人|ぬすびと}になろうかと{迷|まよ}っていたことなど、もう{忘|わす}れていた。{下人|げにん}は{刀|かたな}を{手|て}に{老婆|ろうば}に{飛|と}びかかり、{何|なに}をしているのかと{問|と}い{詰|つ}めた。
>
> {老婆|ろうば}の{答|こた}えはこうだった。{髪|かみ}を{抜|ぬ}いて、かつらにして{売|う}ろうと{思|おも}った。{死人|しにん}の{髪|かみ}を{抜|ぬ}くのは{悪|わる}いことかもしれない。だが、この{女|おんな}も{生|い}きていた{頃|ころ}、{蛇|へび}を{干|ほ}して{魚|さかな}だと{偽|いつわ}り、{役人|やくにん}たちに{売|う}っていた。{飢|う}え{死|じ}にしないためにはそうするしかなかったのだから、それを{悪|わる}いとは{思|おも}わない。{自分|じぶん}がしていることも、{生|い}きるためにやむを{得|え}ないことだ。この{女|おんな}なら、きっと{許|ゆる}してくれるだろう、と。
>
> {聞|き}いているうちに、{下人|げにん}の{心|こころ}に、ある{勇気|ゆうき}が{生|う}まれてきた。それは、さっき{門|もん}の{下|した}で{欠|か}けていた{勇気|ゆうき}だった。{生|い}きるためなら{許|ゆる}されるというのなら、{自分|じぶん}が{老婆|ろうば}から{奪|うば}っても{文句|もんく}は{言|い}えないはずだ。{下人|げにん}はそう{言|い}い{放|はな}つと、{老婆|ろうば}の{着物|きもの}を{剥|は}ぎ{取|と}り、{足|あし}にしがみつく{老婆|ろうば}を{振|ふ}り{払|はら}って、はしごを{駆|か}け{下|お}りた。
>
> しばらくして、{老婆|ろうば}は{死体|したい}の{間|あいだ}から{身|み}を{起|お}こし、はしごの{口|くち}まではっていって、{下|した}をのぞきこんだ。{外|そと}には、ただ{真|ま}っ{暗|くら}な{夜|よる}が{広|ひろ}がっているだけだった。

{仕|つか}える = to serve (a master); {当|あ}て = a prospect, somewhere to go; うずくまる = to crouch;
{問|と}い{詰|つ}める = to press (someone) for an answer; {偽|いつわ}る = to pass off falsely; {役人|やくにん} = an
official (here, palace guards); {言|い}い{放|はな}つ = to declare flatly; {振|ふ}り{払|はら}う = to shake off;
はう = to crawl.

Akutagawa tells the scene of the hair briefly and without lingering; so does this retelling. The
servant's sudden change is the point: a moment earlier he burns with hatred of evil, and a moment
later the old woman's own argument gives him the courage he lacked to do evil himself.

## The last line

The story ends with one short sentence that every Japanese reader knows:

「{下人|げにん}の{行方|ゆくえ}は、{誰|だれ}も{知|し}らない。」 — Where the servant went, no one knows.

The line is quoted here as the standard (definitive) text of 1918 has it; it reads the same in
today's modern-kana editions (school textbooks often print だれ in kana). It wasn't the first ending. The version
of 1915 ended by telling the reader that the servant was already hurrying through the rain into
the city to commit robbery. Akutagawa altered the ending slightly when the story was collected in
his first book, 『{羅生門|らしょうもん}』 (1917), and replaced it with the present line in the collection
『{鼻|はな}』 (1918), whose text became the standard one.

The change matters. The first ending says what the servant did; the last one says only that no
one knows. Readers are left with the dark outside the gate and with a question they must answer
for themselves: did he become a robber, and if he did, was he wrong?

## Survival and morals

The story asks what lesson 20's まじき asks: is there conduct that is unworthy of a human being
whatever the circumstances? Here are some ways Japanese readers discuss it, in the language of
this module.

> {下人|げにん}が{老婆|ろうば}の{着物|きもの}を{奪|うば}ったことは、{人|ひと}としてあるまじき{行為|こうい}なのだろうか。{飢|う}え{死|じ}にを{目前|もくぜん}にした{人間|にんげん}に、{道徳|どうとく}を{説|と}くことができるのか。{老婆|ろうば}は、{生|い}きるためなら{悪|あく}も{許|ゆる}されると{言|い}う。しかし、その{理屈|りくつ}を{認|みと}めれば、{弱|よわ}い{者|もの}から{奪|うば}うことも{正当化|せいとうか}されてしまう。{実際|じっさい}、{下人|げにん}はその{理屈|りくつ}をそのまま{老婆|ろうば}{自身|じしん}に{向|む}けたのである。{生存|せいぞん}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされた{選択|せんたく}と、{自分|じぶん}で{選|えら}んだ{悪事|あくじ}の{境目|さかいめ}はどこにあるのか。{作品|さくひん}は{答|こた}えを{示|しめ}さない。{読者|どくしゃ}{一人一人|ひとりひとり}が{考|かんが}えてしかるべき{問|と}いとして{残|のこ}されているのである。

{目前|もくぜん} = right before one's eyes; {説|と}く = to preach, explain; {境目|さかいめ} = the
borderline; {自身|じしん} = oneself, herself.

A few things to notice:

- The servant's hatred of evil and his decision to do evil come within minutes of each other.
  Akutagawa shows that a person's moral feelings can be strong and still change in an instant.
- The old woman's defence is a chain: the dead woman cheated to survive, so she would forgive me,
  so I may take her hair. The servant adds one more link, and the chain reaches the old woman.
- Akutagawa's narrator often speaks to the reader directly and comments on the servant (once even
  noting that "the author" said earlier the servant was waiting for the rain). This distance is
  part of the story's modern feel.

## Kurosawa's film

In 1950 the director {黒澤|くろさわ}{明|あきら} (澤 is an old form of lesson 1's 沢, off the list)
released a film called 『{羅生門|らしょうもん}』. Despite the title, its plot comes mainly from another
Akutagawa story, 『{藪|やぶ}の{中|なか}』 ("In a Grove"; 藪 is off the list), in which several people
give conflicting accounts of a killing in a forest. From 『{羅生門|らしょうもん}』 the film takes the
ruined gate, where people shelter from the rain and retell the case, and the theft of a garment in
its closing scenes.

The film won the top prize at the Venice Film Festival in 1951 and an honorary Academy Award, and
it was one of the first Japanese films to become widely known abroad. In English, "the Rashomon
effect" is now used for situations in which witnesses give contradictory versions of one event,
an idea that belongs to 『{藪|やぶ}の{中|なか}』 more than to the story you've just read. Japanese has its
own idiom from the same story: {真相|しんそう}は{藪|やぶ}の{中|なか}だ (the truth is lost in the thicket, no
one can say what really happened).

## Words for the story

| Area | Words |
|---|---|
| the setting | {羅生門|らしょうもん}, {荒廃|こうはい}, {荒|あ}れ{果|は}てる, {死体|したい}, {雨宿|あまやど}り |
| the people | {下人|げにん}, {盗人|ぬすびと}, {老婆|ろうば} (lesson 1), {暇|ひま}を{出|だ}す |
| what they do | {生|い}き{延|の}びる, {生存|せいぞん}, {悪事|あくじ}, {引剥|ひはぎ}, かつら |
| the ideas | {良心|りょうしん}, {正当化|せいとうか}, {黒洞々|こくとうとう} |
| the book | {説話|せつわ}, {今昔物語集|こんじゃくものがたりしゅう}, {改稿|かいこう} |

{黒洞々|こくとうとう}たる{夜|よる} ("a pitch-black night") is the phrase Akutagawa uses for the darkness
outside the gate in the story's last paragraph; it's recognition vocabulary. {引剥|ひはぎ} (highway
robbery) is the word the servant uses for what he is about to do.

## Key points

- 『{羅生門|らしょうもん}』: November 1915, 『{帝国文学|ていこくぶんがく}』, under a pen name; based on two tales in
  『{今昔物語集|こんじゃくものがたりしゅう}』; the standard text is the one revised for 『{鼻|はな}』 (1918).
- A dismissed servant, unable to bring himself to steal, meets an old woman taking hair from the
  dead; her argument that survival excuses wrong gives him the courage to rob her.
- The last line, 「{下人|げにん}の{行方|ゆくえ}は、{誰|だれ}も{知|し}らない。」, replaced an ending that said he was
  off to commit robbery: the reader must decide.
- Kurosawa's 1950 film takes its plot from 『{藪|やぶ}の{中|なか}』 and its frame and title from
  『{羅生門|らしょうもん}』; it won the top prize at Venice in 1951.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Japan's postwar economy
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Editorials, documentaries and older colleagues constantly refer to the stages of Japan's economy
since the war: 「{高度成長期|こうどせいちょうき}には…」, 「バブルの{頃|ころ}は…」, 「{石油危機|せきゆきき}のときは…」. This lesson
gives you the outline and the words, from the ruins of 1945 to the long slow years after 1990. It
sticks to dates and events that are well documented, and says where names and periods are
conventions rather than facts. It gives no current figures, makes no forecasts and doesn't judge
any government's policy: those are matters of debate, and they change.

The texts use lesson 19's を{余儀|よぎ}なくされる (being forced by circumstances) and N1 lesson 12's
べく (in order to), as economic history writing does.

## From the ruins to "no longer the postwar era"

In 1945 Japan's cities had been bombed, factories destroyed and food was scarce. The early postwar
years were a time of shortage, inflation and reconstruction ({戦後|せんご}の{復興|ふっこう}; {復興|ふっこう} is
lesson 1's word). Orders connected with the war in Korea, which began in 1950, gave industry a
lift: Japanese calls this {朝鮮特需|ちょうせんとくじゅ}, the "special procurement" boom.

In July 1956 the government's annual economic report, the {経済白書|けいざいはくしょ}, contained a phrase
that became famous: 「もはや{戦後|せんご}ではない」 ("It is no longer the postwar era"). The phrase is usually
explained this way: the economy had recovered to its prewar level, and the report argued that further growth would have to come
from modernization rather than recovery.

## High growth (roughly the mid-1950s to the early 1970s)

The period of {高度経済成長|こうどけいざいせいちょう} is usually dated from about 1955 to the first oil crisis
of 1973. The boundaries are a convention; historians draw them slightly differently. Over these
years the economy grew at around ten per cent a year on average, a figure often quoted in
textbooks.

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1956 | The {経済白書|けいざいはくしょ}: 「もはや{戦後|せんご}ではない」 |
| late 1950s | The {三種|さんしゅ}の{神器|じんぎ}: television, washing machine and refrigerator spread into homes |
| 1960 | The {所得倍増計画|しょとくばいぞうけいかく} (Income Doubling Plan) under Prime Minister {池田勇人|いけだはやと} |
| October 1964 | The {東海道新幹線|とうかいどうしんかんせん} opens (1 October; Tokyo–Shin-Osaka in four hours at the fastest), and the Tokyo Olympics are held |
| 1965–1970 | A long boom, from October 1965 to July 1970 by the Cabinet Office's reference dates, often called いざなぎ{景気|けいき} |
| 1973 | The first oil crisis ({第一次石油危機|だいいちじせきゆきき}) |

Growth had costs. Industrial pollution ({公害|こうがい}) damaged health in several regions, and the
diseases it caused became national issues in the 1960s. Millions of young people left the
countryside for the cities, and the countryside began to empty (lesson 18's {過疎化|かそか}).

The words to know: {好景気|こうけいき} (a boom) and {不景気|ふけいき} (hard times); {景気後退|けいきこうたい} (a downturn);
{国民総生産|こくみんそうせいさん} (GNP), the measure of the time, and {国内総生産|こくないそうせいさん} (GDP, lesson 12), the
measure used today; {経済大国|けいざいたいこく} (an economic power).

## The oil shocks and slower growth

In October 1973, war in the Middle East led Arab oil producers to restrict supply, and the price of
oil jumped. Japan, which imported almost all its oil, was hit hard. Prices surged in what the press
called {狂乱物価|きょうらんぶっか} (runaway inflation), people queued for toilet paper and detergent, and in
1974 the economy shrank for the first time since the war. A second oil shock followed at the end
of the decade. The era of high growth was over; what followed is often called {安定成長|あんていせいちょう}
(stable growth) or simply {低成長|ていせいちょう} (low growth).

{石油危機|せきゆきき}によって、{多|おお}くの{企業|きぎょう}は{生産|せいさん}の{縮小|しゅくしょう}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされた。{一方|いっぽう}で、エネルギーを{節約|せつやく}すべく、{省|しょう}エネルギーの{技術|ぎじゅつ}が{急速|きゅうそく}に{発達|はったつ}した。 — The oil crisis forced many companies to cut production. At the same time, energy-saving technology developed rapidly as people sought to save energy.

## The bubble and its collapse

In September 1985, the finance ministers and central bank governors of five major economies met at
the Plaza Hotel in New York and agreed to bring down the value of the dollar (the {プラザ合意|プラザごうい},
Plaza Accord). The yen rose sharply ({円高|えんだか}, lesson 12's word), and exporters suffered for a time.

What followed was the bubble economy (バブル{経済|けいざい}). Money flowed into land and shares, and
their prices rose far beyond what the underlying economy justified. By the Cabinet Office's dates
the expansion ran from November 1986 to February 1991. Land prices ({地価|ちか}) and share prices
later fell steeply, leaving banks with huge {不良債権|ふりょうさいけん} (bad loans, lesson 12).

In November 1997 several major financial institutions failed within weeks of each other: the
securities firm {山一證券|やまいちしょうけん} (證 is the old form of N2's 証, off the list) announced it would
close, and the {北海道拓殖銀行|ほっかいどうたくしょくぎんこう} failed. The {金融危機|きんゆうきき} (financial crisis) shook
confidence across the country.

{不良債権|ふりょうさいけん}の{処理|しょり}が{遅|おく}れ、{多|おお}くの{企業|きぎょう}が{倒産|とうさん}や{人員削減|じんいんさくげん}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされた。 — The clean-up of bad loans was slow, and many companies were forced into bankruptcy or staff cuts.

## The lost decades and deflation

The years of weak growth after the bubble are commonly called {失|うしな}われた{十年|じゅうねん} (the lost
decade); as the slow growth continued, people began to say {失|うしな}われた{二十年|にじゅうねん} and then
{失|うしな}われた{三十年|さんじゅうねん}. These are common names, not official terms, and economists disagree
about how to measure and explain the period. Over much of it, prices tended to fall slightly year
after year: deflation (デフレ, lesson 12's word). The opposite, inflation, is インフレ (also lesson 12's).

## A short reading

A passage from a high-school textbook-style overview (である style).

> {戦後|せんご}の{日本|にほん}は、{焼|や}け{跡|あと}からの{復興|ふっこう}を{経|へ}て、{一九五〇年代|せんきゅうひゃくごじゅうねんだい}{半|なか}ばから{高度経済成長|こうどけいざいせいちょう}の{時代|じだい}に{入|はい}った。{人々|ひとびと}は{豊|ゆた}かな{生活|せいかつ}を{手|て}に{入|い}れるべく{懸命|けんめい}に{働|はたら}き、{家庭|かてい}にはテレビや{洗濯機|せんたくき}、{冷蔵庫|れいぞうこ}が{次々|つぎつぎ}に{広|ひろ}まった。{一九六四年|せんきゅうひゃくろくじゅうよねん}には{東海道新幹線|とうかいどうしんかんせん}が{開業|かいぎょう}し、{東京|とうきょう}オリンピックが{開|ひら}かれた。しかし{一九七三年|せんきゅうひゃくななじゅうさんねん}の{石油危機|せきゆきき}によって、{日本経済|にほんけいざい}は{大|おお}きな{転換|てんかん}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされる。{一九八〇年代|せんきゅうひゃくはちじゅうねんだい}{後半|こうはん}にはバブル{経済|けいざい}が{生|う}まれたが、それが{崩壊|ほうかい}すると、{長|なが}い{低成長|ていせいちょう}の{時代|じだい}が{続|つづ}いた。この{間|あいだ}に{何|なに}が{得|え}られ、{何|なに}が{失|うしな}われたのか。その{評価|ひょうか}は、{今|いま}も{分|わ}かれている。

{焼|や}け{跡|あと} = the burnt ruins (of bombing); {半|なか}ば = the middle; {転換|てんかん} = a change of
direction. Notice the historical present {余儀|よぎ}なくされる in a past narrative, common in written
history, and べく for the purpose of people's hard work.

## Words for the postwar economy

| Area | Words |
|---|---|
| growth | {高度経済成長|こうどけいざいせいちょう}, {高度成長期|こうどせいちょうき}, {好景気|こうけいき}, {特需|とくじゅ}, {所得倍増|しょとくばいぞう}, {経済大国|けいざいたいこく}, {国民総生産|こくみんそうせいさん} |
| symbols | {三種|さんしゅ}の{神器|じんぎ}, {東海道新幹線|とうかいどうしんかんせん}, {経済白書|けいざいはくしょ} |
| shocks | {石油危機|せきゆきき}, オイルショック, {狂乱物価|きょうらんぶっか}, {不景気|ふけいき}, {景気後退|けいきこうたい}, {低成長|ていせいちょう} |
| the bubble | バブル{経済|けいざい}, {地価|ちか}, {金融危機|きんゆうきき} |
| costs | {公害|こうがい} |

## Key points

- High growth ({高度経済成長|こうどけいざいせいちょう}): roughly the mid-1950s to 1973 (a convention), around ten per
  cent a year on average; 1956 「もはや{戦後|せんご}ではない」; 1960 Income Doubling Plan; October 1964
  Shinkansen and Olympics.
- 1973 first oil crisis, {狂乱物価|きょうらんぶっか}, 1974 the first postwar contraction; then slower growth.
- 1985 Plaza Accord and a strong yen; the bubble (expansion November 1986 – February 1991 by the
  Cabinet Office's dates); bad loans; November 1997 financial failures.
- {失|うしな}われた{十年|じゅうねん} / {二十年|にじゅうねん} / {三十年|さんじゅうねん}: common names for the long slow period; deflation.
- を{余儀|よぎ}なくされる and べく are the grammar of written economic history.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Only here: ならでは, をおいて, にして, にいたっては
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 5 is about scope and manner: how far a statement reaches, what something is like, and in
what way it is done. Lesson 21 singles things out ("only A could", "no one but A", "as for A, it's
even worse"); lesson 22 says what something is covered in or shows signs of; lesson 23 is about
tendencies and likeness; lesson 24 about doing something in one's own way and as befits one's
standing; and lesson 25 about what happens "once" something happens, and "whether or not".

This lesson's four patterns all pick one item out of many:

{職人|しょくにん}ならではの{技|わざ}が{光|ひか}る。 — The skill only a craftsman could have shines through.

{彼女|かのじょ}をおいて、この{役|やく}を{演|えん}じられる{人|ひと}はいない。 — There is no one but her who could play this role.

{名人|めいじん}にして{初|はじ}めて{出|だ}せる{音|おと}だ。 — It's a sound only a master could produce.

{絵|え}も{彫刻|ちょうこく}も{少|すく}ないが、{写真|しゃしん}に{至|いた}っては{一枚|いちまい}もない。 — There are few paintings and sculptures, and as for photographs, there isn't a single one.

The theme is the arts: poetry and literature, painting and calligraphy, carving, pottery and
lacquer, music, and the words of appreciation and criticism. Earlier courses gave you the basics
({美術|びじゅつ}, {作品|さくひん}, {名作|めいさく}, {書道|しょどう}, {評論|ひょうろん}); N1 adds the words of the
critic and the craftsman, and this lesson's kanji let you write carried words such as
{鑑賞|かんしょう}, {漫画|まんが}, {歌舞伎|かぶき} and {俳句|はいく}.

All four patterns are written or formal. ならでは is also common in advertising, travel writing and
reviews; the other three belong to writing, speeches and careful speech.

## N + ならでは: what only A can offer

ならでは follows a noun and says that something is typical of A and found nowhere else, and that
this is a good thing. It is a pattern of praise.

| Form | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| A ならではの B | {京都|きょうと}ならではの{味|あじ} | a taste you get only in Kyoto |
| B は A ならではだ | この{景色|けしき}は{冬|ふゆ}ならではだ | this view belongs to winter alone |
| A ならでは〜ない (to recognize) | {老舗|しにせ}ならでは{出|だ}せない{味|あじ} | a taste only an old shop can produce |

{手作|てづく}りならではの{温|あたた}かみがある。 — It has a warmth that only handmade things have.

{地元|じもと}の{人|ひと}ならではの{情報|じょうほう}を{教|おし}えてもらった。 — I was told things only a local would know.

{子供|こども}ならではの{自由|じゆう}な{発想|はっそう}に{驚|おどろ}かされた。 — I was amazed by the free ideas only a child could have.

Points to remember:

- A is a noun: a person or group ({職人|しょくにん}, {地元|じもと}の{人|ひと}), a place ({京都|きょうと}, この{店|みせ}), a time
  ({冬|ふゆ}, この{季節|きせつ}) or a method or material ({手作|てづく}り, {登|のぼ}り{窯|がま}).
- B is a good quality: {味|あじ}, {魅力|みりょく}, {技|わざ}, {発想|はっそう}, {雰囲気|ふんいき}, {温|あたた}かみ. ならでは isn't
  used for faults. For a mistake typical of beginners, say {初心者|しょしんしゃ}にありがちなミス, not
  ならではのミス.
- It doesn't state a rule about who may do something. "Only members may enter" is
  {会員|かいいん}しか{入|はい}れません or {会員|かいいん}のみ.
- The 〜ない form (ならでは{出|だ}せない) is older written style; you'll read it, but ならではの is the
  form to use.

### ならでは and だけ

だけ states a fact; ならでは adds praise for something characteristic.

この{店|みせ}だけの{料理|りょうり}がある。 — There is a dish this restaurant alone serves. (it's on no other menu)

この{店|みせ}ならではの{料理|りょうり}がある。 — There is a dish that shows what this restaurant is all about. (it's special and typical of the place)

Only だけ works for a plain limit: {日曜|にちよう}だけ{休|やす}みだ (closed on Sundays only), never
{日曜|にちよう}ならでは{休|やす}みだ (that isn't said).

## 〜をおいて〜ない: no one but A

N + をおいて means "leaving A aside", and with a negative it says that A is the only possible one:
"apart from A, there is no…". It is a strong judgement in A's favour, and lives in speeches,
recommendations, editorials and formal conversation.

{彼|かれ}をおいて、{次|つぎ}の{会長|かいちょう}にふさわしい{人|ひと}はいない。 — There is no one but him fit to be the next chairperson.

この{研究|けんきゅう}を{任|まか}せられるのは、{山田|やまだ}{先生|せんせい}をおいてほかにいません。 — Professor Yamada is the only person this research could be entrusted to.

{日本|にほん}の{伝統|でんとう}を{世界|せかい}に{伝|つた}える{場所|ばしょ}として、ここをおいてほかにあるだろうか。 — As a place for showing Japan's traditions to the world, could there be anywhere but here?

Points to remember:

- What follows is negative (いない, ない, {考|かんが}えられない) or a question that expects "no" (〜だろうか,
  {誰|だれ}がいるだろうか). ほかに often comes before it.
- A is usually a person, a place or an occasion, rated very highly.
- {何|なに}をおいても is a set phrase: "before anything else, whatever happens":
  {知|し}らせを{聞|き}いたら、{何|なに}をおいても{駆|か}けつけます (when I hear, I'll come straight away, whatever I'm doing).
- Dictionaries write the verb with the kanji of lesson 13's {措置|そち}; newspapers write をおいて in kana,
  and so does this course.
- It isn't において (in, at: {会議|かいぎ}において, at the meeting), which has no を.

### をおいて and しか

しか〜ない limits: {彼|かれ}しかいない can be resignation ("there's only him"). をおいて〜ない praises:
{彼|かれ}をおいてほかにいない says he is the best possible choice.

## N + にして: only at A, both A and B, in an instant

にして follows a noun. It has three uses, all written or formal.

**1. Aにして{初|はじ}めて / Aにしてようやく: only at the level of A.** A is a person of great skill,
an age or a stage reached after a long time. What follows is something possible only there.

{名人|めいじん}にして{初|はじ}めて{可能|かのう}な{技|わざ}だ。 — It's a technique only a master is capable of.

{五十|ごじゅう}にしてようやく、{師匠|ししょう}の{言葉|ことば}の{意味|いみ}が{分|わ}かった。 — Only at fifty did I finally understand what my teacher had meant.

**2. AにしてB: A and also B.** One person or thing has two roles or qualities. This use is
written.

{彼|かれ}は{医師|いし}にして{作家|さっか}である。 — He is a doctor and also a writer.

この{寺|てら}は{日本|にほん}{最古|さいこ}にして{最大|さいだい}の{木造|もくぞう}{建築|けんちく}だという。 — This temple is said to be both the oldest and the largest wooden building in Japan.

**3. A time word + にして: in just that time.** Set phrases: {一瞬|いっしゅん}にして (in an instant),
{一夜|いちや}にして (overnight), {一代|いちだい}にして (within one generation).

{火事|かじ}で、{百年|ひゃくねん}{続|つづ}いた{工房|こうぼう}が{一夜|いちや}にして{灰|はい}になった。 — In the fire, a workshop that had stood for a hundred years turned to ashes overnight.

With an age, にして also means "at": 「{四十|しじゅう}にして{惑|まど}わず」 (at forty, I was no longer
in doubt) is a well-known line from the Analects of Confucius, quoted in Japanese as a saying.

Don't confuse にして with にしては (for an X; N3): {子供|こども}にしては{上手|じょうず}だ (good, for a child).
にして has no は and no "considering".

## 〜に{至|いた}っては: as for A, the most extreme case

N + に{至|いた}っては comes after several cases have been mentioned (or are in the speaker's mind)
and picks out the most extreme: "and as for A, …". The case is usually a bad or surprising one.

{参加者|さんかしゃ}は{年々|ねんねん}{減|へ}っており、{二十代|にじゅうだい}に{至|いた}っては{一人|ひとり}もいない。 — Participants are falling year by year, and as for people in their twenties, there's not a single one.

{兄|あに}も{姉|あね}も{料理|りょうり}をしないが、{父|ちち}に{至|いた}っては{湯|ゆ}を{沸|わ}かしたこともない。 — Neither my brother nor my sister cooks, and my father has never so much as boiled water.

Points to remember:

- It follows a noun, and that noun is the last and most extreme item of a series (often Aも〜、Bも〜、
  Cに{至|いた}っては〜). It isn't used for the first or only case.
- It's an evaluation: usually critical or amazed, sometimes neutral in reports.
- Style: written and formal speech, and news commentary.
- Its kanji is lesson 26's; N2 wrote にいたる in kana, and this course writes it with kanji now.

> **Review (N2 lesson 26).** 〜に{至|いた}るまで: "everything, right down to": {服装|ふくそう}から{言葉遣|ことばづか}いに
> {至|いた}るまで{厳|きび}しく{言|い}われた (I was told off about everything, from my clothes down to my way of
> speaking). It includes the whole range. 〜に{至|いた}っては singles out the extreme case.
> 〜に{至|いた}って (only when things reached): {事故|じこ}が{起|お}きるに{至|いた}って、ようやく{対策|たいさく}が
> {取|と}られた.
>
> **Review (N2 lesson 21).** 〜に{限|かぎ}らず (not only, not limited to): この{祭|まつ}りは{地元|じもと}の
> {人|ひと}に{限|かぎ}らず、{誰|だれ}でも{参加|さんか}できる. It widens the scope, where ならでは narrows it.

## Choosing between them

| Pattern | What it does | Follows | Feel | Style |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ならではの | only A has this good quality | noun | praise | both; ads and reviews |
| をおいて〜ない | no one / nothing but A | noun | strong praise | written, formal speech |
| にして{初|はじ}めて | only at A's level | noun (person, age) | admiration | written, formal speech |
| AにしてB | A and also B | noun | neutral | written |
| に{至|いた}っては | as for A, the extreme case | noun | critical or amazed | written, formal speech |
| だけ / しか〜ない | a plain limit | noun, verb | neutral | all |

## Words for the arts

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| poetry and literature | {詩|し}, {詩人|しじん}, {詩集|ししゅう}, {詩歌|しいか}, {詩的|してき}, {詠|よ}む, {句|く}, {語句|ごく}, {散文|さんぶん}, {戯曲|ぎきょく}, {叙情|じょじょう}, {叙情的|じょじょうてき}, {叙事詩|じょじし}, {叙述|じょじゅつ}する, {描写|びょうしゃ}する |
| figures of speech | {比喩|ひゆ}, {比喩的|ひゆてき}, {直喩|ちょくゆ}, {隠喩|いんゆ}, {擬人化|ぎじんか}する, {擬音|ぎおん}, {擬態語|ぎたいご} |
| painting and calligraphy | {墨|すみ}, {墨汁|ぼくじゅう}, {水墨画|すいぼくが}, {水彩画|すいさいが}, {色彩|しきさい}, {彩|いろど}る, {彩|いろど}り, {描|えが}く, {構図|こうず}, {余白|よはく}, {遠近法|えんきんほう}, {濃淡|のうたん}, {写実的|しゃじつてき}, {前衛|ぜんえい}, {書家|しょか}, {掛|か}け{軸|じく}, {浮世絵|うきよえ}, {錦絵|にしきえ}, {漫画家|まんがか}, {画風|がふう}, デッサン, アトリエ |

Notes:

- **Figures of speech.** A **[[simile]]** says that one thing is like another, with ような, ように, まるで or
  (lesson 23) ごとく: {雪|ゆき}のように{白|しろ}い{肌|はだ}. It is a {直喩|ちょくゆ}. A **[[metaphor]]** says it
  without "like": {人生|じんせい}は{旅|たび}だ. That is a {隠喩|いんゆ} (also {暗喩|あんゆ}).
  **[[Personification]]** ({擬人化|ぎじんか}) talks about a thing as if it were a person: {風|かぜ}が{歌|うた}う,
  {花|はな}が{笑|わら}う. {比喩|ひゆ} covers all of them.
- {描|えが}く and {描|か}く are the same kanji with two readings. かく is drawing a picture
  ({絵|え}を{描|か}く); えがく is portraying in words or pictures and picturing in the mind
  ({夢|ゆめ}を{描|えが}く), and also drawing shapes ({円|えん}を{描|えが}く).
- {陶器|とうき} is earthenware: thicker, softer, often warm in colour; {磁器|じき} is porcelain: thin, hard
  and white. {陶磁器|とうじき} is both, and {焼|や}き{物|もの} is the everyday word.
- {傑作|けっさく} is an outstanding work; carried {名作|めいさく} a famous classic. In casual speech
  {傑作|けっさく} can also be a joke: それは{傑作|けっさく}だ (that's priceless).
- {情緒|じょうちょ} is the emotional atmosphere a place evokes ({下町|したまち}{情緒|じょうちょ}, {異国|いこく}{情緒|じょうちょ});
  {風情|ふぜい} is a quiet, tasteful charm, often of the seasons. Both are compliments.
- {粋|いき} is the understated chic of old Edo; lesson 30h2 comes back to it as an idea.

## Dialogue: an interview with a lacquer craftsman

A magazine writer, Morita, interviews Ishikawa, a lacquer craftsman, in the workshop. (Formal
speech: an interview.)

```dialogue
# Fifty years of lacquer
もりた: {本日|ほんじつ}はお{忙|いそが}しいところ、ありがとうございます。さっそくですが、{漆|うるし}のお{仕事|しごと}を{始|はじ}められて{何年|なんねん}になりますか。
= Thank you for sparing the time today. To begin: how many years have you been working in lacquer?
いしかわ: {十五|じゅうご}で{弟子入|でしい}りしましたから、もう{五十年|ごじゅうねん}になりますね。
= I became an apprentice at fifteen, so it's been fifty years now.
もりた: この{町|まち}の{漆器|しっき}ならではの{特徴|とくちょう}というと、どんな{点|てん}でしょうか。
= What would you say is unique to this town's lacquerware?
いしかわ: やはり{丈夫|じょうぶ}さでしょうね。{下地|したじ}に{地元|じもと}の{土|つち}を{焼|や}いた{粉|こな}を{混|ま}ぜて、{何度|なんど}も{塗|ぬ}り{重|かさ}ねるんです。{毎日|まいにち}{使|つか}っても、{何十年|なんじゅうねん}ともちますよ。
= Its strength, I'd say. We mix powder made from baked local clay into the base coat and apply coat after coat. Even used every day, it lasts for decades.
もりた: {一|ひと}つの{器|うつわ}に、どのくらい{時間|じかん}がかかるのですか。
= How long does one piece take?
いしかわ: {早|はや}いもので{半年|はんとし}です。{手|て}の{込|こ}んだ{重箱|じゅうばこ}に{至|いた}っては、{一年|いちねん}{以上|いじょう}かかることもあります。
= Half a year for the quick ones. As for an elaborate set of stacking boxes, it can take more than a year.
もりた: {気|き}の{遠|とお}くなるようなお{話|はなし}です。{若|わか}い{頃|ころ}、お{辞|や}めになりたいと{思|おも}われたことはありませんでしたか。
= It makes my head spin. When you were young, did you never want to give it up?

もりた: どんな{方|かた}だったのですか。
= What kind of person was your teacher?
いしかわ: {無口|むくち}な{人|ひと}でしたが、{筆|ふで}を{持|も}たせたら、{師匠|ししょう}をおいてほかにかなう{人|ひと}はいませんでした。
= A person of few words, but with a brush in hand, there was no one who could match my teacher.
もりた: いしかわさんご{自身|じしん}も、{昨年|さくねん}、{人間国宝|にんげんこくほう}に{認定|にんてい}されましたね。
= You yourself were named a Living National Treasure last year.

= Oh no, I've a long way to go. It's only at seventy that I've started to understand lacquer's moods a little.
もりた: {漆|うるし}の{機嫌|きげん}、ですか。
= Lacquer's moods?
いしかわ: ええ。{漆|うるし}は{湿気|しっけ}がないと{固|かた}まらないんです。{梅雨|つゆ}の{頃|ころ}は{早|はや}く{固|かた}まるし、{冬|ふゆ}は{遅|おそ}い。{毎日|まいにち}{違|ちが}うので、{職人|しょくにん}のほうが{漆|うるし}に{合|あ}わせるしかないんですよ。

もりた: {最後|さいご}に、{若|わか}い{方|かた}にひと{言|こと}お{願|ねが}いします。
```

{弟子入|でしい}り = becoming an apprentice; {下地|したじ} = base coat; {重箱|じゅうばこ} = a set of stacking
lacquered boxes for food; {気|き}が{遠|とお}くなる = to feel faint (at the thought); かぶれる = to get a
rash (from a plant or chemical); {無口|むくち} = taciturn; かなう = to match, to be equal to;
{機嫌|きげん} = mood (N3's きげん). Morita's お{辞|や}めになりたい and {思|おも}われた are honorific;
Ishikawa's {私|わたし}などまだまだです is the modest reply to praise. The four patterns: ならではの
(twice), に{至|いた}っては, をおいてほかに〜ない, にしてようやく.
