> {北村|きたむら}は{二十代|にじゅうだい}で{師匠|ししょう}のもとを{離|はな}れ、{生|う}まれ{育|そだ}った{村|むら}に{戻|もど}って{自|みずか}ら{窯|かま}を{築|きず}いた。{以来|いらい}、{土|つち}は{裏山|うらやま}から{掘|ほ}ったものしか{使|つか}わない。「{遠|とお}くの{良|よ}い{土|つち}より、{足元|あしもと}の{土|つち}」というのが{口癖|くちぐせ}だそうだ。{初期|しょき}の{部屋|へや}に{並|なら}ぶ{皿|さら}や{鉢|はち}は{驚|おどろ}くほど{素朴|そぼく}で、{一見|いっけん}すると{地味|じみ}である。だが{説明|せつめい}によれば、どれも{料理|りょうり}を{盛|も}ったときに{初|はじ}めて{完成|かんせい}するように{作|つく}られているという。{飾|かざ}るための{器|うつわ}ではなく、{毎日|まいにち}の{食卓|しょくたく}で{使|つか}うための{器|うつわ}なのだ。
>
> {会場|かいじょう}を{通|とお}して{驚|おどろ}かされるのは、{色|いろ}の{少|すく}なさだ。{北村|きたむら}は{絵付|えつ}けをほとんどしない。{器|うつわ}の{表面|ひょうめん}に{現|あらわ}れる{赤|あか}や{灰色|はいいろ}の{濃淡|のうたん}は、すべて{登|のぼ}り{窯|がま}の{炎|ほのお}と{灰|はい}が{生|う}んだものである。{同|おな}じ{土|つち}、{同|おな}じ{形|かたち}でも、{窯|かま}のどこに{置|お}かれたかで{一点|いってん}ごとに{表情|ひょうじょう}が{異|こと}なる。{窯|かま}の{中|なか}は{千二百度|せんにひゃくど}を{超|こ}え、{火|ひ}を{止|と}めるまでに{五日|いつか}{近|ちか}くかかるという。{作家|さっか}が{完全|かんぜん}には{支配|しはい}できない{火|ひ}に{仕上|しあ}げを{委|ゆだ}ねること、それこそが{登|のぼ}り{窯|がま}ならではの{魅力|みりょく}だと{北村|きたむら}は{語|かた}っている。
>
> {展示|てんじ}の{中盤|ちゅうばん}には、{窯|かま}から{出|だ}した{時点|じてん}でひびが{入|はい}っていた「{失敗作|しっぱいさく}」が、あえて{何点|なんてん}も{並|なら}べられている。{普通|ふつう}なら{割|わ}って{捨|す}てるものを、{北村|きたむら}は{手元|てもと}に{残|のこ}し、{次|つぎ}の{仕事|しごと}の{手|て}がかりにしてきたという。{中|なか}には、ひびを{金|きん}で{継|つ}いで、{花|はな}{入|い}れとして{使|つか}い{続|つづ}けているものもある。{完成品|かんせいひん}だけを{見|み}せる{展覧会|てんらんかい}が{多|おお}い{中|なか}で、この{構成|こうせい}は{作家|さっか}の{六十年|ろくじゅうねん}を{正直|しょうじき}に{物語|ものがた}っている。
>
> {圧巻|あっかん}は、{最後|さいご}の{部屋|へや}に{一枚|いちまい}だけ{置|お}かれた{大皿|おおざら}「{雪原|せつげん}」だ。{白|しろ}い{灰|はい}が{雪|ゆき}のように{降|ふ}り{積|つ}もった{表面|ひょうめん}に、{一筋|ひとすじ}だけ{淡|あわ}い{緑|みどり}が{流|なが}れている。{本人|ほんにん}は「{八十|はちじゅう}にして{初|はじ}めて、{火|ひ}とけんかをしなくなった」と{言|い}う。{若|わか}い{頃|ころ}は{思|おも}いどおりの{色|いろ}を{出|だ}そうとして{火|ひ}と{争|あらそ}い、{窯|かま}を{開|あ}けるたびに{落胆|らくたん}したが、{今|いま}は{火|ひ}が{出|だ}した{答|こた}えをそのまま{受|う}け{入|い}れられるようになったのだという。{長|なが}い{年月|ねんげつ}をかけて{土|つち}と{火|ひ}に{向|む}き{合|あ}ってきた{北村|きたむら}をおいて、この{静|しず}けさに{至|いた}った{作家|さっか}はいないのではないか。
>
> {残念|ざんねん}なのは{展示|てんじ}の{方法|ほうほう}である。{作品|さくひん}の{解説|かいせつ}は{短|みじか}く、{技法|ぎほう}について{知|し}りたい{来場者|らいじょうしゃ}には{物足|ものた}りない。{照明|しょうめい}も{暗|くら}すぎて、{器|うつわ}の{内側|うちがわ}の{色|いろ}がよく{見|み}えない。{外国語|がいこくご}の{案内|あんない}に{至|いた}っては、{入口|いりぐち}の{挨拶文|あいさつぶん}{一枚|いちまい}しかない。{作品|さくひん}の{前|まえ}で{長|なが}く{足|あし}を{止|と}める{人|ひと}が{多|おお}いだけに、{惜|お}しい{点|てん}である。{海外|かいがい}からの{来館者|らいかんしゃ}が{増|ふ}えている{今|いま}、{改善|かいぜん}を{望|のぞ}みたい。
>
> とはいえ、それは{小|ちい}さな{傷|きず}にすぎない。{使|つか}われてこそ{美|うつく}しいという{工芸|こうげい}の{考|かんが}え{方|かた}を、これほど{説得力|せっとくりょく}をもって{示|しめ}す{展覧会|てんらんかい}はめったにない。{会期|かいき}は{来月|らいげつ}{末|まつ}まで。{器|うつわ}が{好|す}きな{人|ひと}はもちろん、{焼|や}き{物|もの}に{関心|かんしん}のなかった{人|ひと}にもぜひ{足|あし}を{運|はこ}んでほしい。

{本格的|ほんかくてき} = full-scale; {回顧展|かいこてん} = retrospective; {鉢|はち} = bowl; {素朴|そぼく} = simple,
unadorned (lesson 28); {絵付|えつ}け = painting designs on ware; {登|のぼ}り{窯|がま} = climbing kiln (a
chain of chambers up a slope); {炎|ほのお} = flame; ひび = crack; あえて = deliberately (lesson 17);
{物語|ものがた}る = to tell the story of; {圧巻|あっかん} = the highlight; {落胆|らくたん} = disappointment (lesson
16); {物足|ものた}りない = not quite satisfying; めったにない = rare (N3's めったに, in kana as in newspapers).

1. Where does Kitamura get the clay, and what does the potter say about it?
2. What makes the colours of Kitamura's ware, according to the review?
3. Why does the reviewer praise the "failures" in the middle of the exhibition?
4. What does the reviewer criticize, and which point is singled out as the worst?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Only from the hill behind the village (「{裏山|うらやま}から{掘|ほ}ったものしか{使|つか}わない」); Kitamura's
   saying is that the clay at your feet is better than good clay from far away.
2. The flames and ash of the climbing kiln, not painting: where each piece stood in the kiln gives
   it its own look. The fire's work is what Kitamura calls the charm only a climbing kiln has
   ({登|のぼ}り{窯|がま}ならではの{魅力|みりょく}).
3. Most exhibitions show only finished pieces; showing the cracked pieces Kitamura kept and learned
   from tells the story of the potter's sixty years honestly.
4. The short explanations, the dim lighting and the lack of foreign-language information; the
   last is the extreme case (に{至|いた}っては): there is only one sheet, the greeting at the entrance.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

The exhibition "A Dialogue of Earth and Fire" at the prefectural art museum is the first
full-scale retrospective of Kitamura Kiyoshi, a potter who has fired ware for nearly sixty years
at a small pottery in the mountains. About two hundred pieces, from the everyday tea bowls of the potter's
youth to the large platters of recent years, are shown in order of date.

In their twenties Kitamura left their teacher, went back to the village where they were born and raised,
and built a kiln of their own. Since then Kitamura has used only clay dug from the hill behind the
village. A favourite saying, we are told, is "Better the clay at your feet than good clay from far
away." The plates and bowls in the first room are surprisingly simple, plain at first glance. But
according to the explanation, each was made to be complete only once food is served on it. They
are not vessels for display but vessels for the table every day.

What strikes you throughout the exhibition is how little colour there is. Kitamura hardly paints
the ware at all. The shades of red and grey on the surface are all the work of the flames and ash
of a climbing kiln. Even with the same clay and the same shape, each piece looks different
depending on where it stood in the kiln. The inside of the kiln goes above 1,200 degrees, and it
is said to take nearly five days before the fire is put out. Leaving the finish to a fire the
artist can never fully control: that, Kitamura says, is the charm only a climbing kiln has.

In the middle of the exhibition, several "failures", pieces that came out of the kiln already
cracked, are deliberately shown. What anyone else would break and throw away, Kitamura kept and
used as a clue for the next work. Some even have their cracks mended with gold and are still in
use as flower vases. When so many exhibitions show only finished pieces, this arrangement tells
the story of the artist's sixty years honestly.

The highlight is a single large platter, "Snowfield", placed alone in the last room. Across a
surface where white ash has settled like snow runs one line of pale green. "Only at eighty have I
stopped fighting with the fire," the potter says. When young, Kitamura fought the fire to get the
colours they wanted and was disappointed every time the kiln was opened; now the potter can accept the
fire's answer as it is. Could any artist other than Kitamura, who has faced earth and fire for so
many years, have reached this stillness?

What is disappointing is the way the work is displayed. The explanations are short and leave
visitors who want to know about technique unsatisfied. The lighting is too dim, too, and the
colours inside the bowls are hard to see. As for information in foreign languages, there is only
one sheet, the greeting at the entrance. Since so many people stop for a long time in front of the
works, this is all the more a pity. With visitors from abroad increasing, I hope this will be
improved.

That said, these are small flaws. Rarely does an exhibition show so convincingly the idea that
crafts are beautiful because they are used. It runs until the end of next month. I hope not only
lovers of ceramics but also people who have never been interested in pottery will go and see it.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{京都|きょうと}ならではの{味|あじ}ですね。
= That's a taste only Kyoto has.
{彼女|かのじょ}をおいて{適任者|てきにんしゃ}はいません。
= There's no one better suited than her.
{名人|めいじん}にして{初|はじ}めてできる{技|わざ}です。
= It's a technique only a master can manage.
{一瞬|いっしゅん}にして{雰囲気|ふんいき}が{変|か}わった。
= The atmosphere changed in an instant.
{若|わか}い{世代|せだい}に{至|いた}っては、{名前|なまえ}も{知|し}らない。
= As for the young generation, they don't even know the name.
```

## Common mistakes

- {私|わたし}ならではのミス isn't used. ならでは praises a good, characteristic quality; for a typical mistake say
  {私|わたし}らしいミス or {私|わたし}にありがちなミス.
- {会員|かいいん}ならでは{入|はい}れます doesn't mean "only members may enter". A rule is {会員|かいいん}のみ or
  {会員|かいいん}しか{入|はい}れません.
- {彼|かれ}をおいて{適任者|てきにんしゃ}がいる: をおいて needs a negative or a "who else?" question after it:
  {適任者|てきにんしゃ}はいない.
- Reading をおいて as において. {会議|かいぎ}において is "at the meeting"; {彼|かれ}をおいて is "apart from
  him".
- {子供|こども}にして{上手|じょうず}だ doesn't mean "good for a child". That's にしては; にして{初|はじ}めて is
  "only at".
- Using に{至|いた}っては for the first or only case. It's the last and most extreme of a series:
  {母|はは}も{兄|あに}も…、{父|ちち}に{至|いた}っては….
- Writing {描|えが}く for every "draw". A picture is {描|か}く; えがく is portraying and imagining.

## Key points

- N + ならではの N: what only A has, praised (not faults, not rules). だけ is the plain fact.
- N + をおいて + negative (or "who else?"): no one but A; strong praise; written, formal speech;
  kana. {何|なに}をおいても = before anything else.
- N + にして: (1) にして{初|はじ}めて / ようやく, only at A's level; (2) AにしてB, A and also B;
  (3) {一瞬|いっしゅん}にして, {一夜|いちや}にして. Not にしては.
- N + に{至|いた}っては: as for A, the extreme case of a series; usually critical; written and formal.
- Simile ({直喩|ちょくゆ}), metaphor ({隠喩|いんゆ}) and personification ({擬人化|ぎじんか}) are all
  {比喩|ひゆ}.
- New kanji: 詩 詠 吟 謡 句 叙 擬 喩 譜 墨 描 彩 彫 陶 漆 窯 瓦 漫 飾 紋 錦 絹 扇 華 麗 雅 粋 匠 傑 鑑 伎 弦.
  Write {鑑賞|かんしょう}, {漫画|まんが}, {漫才|まんざい}, {歌舞伎|かぶき}, {俳句|はいく}, {文句|もんく}, {飾|かざ}る with
  kanji from now on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Covered in: ずくめ, まみれ, めく, ぐるみ
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 21 singled one thing out. This lesson's four suffixes say how far something spreads over a
person, a thing or a group: all over, covered in, with a touch of, all of them together.

{黒|くろ}ずくめの{男|おとこ}が{門|もん}の{前|まえ}に{立|た}っていた。 — A man dressed all in black was standing at the gate.

{子供|こども}たちは{泥|どろ}まみれになって{遊|あそ}んでいる。 — The children are playing, covered in mud.

{日差|ひざ}しが{春|はる}めいてきた。 — The sunshine is starting to feel like spring.

{町|まち}ぐるみで{祭|まつ}りの{準備|じゅんび}をする。 — The whole town gets the festival ready together.

All four follow a noun directly. ずくめ, まみれ and ぐるみ make a noun phrase (〜の + noun, 〜で,
〜だ); めく is a group 1 verb (めいて, めいた). They're at home in writing and in everyday speech
alike, though めく sounds a little literary.

The theme is history: the shogunate and the domains, emperors and the court, castles, walls and
weapons, eras and calendars, and the rise and fall of states. Earlier courses gave you the basics
({歴史|れきし}, {時代|じだい}, {武士|ぶし}, {大名|だいみょう}, {将軍|しょうぐん}, {城下町|じょうかまち}); N1 adds the words of
historians and of historical fiction, and this lesson's kanji let you write {侍|さむらい},
{西暦|せいれき}, {世紀|せいき} and {字幕|じまく}.

## N + ずくめ: nothing but A

ずくめ says that everything about something is A: from head to toe, or one thing after another.

| Form | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| A ずくめの B | {黒|くろ}ずくめの{服装|ふくそう} | clothes that are black from head to toe |
| A ずくめだ | {今年|ことし}はいいことずくめだった | this year was nothing but good things |

{入学式|にゅうがくしき}の{日|ひ}は{初|はじ}めてずくめで、{一日|いちにち}が{長|なが}かった。 — On the day of the entrance ceremony, everything was a first, and the day felt long.

{今回|こんかい}の{大会|たいかい}は{異例|いれい}ずくめだった。 — This year's tournament was one exception after another.

この{寮|りょう}は{規則|きそく}ずくめで、{息|いき}が{詰|つ}まる。 — This dormitory is nothing but rules; it's stifling.

Points to remember:

- It goes with a fairly small set of nouns: colours ({黒|くろ}, {白|しろ}), いいこと / {良|よ}いこと,
  {結構|けっこう} (all fine, often ironic: {結構|けっこう}ずくめの{話|はなし}), ごちそう, {規則|きそく}, {異例|いれい},
  {初|はじ}めて. With other nouns it can sound odd; use ばかり or だらけ.
- It can be good or bad: いいことずくめ is good, {規則|きそく}ずくめ is bad.
- It isn't used for dirt or stains: "covered in mud" is {泥|どろ}まみれ; {泥|どろ}ずくめ isn't used.
- You'll also see it spelled づくめ, from {尽|つ}くす (to use up); ずくめ is the usual modern
  spelling.

## N + まみれ: covered in (something messy)

まみれ says that a surface is covered all over with something unpleasant that sticks to it: mud,
sweat, blood, dust, oil, flour. Figuratively it's used for debt and for corruption.

{雨|あめ}の{中|なか}の{試合|しあい}で、ユニフォームが{泥|どろ}まみれになった。 — In the match in the rain, our kits were covered in mud.

{倉庫|そうこ}から、ほこりまみれの{箱|はこ}が{出|で}てきた。 — A box covered in dust came out of the storeroom.

{夏|なつ}の{現場|げんば}では、{一日|いちにち}で{汗|あせ}まみれになる。 — On a building site in summer you're drenched in sweat within a day.

{彼|かれ}は{事業|じぎょう}に{失敗|しっぱい}して、{借金|しゃっきん}まみれになった。 — His business failed and he ended up up to his ears in debt.

Points to remember:

- It's always bad, and the thing must cover the surface: {花|はな}まみれ (flowers aren't messy) and
  {間違|まちが}いまみれ aren't used (mistakes don't cover a surface; that's {間違|まちが}いだらけ).
- Forms: Aまみれの + noun, Aまみれになる, Aまみれで. Always in kana.
- Typical: {泥|どろ}, {汗|あせ}, {血|ち}, ほこり, {油|あぶら}, {粉|こな}, {借金|しゃっきん}.

## N + めく: with a touch of A

めく after a noun means "to show signs of A, to have something of A about it" without quite being
A. It's a group 1 verb, used mostly as めいてきた (the signs are appearing) and めいた + noun.

{三月|さんがつ}に{入|はい}り、{風|かぜ}がずいぶん{春|はる}めいてきた。 — Now that it's March, the wind has become quite spring-like.

{彼|かれ}は{皮肉|ひにく}めいた{笑|わら}いを{浮|う}かべた。 — He gave a slightly sarcastic smile.

{部長|ぶちょう}の{話|はなし}は、いつも{説教|せっきょう}めいている。 — The section head's talks always sound a bit like a sermon.

{謎|なぞ}めいた{手紙|てがみ}が{届|とど}いた。 — A mysterious letter arrived.

Points to remember:

- The nouns are limited: seasons ({春|はる}めく, {秋|あき}めく), and abstract nouns of speech and
  manner: {皮肉|ひにく}, {冗談|じょうだん}, {謎|なぞ}, {説教|せっきょう} (a lecture), {言|い}い{訳|わけ}, {予言|よげん}
  (prophecy), {脅|おど}し (a threat).
- The negative ({春|はる}めかない) isn't used; say まだ{春|はる}らしくない.
- 〜めかす is "to make it seem like A": {冗談|じょうだん}めかして{本音|ほんね}を{言|い}う (to say what one really
  thinks as if joking). {古|ふる}めかしい (old-fashioned) is built the same way.
- めく is a little literary. In casual speech, っぽい (N3) does a similar job: {皮肉|ひにく}っぽい
  {言|い}い{方|かた}.

## N + ぐるみ: all of A, together

ぐるみ means "including all of A, the whole of A together". It's neutral: what follows decides
whether it's good or bad.

{隣|となり}の{家|いえ}とは{家族|かぞく}ぐるみの{付|つ}き{合|あ}いをしている。 — We're friends with the family next door, children, parents and all.

{商店街|しょうてんがい}では、{町|まち}ぐるみで{防犯|ぼうはん}に{取|と}り{組|く}んでいる。 — The shopping street is working on crime prevention as a whole community.

{会社|かいしゃ}ぐるみの{不正|ふせい}が{明|あき}らかになった。 — Wrongdoing involving the whole company has come to light.

Points to remember:

- Typical: {家族|かぞく}, {町|まち}, {村|むら}, {地域|ちいき}, {会社|かいしゃ}, {組織|そしき}, {学校|がっこう}.
- Forms: Aぐるみの + noun, Aぐるみで.
- With wrongdoing ({会社|かいしゃ}ぐるみの{犯罪|はんざい}), it says the organization itself, not one person,
  was behind it.
- {身|み}ぐるみ{剥|は}がされる is a set phrase: to be stripped of everything one has. The same ぐるみ is
  in ぬいぐるみ (a stuffed toy: something wrapped in cloth).

> **Review (N3).** 〜だらけ: full of, covered with, usually bad: {間違|まちが}いだらけの{答案|とうあん}, {傷|きず}だらけ,
> ほこりだらけ. It is the widest of these: when ずくめ or まみれ doesn't fit, だらけ often does.
>
> **Review (N3 and N2 lesson 24).** 〜っぽい (N3): -ish, tending to, casual: {子供|こども}っぽい, {忘|わす}れっぽい,
> {白|しろ}っぽい. 〜げ (N2): looking, seeming, written: {寂|さび}しげな{顔|かお}.

## ずくめ, まみれ, だらけ: which one?

| | ずくめ | まみれ | だらけ |
|---|---|---|---|
| says | everything is A | the surface is covered with A | full of A, lots of A |
| good or bad | either | bad | mostly bad |
| typical | {黒|くろ}, いいこと, {規則|きそく}, {異例|いれい} | {泥|どろ}, {汗|あせ}, {血|ち}, ほこり, {借金|しゃっきん} | {間違|まちが}い, {傷|きず}, ほこり, {穴|あな} |
| only this one | {黒|くろ}ずくめの{男|おとこ} | {汗|あせ}まみれのシャツ | {間違|まちが}いだらけの{作文|さくぶん} |

> {手|て}がかりになっているのは、{藩|はん}の{記録|きろく}である。{藩主|はんしゅ}の{子孫|しそん}の{家|いえ}の{蔵|くら}から、{石垣|いしがき}の{修理|しゅうり}について{記|しる}した{古文書|こもんじょ}が{見|み}つかった。{日付|ひづけ}は{旧暦|きゅうれき}で{書|か}かれており、{今|いま}の{暦|こよみ}に{直|なお}すと、{修理|しゅうり}は{真冬|まふゆ}に{行|おこな}われていたことが{分|わ}かる。ただ、その{中|なか}には{謎|なぞ}めいた{記述|きじゅつ}もある。「{北|きた}の{角|かど}の{石|いし}、{動|うご}かすべからず」とだけ{書|か}かれ、{理由|りゆう}は{何|なに}も{記|しる}されていないのだ。{石垣|いしがき}{全体|ぜんたい}を{支|ささ}える{要|かなめ}の{石|いし}なのか、それとも{信仰|しんこう}に{関|かか}わる{石|いし}なのか、{専門家|せんもんか}の{間|あいだ}でも{意見|いけん}が{分|わ}かれている。{工事|こうじ}チームは、ひとまず{記録|きろく}どおり、その{石|いし}には{手|て}を{触|ふ}れないことにした。
>
> {作業|さぎょう}を{支|ささ}えているのは、{町|まち}の{人々|ひとびと}だ。{週末|しゅうまつ}になると、{高校生|こうこうせい}から{八十代|はちじゅうだい}の{住民|じゅうみん}までが{集|あつ}まり、{職人|しょくにん}の{指示|しじ}に{従|したが}って{小|ちい}さな{石|いし}を{運|はこ}ぶ。{雨|あめ}の{日|ひ}には{全員|ぜんいん}が{泥|どろ}まみれになるが、{不満|ふまん}を{言|い}う{人|ひと}はほとんどいない。{家族|かぞく}ぐるみで{参加|さんか}している{人|ひと}も{多|おお}く、「{孫|まご}が{大人|おとな}になったとき、この{石|いし}はおじいちゃんが{運|はこ}んだんだと{言|い}えるのがうれしい」と{笑|わら}う{人|ひと}もいた。{作業|さぎょう}の{後|あと}、{汗|あせ}まみれのまま{皆|みな}で{弁当|べんとう}を{広|ひろ}げるのが{恒例|こうれい}になっている。
>
> もちろん、いいことずくめではない。{費用|ひよう}の{大半|たいはん}は{国|くに}と{県|けん}の{補助|ほじょ}に{頼|たよ}っており、{予算|よさん}が{削|けず}られれば{工事|こうじ}は{止|と}まる。{観光|かんこう}{資源|しげん}として{期待|きたい}する{声|こえ}がある{一方|いっぽう}で、「{石垣|いしがき}より{先|さき}に{道路|どうろ}を{直|なお}してほしい」という{住民|じゅうみん}もいる。
>
> それでも、{石|いし}を{一|ひと}つ{積|つ}むごとに、{町|まち}の{人々|ひとびと}は{四百年|よんひゃくねん}{前|まえ}の{誰|だれ}かと{一緒|いっしょ}に{働|はたら}いているのかもしれない。{石垣|いしがき}が{元|もと}の{姿|すがた}に{戻|もど}る{頃|ころ}には、{今|いま}{石|いし}を{運|はこ}んでいる{高校生|こうこうせい}たちも{大人|おとな}になっているだろう。{春|はる}めいてきた{城跡|しろあと}の{堀|ほり}の{水面|みなも}に、{今年|ことし}も{桜|さくら}が{映|うつ}り{始|はじ}めた。

{崩|くず}れ{落|お}ちる = to collapse; {象徴|しょうちょう} = symbol; {運命|うんめい}をたどる = to meet the same fate;
{重機|じゅうき} = heavy machinery; {代々|だいだい} = for generations; {石工|いしく} = stonemason; {詰|つ}め{方|かた} =
the way of packing; {子孫|しそん} = descendants; {記述|きじゅつ} = a written passage; 〜べからず = "must not"
(lesson 20); {要|かなめ} = the key point; {恒例|こうれい} = a regular custom; {補助|ほじょ} = subsidy;
{城跡|しろあと} = castle ruins; {水面|みなも} = the surface of the water (literary).

1. Why did the town start rebuilding the wall, and why will it take about ten years?
2. What makes the old document "mysterious", and what did the team decide?
3. What are the two problems the writer mentions?
4. In the last paragraph, what does the writer suggest the townspeople are doing as they carry the stones?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Part of the wall collapsed in an earthquake five years ago. Instead of using heavy machinery,
   they return every fallen stone to its original place by the old methods, a little at a time.
2. It says only that the stone at the north corner must not be moved, with no reason given; experts
   disagree about why. The team decided, for now, not to touch that stone, as the record says.
3. Money: most of the cost depends on national and prefectural subsidies, so budget cuts would stop
   the work; and opinion: some residents would rather have the roads repaired first.
4. Working together with someone from four hundred years ago (the builders of the original wall).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

In this castle town of about thirty thousand people, the whole community is now at work rebuilding
the castle's stone walls. It began when part of the walls, built at the start of the Edo period,
collapsed in an earthquake five years ago.

The castle was built at the end of the Warring States period, and its keep was pulled down early in
the Meiji era. After the domains were abolished, castles were seen as symbols of an old age, and many
castles across the country met the same fate. All that remained were the stone walls and the moat.
Even so, for the townspeople the walls are still the face of the town, coloured by cherry blossoms in
spring and autumn leaves in autumn.

The work is one exception after another. First, every single fallen stone is collected, numbered and
put back in its original place. New stones are used as little as possible. What heavy machinery
could do in a few months is being done little by little by the old methods, so completion is expected
to take ten years. The way of laying the stones is a skill handed down for generations in a family of
craftsmen, and the person directing the work is a stonemason in their seventies who inherited that skill.
They say the strength of a wall depends on how the small stones are packed deep inside, where you
can't see them.

The clue is the domain's records. An old document describing repairs to the walls was found in the
storehouse of the family descended from the domain lords. Its dates are written in the old calendar,
and converted to today's calendar they show that the repairs were done in midwinter. But it also
contains a mysterious passage. It says only, "The stone at the north corner must not be moved," with
no reason at all. Whether it is a keystone that supports the whole wall or a stone connected with
some belief, even the experts disagree. For now, the team has decided to follow the record and not to
touch that stone.

The work is supported by the townspeople. At weekends residents from high-school students to people
in their eighties gather and carry small stones as the craftsmen direct. On rainy days everyone ends
up covered in mud, but hardly anyone complains. Many take part as whole families, and one person
laughed, "I'm glad that when my grandchild grows up, I'll be able to say Grandpa carried this stone."
After the work, it has become the custom for everyone to open their lunch boxes together, still
drenched in sweat.

Of course, it isn't all good news. Most of the cost depends on subsidies from the national and
prefectural governments, and if the budget is cut, the work will stop. While some hope it will become
a tourist attraction, some residents say, "I'd rather they fixed the roads before the walls."

Even so, with each stone they lay, the townspeople may be working alongside someone from four hundred
years ago. By the time the walls are back as they were, the high-school students carrying stones now
will be adults. On the surface of the moat of the castle ruins, where spring is in the air, the cherry
blossoms have begun to be reflected again this year.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{黒|くろ}ずくめの{服|ふく}で{現|あらわ}れた。
= They turned up dressed all in black.
{子供|こども}たちは{泥|どろ}まみれだ。
= The children are covered in mud.
だいぶ{春|はる}めいてきましたね。
= It's getting quite spring-like, isn't it?
{家族|かぞく}ぐるみで{付|つ}き{合|あ}っています。
= Our families are friends.
いいことずくめの{一年|いちねん}でした。
= It was a year of nothing but good things.
```

## Common mistakes

- {泥|どろ}ずくめ and {汗|あせ}ずくめ aren't used. Dirt and sweat that cover a surface take まみれ; ずくめ is for "everything
  is A" ({黒|くろ}ずくめ, いいことずくめ).
- {間違|まちが}いまみれ isn't used. まみれ is something messy covering a surface; many mistakes are
  {間違|まちが}いだらけ.
- {花|はな}まみれの{庭|にわ} isn't said. まみれ is always unpleasant: a garden full of flowers is {花|はな}でいっぱい.
- {春|はる}めかない isn't used. めく has no negative in use: まだ{春|はる}らしくない.
- Using めく with any noun: {先生|せんせい}めいた is rare. めく takes seasons and a few abstract nouns
  ({皮肉|ひにく}, {冗談|じょうだん}, {謎|なぞ}, {説教|せっきょう}); for "like a teacher" say {先生|せんせい}らしい or
  {先生|せんせい}のような.
- Thinking ぐるみ is always bad. {家族|かぞく}ぐるみの{付|つ}き{合|あ}い is warm; only the context
  ({会社|かいしゃ}ぐるみの{不正|ふせい}) makes it bad.
- {皇帝|こうてい} for Japan's emperor: that's {天皇|てんのう}.

## Key points

- N + ずくめ: nothing but A (black clothes, good things, rules, exceptions); good or bad; a limited set
  of nouns.
- N + まみれ: covered all over with something messy that sticks (mud, sweat, blood, dust, debt); bad.
- N + めく / めいた: showing signs of A ({春|はる}めく) or with a touch of A ({皮肉|ひにく}めいた); limited
  nouns; no negative.
- N + ぐるみ: all of A together ({家族|かぞく}ぐるみ, {町|まち}ぐるみ, {会社|かいしゃ}ぐるみ); neutral.
- だらけ (N3) is the widest: full of, usually bad.
- New kanji: 藩 幕 侍 帝 姫 殿 摂 庶 仙 堀 塀 垣 郭 邸 倉 籠 刀 矢 昭 暦 紀 弥 唐 呉 鎌 滅 鎮 伐 没 拓 陵 甲.
  Write {侍|さむらい}, {西暦|せいれき}, {世紀|せいき}, {字幕|じまく}, {絶滅|ぜつめつ} with kanji from now on.

the lesson.

lessons.title: Tendencies and likeness: きらいがある, ごとき, ごとく, んばかり
topics: ごとき and ごとく
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson is about two things the written language says with patterns of its own. The first is
**[[tendency]]**: what someone is inclined to do, usually something unwelcome. The second is
**[[likeness]]**: what something resembles, or seems about to do.

{彼|かれ}は{何|なん}でも{一人|ひとり}で{抱|かか}え{込|こ}むきらいがある。 — He tends to take everything on by himself.

{前述|ぜんじゅつ}のごとく、この{地域|ちいき}は{雨|あめ}が{少|すく}ない。 — As stated above, this region gets little rain.

{会場|かいじょう}は{割|わ}れんばかりの{拍手|はくしゅ}に{包|つつ}まれた。 — The hall was filled with applause fit to bring the roof down.

{子供|こども}たちは{待|ま}ってましたとばかりに{外|そと}へ{飛|と}び{出|だ}した。 — The children rushed outside as if they'd been waiting for this.

All four are written or literary. In conversation you'd use 〜がちだ, 〜ところがある, ように / みたいに and
〜そうなほど instead; you'll hear these four in speeches, news commentary and storytelling, and read
them everywhere.

The theme is the earth: mountains and valleys, coasts and the sea, volcanoes and floods, caves and
deserts, soil and fields. Earlier courses gave you the landscape and disaster words ({地形|ちけい}, {半島|はんとう}, {平野|へいや},
{被災|ひさい}); this lesson adds the words of geography books, travel writing and disaster
reports, and lets you write {洪水|こうずい} and {揺|ゆ}れる with kanji.

## 〜きらいがある: a bad tendency

〜きらいがある says that a person, a group or an institution tends to do something the speaker
considers undesirable. It's a critical, written pattern.

| Before きらいがある | Example |
|---|---|
| verb, dictionary form | {物事|ものごと}を{大|おお}げさに{言|い}うきらいがある |
| verb, ない form | {人|ひと}の{話|はなし}を{最後|さいご}まで{聞|き}かないきらいがある |
| noun + の | {説明|せつめい}{不足|ぶそく}のきらいがある |

{最近|さいきん}の{報道|ほうどう}は、{一|ひと}つの{事件|じけん}を{必要|ひつよう}{以上|いじょう}に{大|おお}きく{扱|あつか}うきらいがある。 — Recent reporting tends to make more of a single incident than it needs to.

{私|わたし}には、{忙|いそが}しくなると{返事|へんじ}を{後回|あとまわ}しにするきらいがある。 — I have a tendency to put off replying when I get busy.

{彼|かれ}の{論文|ろんぶん}は、{結論|けつろん}を{急|いそ}ぎすぎるきらいがある。 — His papers tend to rush to their conclusions.

Points to remember:

- Only for undesirable tendencies of behaviour or thinking. A good habit isn't a きらい: "she
  tends to get up early" is {早起|はやお}きする{習慣|しゅうかん}がある; {早起|はやお}きするきらいがある isn't used.
- Not for nature or statistics: "basins tend to be hot in summer" is {盆地|ぼんち}は{夏|なつ}に{暑|あつ}くなる
  {傾向|けいこう}がある; {暑|あつ}くなるきらいがある isn't used. きらいがある is a judgement of conduct.
- It's used of other people and groups, and of oneself when owning up to a fault.
- The きらい is the noun of {嫌|きら}う (to dislike), here meaning "a leaning"; it's written in kana in this
  pattern.

| Pattern | What it says | Good or bad | Style |
|---|---|---|---|
| 〜がちだ (N3) | something (often unwanted) happens often | mostly bad | everyday |
| 〜{傾向|けいこう}がある (N3) | a tendency in facts or numbers | neutral | neutral, reports |
| 〜きらいがある | a person's or group's bad leaning | critical | written, formal |
| 〜やすい (N4) | easily, prone to (physically) | neutral | everyday |

## ごとく, ごとき, ごとし: like (written)

ごとし is the classical word for "like, as if" (modern ようだ). Modern writing uses three of its
forms, joined like ようだ: noun + の, or a verb + (が).

| Form | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 〜のごとく / 〜がごとく | adverb: "as, like" before a verb | {前述|ぜんじゅつ}のごとく, {湯水|ゆみず}のごとく{使|つか}う |
| 〜のごとき / 〜がごとき | before a noun | {夢|ゆめ}のごとき{日々|ひび} |
| 〜のごとし | at the end of a sentence | {光陰|こういん}{矢|や}のごとし |

{例|れい}のごとく、{会議|かいぎ}は{予定|よてい}より{長引|ながび}いた。 — As usual, the meeting ran over.

{彼|かれ}は{親|おや}の{財産|ざいさん}を{湯水|ゆみず}のごとく{使|つか}った。 — He spent his parents' money like water.

{山|やま}のごとき{書類|しょるい}を{前|まえ}に、{途方|とほう}に{暮|く}れた。 — Faced with a mountain of paperwork, I was at a loss.

{光陰|こういん}{矢|や}のごとし。 — Time flies like an arrow. (a saying)

Points to remember:

- It's written style, also heard in formal speeches. In speech say ように / ような / みたいに.
- Verb + がごとく is more literary than verb + ごとく: {飛|と}ぶがごとく{走|はし}り{去|さ}った (sped away as
  if flying).
- ごとし at the end of a sentence survives mostly in sayings; lesson 26 teaches it as a classical
  form. None of these forms is a drill form.
- Dictionaries write it with lesson 26's kanji 如; this course writes ごとし / ごとく / ごとき in kana,
  as newspapers do.
- Set phrases: {例|れい}のごとく (as usual), {前述|ぜんじゅつ}のごとく / {以下|いか}のごとく (as above / as
  follows), {周知|しゅうち}のごとく (as is well known).

### N + ごとき: "the likes of"

Straight after a noun, without の, ごとき looks down on the person: "the likes of A, a mere A".
Used of oneself it's humble; of others, scornful.

{私|わたし}ごときに、こんな{大役|たいやく}が{務|つと}まるでしょうか。 — Could the likes of me really fill such an important role? (humble)

あんな{若造|わかぞう}ごときに{負|ま}けてたまるか。 — I won't lose to the likes of that young upstart! (scornful)

Never use it of the person you're talking to or of someone you respect. With の, the meaning is
"like": {彼|かれ}のごとき{人物|じんぶつ} (a man such as he), which isn't scornful.

## ない stem + んばかり: as if about to

The ない stem + んばかり says that something looks just about to happen, though it doesn't:
"fit to, almost, as if about to". する becomes せんばかり.

| Verb | ない stem + んばかり |
|---|---|
| {泣|な}く | {泣|な}かんばかり |
| {割|わ}れる | {割|わ}れんばかり |
| あふれる | あふれんばかり |
| {飛|と}びかかる | {飛|と}びかからんばかり |
| する | せんばかり |

{彼女|かのじょ}は{泣|な}かんばかりに{頼|たの}み{込|こ}んだ。 — She begged, almost in tears.

{箱|はこ}からあふれんばかりの{花|はな}が{届|とど}いた。 — Flowers arrived, almost spilling out of the box.

{彼|かれ}は{今|いま}にも{飛|と}びかからんばかりの{勢|いきお}いで{怒鳴|どな}った。 — He shouted as if he was about to leap at someone.

Points to remember:

- Forms: 〜んばかりに + verb, 〜んばかりの + noun, 〜んばかりだ.
- It describes what an observer sees: other people's faces and actions, a crowd, a scene. It isn't
  used for your own intention ("I was about to cry" is {泣|な}きそうだった).
- Written and literary; in speech, 〜そうなほど / 〜そうなくらい.
- The ん is the classical auxiliary む / ん ("will, about to", 05h2's classical auxiliaries), the same
  ん as in lesson 12's んがため.

## 〜とばかりに: as if to say

Words in quotation (or a plain form) + とばかりに: someone acts in a way that seems to say
something, without saying it.

{彼|かれ}は「もう{帰|かえ}れ」とばかりに{時計|とけい}を{見|み}た。 — He glanced at the clock as if to say "Go home."

{店|みせ}はここぞとばかりに{値段|ねだん}を{上|あ}げた。 — The shop seized its moment and raised prices.

Points to remember:

- The person is someone else, seen from outside.
- Set phrases: ここぞとばかりに (seizing the moment), {待|ま}ってましたとばかりに (as if they'd been
  waiting for it).
- 〜と{言|い}わんばかりに is the same idea with んばかり: {迷惑|めいわく}だと{言|い}わんばかりの{顔|かお} (a face that
  all but said "you're a nuisance").

> **Review (N2 lesson 24).** 〜かのように: as if (often contrary to fact): {彼|かれ}は{何|なに}もなかったかのように
> {笑|わら}った. んばかり is "as if about to"; かのように is "as if it were so".
>
> **Review (N3).** 〜がち (often): {冬|ふゆ}は{風邪|かぜ}をひきがちだ. 〜{傾向|けいこう}がある (there is a tendency):
> {若者|わかもの}の{読書|どくしょ}{時間|じかん}は{減|へ}る{傾向|けいこう}にある.

## Saying what something is like

| Pattern | Meaning | Style |
|---|---|---|
| ようだ / みたいだ (N4) | like, as if | everyday (みたい casual) |
| 〜のごとく / ごとき / ごとし | like | written, literary |
| かのように (N2) | as if (it isn't really so) | written and speech |
| んばかり | as if about to | written, literary |
| とばかりに | as if to say | written, storytelling |
| N + ごとき | the likes of | humble or scornful |

## Words for the earth

| Topic | Words |

## Dialogue: a guided walk on the coast

A guide, Takahashi, takes a group along a stretch of rocky coast. Mari and Ken are on the tour.
(The guide speaks polite, slightly formal Japanese; the visitors are polite with the guide and
casual with each other.)

```dialogue

たかはし: {皆様|みなさま}、{足元|あしもと}にお{気|き}をつけください。ここから{先|さき}は{岩|いわ}がぬれていて、{滑|すべ}りやすくなっております。

まり: わあ、すごい{崖|がけ}。{下|した}の{海|うみ}、{渦|うず}を{巻|ま}いてますね。
= Wow, what a cliff. The sea down there is swirling.
たかはし: ええ、この{辺|あた}りは{潮|しお}の{流|なが}れが{速|はや}いんです。{満潮|まんちょう}になると、あの{洞窟|どうくつ}の{入口|いりぐち}まで{水|みず}が{来|き}ます。

けん: {写真|しゃしん}を{撮|と}るなら、もう{少|すこ}し{前|まえ}に{出|で}たほうがいいかな。
= If I want a photo, maybe I should go a bit further forward.
たかはし: あ、そのロープより{先|さき}には{出|で}ないでください。{写真|しゃしん}に{夢中|むちゅう}になると、{皆様|みなさま}{崖|がけ}に{近|ちか}づきすぎるきらいがありまして…。

= Sorry.
```

ロープ = rope; {竜|りゅう} = dragon (lesson 30's kanji); {昇|のぼ}る = to rise; カモメ = gull; {狙|ねら}う = to go for,
to aim at (lesson 11); ひんやり = pleasantly cool (N2); {満|み}ち{引|ひ}き = the ebb and flow. The guide's
きらいがありまして is a gentle way to criticize the customers: it says "people tend to" without naming
Ken. {昇|のぼ}るがごとき is guidebook style, a little literary for effect.

>
> {高度|こうど}{成長期|せいちょうき}{以降|いこう}、{都市|とし}が{広|ひろ}がるにつれ、こうした{低地|ていち}は{次々|つぎつぎ}に{住宅地|じゅうたくち}に{変|か}わった。{開発|かいはつ}{業者|ぎょうしゃ}の{中|なか}には、{地価|ちか}の{安|やす}さに{目|め}をつけ、ここぞとばかりに{宅地|たくち}を{売|う}り{出|だ}したところもある。{買|か}う{側|がわ}も、{駅|えき}からの{近|ちか}さや{値段|ねだん}ばかりに{目|め}を{奪|うば}われ、{土地|とち}の{過去|かこ}にまで{関心|かんしん}を{払|はら}わなかった。
>
> もちろん、{開発|かいはつ}そのものが{悪|わる}いわけではない。{低地|ていち}の{開発|かいはつ}がなければ、{都市|とし}に{集|あつ}まる{人々|ひとびと}に{十分|じゅうぶん}な{住宅|じゅうたく}を{用意|ようい}することはできなかっただろう。{排水|はいすい}{設備|せつび}の{整備|せいび}や、{土|つち}を{盛|も}って{地面|じめん}を{高|たか}くする{工事|こうじ}など、{危険|きけん}を{減|へ}らす{工夫|くふう}も{重|かさ}ねられてきた。{問題|もんだい}は、そうした{対策|たいさく}があることで、{住|す}む{人|ひと}が{土地|とち}の{弱|よわ}さを{忘|わす}れてしまうことにある。{対策|たいさく}が{進|すす}めば{進|すす}むほど{危険|きけん}が{見|み}えにくくなるという、{皮肉|ひにく}な{面|めん}があるのだ。
>
> {大雨|おおあめ}の{夜|よる}、あふれんばかりの{川|かわ}を{前|まえ}にして{初|はじ}めて{危険|きけん}に{気|き}づくのでは{遅|おそ}い。{自治体|じちたい}が{作|つく}るハザードマップには、{浸水|しんすい}が{予想|よそう}される{区域|くいき}が{示|しめ}されている。{家|いえ}を{選|えら}ぶ{際|さい}には、{地図|ちず}を{開|ひら}き、その{土地|とち}がかつて{何|なん}であったのかを{確|たし}かめたい。{古|ふる}い{地形図|ちけいず}は、{図書館|としょかん}や{行政|ぎょうせい}のウェブサイトで{誰|だれ}でも{見|み}ることができる。
>
> {周知|しゅうち}のごとく、{日本|にほん}は{山|やま}が{多|おお}く{平地|へいち}が{少|すく}ない。{人|ひと}が{住|す}める{土地|とち}には{限|かぎ}りがあり、{低地|ていち}での{暮|く}らしをすべてやめることはできない。だからこそ、{堤防|ていぼう}に{守|まも}られていると{過信|かしん}せず、{水|みず}は{必|かなら}ず{低|ひく}い{所|ところ}へ{流|なが}れるという{当|あ}たり{前|まえ}の{事実|じじつ}を、{改|あらた}めて{心|こころ}に{刻|きざ}むべきである。{堤防|ていぼう}は{私|わたし}たちを{守|まも}ってくれるが、{考|かんが}えることまで{代|か}わってはくれない。

{決壊|けっかい}する = to burst (of an embankment); {相次|あいつ}ぐ = to happen one after another; {家財|かざい} =
household goods; {口|くち}をそろえる = to say with one voice; {治水|ちすい} = flood control; {想定|そうてい} =
what was assumed (the design limit); {万能|ばんのう} = all-powerful; {水位|すいい} = water level;
{成|な}り{立|た}ち = how something came to be; {地価|ちか} = land prices; {宅地|たくち} = residential land;
{排水|はいすい} = drainage; {盛|も}る = to pile up; {地形図|ちけいず} = topographic map; {周知|しゅうち} = common
knowledge; {過信|かしん}する = to put too much faith in; {刻|きざ}む = to engrave (here: to take to heart).

1. What does the editorial say "we" tend to think, and why is it a problem?
2. What did old maps show about the places that were badly flooded?
3. What does the writer grant in favour of developing low ground, and what is the "ironic" side?
4. What does the writer recommend doing before choosing a house?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. That if there are embankments and dams there won't be flood damage (〜と{考|かんが}えるきらいがある).
   Embankments aren't all-powerful against rain beyond what they were designed for; the one that burst
   met national standards, and many people stayed at home even as the water rose.
2. That many of them were rice fields, dry fields or marshes until a few decades ago: low ground where
   water collects, which is why people once didn't build there. Some place names still contain
   "marsh" or "pond".
3. Without it, cities couldn't have housed the people moving into them, and drainage and raising the
   ground have reduced the risk. The irony is that the more the measures advance, the harder the
   danger is to see, because residents forget how weak the land is.
4. Open a map and check what the land used to be; the hazard map shows areas expected to flood, and old
   topographic maps can be seen in libraries and on government websites.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

This year again there was record rainfall in many places, and one after another, river embankments
burst and flooded residential areas. Many people lost their household goods overnight. Many of the
residents hit by the disaster say with one voice, "I never imagined the water would come this far."

We tend to think that as long as there are embankments and dams, floods won't happen. Certainly,
modern flood-control works have reduced the great floods of the past. But embankments aren't
all-powerful against rain beyond what they were designed for. The embankment that burst this time,
too, was a fine structure that met national standards. It is said that many people stayed in their
homes even as the river rose to the top edge of the embankment.

Looking at the worst-hit districts on old maps tells you something interesting. Many of them were low
ground that was rice fields, dry fields or marshes until a few decades ago. Precisely because water
collects easily there, people in the past didn't build houses on such land, and used it for paddies.
Quite a few places still have the characters for "marsh" or "pond" in their names. The land remembers
how it came to be. One day the water comes back, as if it had remembered its old path.

From the period of high growth onwards, as the cities spread, such low ground was turned into housing
one area after another. Some developers, seizing on the low land prices, took their chance to sell it
off as building plots. The buyers, too, looking only at the distance to the station and the price,
paid no attention to the land's past.

Of course, development itself isn't bad. Without developing low ground, it would have been impossible
to provide enough housing for the people pouring into the cities. Ways of reducing the danger, such as
building drainage and raising the ground with earth, have also been put in place. The problem is that,
because such measures exist, the people who live there forget how weak the land is. There is an
ironic side: the further the measures go, the harder the danger becomes to see.

To notice the danger only on a night of heavy rain, standing before a river on the point of
overflowing, is too late. The hazard maps that local governments produce show the areas expected to
flood. When choosing a home, we should open a map and check what the land used to be. Old
topographic maps can be seen by anyone at libraries and on government websites.

As is well known, Japan has many mountains and little flat land. The land people can live on is
limited, and we can't give up living on low ground altogether. That is exactly why we should not put
too much faith in the embankments that protect us, and should take to heart once more the obvious
fact that water always flows to low places. Embankments protect us, but they can't do our thinking
for us.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{彼|かれ}は{物事|ものごと}を{大|おお}げさに{言|い}うきらいがある。
= He tends to exaggerate things.
{例|れい}のごとく、{会議|かいぎ}が{長引|ながび}いた。
= As usual, the meeting ran over.
{私|わたし}ごときにはもったいないお{言葉|ことば}です。
= Such kind words are wasted on the likes of me.
{割|わ}れんばかりの{拍手|はくしゅ}が{起|お}こった。
= Applause fit to bring the roof down broke out.
{待|ま}ってましたとばかりに{手|て}を{挙|あ}げた。
= They put up a hand as if they'd been waiting for the chance.
```

## Common mistakes

- {早起|はやお}きするきらいがある isn't used. きらいがある is only for bad tendencies; a good habit is
  {早起|はやお}きする{習慣|しゅうかん}がある.
- {夏|なつ}は{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}るきらいがある isn't used. Weather and statistics aren't conduct: {雨|あめ}が{多|おお}い,
  {降|ふ}る{傾向|けいこう}がある.
- {私|わたし}は{泣|な}かんばかりにした isn't used for "I nearly cried". んばかり describes how something looks to an
  observer; for yourself, {泣|な}きそうになった.
- {泣|な}くばかり doesn't mean "almost crying". The form is the ない stem + んばかり: {泣|な}かんばかり; {泣|な}くばかり
  means "does nothing but cry".
- Calling a guest {先生|せんせい}ごとき: N + ごとき (no の) is scornful of others. With の it's just
  "like": {先生|せんせい}のごとき{立派|りっぱ}な{方|かた}.
- ごとく in casual speech: {例|れい}のごとく is a set phrase people say jokingly, but in general use
  ように / みたいに when talking.

## Key points

- 〜きらいがある (dictionary / ない form, noun + の): tends to (a bad leaning of a person or group);
  critical, written; not for good habits or nature.
- ごとし (classical ようだ): 〜のごとく + verb, 〜のごとき + noun, 〜のごとし at the end (sayings); written; kana.
  N + ごとき without の: "the likes of" (humble about oneself, scornful of others).
- ない stem + んばかり(に / の): as if about to; する → せんばかり; an observer's view; literary.
- 〜とばかりに: as if to say; ここぞとばかりに, {待|ま}ってましたとばかりに.
- Tendency (きらいがある, がち, {傾向|けいこう}) and likeness (ようだ, ごとく, かのように, んばかり) are
  the two ideas of this lesson.
- New kanji: 岳 峡 峰 崖 渓 丘 洞 窟 穴 沼 湧 潮 洪 漂 浸 渦 滝 滴 噴 揺 遭 亜 殻 貝 礁 漠 堤 壌 肥 畑 牧 耕.
  Write {洪水|こうずい} and {揺|ゆ}れる with kanji from now on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: In its own way: なりに, たる, たるもの, と相まって
topics: たる and たるもの
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson is about manner and standing: doing something in one's own way, being what one's
title says, two things combining, and falling short of one's position.

{子供|こども}なりに{考|かんが}えて{出|だ}した{答|こた}えだ。 — It's an answer the child came up with, thinking it through as a child can.

{教師|きょうし}たるもの、{生徒|せいと}の{手本|てほん}でなければならない。 — Anyone who is a teacher must be an example to the pupils.

{才能|さいのう}と{努力|どりょく}が{相|あい}まって、{彼女|かのじょ}は{成功|せいこう}した。 — Talent and hard work together brought her success.

{大臣|だいじん}ともあろう{人|ひと}が、そんなことを{言|い}うとは。 — That someone in a minister's position should say such a thing!

なりに belongs to everyday speech as much as to writing. たる, たるもの, と{相|あい}まって and ともあろう are
written and formal: editorials, speeches, formal letters and, for ともあろう, indignant comment.

The theme is speech and manners: praise and blame, requests, promises and refusals, silence and
ambiguity, politeness, and forms of address and names. You met keigo in N4 and N3
({尊敬語|そんけいご}, {謙譲語|けんじょうご}, {言葉遣|ことばづか}い); this lesson adds the words people use about speech, and lets you
write {褒|ほ}める, {黙|だま}る, {冗談|じょうだん}, {勧|すす}める, {尋|たず}ねる, {遠慮|えんりょ}, {丁寧|ていねい} and {癖|くせ} with
kanji.

## N / plain form + なりに: in one's own way

なりに says that someone or something does what it can within its own limits, or has its own
logic. A may be small, young, inexperienced or simply "that particular one".

| Before なりに | Example |
|---|---|
| noun | {子供|こども}なりに, {私|わたし}なりに, {素人|しろうと}なりに |
| い-adjective | {狭|せま}いなりに, {若|わか}いなりに |
| verb or clause, plain form | {知|し}らないなりに, {経験|けいけん}が{少|すく}ないなりに |

{狭|せま}い{部屋|へや}だが、{狭|せま}いなりに{工夫|くふう}して{暮|く}らしている。 — It's a small flat, but I make it work as best a small place allows.

{彼|かれ}には{彼|かれ}なりの{理由|りゆう}があったのだろう。 — He must have had his own reasons.

{私|わたし}なりに{精|せい}いっぱい{頑張|がんば}ったつもりです。 — I did my best, in my own way.

Points to remember:

- なりの + noun: {私|わたし}なりの{考|かんが}え (my own view), {彼|かれ}なりのやり{方|かた}.
- それなりに / それなりの: "reasonably, to a fitting degree, in its own way": それなりの{準備|じゅんび}が
  {必要|ひつよう}だ (it needs a fitting amount of preparation), それなりにおいしい (it's good enough, in its
  way).
- It implies a limit, so don't use it of people above you: {先生|せんせい}なりに{頑張|がんば}った sounds
  condescending. Use it of yourself (modestly), of children and beginners, or of each person's own way.
- This isn't lesson 1's なり (as soon as) or lesson 8's なり〜なり (or the like): those follow verbs in
  other ways and mean other things.

## N + たる / たるもの: being, and being worthy of the name

N + たる + noun means "who is an N, and should be one in full": the standard that the title or role
carries. たるもの (or たる{者|もの}) at the start of a sentence sets out what such a person must do.

{一国|いっこく}の{首相|しゅしょう}たる{人物|じんぶつ}が、{国民|こくみん}にうそをついてはならない。 — A person who is a country's prime minister must not lie to the people.

{指導者|しどうしゃ}たる{者|もの}は、{自|みずか}らの{言葉|ことば}に{責任|せきにん}を{持|も}つべきだ。 — Anyone who leads must take responsibility for their own words.

{医師|いし}たるもの、{患者|かんじゃ}の{話|はなし}に{耳|みみ}を{傾|かたむ}けなければならない。 — A doctor, being a doctor, must listen to the patient.

Points to remember:

- The noun before たる is a role, rank or status ({教師|きょうし}, {医師|いし}, {首相|しゅしょう}, {指導者|しどうしゃ}, {法治国家|ほうちこっか}).
- たるもの〜 usually ends in べきだ, なければならない or てはならない: it states a duty.
- Written and formal (speeches, editorials, mottoes). It can sound pompous in conversation.
- たる is the attributive of the classical たり ("to be"); 26 comes back to classical forms. Written
  in kana.

## 〜と{相|あい}まって: combined with

AとBが{相|あい}まって, or A と{相|あい}まって B: two factors work together and produce a stronger result.
The result may be good or bad.

{円安|えんやす}と{相|あい}まって、{外国|がいこく}からの{観光客|かんこうきゃく}が{急増|きゅうぞう}している。 — Combined with the weak yen, the number of visitors from abroad is shooting up.

{美|うつく}しい{景色|けしき}と{相|あい}まって、{料理|りょうり}が{一層|いっそう}おいしく{感|かん}じられた。 — With the beautiful view, the food tasted all the better.

{寝不足|ねぶそく}と{疲|つか}れが{相|あい}まって、{集中|しゅうちゅう}できなかった。 — Lack of sleep and tiredness together left me unable to concentrate.

Points to remember:

- It follows a noun; the result comes after it. Before a noun: 〜と{相|あい}まった{効果|こうか}.
- It's about combined causes, not simple addition: "A and also B" is AもBも or Aに{加|くわ}えてB.
- Written and formal speech; in conversation, 〜も{重|かさ}なって.
- 相 is read あい here, as in {相手|あいて}; the course writes it with kanji.

## N + ともあろう: someone of that standing

N + ともあろう + {人|ひと} / {者|もの} / {方|かた} / noun + が: "someone in A's position, of all people". It
criticizes behaviour unworthy of the role, and usually ends in surprise or disapproval
(〜とは, 〜なんて, {信|しん}じられない, {情|なさ}けない).

{警察官|けいさつかん}ともあろう{者|もの}が{交通|こうつう}{違反|いはん}をするなんて。 — A police officer, of all people, breaking traffic rules!

{一流|いちりゅう}ホテルともあろうところが、こんな{初歩的|しょほてき}なミスをするとは{思|おも}わなかった。 — I never thought a first-class hotel would make such a basic mistake.

Points to remember:

- The noun is a role or status that comes with expectations: {大臣|だいじん}, {教師|きょうし}, {医者|いしゃ},
  {社長|しゃちょう}, {専門家|せんもんか}, {一流|いちりゅう}{企業|きぎょう}.
- たる states the standard; ともあろう says someone has fallen short of it. Compare:
  {教師|きょうし}たるもの、{時間|じかん}を{守|まも}るべきだ (a teacher should be punctual) and
  {教師|きょうし}ともあろう{人|ひと}が{遅刻|ちこく}するとは (a teacher, of all people, being late!).
- Written and formal speech, but also common when people complain.

> **Review (N3).** 〜として (as, in the role of): {代表|だいひょう}として{参加|さんか}する. 〜にとって (for, from the
> point of view of): {私|わたし}にとって{大切|たいせつ}な{人|ひと}. Both are neutral; たる and ともあろう add the
> expectations that go with the role.

## Roles and expectations

| Pattern | Says | Feel | Style |
|---|---|---|---|
| 〜として (N3) | in the role of | neutral | all |
| 〜なりに / なりの | in A's own (limited) way | modest, understanding | all |
| N + たる / たるもの | someone who is truly A (must…) | the ideal, a duty | written, formal |
| N + ともあろう | someone of A's standing (fell short) | criticism, surprise | written, formal speech |
| 〜と{相|あい}まって | combined with | neutral | written, formal |

## Words for speech and manners

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| praise and honour | {名誉|めいよ}, {名誉毀損|めいよきそん}, {不名誉|ふめいよ}, {名誉職|めいよしょく}, {誉|ほま}れ, {栄誉|えいよ}, {褒美|ほうび}, {褒賞|ほうしょう}, {褒|ほ}め{言葉|ことば}, {称賛|しょうさん}する, {絶賛|ぜっさん}する, {賛辞|さんじ}, {感銘|かんめい}, {座右|ざゆう}の{銘|めい}, {熱烈|ねつれつ}, {謝意|しゃい} |
| blame and scorn | {嘲笑|ちょうしょう}する, {嘲|あざけ}る, {自嘲|じちょう}, {罵|ののし}る, {罵倒|ばとう}する, {罵声|ばせい}, {非難|ひなん}する, {苦言|くげん}, {陰口|かげぐち}, {暴言|ぼうげん}, {難癖|なんくせ}, {毀損|きそん}する, {痛烈|つうれつ}, {強烈|きょうれつ}, {言葉尻|ことばじり}, {揚|あ}げ{足|あし} |
| asking and urging | {勧誘|かんゆう}する, {勧告|かんこく}する, {勧|すす}め, {促|うなが}す, {促進|そくしん}する, {尋問|じんもん}する, {召集|しょうしゅう}する |
| saying yes and no | {承諾|しょうだく}する, {快諾|かいだく}する, {受諾|じゅだく}する, {諾否|だくひ}, {許諾|きょだく}, {断|ことわ}り, {謝絶|しゃぜつ}, {弁解|べんかい}する, {前言|ぜんげん} |
| promises and gifts | {誓約|せいやく}, {確約|かくやく}する, {口約束|くちやくそく}, {贈呈|ぞうてい}する, {進呈|しんてい}する, {謹呈|きんてい}, {呈|てい}する, {露呈|ろてい}する, {頂戴|ちょうだい}する |
| silence and ambiguity | {沈黙|ちんもく}, {黙認|もくにん}する, {黙々|もくもく}と, {暗黙|あんもく}, {黙|だま}り{込|こ}む, {口|くち}ごもる, {冗長|じょうちょう}, {曖昧|あいまい}, {遠回|とおまわ}し, {口止|くちど}め, {一拍|いっぱく} |
| consideration | {配慮|はいりょ}する, {考慮|こうりょ}する, {熟慮|じゅくりょ}, {無遠慮|ぶえんりょ}, {不慮|ふりょ} |
| politeness and manner | {丁重|ていちょう}, {丁寧語|ていねいご}, {恭|うやうや}しい, {静粛|せいしゅく}, {粛々|しゅくしゅく}と, {厳粛|げんしゅく}, {自粛|じしゅく}する, {無礼|ぶれい}, {前置|まえお}き, {建前|たてまえ}, {社交辞令|しゃこうじれい}, お{世辞|せじ}, リップサービス, {物腰|ものごし}, エチケット, ニュアンス, ジェスチャー |

Suzuki, in their first year at a trading company, asks the section chief, Tanaka, for advice.
(Office speech: Suzuki is polite; Tanaka is friendly and plain.)

```dialogue

たなか: それは{無理|むり}だろう。{工場|こうじょう}も{手|て}いっぱいだし。
= That's impossible, surely. The factory's at full capacity.
すずき: ですが、{長年|ながねん}のお{客様|きゃくさま}なので、どうお{断|ことわ}りすればいいか…。
= But they're a long-standing customer, so I don't know how to say no…

たなか: {例|たと}えば、{一部|いちぶ}だけ{先|さき}に{納品|のうひん}するとか。{先方|せんぽう}の{事情|じじょう}も、うちの{事情|じじょう}も{考慮|こうりょ}してね。
```

of response; {納期|のうき} = delivery date; {手|て}いっぱい = fully occupied; {納品|のうひん}する = to deliver
goods; {誠実|せいじつ} = sincere (lesson 17); {仕入|しい}れ = buying in stock; {文面|ぶんめん} = the wording of a
letter. The client's {御社|おんしゃ}ともあろう{会社|かいしゃ} is pressure dressed as a compliment: "a company of your

>
> {大切|たいせつ}なのは、{曖昧|あいまい}さを{一方的|いっぽうてき}に{否定|ひてい}することでも、{美徳|びとく}として{守|まも}ることでもありません。{場面|ばめん}と{相手|あいて}に{応|おう}じて、はっきり{言|い}うべきときと、{言葉|ことば}を{和|やわ}らげるべきときを{見分|みわ}ける{力|ちから}です。{言葉|ことば}は{道具|どうぐ}であり、{正|ただ}しい{使|つか}い{方|かた}は{一|ひと}つではありません。{来週|らいしゅう}は、{実際|じっさい}の{会話|かいわ}の{録音|ろくおん}を{聞|き}きながら、この{点|てん}をさらに{考|かんが}えてみましょう。

{行為|こうい} = an act; {言葉|ことば}を{濁|にご}す = to be evasive (lesson 25); {傷|きず}つける = to hurt;
{間|ま}の{取|と}り{方|かた} = the use of pauses; ぼかす = to blur, to leave vague; {型|かた} = a pattern, a
model; {共有|きょうゆう}する = to share; すれ{違|ちが}い = a misunderstanding (passing each other by);
{正面|しょうめん}から = head-on; {検討|けんとう}する = to consider; {美徳|びとく} = a virtue; {和|やわ}らげる = to soften.

1. Why does the lecturer call indirect refusals "the speaker's own consideration" rather than mere
   vagueness?
2. How do listeners usually understand 「{考|かんが}えておきます」, and what helps them?
3. What happened to the international student, and why?
4. Why does the lecturer bring up a minister in the Diet?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Because saying "no" outright might hurt the other person; the indirect answer is a way, in the
   speaker's own fashion (なりの), of refusing without damaging the relationship.
2. They usually understand it correctly as a refusal without being told; tone, pauses and facial
   expression, together with the words (と{相|あい}まって), carry the message.
3. Told 「{考|かんが}えておきます」, the student waited a week for an answer: someone who doesn't share the
   habit may not understand the indirect refusal.
4. To show that people with public responsibility are criticized more harshly for vague answers: a
   minister, of all people (ともあろう), shouldn't just repeat "we'll consider it"; a politician
   (たるもの) should take responsibility for their words.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Today I'd like to think about the act of refusing. When you turn down an invitation, what words do
you use? Probably not many of you say outright, "I won't go." Isn't it more common to be evasive,
with "That day's a bit…", or to answer, "I'll think about it"?

Indirect refusals like these are often criticized as "vague". Certainly there are times when it's
hard to tell whether the other person is really refusing. But I see this not as mere vagueness, but
as the speaker's own kind of consideration. Say "no" outright and you might hurt the other person's
feelings. It's that person's way of refusing without damaging the relationship.

What's interesting is that, in most cases, listeners take the meaning correctly. That "I'll think
about it" means "I'm afraid not" is understood without being explained. The tone, the pauses and
the facial expression convey more than the words themselves. You could say that the words and the
expression combine into one message.

One Japanese teacher, I'm told, teaches learners: "When you refuse, first apologize, then give a
lightly blurred reason, and finally connect it to a next time." "I'm sorry, I've got something on
that day. Please ask me again." It may not be perfect, but as a pattern beginners can use in a
beginner's way, I think it's well made.

However, this approach doesn't always work. With someone who doesn't share the same habits, an
indirect way of putting things may not get through. In fact, I once heard an international student
say, "I was told 'I'll think about it', so I waited a week for an answer." As both workplaces and
schools become more international, misunderstandings over refusals may be happening more easily
than before.

There's one more issue: position. When people with public responsibility use vague language,
the criticism is all the harsher. If a minister, of all people, doesn't answer questions in the Diet
head-on and only repeats "we will consider it", the public won't be satisfied. A politician, being a
politician, should take responsibility for their own words: that is the point.

What matters isn't rejecting vagueness out of hand, nor guarding it as a virtue. It's the ability to
tell, according to the situation and the person, when to speak clearly and when to soften one's
words. Words are tools, and there's more than one right way to use them. Next week, let's think
about this further while listening to recordings of real conversations.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{私|わたし}なりに{考|かんが}えてみました。
= I've thought about it in my own way.
{教師|きょうし}たるもの、{時間|じかん}は{守|まも}るべきです。
= A teacher should above all be punctual.
{好天|こうてん}と{相|あい}まって、{会場|かいじょう}は{大|おお}にぎわいだった。
= With the fine weather on top of everything, the venue was packed.
{専門家|せんもんか}ともあろう{人|ひと}が、そんな{間違|まちが}いを。
= An expert, of all people, making a mistake like that!
それなりの{理由|りゆう}があるはずです。
= There must be a good enough reason.
```

## Common mistakes

- {先生|せんせい}なりに{頑張|がんば}っていらっしゃる isn't used of a superior. なりに implies limits; it sounds condescending about a
  superior. Say {先生|せんせい}も{懸命|けんめい}に{取|と}り{組|く}んでいらっしゃる.
- Confusing なりに with lesson 1's なり: {帰|かえ}るなり{寝|ね}た (went to bed as soon as I got home) is a
  different pattern from {子供|こども}なりに{考|かんが}えた.
- ×{教師|きょうし}たるもの、{遅刻|ちこく}した. たるもの sets out a duty, so it ends in べきだ / なければならない;
  for a teacher who was late, use ともあろう: {教師|きょうし}ともあろう{人|ひと}が{遅刻|ちこく}した.
- {田中|たなか}さんともあろう{人|ひと}が isn't the usual use. ともあろう follows a role or rank, not a name (with a well-known name, あの〜ともあろう{人|ひと}が is heard).
- Using と{相|あい}まって for a simple "and": "she speaks English and French" is {英語|えいご}もフランス{語|ご}も
  {話|はな}せる; と{相|あい}まって is two causes combining into one effect.
- Writing いただく with a kanji: the course writes it in kana; {頂戴|ちょうだい} and {戴冠式|たいかんしき} keep their
  kanji.

## Key points

- N / plain form + なりに / なりの: in A's own (limited) way; それなりに / それなりの (reasonably, fittingly);
  not of superiors.
- N + たる + N, N + たるもの〜べきだ: someone who is truly A, and the duty that goes with it; written.
- A と{相|あい}まって B / AとBが{相|あい}まって: combined with, producing an effect; written and formal.
- N + ともあろう + {人|ひと} / {者|もの} が: someone of A's standing, of all people (criticism).
- New kanji: 誉 褒 嘲 罵 毀 銘 烈 召 呈 勧 促 諾 尋 慮 冗 黙 曖 昧 癖 戴 丁 寧 粛 痴 恭 挟 拍 旦 那 翁 俊 斎.
  Write {褒|ほ}める, {黙|だま}る, {冗談|じょうだん}, {勧|すす}める, {尋|たず}ねる, {遠慮|えんりょ}, {癖|くせ}, {丁寧|ていねい}, {愚痴|ぐち},
  {拍手|はくしゅ}, {召|め}し{上|あ}がる and {催促|さいそく} with kanji from now on.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Once it happens: が最後, たら最後, ようが〜まいが, ずとも
topics: が最後 and たら最後
ようと and ようが
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last core lesson of module 5 is about conditions that leave no way out: once something happens,
the result is certain; whether or not something happens, it makes no difference; no matter what
anyone does; even without doing something.

あの{店|みせ}に{入|はい}ったが{最後|さいご}、{何|なに}か{買|か}わずには{出|で}られない。 — Once you go into that shop, you can't come out without buying something.

{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}ろうが{降|ふ}るまいが、{試合|しあい}は{行|おこな}われる。 — Rain or no rain, the match goes ahead.

{誰|だれ}が{何|なん}と{言|い}おうと、{私|わたし}は{行|い}く。 — Whatever anyone says, I'm going.

{言|い}わずとも{分|わ}かる。 — It goes without saying. (You understand without being told.)

たら{最後|さいご} and ようが / ようと are common in speech; が{最後|さいご}, ようが〜まいが and ずとも are more
written. All of them use forms you already know: the た form, the volitional, N2's まい and the
written negative ず.

The theme is the senses and appearance: light and darkness, colours, scent and smell, texture,
clothes and sewing, looks and atmosphere. N2 lesson 24 gave you cloth and appearance ({生地|きじ},
{身|み}なり); this lesson adds the words of description, the vocabulary of stories and
essays, and lets you write {化粧|けしょう} with kanji.

## 〜たが{最後|さいご} / 〜たら{最後|さいご}: once that happens, there's no going back

The た form + が{最後|さいご} (written) or たら{最後|さいご} (spoken) says that once A happens, B follows and
can't be stopped or undone. B is usually unwelcome, or at least extreme.

{彼|かれ}は{一度|いちど}{話|はな}し{始|はじ}めたら{最後|さいご}、{二時間|にじかん}は{止|と}まらない。 — Once he starts talking, he won't stop for two hours.

この{秘密|ひみつ}を{知|し}られたが{最後|さいご}、もうこの{町|まち}にはいられない。 — Once this secret gets out, I won't be able to stay in this town.

{布団|ふとん}に{入|はい}ったら{最後|さいご}、{朝|あさ}まで{起|お}きられない。 — Once I get into bed, I can't get up again until morning.

Points to remember:

- A is one action or event; B is the inevitable consequence, often with 〜ない, {二度|にど}と〜ない,
  〜まで〜ない, 〜しかない.
- B is mostly the present or future (a habit, a prediction, a warning). In stories it can be past:
  {彼|かれ}は{家|いえ}を{出|で}たが{最後|さいご}、{二度|にど}と{戻|もど}らなかった.
- It's stronger than ば / たら alone: it stresses that there's no turning back. It's also often used
  humorously about one's own weaknesses.
- {最後|さいご} is N4's さいご, written with kanji in this course.

## 〜(よ)うが〜まいが / 〜(よ)うと〜まいと: whether or not

The volitional + が, then the same verb + まい + が (or と…と): "whether A or not A", the result is the
same. まい (N2 lesson 18) is the written negative of will or guess.

| Verb | volitional + が | + まいが |
|---|---|---|
| {行|い}く | {行|い}こうが | {行|い}くまいが |
| {来|く}る | {来|こ}ようが | {来|く}るまいが / {来|こ}まいが |
| する | しようが | するまいが / しまいが |
| {食|た}べる (group 2) | {食|た}べようが | {食|た}べるまいが / {食|た}べまいが |
| いる | いようが | いまいが |

{彼|かれ}が{来|こ}ようが{来|く}るまいが、{会議|かいぎ}は{予定|よてい}どおり{始|はじ}める。 — Whether he comes or not, the meeting starts as planned.

{信|しん}じようと{信|しん}じまいと、これは{本当|ほんとう}にあった{話|はなし}だ。 — Believe it or not, this really happened.

Points to remember:

- まい joins the dictionary form of group 1 verbs ({行|い}くまい); group 2 verbs take the dictionary form or
  the ない stem ({食|た}べるまい / {食|た}べまい); する and {来|く}る have several forms.
- B is a decision or a fact that A doesn't affect. It isn't used when B depends on A.
- The pattern ending in が is a little more written; と〜まいと is equally common.

## Question word + 〜(よ)うが / 〜(よ)うと: no matter

With a question word (or どんなに, たとえ), the volitional + が / と means "no matter who / what / how".
い-adjectives use 〜かろう, な-adjectives and nouns 〜だろう / 〜であろう.

{誰|だれ}が{何|なん}と{言|い}おうと、{決|き}めたことは{変|か}えない。 — Whatever anyone says, I won't change my decision.

どんなに{高|たか}かろうが、{必要|ひつよう}なものは{買|か}う。 — However expensive it is, I'll buy what I need.

たとえ{雨|あめ}だろうと、{出発|しゅっぱつ}する。 — Even if it rains, we'll set off.

Points to remember:

- It's the strong, slightly formal cousin of N4's 〜ても: {誰|だれ}が{何|なん}と{言|い}っても.
- The second half states the speaker's will or a fixed fact, unaffected by A.
- {高|たか}かろう and {静|しず}かであろう are written forms; in speech, {高|たか}くても, {静|しず}かでも.

## ない stem + ずとも: even without

The ない stem + ずとも (the written negative ず + とも, "even if") means "even without doing A":
{言|い}わずとも, {急|いそ}がずとも. する → せずとも; {来|く}る → {来|こ}ずとも (rare).

{説明|せつめい}せずとも、{見|み}れば{分|わ}かるはずだ。 — It should be clear just from looking, without any explanation.

そんなに{急|いそ}がずとも、{間|ま}に{合|あ}いますよ。 — You'll make it even without rushing like that.

Points to remember:

- Written and literary; in speech, 〜なくても.
- Set phrases: {言|い}わずとも{分|わ}かる (it goes without saying), {言|い}わずと{知|し}れた (well known: {言|い}わずと
  {知|し}れた{名店|めいてん}). {言|い}わずもがな (needless to say) is a related classical phrase.
- ず isn't a drill form; N3 lesson 26 taught it as the written negative.

> **Review (N2 lesson 25).** 〜ものなら (if you could): {行|い}けるものなら{行|い}きたい. 〜(よ)うものなら (if you
> were to, something bad would follow): {遅刻|ちこく}しようものなら、{厳|きび}しく{叱|しか}られる. Like が{最後|さいご}, ようものなら
> warns of a consequence; it is hypothetical, while が{最後|さいご} describes what always happens.

## No way out: comparing the patterns

| Pattern | Says | Second half | Style |
|---|---|---|---|
| 〜たとたん (N3) | just as A happened, B (unexpected) | a past event | everyday |
| 〜たら{最後|さいご} / たが{最後|さいご} | once A happens, B can't be stopped | a certain (bad) result | speech / written |
| 〜(よ)うものなら (N2) | if you were to A, something bad | a warning | everyday, a little stiff |
| 〜(よ)うが〜まいが | whether A or not | unaffected decision or fact | written, formal speech |
| question word + 〜(よ)うと | no matter who / what / how | the speaker's will | both |
| 〜ても (N4) | even if | anything | everyday |
| 〜ずとも | even without A | a result still reached | written |

## Words for the senses and appearance

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| light and darkness | {輝|かがや}く, {輝|かがや}き, {輝|かがや}かしい, {瞬|またた}く, {瞬間|しゅんかん}, {瞬時|しゅんじ}, {暗闇|くらやみ}, {闇|やみ}, {夕闇|ゆうやみ}, {闇夜|やみよ}, {真|ま}っ{暗|くら}, {薄暗|うすぐら}い, {暁|あかつき}, {日陰|ひかげ}, {木陰|こかげ}, {陰|かげ}る, {陰気|いんき}, {陰影|いんえい}, {明暗|めいあん}, まぶしい, {光景|こうけい} |
| clear and cloudy | {澄|す}む, {澄|す}ます, {濁|にご}る, {濁|にご}り, {濁|にご}す, {濁音|だくおん}, {泡|あわ}, {泡立|あわだ}つ, {気泡|きほう}, {発泡|はっぽう}, {灰|はい}, {灰皿|はいざら}, {石灰|せっかい} |
| colours | {灰色|はいいろ}, {紺|こん}, {紺色|こんいろ}, {濃紺|のうこん}, {紫|むらさき}, {紫色|むらさきいろ}, {紫外線|しがいせん}, {朱色|しゅいろ}, {朱肉|しゅにく}, {淡|あわ}い, {淡々|たんたん}と, {淡水|たんすい}, {原色|げんしょく}, {色調|しきちょう}, {艶|つや}, {色艶|いろつや}, あでやか, {艶|つや}っぽい, {色白|いろじろ}, ベージュ, パステル, グラデーション, コントラスト, シルエット |
| scent and smell | {臭|くさ}い, {臭|くさ}み, {悪臭|あくしゅう}, {口臭|こうしゅう}, {消臭|しょうしゅう}, {汗臭|あせくさ}い, {面倒臭|めんどうくさ}い, {芳|かんば}しい, {芳香|ほうこう}, {薫風|くんぷう} |
| the senses | {五感|ごかん}, {視覚|しかく}, {聴覚|ちょうかく}, {触覚|しょっかく}, {味覚|みかく}, {質感|しつかん} |
| shape and texture | {凸凹|でこぼこ}, {凸|とつ}, {凹|おう}, へこむ |
| clothes and sewing | {柄|がら}, {花柄|はながら}, {大柄|おおがら}, {小柄|こがら}, {縫|ぬ}う, {縫|ぬ}い{目|め}, {縫|ぬ}い{物|もの}, {縫製|ほうせい}, {裁縫|さいほう}, {繕|つくろ}う, {修繕|しゅうぜん}する, {裸|はだか}, {丸裸|まるはだか}, {裸眼|らがん}, {袖|そで}, {半袖|はんそで}, {長袖|ながそで}, {袖口|そでぐち}, {振袖|ふりそで}, {装|よそお}い, {着|き}こなす, {染|し}み |
| the face and make-up | {頬|ほお}, {頬張|ほおば}る, {化粧品|けしょうひん}, {化粧水|けしょうすい}, {化粧室|けしょうしつ}, {薄化粧|うすげしょう} |
| looks and atmosphere | {雰囲気|ふんいき}, {眺|なが}める, {眺|なが}め, {眺望|ちょうぼう}, {爽|さわ}やか, {爽快|そうかい}, {醜|みにく}い, {醜態|しゅうたい}, {閑静|かんせい}, {閑散|かんさん}, {閑古鳥|かんこどり}, {鈴|すず}, {鈴虫|すずむし}, {風鈴|ふうりん} |
| other words | {間柄|あいだがら}, {手柄|てがら}, {事柄|ことがら}, {芳名|ほうめい}, {闇雲|やみくも}, {瞬発力|しゅんぱつりょく}, {言|い}わずもがな |

Notes:

- {澄|す}む (to be clear) sounds like N5's {住|す}む and carried {済|す}む; it's a different word. {耳|みみ}を{澄|す}ます is to
  listen hard; {澄|す}ました{顔|かお} is a prim, unconcerned face.
- {淡|あわ}い is pale (colour) or faint (hope, feelings); {淡々|たんたん}と is calmly, without showing feeling;
  {冷淡|れいたん} (lesson 17) is cold-hearted.
- におう is one word with two spellings: lesson 1's {匂|にお}う for smells in general or pleasant ones,
  {臭|にお}う for bad ones ({生|なま}ゴミが{臭|にお}う). In the same way かおる can be written {香|かお}る or, in
  letters and poetry, {薫|かお}る ({風|かぜ}{薫|かお}る{五月|ごがつ}).
- {芳|かんば}しい (fragrant) is used mostly in the negative today: {結果|けっか}が{芳|かんば}しくない (the results
  aren't good).
- {柄|がら} is a pattern ({花柄|はながら}) and also build or character ({大柄|おおがら}, {小柄|こがら}, {柄|がら}が{悪|わる}い);
  {人柄|ひとがら} (lesson 17) is a person's character. In {間柄|あいだがら}, {手柄|てがら} and {事柄|ことがら} it has drifted
  to "relation, deed, matter".
- {雰囲気|ふんいき} is often mispronounced ふいんき; the standard reading is ふんいき.
- {暁|あかつき} is dawn, and 〜の{暁|あかつき}には means "when (something) is achieved": {優勝|ゆうしょう}の{暁|あかつき}には.

## Kanji

Thirty-two kanji: light, darkness and shape; clear water and colours; scent, feeling and
atmosphere; and clothes and the face.

### Light, darkness and shape

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 輝 | shine | キ | かがや(く) | 15 | {輝|かがや}く, {輝|かがや}き, {輝|かがや}かしい |
| 瞬 | blink, instant | シュン | またた(く) | 18 | {瞬間|しゅんかん}, {瞬時|しゅんじ}, {瞬|またた}く, {瞬発力|しゅんぱつりょく}; lesson 6's {一瞬|いっしゅん} |
| 闇 | darkness | — | やみ | 17 | {闇|やみ}, {暗闇|くらやみ}, {夕闇|ゆうやみ}, {闇雲|やみくも} |
| 暁 | dawn | ギョウ | あかつき | 12 | {暁|あかつき} |
| 陰 | shade, shadow | イン | かげ, かげ(る) | 11 | {日陰|ひかげ}, {木陰|こかげ}, {陰気|いんき}, {陰影|いんえい}, {陰|かげ}る |
| 眺 | gaze | チョウ | なが(める) | 11 | {眺|なが}める, {眺|なが}め, {眺望|ちょうぼう} |
| 凸 | convex | トツ | — | 5 | {凸凹|でこぼこ}, {凸|とつ} |
| 凹 | concave | オウ | — | 5 | {凸凹|でこぼこ}, {凹|おう} |

- {凸凹|でこぼこ} is a special reading of the two kanji together; alone they're トツ and オウ ({凸|とつ}レンズ,
  {凹|おう}レンズ). "Dented" (へこむ) is often printed with 凹, but that reading isn't in the jōyō table.
- 輝 (光 + 軍) and lesson 19's 揮 ({指揮|しき}, with the hand 扌) share 軍 and キ.
- 闇 is a sound (音) shut inside a gate (門): you can hear but not see.
- かげ is written 陰 for shade, the side away from the light ({日陰|ひかげ}, {木陰|こかげ}) and the hidden side
  ({陰口|かげぐち}, lesson 24), and 影 for a shadow or silhouette (carried かげ).
- 瞬 has 18 strokes: 目 (eye) and 舜.


<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

When I came out of the station, dusk was already beginning to wrap the town. The little station,
where I got off for the first time in ten years, looked much smaller and shabbier than in my memory.
A slightly cool end-of-summer wind brushed my cheek.

My grandmother's house is at the edge of a quiet residential area up the hill from the station.
When I opened the front door, there was a smell of old wood and tatami. It was the smell I breathed
every summer holiday as a child. Under the eaves, a faded wind chime was ringing towards the empty
garden.

It has been three months since my grandmother died. My mother had asked me to choose a keepsake
before the house was let go, and so I had come here alone. Inside, the house was dim, and when I
opened a window the damp night air flowed in. On the table in the living room, the sewing box my
grandmother had used to the very end lay open. One needle still had navy thread in it.

When I opened the chest of drawers in the back room, the sharp smell of mothballs stung my nose. In
the top drawer, a single navy kimono lay carefully folded. When I picked it up, the cool, smooth
feel of the silk reached my fingers. Along the cuff of the sleeve ran fine stitches. It had been
mended many times.

My grandmother was a woman of few words. When she praised and when she scolded, her words were
short. Yet somehow, as a child, I always knew what she was thinking.

"You know, once you put your arms in the sleeves of this kimono, you can't wear any other." She said
that to me when I was small, and laughed mischievously. Rain or snow, when New Year came she always
put on this kimono and went to the shrine nearby for the first visit of the year. Whether anyone was
watching or not, with her back straight and her sash tied smartly.

According to my mother, this kimono was one of the few things my grandmother brought with her when
she married into the family. In the hard years after the war she exchanged her other kimonos for
rice and vegetables, but this one, it seems, she could never bring herself to part with.

I spread the kimono out on my lap. In the pale light coming through the window, the deep navy seemed
to shine quietly. There was no showy pattern at all. But looking closely, I saw a small flower
embroidered near the collar in the same navy thread. It looked like a cherry blossom, or perhaps a
plum. When I traced it with a finger, I could feel the thread rising faintly. When my grandmother
had embroidered it, and why, I don't know. And yet I felt I understood without having to ask.

When I happened to look up, the world outside the window had sunk completely into darkness. Through
a gap in the clouds a single star was twinkling. In the garden the bell crickets had begun to sing.
I folded the kimono again with care and held it to my chest. Whatever anyone might say, I thought,
this one thing I would take back with me to Tokyo.
