## Common mistakes

- ×{入|はい}るが{最後|さいご}. が{最後|さいご} and たら{最後|さいご} take the た form: {入|はい}ったが{最後|さいご}, {入|はい}ったら{最後|さいご}.
- Using が{最後|さいご} for a happy, ordinary result: {薬|くすり}を{飲|の}んだが{最後|さいご}、{治|なお}った isn't used. It's for a result
  that can't be stopped or undone; for a simple result, use たら: {薬|くすり}を{飲|の}んだら{治|なお}った.
- ×{行|い}こうが{行|い}かないが. The second half uses まい: {行|い}こうが{行|い}くまいが, or {行|い}こうと{行|い}くまいと.
- Forgetting かろう with い-adjectives: the standard written form is どんなに{高|たか}かろうが. {高|たか}いだろうが is
  heard in speech but sounds loose; in conversation, どんなに{高|たか}くても is the natural choice.
- ×{言|い}わないずとも. ずとも joins the ない stem: {言|い}わずとも; する → せずとも.
- Reading {雰囲気|ふんいき} as ふいんき. It's ふんいき.

## Key points

- た form + が{最後|さいご} / たら{最後|さいご}: once A happens, B is certain and irreversible (usually bad).
- 〜(よ)うが〜まいが / 〜(よ)うと〜まいと: whether or not; the result is unaffected.
- Question word / どんなに / たとえ + 〜(よ)うが / 〜(よ)うと: no matter; い-adjectives 〜かろう, nouns and
  な-adjectives 〜だろう / 〜であろう.
- ない stem + ずとも: even without (written); {言|い}わずとも, せずとも; in speech 〜なくても.
- New kanji: 輝 瞬 闇 暁 陰 眺 凸 凹 澄 濁 泡 淡 灰 紺 紫 朱 艶 爽 醜 臭 薫 芳 閑 雰 鈴 頬 粧 柄 縫 繕 裸 袖.
  Write {化粧|けしょう} with kanji from now on; {凸凹|でこぼこ} is a special reading.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Dazai Osamu and "Run, Melos!"
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This honors lesson reads one of the best-known short stories in Japanese, {太宰治|だざいおさむ}'s
『{走|はし}れメロス』 ("Run, Melos!"). Most Japanese adults met it at school, and its first line is
widely quoted and parodied. You'll read about the writer, the
story's sources, its opening in the original, and the whole plot retold in modern Japanese that
uses this module's grammar ({倒|たお}れんばかり, 〜ようが〜まいが, {聞|き}かずとも).

## The writer

{太宰治|だざいおさむ} is a pen name; the writer was born {津島修治|つしましゅうじ} on 19 June 1909, in the village of
{金木|かなぎ} in Aomori Prefecture (today part of Goshogawara City). He became one of the most widely read
Japanese novelists of the twentieth century. He died in June 1948, still in his thirties. His best-known novels
are 『{人間失格|にんげんしっかく}』 ("No Longer Human") and 『{斜陽|しゃよう}』 ("The Setting Sun"); both are
much darker than 『{走|はし}れメロス』, and many readers are surprised that the same writer produced
both. His works have been in the public domain in Japan since 1999, fifty years after his death
under the law of the time.

All three kanji of his name are on the course list: {太|だ}, {宰|ざい} (lesson 13's {宰相|さいしょう}) and
{治|おさむ}. The name is a special reading as a whole: learn it as {太宰治|だざいおさむ}.

## The story and its sources

『{走|はし}れメロス』 first appeared in the May 1940 issue of the magazine 『{新潮|しんちょう}』. At its end Dazai
added a short note, 「{古伝説|こでんせつ}と、シルレルの{詩|し}から。」 ("From an old legend and Schiller's poem").
Schiller's poem is the ballad known in Japanese as 「{人質|ひとじち}」 ("The Hostage"); Dazai is said to
have worked from a Japanese translation of it. The legend behind the poem is a story of two
friends set in ancient Syracuse, one of whom stands surety for the other with his life. So the story is a
{翻案|ほんあん} (an adaptation), not an original plot: what is Dazai's own is the voice, quick,
emotional and often funny, and the way Melos argues with himself as he runs.

It is set in Syracuse (シラクス in the story) under a king, {暴君|ぼうくん}ディオニス, who trusts no one.
The hero, メロス, is a herdsman from a village some forty kilometres away (ten {里|り}, the old unit of distance); his
friend セリヌンティウス is a stonemason ({石工|いしく}) in the city.

The story has long been printed in junior-high-school Japanese textbooks, commonly for the
second year. Ask a Japanese friend to recite its first sentence: many can.

## The opening

The first two sentences, in modern kana and shinjitai (the spelling of the modernized editions):

> メロスは{激怒|げきど}した。{必|かなら}ず、かの{邪智暴虐|じゃちぼうぎゃく}の{王|おう}を{除|のぞ}かなければならぬと{決意|けつい}した。

— Melos was enraged. He resolved that he must at all costs rid the land of that wicked, cruel king.

- {激怒|げきど}する (to be enraged) is a carried word; the short, blunt first sentence is what makes the
  opening famous.
- かの is the literary "that" (あの). {邪智暴虐|じゃちぼうぎゃく} is a four-character compound: {邪智|じゃち} (cunning,
  wicked cleverness; 智 is outside the course list) and {暴虐|ぼうぎゃく} (tyranny, cruelty; lesson 18's
  {虐待|ぎゃくたい} has the same 虐).
- ならぬ is the written negative ぬ (N2 lesson 26) on なる: ならない. Dazai's narrator uses ぬ and
  older forms all through the story, which gives it the tone of a legend told aloud.
- {除|のぞ}く here is "to remove, get rid of" a person.

## The story retold

The rest of this section is a retelling in modern Japanese, written for this course. The words in
it are glossed below.

> {昔|むかし}、シラクスという{町|まち}に、ディオニスという{王|おう}がいた。{王|おう}は{人|ひと}を{信|しん}じることができず、{家族|かぞく}や{家臣|かしん}を{次々|つぎつぎ}に{処刑|しょけい}していた。
>
> {村|むら}の{牧人|ぼくじん}メロスは、{妹|いもうと}の{結婚|けっこん}の{準備|じゅんび}のために{町|まち}へ{来|き}て、この{話|はなし}を{聞|き}いた。{激怒|げきど}したメロスは{王|おう}を{除|のぞ}こうと{城|しろ}に{乗|の}り{込|こ}み、たちまち{捕|と}らえられた。
>
> {死刑|しけい}を{言|い}い{渡|わた}されたメロスは、{王|おう}に{頼|たの}んだ。「{妹|いもうと}の{結婚式|けっこんしき}を{挙|あ}げさせてください。{三日目|みっかめ}の{日暮|ひぐ}れまでに、{必|かなら}ず{戻|もど}ってきます」。{身代|みが}わりとして、{竹馬|ちくば}の{友|とも}である{石工|いしく}のセリヌンティウスが{町|まち}に{残|のこ}された。{王|おう}は、{少|すこ}し{遅|おく}れて{来|く}れば{命|いのち}は{助|たす}けてやる、とメロスにささやいた。{人|ひと}は{必|かなら}ず{裏切|うらぎ}るものだと{信|しん}じていたのだ。
>
> メロスは{夜通|よどお}し{走|はし}って{村|むら}へ{帰|かえ}り、{妹|いもうと}の{式|しき}を{挙|あ}げた。{王|おう}が{信|しん}じようが{信|しん}じまいが、{約束|やくそく}は{必|かなら}ず{守|まも}る。そう{心|こころ}に{決|き}めて、{三日目|みっかめ}の{朝|あさ}、{再|ふたた}び{町|まち}へ{向|む}かって{走|はし}り{出|だ}した。
>
> {帰|かえ}り{道|みち}は{苦難|くなん}の{連続|れんぞく}だった。{降|ふ}り{続|つづ}いた{大雨|おおあめ}で{川|かわ}があふれ、{橋|はし}が{流|なが}されていた。メロスは{濁流|だくりゅう}に{飛|と}び{込|こ}み、{泳|およ}いで{渡|わた}った。{峠|とうげ}では{山賊|さんぞく}に{襲|おそ}われたが、{三人|さんにん}を{倒|たお}して{逃|のが}れた。
>
> {強|つよ}い{日差|ひざ}しの{中|なか}で、メロスはついに{倒|たお}れた。もう{走|はし}れない。{友|とも}を{裏切|うらぎ}っても{仕方|しかた}がない、という{思|おも}いさえ{頭|あたま}をよぎった。そのとき、{岩|いわ}の{間|あいだ}から{水|みず}の{湧|わ}く{音|おと}が{聞|き}こえた。{一口|ひとくち}{飲|の}むと、{体|からだ}に{力|ちから}が{戻|もど}ってきた。
>
> メロスは{再|ふたた}び{走|はし}った。{日|ひ}は{沈|しず}みかけている。{服|ふく}は{破|やぶ}れ、{今|いま}にも{倒|たお}れんばかりの{姿|すがた}で、メロスは{刑場|けいじょう}に{飛|と}び{込|こ}んだ。セリヌンティウスが{処刑|しょけい}される{寸前|すんぜん}だった。
>
> {二人|ふたり}は、{一度|いちど}だけ{相手|あいて}を{疑|うたが}ったことを{打|う}ち{明|あ}け、{互|たが}いの{頬|ほお}を{打|う}ってから、{固|かた}く{抱|だ}き{合|あ}った。{言葉|ことば}にせずとも、{二人|ふたり}には{分|わ}かっていた。{信|しん}じ{合|あ}う{心|こころ}は{本物|ほんもの}だったのだ。その{様子|ようす}を{見|み}ていた{王|おう}は、{自分|じぶん}も{仲間|なかま}に{入|い}れてほしいと{頼|たの}んだ。
>
> {群衆|ぐんしゅう}の{歓声|かんせい}の{中|なか}、{一人|ひとり}の{少女|しょうじょ}が{赤|あか}いマントを{差|さ}し{出|だ}した。メロスは、{自分|じぶん}がほとんど{裸|はだか}であることに{気|き}づき、{顔|かお}を{真|ま}っ{赤|か}にした。

{牧人|ぼくじん} = herdsman; {乗|の}り{込|こ}む = to march in; {捕|と}らえる = to seize; {言|い}い{渡|わた}す = to
sentence; {日暮|ひぐ}れ = nightfall; {身代|みが}わり = a substitute, a hostage in someone's place;
{竹馬|ちくば}の{友|とも} = a friend since childhood; ささやく = to whisper; {夜通|よどお}し = all night; {苦難|くなん}の{連続|れんぞく}
= one hardship after another; {濁流|だくりゅう} = a muddy torrent (lesson 25's 濁); {峠|とうげ} = mountain pass
(lesson 10); {山賊|さんぞく} = bandits (lesson 11); よぎる = to cross (one's mind); {刑場|けいじょう} = place of
execution; {寸前|すんぜん} = just before; {打|う}ち{明|あ}ける = to confess; {群衆|ぐんしゅう} = crowd.

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Long ago, in a city called Syracuse, there was a king called Dionys. The king could trust no one,
and he was putting his family and his retainers to death one after another.

Melos, a herdsman from a village, came to the city to prepare for his sister's wedding and heard
this. Enraged, Melos marched into the castle meaning to rid the land of the king, and was seized
at once.

Sentenced to death, Melos asked the king: "Let me hold my sister's wedding. I will certainly be
back by nightfall on the third day." As a hostage in his place, his childhood friend Selinuntius,
a stonemason, was kept in the city. The king whispered to Melos that if he came back a little
late, his life would be spared. He believed people always betray each other.

Melos ran all night back to his village and held his sister's wedding. Whether the king believed
it or not, he would keep his promise. Having made up his mind, on the morning of the third day he
set off running back to the city.

The way back was one hardship after another. The river had overflowed after days of heavy
rain, and the bridge had been swept away. Melos dived into the muddy torrent and swam across. On
the pass he was attacked by bandits, but he knocked down three of them and escaped.

In the strong sunshine, Melos finally collapsed. He could run no more. Even the thought that it
couldn't be helped if he betrayed his friend crossed his mind. Just then he heard the sound of
water welling up between the rocks. When he drank a mouthful, his strength came back.

Melos ran again. The sun was about to set. His clothes torn, looking as though he might collapse
at any moment, Melos burst into the place of execution. It was just before Selinuntius was to be
put to death.

The two confessed that each had doubted the other just once, struck each other on the cheek, and
then held each other tight. They didn't need words to know it: their trust in each other was
real. The king, who had been watching, asked to be let into their friendship too.

Amid the cheers of the crowd, a girl held out a red cloak. Melos realized he was almost naked, and
turned bright red.

</details>

Notes on the retelling:

- {倒|たお}れんばかり (lesson 23): looking as if he might collapse; {信|しん}じようが{信|しん}じまいが (lesson 25):
  whether or not the king believed it; {言葉|ことば}にせずとも (lesson 25): without putting it into words.
- In the original, the last line is about the "hero" ({勇者|ゆうしゃ}) blushing: a joke at the end of a
  heroic story. Dazai's narrator is often half serious, half amused.
- The original is told in a lively, old-fashioned style with many ぬ and である forms; the retelling
  uses plain modern narrative.

## Why it is read

The story is about {信実|しんじつ} (sincerity, keeping faith: the original's own word) and friendship,
and about a king who has decided that trust is foolish. Schools like it because it is short, has a
clear plot and raises good questions: Was Melos right to put his friend's life at risk? Is a
promise worth keeping when no one would blame you for breaking it? Why do both friends confess a
doubt before they embrace? Readers have also noticed that Melos is far from perfect: rash, quick to
anger, tempted to give up. That is part of the story's charm.

## Words from this lesson

{暴君|ぼうくん}, {処刑|しょけい}する, {刑場|けいじょう}, {信実|しんじつ}, {勇者|ゆうしゃ}, {赤面|せきめん}する, {濁流|だくりゅう}, {邪悪|じゃあく},
{竹馬|ちくば}の{友|とも}, {友|とも}, {王|おう}, {正直者|しょうじきもの}, {日没|にちぼつ}, {刻限|こくげん}, {走|はし}り{抜|ぬ}く, {生誕|せいたん},
{没年|ぼつねん}, {人間不信|にんげんふしん}, {自伝的|じでんてき}. Carried words: {激怒|げきど} (rage, N2), and {文豪|ぶんごう} (a literary giant, N2's
ぶんごう), to write in kanji now: its second kanji is lesson 17's.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Haiku and waka
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

N3's honors lesson on haiku taught you to count five, seven, five, to spot a season word and a
cutting word, and to read three famous haiku (the old pond, the rape blossom and the harvest moon).
This lesson goes further: three more haiku each by the three great masters of the Edo period, the
older and longer form of court poetry, **[[waka]]**, and the famous anthology of a hundred waka that
many Japanese families still play as a card game at New Year.

> **Review (N3 honors).** A **[[haiku]]** ({俳句|はいく}) has 5-7-5 morae (sounds counted as in kana:
> きょう is two, がっこう four). It usually contains a **[[kigo]]** ({季語|きご}), a word that places it in a
> season, and often a **[[kireji]]** ({切|き}れ{字|じ}), a "cutting word" such as や, かな or けり that makes a
> pause and adds feeling.

The poems are given as printed in the sources this course checked (named in the course notes),
with the old kana spelling where they have it, then a reading in modern kana and an English
rendering of our own. Lesson 05h2 taught historical kana usage: here you'll see it at work
(よこたふ = よこたう, いたづら = いたずら). The kanji of the poets' names {芭蕉|ばしょう} and {蕪村|ぶそん} and of a
few words in the poems ({蝉|せみ}, {蛙|かわず}, {雀|すずめ}) are outside the course list.

## Forms, words and seasons

| Form | Pattern | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| waka ({和歌|わか}) | 5-7-5-7-7 (31 morae) | classical court poetry (the oldest anthologies are from the 8th century); the form is today called {短歌|たんか} |
| haiku ({俳句|はいく}) | 5-7-5 (17 morae) | grew out of the opening verse ({発句|ほっく}) of linked verse ({連歌|れんが}) |

- A waka has an upper verse ({上|かみ}の{句|く}, 5-7-5) and a lower verse ({下|しも}の{句|く}, 7-7). Poets of waka are
  {歌人|かじん}; poets of haiku are {俳人|はいじん}. A book of waka is a {歌集|かしゅう}, of haiku a {句集|くしゅう}; a
  gathering to compose haiku is a {句会|くかい}.
- A {歳時記|さいじき} is a dictionary of season words, arranged by season, with example poems. Season
  words follow the old calendar, so the seasons start earlier than you'd expect: spring begins in
  early February.
- Two techniques of waka: a {掛詞|かけことば} is a pivot word with two meanings at once (ながめ = "gazing" and
  "long rain"), and a {枕詞|まくらことば} is a fixed epithet that introduces a word (ひさかたの before {光|ひかり},
  "light", and words for the sky).
- A {辞世|じせい} is a poem written just before one's death. Lesson 24's {翁|おう} appears after the names of
  revered old poets: {芭蕉翁|ばしょうおう}.

## Three haiku by Bashō

{松尾芭蕉|まつおばしょう} (1644–1694) was born in Iga, in today's Mie Prefecture, and died in Osaka while
travelling. His most famous journey, through the north of Honshū in 1689, became the travel book
『おくのほそ{道|みち}』; all three of these haiku are from it.

> {閑|しず}かさや{岩|いわ}にしみ{入|い}る{蝉|せみ}の{声|こえ}

しずかさや / いわにしみいる / せみのこえ. Such stillness: into the rocks soaks the cicadas' cry.
Season word: {蝉|せみ} (summer). Cutting word: や. Written at the mountain temple {立石寺|りっしゃくじ}
(Yamadera) in Yamagata. Note lesson 25's 閑 ({閑静|かんせい}); しず(か) is not a jōyō reading of it, so outside poems
this word is written {静|しず}か. The text of 『おくのほそ{道|みち}』 itself, and many haiku books, print it {閑|しずか}さや{岩|いわ}にしみ{入|いる}{蝉|せみ}の{声|こえ}, with the same reading. The stillness is so deep that even the
loud cicadas seem to sink into the stone.

> {夏草|なつくさ}や{兵|つわもの}どもが{夢|ゆめ}の{跡|あと}

なつくさや / つわものどもが / ゆめのあと. Summer grass: all that is left of warriors' dreams. Season
word: {夏草|なつくさ} (summer). Cutting word: や. Written at Hiraizumi, where a great family of warriors
had been destroyed five centuries earlier. {兵|つわもの} is an old word for "warrior" (lesson 14's 兵,
read ヘイ in {兵士|へいし}; つわもの isn't a jōyō reading); one source prints the last word in kana, {夢|ゆめ}のあと.

> {荒海|あらうみ}や{佐渡|さど}によこたふ{天河|あまのがわ}

あらうみや / さどによこたう / あまのがわ. The wild sea: lying across to Sado, the River of Heaven.
Season word: {天河|あまのがわ} (the Milky Way, autumn in the old calendar). Cutting word: や. よこたふ is
historical kana for よこたう (to lie across), and {天河|あまのがわ} is usually written {天|あま}の{川|がわ} today.
Written facing the island of Sado on the Sea of Japan coast.

## Three haiku by Buson

{与謝蕪村|よさぶそん} (1716–1784; he died at the very end of 1783 by the old calendar) was born near Osaka
and was a painter as well as a poet; his haiku are often called pictorial.

> {春|はる}の{海|うみ}{終日|ひねもす}のたりのたりかな

はるのうみ / ひねもすのたり / のたりかな. The spring sea: all day long, rising and falling, rising
and falling. Season word: {春|はる}の{海|うみ} (spring). Cutting word: かな. {終日|ひねもす} is an old word for "all
day long" (today しゅうじつ in writing); のたりのたり is an onomatopoeia of slow, lazy waves. One
source prints かな as {哉|かな}, the old kanji for it.

> {夏河|なつかわ}を{越|こ}すうれしさよ{手|て}に{草履|ぞうり}

なつかわを / こすうれしさよ / てにぞうり. The joy of wading across a summer stream, sandals in hand.
Season word: {夏河|なつかわ} (summer). よ here works like a cutting word. {草履|ぞうり} is lesson 9's special
reading.

> しら{梅|うめ}に{明|あく}る{夜|よ}ばかりとなりにけり

しらうめに / あくるよばかりと / なりにけり. Now there are only nights that dawn on white plum
blossom. Season word: しら{梅|うめ}, white plum (early spring). Cutting word: けり. Buson's death poem
({辞世|じせい}), spoken on his deathbed in the last month of the year. {明|あく}る (read あくる; one source
prints {明|あ}くる) is the classical form of {明|あ}ける; the middle part has eight morae, one more than usual.

## Three haiku by Issa

{小林一茶|こばやしいっさ} (1763–1827 by the old calendar; early 1828 by ours) was born in Kashiwabara, in the
mountains of Nagano, and wrote about small creatures, children and his own hard life with humour
and sympathy. All the kanji of his name are on the course list.

> {雀|すずめ}の{子|こ}そこのけそこのけ{御馬|おうま}が{通|とお}る

すずめのこ / そこのけそこのけ / おうまがとおる. Little sparrow, out of the way, out of the way: a
fine horse is coming through. Season word: {雀|すずめ}の{子|こ}, a young sparrow (spring). そこのけ is "get
out of there"; {御馬|おうま} (one source prints お{馬|うま}) is the horse of some great person, teased by
the polite お.

> {我|われ}と{来|き}て{遊|あそ}べや{親|おや}のない{雀|すずめ}

われときて / あそべやおやの / ないすずめ. Come and play with me, little sparrow with no parents.
Season word: {親|おや}のない{雀|すずめ} (a motherless young sparrow, spring). Cutting word: や. Issa lost his
mother when he was a small child; readers usually hear the poet in the sparrow.

> {痩|や}せ{蛙|がえる}まけるな{一茶|いっさ}{是|これ}にあり

やせがえる / まけるないっさ / これにあり. Skinny frog, don't give up: Issa is here with you. Season
word: {蛙|かわず} / かえる (spring). The frogs are fighting, and Issa cheers on the weakest. Sources print it
{痩蛙|やせがえる}まけるな{一茶|いっさ}{是|これ}にあり (with the old {是|これ} for これ) or {痩|や}せ{蛙|がえる}まけるな{一茶|いっさ}これにあり.

## Waka and the Hundred Poets

『{百人一首|ひゃくにんいっしゅ}』 ("one poem each by a hundred poets") usually means the
『{小倉|おぐら}{百人一首|ひゃくにんいっしゅ}』, a selection of waka from the seventh to the thirteenth century,
traditionally credited to the poet {藤原定家|ふじわらのていか} (also read さだいえ) in the early Kamakura period;
another theory names a different compiler. Since the Edo period it has been printed as a card
game (karuta: カルタ or かるた). In the usual game, a reader reads a poem from a {読|よ}み{札|ふだ} (a card with
the whole poem), and players race to find and take the {取|と}り{札|ふだ}, which carries only the lower
verse in kana: the fastest know every poem by heart and move as soon as they hear the first sounds.
Competitive karuta ({競技|きょうぎ}かるた), with standard rules, began in the Meiji era and has national
championships today.

> {天|あま}の{原|はら}ふりさけ{見|み}れば{春日|かすが}なる{三笠|みかさ}の{山|やま}に{出|い}でし{月|つき}かも
>
> — {安倍仲麿|あべのなかまろ} (No. 7)

あまのはら / ふりさけみれば / かすがなる / みかさのやまに / いでしつきかも. When I look up far across
the plain of heaven: is that the moon that rose over Mount Mikasa at Kasuga? The poet went to Tang
China as a young scholar in the eighth century, with an envoy mission (lesson 22's {遣唐使|けんとうし}). He served the Tang court for decades; when
at last he set out for home, his ship was blown off course, and he died in China without seeing
Japan again. The poem is said to have been composed at a farewell feast before that voyage, though
the sources differ. ふりさけ{見|み}る is "to look up far"; かも at the end expresses wonder.
His name's last kanji is outside the course list, and the {三笠|みかさ} of the mountain's name has an
off-list second kanji.

> {花|はな}の{色|いろ}は{移|うつ}りにけりないたづらにわが{身|み}{世|よ}にふるながめせしまに
>
> — {小野小町|おののこまち} (No. 9)

はなのいろは / うつりにけりな / いたずらに / わがみよにふる / ながめせしまに. The colour of the
blossoms has faded, all in vain, while I passed my days in the world gazing out at the long rains.
Two pivot words ({掛詞|かけことば}): ふる is both {経|ふ}る (to pass time) and {降|ふ}る (to fall, of rain), and ながめ
is both {眺|なが}め (gazing, lesson 25) and {長雨|ながめ} (long rain). The faded blossoms are also the
poet's own beauty. いたづら is historical kana for いたずら, "in vain"; one source prints {移|うつ}り in
kana.

> ひさかたの{光|ひかり}のどけき{春|はる}の{日|ひ}にしづ{心|ごころ}なく{花|はな}の{散|ち}るらむ
>
> — {紀友則|きのとものり} (No. 33)

ひさかたの / ひかりのどけき / はるのひに / しずごころなく / はなのちるらん. On a spring day of such
gentle light, why do the blossoms fall with such restless hearts? ひさかたの is a pillow word
({枕詞|まくらことば}) for {光|ひかり}; のどけき is "calm, peaceful"; しづ{心|ごころ} (historical kana for しずごころ) is
"a quiet heart"; 〜らむ asks "why?". Lesson 22's 紀 is in the poet's family name.

## Write your own

Choose a season word from lesson 2's nature words ({夜桜|よざくら} spring, {雷|かみなり} summer, {稲妻|いなずま} autumn,
{初霜|はつしも} winter), put a cutting word after it, and add a concrete picture in 7-5. Two examples
written for this course:

> {初霜|はつしも}や{庭|にわ}の{小石|こいし}の{白|しろ}くなる

はつしもや / にわのこいしの / しろくなる. First frost: the pebbles in the garden turn white.

> {夜桜|よざくら}や{屋台|やたい}の{明|あ}かり{遠|とお}ざかる

よざくらや / やたいのあかり / とおざかる. Cherry blossoms at night: the lights of the stalls grow
distant.

Count your morae with kana, don't explain your feeling (show the picture instead), and use one
season word, not two.

## Words from this lesson

{和歌|わか}, {短歌|たんか}, {歌人|かじん}, {俳人|はいじん}, {切|き}れ{字|じ}, {上|かみ}の{句|く}, {下|しも}の{句|く}, {掛詞|かけことば}, {枕詞|まくらことば},
{読|よ}み{札|ふだ}, {取|と}り{札|ふだ}, {句集|くしゅう}, {歌集|かしゅう}, {句会|くかい}, {歳時記|さいじき}, {辞世|じせい}, {発句|ほっく}, {連歌|れんが},
{写生|しゃせい}, {名句|めいく}. Carried words to write in kanji: {俳句|はいく} and {季語|きご}.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete
the lesson.

lessons.title: Literary forms: べし, ごとし, ざる, をして, しめる
topics: ざる and the two ぬ
をして and しめる
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The last module is about Japanese on the page at its most demanding, and about the test itself.
Lessons 26–28 take the three kinds of text that make N1 reading hard: literary prose (this
lesson), the vocabulary that dense texts are built from (27) and academic and official writing
(28). Lesson 29 is a full set of exam-style practice and lesson 30 is the exam and a review.

This lesson gathers the **[[literary forms]]** you have been meeting one by one since N2 and adds the
last few. A literary form is a piece of older Japanese that modern writing keeps for weight,
rhythm or a touch of the past. Many of them are **[[classical forms]]**: endings of classical
Japanese, the written language before the twentieth century, that survive in proverbs, set
phrases, mottos, titles and a certain kind of essay. You will rarely write them, but N1 texts use
them without warning, and a learner who stumbles on {知|し}られざる or {言|い}わしめた loses the
thread of the sentence.

{継続|けいぞく}は{力|ちから}なり。 — Perseverance is strength. (A school motto: なり is the classical である.)

{光陰|こういん}{矢|や}のごとし。 — Time flies like an arrow. (ごとし is the classical ようだ.)

{学生|がくせい}は{学業|がくぎょう}に{励|はげ}むべし。 — Students shall apply themselves to their studies. (べし: "shall, must".)

{彼|かれ}の{演奏|えんそう}は、{世界|せかい}の{名手|めいしゅ}をして「{天才|てんさい}だ」と{言|い}わしめた。 — Their playing made even the world's finest players call them a genius.

The theme is thought and value: philosophy and ethics, logic, the self, faith and fate, and the
ordinary and the extraordinary. The reading is an essay in a literary style about an ordinary life.

> **Review (N2 lesson 26 and this course).** You know the written style (である, であろう, 〜ねばならない),
> the negative ぬ before nouns ({知|し}らぬ{間|ま}に, {予期|よき}せぬ), 〜べく "in order to" (lesson 12),
> 〜まじき and 〜べからず (lesson 20), 〜ごとき and 〜ごとく (lesson 23) and 〜たりとも (lesson 6). This
> lesson puts them into one system. The reference sheet "Literary and academic style" has the
> tables.

## 〜べし: "shall, must" from classical Japanese

べし is the classical auxiliary behind N3's 〜べきだ. It follows the dictionary form; する gives
すべし or するべし. Like any classical ending it has several forms, and you already know three of
them.

| Form | Job | Example | Met in |
|---|---|---|---|
| べし | ends a sentence | {心|こころ}すべし (take care) | this lesson |
| べき | before a noun, and べきだ / べきである | {守|まも}るべき{約束|やくそく} | N3 |
| べく | joins clauses: "in order to" | {解決|かいけつ}すべく{努力|どりょく}する | lesson 12 |
| べからず | "must not" (notices) | {立|た}ち{入|い}るべからず | lesson 20 |
| べからざる | before a noun: "that must not be" | {欠|か}くべからざる{存在|そんざい} | lesson 20 |

In modern Japanese, sentence-final べし lives in four places.

1. **Rules, mottos and instructions with an old-fashioned ring**: school and company mottos, old
   regulations, the instructions in a dojo.

{道具|どうぐ}は{使|つか}ったら{手入|てい}れすべし。 — Tools must be cared for after use.

{会員|かいいん}は{本会|ほんかい}の{規則|きそく}を{守|まも}るべし。 — Members shall observe the rules of this society.

2. **Set phrases and proverbs**, where べし often keeps its older senses ("can, is bound to"):

| Phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {推|お}して{知|し}るべし | you can guess the rest ("push on and you will know") |
| {恐|おそ}るべし / {恐|おそ}るべき + noun | formidable, fearsome ({恐|おそ}るべき{才能|さいのう}) |
| {後生|こうせい}{畏|おそ}るべし | the young are to be held in awe (they may surpass us; from the Analects) |
| 〜べくして〜 | was bound to: {起|お}こるべくして{起|お}きた{事故|じこ} |

{恐|おそ}るべき keeps the classical verb {恐|おそ}る (modern {恐|おそ}れる): {恐|おそ}れるべき{才能|さいのう}
would mean a talent one *ought* to fear. {起|お}こるべくして{起|お}きた means "happened as it was bound
to": the accident was the result of known causes, so it is a criticism.

3. **Headlines, advertising and the internet**, playfully: 「この{夏|なつ}、{行|い}くべし」 (you've got to
   go this summer). It sounds like an order from an old master, which is the joke.
4. **Old texts and historical fiction**, where it also means "will surely" and "should be able
   to". Recognize it there; don't use those senses.

The negative of sentence-final べし is べからず ("must not"), lesson 20's notice form; a literary
alternative is 〜べきではない. べし has no past: write 〜べきだった.

## 〜ごとし: "like, as"

ごとし is the classical ようだ. Lesson 23 taught its two living forms; here is the whole set.

| Form | Job | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ごとし | ends a sentence (proverbs, aphorisms) | {光陰|こういん}{矢|や}のごとし |
| ごとき + noun | "like, such as" before a noun | {夢|ゆめ}のごとき{日々|ひび} |
| ごとく | "as, like" before a verb or a comma | {前述|ぜんじゅつ}のごとく / {例|れい}のごとく |

It follows a noun + の, or a verb + が (or かの): {水|みず}の{流|なが}れるがごとく, {何事|なにごと}もなかったかのごとく.

{人生|じんせい}は{旅|たび}のごとし。 — Life is like a journey.

{過|す}ぎたるは{猶|なお}{及|およ}ばざるがごとし。 — Too much is as bad as too little. (A proverb with two classical forms: {過|す}ぎたる, "having gone too far", and {及|およ}ばざる, "falling short".)

{彼|かれ}は{何事|なにごと}もなかったかのごとく{話|はな}し{続|つづ}けた。 — They carried on talking as if nothing had happened.

{例|れい}のごとく{会議|かいぎ}は{一時間|いちじかん}{延|の}びた。 — As usual, the meeting overran by an hour.

- ごとし at the end of a sentence is for proverbs and deliberately weighty statements. In your own
  writing, ようだ and ようである are always right.
- {例|れい}のごとく ("as usual", often with a sigh) and {前述|ぜんじゅつ}のごとく / {以下|いか}のごとく
  ("as stated above / as follows") are everyday written Japanese.
- Lesson 23's N + ごとき of contempt or modesty ({私|わたし}ごとき) is the same ごとき.

## 〜ざる and the two kinds of ぬ

### ざる: "not", before a noun

ざる is the noun-modifying form of ず: the classical negative that N3 taught you in {降|ふ}らず、 and
N2 17 in 〜ざるを{得|え}ない. It follows the ない stem: {知|し}られ + ざる, {見|み} + ざる; する becomes
せざる. Most uses are fixed phrases before a noun.

| Phrase | Meaning | Modern |
|---|---|---|
| {知|し}られざる + noun | little-known, unknown to most | あまり{知|し}られていない |
| {招|まね}かれざる{客|きゃく} | an uninvited, unwelcome guest | {招|まね}かれていない{客|きゃく} |
| {予期|よき}せざる + noun | unforeseen | {予想|よそう}しなかった |
| 〜ならざる + noun | that is not: {天才|てんさい}ならざる{身|み} | {天才|てんさい}ではない{身|み} |
| {欠|か}くべからざる | indispensable (lesson 20) | なくてはならない |
| {見|み}ざる{聞|き}かざる{言|い}わざる | see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil | |

{知|し}られざる{名作|めいさく}を{紹介|しょうかい}する{番組|ばんぐみ}が{好評|こうひょう}だ。 — A programme introducing little-known masterpieces has been well received.

ならざる is なり (the classical である, below) + ざる: {人|ひと}ならざるもの is "a being that is not
human". The three monkeys of {見|み}ざる{聞|き}かざる{言|い}わざる are a pun: ざる sounds like
{猿|さる} (monkey) when voiced.

### Two kinds of ぬ

N2 taught the negative ぬ: {知|し}らぬ, {見知|みし}らぬ{人|ひと}. Classical Japanese also had a
**[[perfective]]** ぬ ("has done, has happened"), and modern Japanese keeps a few famous examples of it.
They look the same, so tell them apart by what comes before:

| | Attaches to | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| negative ぬ | the ない stem | {知|し}らぬ, {来|こ}ぬ{人|ひと} | doesn't know; a person who doesn't come |
| perfective ぬ | the ます stem | {風立|かぜた}ちぬ, {秋|あき}{来|き}ぬ | the wind has risen; autumn has come |

{風立|かぜた}ちぬ (the wind has risen) is the title of Hori Tatsuo's novel, finished in 1937, and of
Miyazaki Hayao's 2013 animated film; it does not mean "the wind doesn't rise". The clearest pair is
{来|く}る: {来|こ}ぬ (こぬ) is "doesn't come", {来|き}ぬ (きぬ) is "has come". Furigana settle it on the
page; in a title without furigana, the ます stem ({立|た}ち, {来|き}) tells you it's perfective.
The perfective ぬ is for recognition only, and neither ぬ is a drill form.

## 〜をして〜しめる: "make someone do", in writing

しめる is the classical causative, the ancestor of させる. It follows the ない stem, like させる:
{言|い}わ + しめる, {行|い}か + しめる; する becomes せしめる. The person made to act is marked by
をして (written for に).

| Modern | Written |
|---|---|
| {彼|かれ}に「{天才|てんさい}だ」と{言|い}わせた | {彼|かれ}をして「{天才|てんさい}だ」と{言|い}わしめた |
| {人々|ひとびと}に{涙|なみだ}を{流|なが}させた | {人々|ひとびと}をして{涙|なみだ}を{流|なが}さしめた |
| {人|ひと}を{感動|かんどう}させる | {人|ひと}をして{感動|かんどう}せしめる |

Today the pattern has one main use: praise. 〜をして〜と{言|い}わしめた says that someone's
achievement was so great it drew words from a person who would not say them lightly:

その{新人|しんじん}の{作品|さくひん}は、{厳|きび}しいことで{知|し}られる{批評家|ひひょうか}をして「{十年|じゅうねん}に{一人|ひとり}の{才能|さいのう}」と{言|い}わしめた。 — That newcomer's work made a critic known for severity call them "a talent that comes once in ten years".

- The subject is a work, an achievement or an event, and the sentence is past and written. You
  won't hear it in conversation except as a joke.
- をして also works with ordinary させる in writing: {何|なに}が{彼|かれ}をしてそうさせたのか (what made
  them do that?).
- Don't confuse the classical しめる with the everyday verb せしめる "to wangle, to pocket"
  ({小遣|こづか}いをせしめる, to wheedle pocket money out of someone), a different word in casual speech.
- しめる is not a drill form.

## なり: the classical である

なり is the classical assertion ("is"). It survives in mottos, proverbs and a few set formulas:

| Phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {継続|けいぞく}は{力|ちから}なり | perseverance is strength |
| {時|とき}は{金|かね}なり | time is money |
| {本日|ほんじつ}は{晴天|せいてん}なり | "today is fine weather" (the phrase for testing a microphone) |
| {金|きん}〜{円|えん}なり | the sum of … yen (on receipts and envelopes, often with a kanji outside N1) |
| さもありなん | that's only to be expected (なん is the perfective ぬ + the classical む: "surely it would be so") |

The answer しかり ("so it is", as in 〜もまたしかり, "the same goes for …") is written in kana in
this course: しか isn't a jōyō reading of its kanji. In {天才|てんさい}ならざる, なり meets ざる.

> **Review (lessons 6 and 21).** 〜たりとも〜ない ({一円|いちえん}たりとも{無駄|むだ}にできない) and
> N + にして ({四十|しじゅう}にして{惑|まど}わず, "at forty I had no more doubts", from the Analects; and
> {名人|めいじん}にして{初|はじ}めてできる) are literary forms too. たりとも contains the classical
> assertion たり; にして is the classical continuative of なり.

## The classical forms in this course, side by side

| Form | Classical role | Modern equivalent | Where you met it |
|---|---|---|---|
| ず / ざる | negative (continuative / before nouns) | ない | N3; this lesson |
| ぬ | negative before nouns; perfective after the ます stem | ない; た | N2 26; this lesson |
| まい | negative guess or will | ないだろう / ないつもりだ | N2 18 |
| べし / べき / べく | duty, recommendation; purpose | べきだ; ために | N3; 12; this lesson |
| べからず / べからざる | prohibition | てはいけない | 20 |
| まじき | unworthy of | べきではない | 20 |
| ごとし / ごとき / ごとく | likeness | ようだ / ような / ように | 23; this lesson |
| ん (= む) | will, intention | う / よう | 12 (んがため), 23 (んばかり) |
| ずとも | even without | なくても | 25 |
| たる | being (worthy of the name) | である | 24 |
| なり | assertion | である | this lesson |
| しめる | causative | させる | this lesson |

None of these is drilled in the conjugation drills, which stay with the N5 and N4 forms. Lesson
5h2 and 15h1 met them in classical texts; here they are in modern ones.

## Literary prose and editorial prose

An editorial and a literary essay may both end their sentences in である, but they read
differently. N1 gives you both, and the questions differ too: an editorial asks "what is the
writer's claim?", literary prose asks "what does the narrator feel, and why?"

| | Editorial and argument | Literary prose (essays, fiction) |
|---|---|---|
| Aim | persuade: claim, grounds, conclusion | show: a scene, a feeling, a turn of mind |
| Sentence endings | である, と{考|かんが}えられる, べきである | narrative past (た), である for reflection, sometimes the present for vividness |
| Vocabulary | kango: {課題|かだい}, {是正|ぜせい}, {懸念|けねん} | native words and images: {霜|しも}の{降|お}りた{草|くさ}, {刃|は}を{研|と}ぐ |
| Classical forms | few: べく, ざるを{得|え}ない | for rhythm and weight: ぬ, ごとし, べし, ざる |
| What is left unsaid | little: the logic is explicit | much: feelings shown through actions and objects |
| Connectors | しかし, したがって, つまり | fewer; the order of scenes carries the logic |

Reading literary prose for the exam: follow the narrator's changes of mind (they usually turn on
an event), notice what objects stand for (a tool, a season), and look for the sentence where the
narrator names what they have understood. That sentence is almost always the answer to the last
question.

## Words for thought and value

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| Philosophy | {哲学|てつがく}, {哲学者|てつがくしゃ}, {思想|しそう}, {思考|しこう}, {観念|かんねん}, {概念|がいねん}, {抽象|ちゅうしょう}, {抽象的|ちゅうしょうてき}, {真理|しんり}, {命題|めいだい}, {普遍|ふへん}, {普遍的|ふへんてき}, {理性|りせい}, {感性|かんせい}, {主観|しゅかん}, {客観|きゃっかん}, {主体|しゅたい}, {認識|にんしき}する, {自明|じめい}, イデオロギー (lesson 13), パラドックス, ジレンマ |
| Ethics | {倫理|りんり}, {倫理的|りんりてき}, {善悪|ぜんあく}, {善|ぜん}, {善人|ぜんにん}, {善意|ぜんい}, {最善|さいぜん}, {偽善|ぎぜん}, {善|よ}し{悪|あ}し, {道理|どうり}, {理念|りねん}, モラル (lesson 17), タブー |
| The self | {自己|じこ}, {自我|じが}, {自尊心|じそんしん}, {自負|じふ}, {自覚|じかく}する, {己|おのれ}, {自己満足|じこまんぞく}, {自己中心的|じこちゅうしんてき}, {利己的|りこてき}, エゴ, アイデンティティ |
| Faith and fate | {信仰|しんこう}, {悟|さと}る, {悟|さと}り, {仰|あお}ぐ, {崇高|すうこう} (lesson 8), {神秘|しんぴ}, {奇跡|きせき}, {運命|うんめい}, {宿命|しゅくめい}, {因果|いんが}, {因縁|いんねん} (lesson 7) |
| Ordinary and extraordinary | {平凡|へいぼん}, {非凡|ひぼん}, {凡人|ぼんじん}, {奇妙|きみょう}, {奇抜|きばつ}, {奇怪|きかい}, {妙|みょう}, {微妙|びみょう}, {絶妙|ぜつみょう}, {唯一|ゆいいつ}, {唯一無二|ゆいいつむに}, {好奇心|こうきしん} |
| Harshness and folly | {残酷|ざんこく}, {過酷|かこく}, {愚|おろ}か, {愚者|ぐしゃ}, {愚直|ぐちょく}, {堕落|だらく}する, {臆病|おくびょう} (lesson 17), {臆測|おくそく}, {臆|おく}する |
| Time and calm | {生涯|しょうがい}, {天涯孤独|てんがいこどく}, {悠久|ゆうきゅう}, {悠然|ゆうぜん}, {恒久|こうきゅう}, {恒常|こうじょう}, {恒例|こうれい}, {泰然|たいぜん}, {安泰|あんたい} |

{主観|しゅかん} and {客観|きゃっかん} are nouns; the carried {主観的|しゅかんてき} and {客観的|きゃっかんてき} are

> {祖父|そふ}が{亡|な}くなったのは、その{翌年|よくねん}の{冬|ふゆ}だった。{享年|きょうねん}{八十八|はちじゅうはち}。{小|ちい}さな{葬儀|そうぎ}になるだろうと{思|おも}っていたが、{当日|とうじつ}は{思|おも}いがけず{大勢|おおぜい}の{人|ひと}が{集|あつ}まった。{近所|きんじょ}の{老人|ろうじん}、{商店街|しょうてんがい}の{店主|てんしゅ}、{見知|みし}らぬ{若|わか}い{夫婦|ふうふ}。{遺影|いえい}の{祖父|そふ}は、{少|すこ}し{照|て}れくさそうに{笑|わら}っていた。{聞|き}けば{祖父|そふ}は、{壊|こわ}れた{戸|と}や{傾|かたむ}いた{棚|たな}を、{頼|たの}まれるたびに{黙|だま}って{直|なお}していたのだという。お{金|かね}はほとんど{受|う}け{取|と}らなかったらしい。{若|わか}い{夫婦|ふうふ}は、{雨漏|あまも}りのする{古|ふる}い{家|いえ}を{借|か}りたとき、{祖父|そふ}が{一週間|いっしゅうかん}かけて{床|ゆか}を{張|は}り{替|か}えてくれたのだと{話|はな}し、{何度|なんど}も{頭|あたま}を{下|さ}げた。{家族|かぞく}の{誰|だれ}も{知|し}らなかった、{知|し}られざる{一面|いちめん}である。{名|な}もない{一人|ひとり}の{職人|しょくにん}の{生涯|しょうがい}が、{多|おお}くの{人|ひと}をして{涙|なみだ}を{流|なが}さしめたのだ。
>
> {葬儀|そうぎ}の{帰|かえ}り{道|みち}、{私|わたし}は{長|なが}い{間|あいだ}の{思|おも}い{違|ちが}いに{気|き}づかされた。{非凡|ひぼん}なものは、どこか{遠|とお}くにあるのではない。{同|おな}じ{仕事|しごと}を{丹念|たんねん}に{繰|く}り{返|かえ}し、{頼|たの}まれれば{黙|だま}って{手|て}を{貸|か}す。その{積|つ}み{重|かさ}ねこそが、{一人|ひとり}の{人間|にんげん}を{唯一無二|ゆいいつむに}の{存在|そんざい}にするのではないか。{奇跡|きせき}とは、{平凡|へいぼん}な{日々|ひび}が{気|き}づかぬうちに{織|お}り{上|あ}げる{一枚|いちまい}の{布|ぬの}のごときものなのかもしれない。{思|おも}えば、{古今|ここん}の{哲学者|てつがくしゃ}の{中|なか}にも、{日々|ひび}の{暮|く}らしの{中|なか}に{真理|しんり}を{見|み}た{人|ひと}は{少|すく}なくない。{善|ぜん}とは、{抽象的|ちゅうしょうてき}な{概念|がいねん}である{前|まえ}に、{傾|かたむ}いた{棚|たな}を{直|なお}すという{具体的|ぐたいてき}な{行|おこな}いなのだ。{祖父|そふ}は{本|ほん}こそ{読|よ}まなかったが、{私|わたし}などよりはるかに{深|ふか}く、それを{知|し}っていたのであろう。
>
> それから{私|わたし}の{暮|く}らしが{劇的|げきてき}に{変|か}わったわけではない。{相変|あいか}わらず{平凡|へいぼん}な{会社員|かいしゃいん}として{働|はたら}き、{満員電車|まんいんでんしゃ}に{揺|ゆ}られている。ただ、{同|おな}じ{道|みち}を{歩|ある}く{朝|あさ}が、{以前|いぜん}ほど{退屈|たいくつ}ではなくなった。{霜|しも}の{形|かたち}は{毎朝|まいあさ}{違|ちが}い、{川|かわ}の{色|いろ}も{季節|きせつ}ごとに{移|うつ}ろう。{見|み}ようとしなかっただけで、{世界|せかい}は{初|はじ}めから{奇妙|きみょう}なほど{豊|ゆた}かだったのである。
>
> {今|いま}、{私|わたし}の{机|つくえ}の{上|うえ}には{祖父|そふ}の{古|ふる}い{道具|どうぐ}が{一|ひと}つ{置|お}いてある。{使|つか}い{方|かた}も{満足|まんぞく}に{知|し}らぬ{私|わたし}だが、ときどき{取|と}り{出|だ}しては{布|ぬの}で{拭|ふ}いている。{刃|は}の{研|と}ぎ{方|かた}を{教|おそ}わっておかなかったことを、{今|いま}になって{悔|く}やんでいる。{明日|あす}もまた、ありふれた{一日|いちにち}が{来|く}るだろう。それを{丹念|たんねん}に{生|い}きるべし。{祖父|そふ}が{生|い}きていたら、きっとそう{言|い}うにちがいない。

{冬|ふゆ}{来|き}ぬ = winter has come (the perfective ぬ: {来|き}, the ます stem); {口調|くちょう} = a
tone, a way of speaking; とかく = all too readily (written); {大工|だいく} = a carpenter; {研|と}ぐ =
to sharpen; {装|よそお}う = to put on, pretend; {就|つ}く = to take up (a job); {聞|き}けば = I'm told,
it turns out; {一面|いちめん} = a side (of a person); {織|お}り{上|あ}げる = to weave (to the end);
{満足|まんぞく}に = properly, adequately (with a negative); {整然|せいぜん}と = in neat order; {難解|なんかい} = hard to understand; {夜|よ}を{徹|てっ}する = to stay up all night; {遺影|いえい} = a portrait of the dead (at a funeral); {照|て}れくさい = embarrassed; {帰省|きせい}する = to go back to one's home town; {黙々|もくもく}と = silently, without a word; {分|わ}からん = {分|わ}からない (ん is the spoken ぬ); {雨漏|あまも}り = a leaking roof; {張|は}り{替|か}える = to replace (a floor, paper or cloth); {移|うつ}ろう = to change, pass (literary). Find the literary forms: {来|き}ぬ, ごとし,
すべし, {極|きわ}まりない, まだ{見|み}ぬ, ならざる, ごとくには, {生|い}きられぬ, {分|わ}からん, {笑|わら}われるべき, {知|し}られざる,
をして〜{流|なが}さしめた, {気|き}づかぬうちに, ごときもの, であろう, {知|し}らぬ, べし.

1. How did the writer see the grandfather's life as a teenager, and what did the writer want instead?
2. What happened one summer when the writer came home, and how does the writer judge it now?
3. What did the writer learn at the funeral, and what does 「{知|し}られざる{一面|いちめん}」 refer to?
4. What is the writer's view of the extraordinary at the end, and how does the last paragraph echo the second?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. As utterly boring ({退屈|たいくつ}{極|きわ}まりない): the same things repeated day after day. The writer
   longed for the unusual and craved a world not yet seen (まだ{見|み}ぬ{世界|せかい}).
2. The writer showed off ideas from university (people should be free, life must have meaning);
   the grandfather, still working, said only that he didn't understand difficult things, but that
   shelves are better not leaning. The writer laughed at this as a simple craftsman's remark, and
   now sees that the one who deserved to be laughed at was the writer ({笑|わら}われるべきは{私|わたし}のほう).
3. That the grandfather had quietly repaired doors and shelves for anyone who asked, taking almost
   no money (the young couple's floor, for example). This was the "little-known side" of him that
   even the family didn't know, and it brought many people to tears.
4. The extraordinary isn't somewhere far away: it is the accumulation of ordinary days done with
   care, like a cloth woven without one noticing; goodness is a concrete act (straightening a
   shelf) before it is a concept, and the world was rich all along. The grandfather's motto 「{手入|てい}れすべし」 in
   paragraph 2 returns as 「{丹念|たんねん}に{生|い}きるべし」, and the writer now cares for the grandfather's tool.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Winter has come again this year. Murmuring this in the manner of an old poem, I was walking along
the path by the river. The frosted grass glittered in the morning sun. In the cold air, my breath was white. Every morning I walk the
same path, cross the same bridge and buy bread at the same shop. "Time flies like an arrow," as the
saying goes, and looking back, such ordinary days pass in an instant. Human beings are creatures
all too ready to seek something extraordinary somewhere other than where they are.

So was I, when I was young. My grandfather was a carpenter in the town, a person of few words. He
rose earlier than anyone in the morning, and when his work was done he always cared for his tools. In his workshop, well-worn tools stood in neat rows, and the scent of wood always hung in the air.
"After you use your tools, look after them" was the one thing he was always saying, and the sight
of him sharpening a blade did not change for decades. To me as a teenager, his life looked utterly
boring. What meaning could there be in a life of repeating the same things? I longed for the
unusual and craved a world I had never seen.

At university I studied philosophy. I shut myself up in the library poring over difficult books, and argued through the night with friends. The philosophers of all ages had pursued universal truths that
transcend time and place. What is the good? What is the self? As I juggled abstract concepts, I
felt I had become someone rather important. Thinking about it now, that was no more than the small
pride of an ordinary person putting on the airs of an extraordinary one. A few years after
graduating, unable to find the kind of work I had imagined, I at last realized my own limits. One
who is not a genius cannot live as a genius does.

Whenever I went home, my grandfather was in his workshop, silently shaping wood. One summer, full
of myself, I laid out the words I had just learned at university: that human beings ought to be
free, that life must have meaning. My grandfather listened without stopping his work, and in the
end said just one thing: "I don't understand difficult things. But it's better if shelves don't
lean." I laughed at the answer as the remark of a simple, stubborn craftsman. Only much later did I
learn that the one who deserved to be laughed at was me.

My grandfather died in the winter of the following year, at the age of eighty-eight. I had thought
it would be a small funeral, but on the day, unexpectedly, a great many people came: old people
from the neighbourhood, the owners of shops on the high street, a young couple I didn't know. In the funeral portrait, my grandfather was smiling, a little embarrassed. It
turned out that whenever he was asked, my grandfather had quietly mended broken doors and leaning
shelves. He seems to have taken almost no money for it. The young couple told us that when they had rented an old house with a leaking roof, he had spent a week relaying its floor, and they bowed again and again. It was a side of him no one in the family
had known. The life of one nameless craftsman had moved many people to tears.

On the way home from the funeral, I was made to see a misunderstanding I had held for a long time.
The extraordinary is not somewhere far away. To repeat the same work with care, and to lend a hand
in silence when asked: is it not the accumulation of such things that makes one human being unlike
any other? A miracle may be something like a single cloth that ordinary days weave without our
noticing. Come to think of it, among the philosophers of every age there are not a few who saw the
truth in everyday life. Goodness, before it is an abstract concept, is a concrete act: setting a
leaning shelf straight. My grandfather never read the books, but he surely knew this far more deeply
than I did.

It's not that my life has changed dramatically since then. I still work as an ordinary office
worker and ride packed trains. But the mornings when I walk the same path are not as dull as they
were. The frost has a different shape every morning, and the colour of the river shifts with the
seasons. It was only that I hadn't tried to see: the world had been strangely rich from the start.

Now one of my grandfather's old tools lies on my desk. I hardly know how to use it properly, but
from time to time I take it out and wipe it with a cloth. Now I regret never having learned from him how to sharpen a blade. Tomorrow, too, an ordinary day will come.
Live it with care. If my grandfather were alive, I'm sure that is what he would say.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{継続|けいぞく}は{力|ちから}なり。
= Perseverance is strength.
{光陰|こういん}{矢|や}のごとし。
= Time flies like an arrow.
{推|お}して{知|し}るべし。
= You can guess the rest.
{知|し}られざる{名作|めいさく}を{紹介|しょうかい}します。
= I'll introduce a little-known masterpiece.
{例|れい}のごとく、{会議|かいぎ}は{長引|ながび}いた。
= As usual, the meeting dragged on.
{彼|かれ}の{演奏|えんそう}は、{名手|めいしゅ}をして{天才|てんさい}と{言|い}わしめた。
= Their playing made even the masters call them a genius.
```

Read classical forms in full and evenly: べし, ごとし and ざる are never shortened. In
{来|こ}ぬ / {来|き}ぬ the furigana is the whole difference, so read what is printed.

## Common mistakes

- {恐|おそ}れるべき{才能|さいのう} for "a formidable talent": it says a talent one ought to fear. The fixed
  phrase keeps the classical verb: {恐|おそ}るべき.
- Reading {風立|かぜた}ちぬ or {秋|あき}{来|き}ぬ as negatives. After the ます stem, ぬ is perfective:
  "has risen", "has come".
- ×{知|し}るざる, ×{見|み}るざる. ざる follows the ない stem: {知|し}らざる, {見|み}ざる; する → せざる.
- ×{言|い}いしめた. しめる follows the ない stem like させる: {言|い}わしめた; する → せしめる.
- Using 〜をして〜しめる in conversation, or for something unremarkable. It's written and mostly
  praises a great achievement.
- ×{行|い}くべしだった. べし has no past: {行|い}くべきだった.
- Ending your own essay sentences in ごとし or べし. In modern writing, use ようだ and べきである; keep
  the classical endings for quotations, mottos and deliberate effect.
- Reading {出納|すいとう} as しゅつのう, or {夏至|げし} as かし.

## Key points

- Literary forms are older Japanese kept for weight and rhythm; most are classical forms. Recognize
  them; write them sparingly.
- べし (shall, must; mottos, rules, set phrases): べき, べく, べからず, べからざる are its other forms.
  {推|お}して{知|し}るべし, {恐|おそ}るべき, 〜べくして〜.
- ごとし (like): ごとき + noun, ごとく + verb; N の / V が ごとし. {例|れい}のごとく, {前述|ぜんじゅつ}のごとく.
- ざる (not, before nouns): {知|し}られざる, {招|まね}かれざる{客|きゃく}, ならざる.
- ぬ: negative after the ない stem ({知|し}らぬ), perfective after the ます stem ({風立|かぜた}ちぬ).
- 〜をして〜しめる: written causative, mostly praise: {言|い}わしめた; する → せしめる.
- なり: classical である in mottos ({継続|けいぞく}は{力|ちから}なり).
- Literary prose shows; editorials argue. Follow the narrator's turns and the objects that carry
  meaning.
- New kanji: 哲 倫 抽 概 唯 恒 遍 矛 盾 善 己 悟 仰 貞 納 享 臆 至 甚 奇 妙 酷 凡 愚 貴 悠 涯 泰 如 堕 渇 丹.

lessons.title: Words and set expressions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

N1 texts are dense because their words are. A single sentence of an editorial may hold a
**[[compound verb]]** whose meaning has drifted far from its parts, a **[[four-character compound]]**,
an **[[idiom]]** and three kango that a conversation would put in native words. The N1 vocabulary
questions test exactly this: a word chosen for a context, a paraphrase in other words, and the
one sentence that uses a word correctly. Unlike N2, the N1 has no word-formation questions; this
lesson teaches how words are built so that you can read them, not so that you can fill in a
prefix.

{彼|かれ}の{説明|せつめい}には{首尾一貫|しゅびいっかん}した{論理|ろんり}があり、{専門家|せんもんか}も{舌|した}を{巻|ま}いた。 — Their explanation had logic that held together from start to finish, and even the specialists were amazed.

{新|あたら}しい{発見|はっけん}が{定説|ていせつ}を{覆|くつがえ}し、{研究|けんきゅう}の{流|なが}れは{徐々|じょじょ}に{変|か}わりつつある。 — A new discovery has overturned the accepted theory, and the course of research is gradually changing.

The theme is abstract words: degree and extent, change and its speed, agreement and difference,
obstruction, order and position, and words of time. The reading is an explanatory essay on how
words change their meaning.

## Compound verbs: when the second verb changes the meaning

A compound verb joins the ます stem of one verb to another: {思|おも}い + {込|こ}む. The second verb
often stops meaning what it means alone and becomes a kind of suffix. The N1 tests the figurative
senses, so learn each second element as a family.

| Second verb | What it adds | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| 〜{込|こ}む | into; deeply, wholly | {打|う}ち{込|こ}む (throw oneself into), {溶|と}け{込|こ}む (fit in), {追|お}い{込|こ}む (corner), {見込|みこ}む (anticipate), {思|おも}い{込|こ}む (be convinced: carried) |
| 〜{切|き}る | completely; decisively | {言|い}い{切|き}る (state flatly), {割|わ}り{切|き}る (take a practical view), {踏|ふ}み{切|き}る (take the plunge; lesson 15's word), {使|つか}い{切|き}る (use up) |
| 〜{抜|ぬ}く | through to the end; out | {見抜|みぬ}く (see through), {考|かんが}え{抜|ぬ}く (think through), {生|い}き{抜|ぬ}く (survive to the end) |
| 〜{返|かえ}す | back; again | {繰|く}り{返|かえ}す (repeat), {言|い}い{返|かえ}す (answer back), {見返|みかえ}す (look again; show them) |
| 〜{尽|つ}くす | exhaustively, to the full | {知|し}り{尽|つ}くす (know inside out), {立|た}ち{尽|つ}くす (stand rooted to the spot) |
| 〜{損|そこ}なう | fail to; do wrongly | {見損|みそこ}なう (misjudge; miss seeing), {言|い}い{損|そこ}なう (misspeak), {聞|き}き{損|そこ}なう (mishear) |
| 〜かねる | can't bring oneself to (N2) | {決|き}めかねる (can't decide), {見|み}かねて (unable to stand by and watch) |

The meaning drifts in a typical way: from a physical action to an attitude or a decision.

| Verb | Literal sense | Figurative sense (the one tested) |
|---|---|---|
| {割|わ}り{切|き}る | divide with no remainder | treat something in a businesslike way, without feelings |
| {踏|ふ}み{切|き}る | take off (in a jump) | go ahead with a bold decision |
| {打|う}ち{込|こ}む | drive in (a nail, a stake) | devote oneself to |
| {見損|みそこ}なう | miss seeing | think too well of someone, then be disappointed |
| {立|た}ち{尽|つ}くす | stand to the end | stand motionless, stunned |

{仕事|しごと}は{仕事|しごと}と{割|わ}り{切|き}ることにした。 — I decided to treat work as just work.

{会社|かいしゃ}は{赤字|あかじ}の{工場|こうじょう}の{閉鎖|へいさ}に{踏|ふ}み{切|き}った。 — The company went ahead with closing the loss-making factory.

{君|きみ}がそんなことを{言|い}うとは、{見損|みそこ}なったよ。 — I never thought you'd say that. I misjudged you.

- 〜{切|き}れない and 〜{切|き}れる are common: {言|い}い{切|き}れない (can't say for certain), {数|かぞ}え{切|き}れない
  (countless), {待|ま}ち{切|き}れない (can't wait).
- 〜{抜|ぬ}く adds effort: {考|かんが}え{抜|ぬ}いた{末|すえ}に is "after thinking it through to the end". Compare
  {追|お}い{抜|ぬ}く (overtake), where 抜 keeps its sense of passing.
- Write the second verb in kanji when it keeps a meaning ({込|こ}む, {切|き}る, {抜|ぬ}く); the
  grammatical 〜かねる stays in kana, as in N2.

## Kango and wago: two words for one idea

Many ideas have a **[[kango]]** (a Sino-Japanese word, read in on'yomi) and a **[[wago]]** (a native word,
read in kun'yomi). The kango is more formal and abstract; the wago is more concrete and spoken.
Paraphrase questions often pair them.

| Kango (written, formal) | Wago (everyday) | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| {遂行|すいこう}する | やり{遂|と}げる | carry out, see through |
| {阻止|そし}する | {食|く}い{止|と}める | stop, prevent |
| {妨害|ぼうがい}する | {邪魔|じゃま}する, {妨|さまた}げる | obstruct |
| {一致|いっち}する | {合|あ}う | agree, match |
| {返還|へんかん}する | {返|かえ}す | return |
| {補充|ほじゅう}する | {補|おぎな}う, {足|た}す | replenish |
| {緩和|かんわ}する | {和|やわ}らげる, {緩|ゆる}める | ease |
| {縮小|しゅくしょう}する | {縮|ちぢ}める | reduce |
| {潜在|せんざい}する | {潜|ひそ}む | lie hidden |
| {差異|さい} | {違|ちが}い | difference |

{邪魔|じゃま} is a kango too, but an everyday one. Not every pair is exact: {返還|へんかん}する is for
territory, land and property handed back formally; you {返|かえ}す a library book.

{両国|りょうこく}の{努力|どりょく}で、{国境|こっきょう}の{紛争|ふんそう}の{拡大|かくだい}を{食|く}い{止|と}めた。 — The two countries' efforts stopped the border dispute from spreading.

{政府|せいふ}は{感染|かんせん}の{拡大|かくだい}を{阻止|そし}するため、{新|あら}たな{措置|そち}を{講|こう}じた。 — The government took new measures to block the spread of the infection.

## Four-character compounds

A {四字熟語|よじじゅくご} (four-character compound, N2 15h2) is a set expression of four kanji, many
from Chinese classics and Buddhism. Most are built from two pairs: {本末|ほんまつ} (root and branch
tips) + {転倒|てんとう} (turned over) = "putting the cart before the horse". Knowing the structure
helps you read the ones you haven't met.

| Compound | Reading | Meaning | Usually used as |
|---|---|---|---|
| {臨機応変|りんきおうへん} | りんきおうへん | adapting to circumstances | 〜に{対応|たいおう}する |
| {本末転倒|ほんまつてんとう} | ほんまつてんとう | priorities backwards | 〜だ |
| {以心伝心|いしんでんしん} | いしんでんしん | understanding without words | 〜で{伝|つた}わる |
| {千差万別|せんさばんべつ} | せんさばんべつ | endlessly varied | 〜だ |
| {異口同音|いくどうおん} | いくどうおん | with one voice | 〜に{言|い}う |
| {半信半疑|はんしんはんぎ} | はんしんはんぎ | half in doubt | 〜で |
| {自業自得|じごうじとく} | じごうじとく | one's own fault | 〜だ |
| {首尾一貫|しゅびいっかん} | しゅびいっかん | consistent throughout | 〜した, 〜している |
| {前代未聞|ぜんだいみもん} | ぜんだいみもん | unheard of | 〜の + noun |
| {一朝一夕|いっちょういっせき} | いっちょういっせき | overnight | 〜には〜ない |
| {言語道断|ごんごどうだん} | ごんごどうだん | outrageous | 〜だ |
| {優柔不断|ゆうじゅうふだん} | ゆうじゅうふだん | indecisive | 〜な, 〜だ |

- **Reading traps**: {異口同音|いくどうおん} (いく, not いこう), {言語道断|ごんごどうだん} (ごんご, not げんご),
  {前代未聞|ぜんだいみもん} (みもん, not みぶん), {一朝一夕|いっちょういっせき} (いっせき, not いちゆう).
  Buddhist readings are behind several of them.
- **Patterns**: parallel pairs ({半信半疑|はんしんはんぎ}: half-believe, half-doubt; {自業自得|じごうじとく}: one's
  own deeds, one's own reward), two halves that say the same thing ({千差万別|せんさばんべつ}: a thousand differences, ten thousand distinctions), and subject + predicate
  ({本末転倒|ほんまつてんとう}).
- Most are nouns that take だ, の or に. {一朝一夕|いっちょういっせき} almost always comes with a negative:
  {一朝一夕|いっちょういっせき}には{身|み}につかない.
- You have met others already: {試行錯誤|しこうさくご} (lesson 9), {唯一無二|ゆいいつむに} (26),
  {天涯孤独|てんがいこどく} (26), and N2's {一石二鳥|いっせきにちょう}, {適材適所|てきざいてきしょ},
  {我田引水|がでんいんすい}, {一長一短|いっちょういったん}.
- In essays, one four-character compound in a paragraph gives weight; three in a sentence sounds
  like a speech by a company president. Use them where a plain phrase would be longer.

## Idioms with the body

A {慣用句|かんようく} (idiom) is a set phrase whose meaning isn't the sum of its words. Body parts give
Japanese hundreds of them; these are the N1-level ones this lesson adds. Each has a fixed verb and
often a fixed tone (praise, criticism).

| Idiom | Literally | Meaning | Tone |
|---|---|---|---|
| {腹|はら}を{割|わ}る | split one's belly | speak frankly ({腹|はら}を{割|わ}って{話|はな}す) | positive |
| {肩|かた}を{並|なら}べる | line up shoulders | be on a par with | neutral |
| {舌|した}を{巻|ま}く | roll one's tongue | be amazed at someone's skill | praise |
| {眉|まゆ}をひそめる | knit one's brows | frown in disapproval | criticism |
| {目|め}に{余|あま}る | be too much for the eye | be too bad to overlook | criticism |
| {口|くち}を{挟|はさ}む | put one's mouth in | butt in | mild criticism |
| {手|て}を{焼|や}く | burn one's hands | have one's hands full with | complaint |
| {腰|こし}を{据|す}える | set one's hips | settle down to something seriously | positive |

{議長|ぎちょう}は、{会議|かいぎ}の{途中|とちゅう}で{何度|なんど}も{口|くち}を{挟|はさ}む{委員|いいん}に{眉|まゆ}をひそめた。 — The chair frowned at the committee member who kept butting in during the meeting.

- The verb is fixed: the idioms are not {腹|はら}を{開|ひら}く or {舌|した}を{回|まわ}す. Usage questions swap it.
- The tone is fixed too: {舌|した}を{巻|ま}く is admiration only, so you can't {舌|した}を{巻|ま}く at a
  failure. {目|め}に{余|あま}る always criticizes.
- ひそめる is in kana: its kanji is outside N1.

## How dictionaries mark words and idioms

A Japanese monolingual dictionary ({国語辞典|こくごじてん}) lists a word under its reading, in kana
(あいうえお) order, with the written forms in brackets. Senses are numbered; a usage marked as colloquial
(〔{俗|ぞく}〕 or 「{俗|ぞく}に」) or as a newer use is often noted after the original sense. Idioms are
usually listed under their head noun ({腹|はら} → {腹|はら}を{割|わ}る), marked as an idiom, and
four-character compounds usually have their own entries. Examples ({用例|ようれい}) follow each sense.
Dictionaries differ in their marks; the introduction ({凡例|はんれい}) of each explains its own.

When you meet a word whose meaning seems to clash with its context, look for a later sense in the
entry: the meaning the text uses may be the newer one, or the older one.

> {意味|いみ}が{逆転|ぎゃくてん}する{例|れい}もある。「やばい」はもともと{危険|きけん}や{不都合|ふつごう}を{表|あらわ}す{言葉|ことば}だったが、{今|いま}では{若|わか}い{世代|せだい}を{中心|ちゅうしん}に「すばらしい」の{意味|いみ}でも{使|つか}われる。「{微妙|びみょう}」も、「{細|こま}やかで{言|い}い{表|あらわ}しがたい」という{本来|ほんらい}の{意味|いみ}から、「あまりよくない」を{遠回|とおまわ}しに{伝|つた}える{言葉|ことば}へと{変化|へんか}を{遂|と}げつつある。{強|つよ}い{言葉|ことば}は{使|つか}われるうちに{力|ちから}を{失|うしな}い、{直接|ちょくせつ}{言|い}いにくいことは{別|べつ}の{言葉|ことば}に{包|つつ}まれる。こうした{現象|げんしょう}は{日本語|にほんご}に{限|かぎ}らず、{多|おお}くの{言語|げんご}で{見|み}られるという。
>
> {比喩|ひゆ}もまた、{言葉|ことば}を{動|うご}かす{大|おお}きな{力|ちから}である。「{割|わ}り{切|き}る」は{本来|ほんらい}、{割|わ}り{算|ざん}で{余|あま}りが{出|で}ないことを{言|い}う。それが{人|ひと}の{態度|たいど}に{転|てん}じ、{感情|かんじょう}を{交|まじ}えずに{物事|ものごと}を{処理|しょり}するという{意味|いみ}になった。「{踏|ふ}み{切|き}る」も、{跳躍|ちょうやく}の{際|さい}に{地面|じめん}を{強|つよ}く{蹴|け}る{動作|どうさ}から、{思|おも}い{切|き}った{決断|けつだん}を{表|あらわ}すようになった。{具体的|ぐたいてき}な{動作|どうさ}の{言葉|ことば}が、やがて{抽象的|ちゅうしょうてき}な{意味|いみ}を{帯|お}びる。「{腹|はら}を{割|わ}る」も、{腹|はら}の{中|なか}、つまり{本心|ほんしん}を{開|ひら}いて{見|み}せるという{比喩|ひゆ}から{来|き}ている。{慣用句|かんようく}の{多|おお}くは、こうして{生|う}まれたものだ。

{改訂|かいてい} = revision (lesson 6's word); {営|いとな}み = workings, activity; {略語|りゃくご} = an abbreviation; {時機|じき} = the right moment, an opportunity; {満|み}ち{引|ひ}き = the ebb and flow (of the tide); {物悲|ものがな}しい = vaguely sad; {力量|りきりょう} =
ability, capacity; {精一杯|せいいっぱい} = with all one's might; けんそん = modesty (its second kanji is
outside N1); {的|まと} = a target ({議論|ぎろん}の{的|まと}, the focus of debate); {少|すく}なからず = not a
few; {遠回|とおまわ}しに = indirectly; {交|まじ}える = to mix in; {帯|お}びる = to take on (a quality);
{退|しりぞ}ける = to reject; {正誤|せいご} = right and wrong; {書|か}き{留|と}める = to write down; かといって = but that doesn't mean. 「{全然|ぜんぜん}」 with positives:
the writer reports a claim ({指摘|してき}がある) without endorsing it; that is the kind of hedge
lesson 28 teaches.

1. What does 「{役不足|やくぶそく}」 originally mean, and why is the new use risky?
2. What does the writer conclude from the older uses of 「{全然|ぜんぜん}」?
3. What two forces of change does the writer describe in paragraphs 6 and 7?
4. What attitude to change does the writer recommend?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. That the role given is too light for the person's ability. Many now use it to mean their own
   ability falls short; the two senses are opposites, so words meant modestly may sound arrogant
   ({傲慢|ごうまん}) to some listeners. ({潮時|しおどき} shows a softer shift of the same kind: once the
   right moment to do something, now often the time to withdraw.)
2. That the rule "{全然|ぜんぜん} goes with a negative" may itself be a convention of one period: what counts
   as correct Japanese differs from era to era.
3. Words reversing or softening their meaning (strong words lose force; things hard to say are
   wrapped in other words: やばい, {微妙|びみょう}) and metaphor (words for concrete actions take on
   abstract meanings: {割|わ}り{切|き}る, {踏|ふ}み{切|き}る, and many idioms).
4. Neither rejecting every new use nor accepting everything: know that a word may have several
   meanings and choose according to the listener and the situation.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Dictionaries are revised every few years. Each time, new words are added, old words disappear,
and new senses are written into words that already exist. Not a few people frown at such changes
and lament "the corruption of the language". But words do not change overnight: they change their
shape gradually, over a long time. If we understand that process, we can see that much of what is
called "corruption" is in fact the natural working of language.

Change in language comes in several types. When new things and ideas appear, words are needed to
name them: loanwords are taken in, and long words are shortened. The speed at which abbreviations
are born, as "smartphone" became 「スマホ」, is astonishing. But what is truly interesting is the
way the meanings of existing words gradually shift. Because the form stays the same while the
content is replaced, the very people using a word often take part in the change without noticing.

An easy example is 「{役不足|やくぶそく}」. Originally it means that the role one is given is too light compared
with one's ability. Today, however, many people use it to mean that their own ability isn't
enough, as in "This role is beyond me, but I'll do my utmost." The two meanings are exact
opposites, and words intended as modesty may, to some listeners, sound arrogant. Many dictionaries
give the original meaning and then note that the mistaken use has spread.

There are other examples like this. 「{潮時|しおどき}」 was originally the time of the tide's ebb and flow, and
from that, the right moment for doing something. In recent years, though, it is often used, as in
"It's about time," to mean the moment to step back or to bring something to an end. The two agree
in expressing timing, but the forward-looking ring has faded and the word has taken on a somewhat
melancholy nuance. With only a slight shift in the centre of its meaning, a word's expression can
change this much.

「{全然|ぜんぜん}」 is another word that is often the focus of debate. Using it with positive forms, as in
"totally fine", is often criticized as the corrupted Japanese of young people. But it has been
pointed out that novels of the Meiji and Taishō periods contain not a few examples of {全然|ぜんぜん} in
positive sentences. The common sense that it belongs with negatives may itself be no more than a
rule born in a particular period. The answer to the question of what "correct Japanese" is differs
from era to era.

There are also cases where a meaning is reversed. 「やばい」 was originally a word for danger or
inconvenience, but now, among younger people especially, it is also used to mean "fantastic".
「{微妙|びみょう}」, too, is changing from its original meaning, "delicate and hard to put into words", into a
word that conveys "not very good" indirectly. Strong words lose their force as they are used, and
things that are hard to say directly are wrapped in other words. Such phenomena are said to be
found in many languages, not only Japanese.

Metaphor, too, is a great force that moves words. 「{割|わ}り{切|き}る」 originally refers to division
leaving no remainder. That shifted to a human attitude and came to mean dealing with things
without letting feelings in. 「{踏|ふ}み{切|き}る」 likewise came from the action of kicking hard against the
ground at take-off in a jump to express a bold decision. Words for concrete actions eventually take
on abstract meanings. 「{腹|はら}を{割|わ}る」 ("split one's belly") likewise comes from the image of opening up what is inside one's belly, one's true feelings, for others to see. Many idioms were born this way.

So how should we face changes in the language? To reject every new usage as a mistake is to ignore
the history of language. But that doesn't mean accepting everything: that could open unexpected
gaps with people of other generations. What matters, surely, is to know that one word can have
several meanings and to choose according to the person and the situation. Is it not the belief that a word has only one right answer that impoverishes language? The dictionary, too, is not a judge ruling on right and wrong in words but a recorder who writes down their progress. No one can stop language
from changing. But anyone can choose their words knowing how they have changed.

</details>

## Say it

```speak
{腹|はら}を{割|わ}って{話|はな}しましょう。
= Let's talk frankly.
{言語道断|ごんごどうだん}だ。
= That's outrageous.
{異口同音|いくどうおん}に{賛成|さんせい}した。
= They agreed with one voice.
{語学|ごがく}は{一朝一夕|いっちょういっせき}には{身|み}につかない。
= You don't learn a language overnight.
{仕事|しごと}は{仕事|しごと}と{割|わ}り{切|き}っている。
= I treat work as just work.
{景気|けいき}に{回復|かいふく}の{兆|きざ}しが{見|み}える。
= There are signs of recovery in the economy.
```

Four-character compounds usually carry one accent for the whole, often on the first part
({臨機応変|りんきおうへん} and {本末転倒|ほんまつてんとう} both fall after the first mora); say them as one word,
not as two pairs.

## Common mistakes

- {腹|はら}を{開|ひら}いて{話|はな}す or {舌|した}を{回|まわ}す for the idioms. The verb of an idiom is fixed: {腹|はら}を{割|わ}る,
  {舌|した}を{巻|ま}く.
- {舌|した}を{巻|ま}く for a failure, or {目|め}に{余|あま}る as praise. The tone of an idiom is fixed too.
- Reading {異口同音|いくどうおん} as いこうどうおん, {言語道断|ごんごどうだん} as げんごどうだん, {下旬|げじゅん} as
  かじゅん.
- {一朝一夕|いっちょういっせき} with a positive ({一朝一夕|いっちょういっせき}に{上達|じょうたつ}した is not used). It goes with a
  negative: {一朝一夕|いっちょういっせき}には{上達|じょうたつ}しない.
- {役不足|やくぶそく} for "not up to the job". That's {力不足|ちからぶそく}; {役不足|やくぶそく} says the job is
  beneath you.
- {返還|へんかん}する for everyday returns ({本|ほん}を{返還|へんかん}する sounds like a treaty). Use {返|かえ}す; {返還|へんかん}する is
  for territory and property returned formally.
- {異常|いじょう} for "unprecedented" ({異常|いじょう}の{人事|じんじ} isn't said). {異例|いれい}の{人事|じんじ} breaks with custom;
  {異常|いじょう} is abnormal and worrying.
- Taking a compound verb literally: {踏|ふ}み{切|き}る in an editorial about a company is a decision,
  not a jump.

## Key points

- Compound verbs: learn the second verb as a family (〜{込|こ}む, 〜{切|き}る, 〜{抜|ぬ}く, 〜{返|かえ}す,
  〜{尽|つ}くす, 〜{損|そこ}なう); the figurative sense ({割|わ}り{切|き}る, {踏|ふ}み{切|き}る, {見損|みそこ}なう) is
  the one tested.
- Kango and wago pairs ({阻止|そし}する / {食|く}い{止|と}める) differ in register; paraphrase questions
  pair them.
- Four-character compounds: two pairs; watch the readings ({異口同音|いくどうおん}, {言語道断|ごんごどうだん}) and
  the usual frame ({一朝一夕|いっちょういっせき}には〜ない).
- Idioms: fixed verb, fixed tone ({舌|した}を{巻|ま}く praises, {眉|まゆ}をひそめる criticizes).
- Words change by reversal, softening and metaphor; dictionaries record both senses.
- New kanji: 致 異 殊 逸 既 即 幾 僅 遂 貫 徐 累 旺 旬 暫 兆 妨 阻 覆 還 充 据 潜 箇 隅 距 狭 縦 繰 緩 裕 沿.

lessons.title: Academic Japanese: ひいては, ならびに, ないし, いわんや
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

The N1 reading section ends with its hardest tasks: a long text whose main claim you must find
(**[[thematic comprehension]]**), and passages with gaps where you choose the connector, the
reference word or the sentence ending that fits (**[[text grammar]]**). Both reward a reader who knows
the **[[academic register]]**: the vocabulary, connectors and hedges of papers, reports, official
documents and the more serious essays. This lesson teaches the connectors that ordinary writing
lacks, the levels of "and" and "or" in laws and rules, the scale of hedged claims, and how an
academic paper is built.

{本研究|ほんけんきゅう}は、{地域|ちいき}の{活性化|かっせいか}、ひいては{国全体|くにぜんたい}の{経済|けいざい}{成長|せいちょう}に{資|し}するものと{考|かんが}えられる。 — This research is thought likely to contribute to the revival of the regions and, by extension, to the economic growth of the whole country.

{申請|しんせい}は{本人|ほんにん}{又|また}は{代理人|だいりにん}が{行|おこな}うものとする。 — Applications shall be made by the person concerned or by an agent.

{結果|けっか}は{三|さん}ないし{五日|いつか}で{通知|つうち}される。 — The results are sent out within three to five days.

The theme is research and academic writing: analysis and hypotheses, the parts and wording of a
paper, measurement and statistics, citation, and the terms of logic. The reading is a short
academic article built on an invented survey.

## Connectors of academic writing

### ひいては: and by extension

A、ひいては B joins two results, where B is the wider consequence of A: "A, and in turn B". Both
are usually nouns, and B is bigger than A (a person → a society, a town → a country).

{一人|ひとり}ひとりの{健康|けんこう}への{投資|とうし}は、{医療費|いりょうひ}の{削減|さくげん}、ひいては{社会|しゃかい}{全体|ぜんたい}の{活力|かつりょく}につながる。 — Investing in each person's health leads to lower medical costs and, by extension, to the vitality of society as a whole.

It's written. In speech, people say さらには or {結局|けっきょく}は{社会|しゃかい}{全体|ぜんたい}のためにもなる. Don't use it
for a simple "and also": the second item must follow from the first.

### ないし: from A to B; or

ないし has two jobs. Between numbers it gives a range ("from … to"); between nouns it is a formal
"or".

| Use | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| range | {三|さん}ないし{五年|ごねん} | three to five years |
| or | {本人|ほんにん}ないし{家族|かぞく} | the person or a family member |

{回復|かいふく}には{二|に}ないし{三週間|さんしゅうかん}を{要|よう}する。 — Recovery takes two to three weeks.

### {否|いな}: no, or rather; whether or not

{否|いな} is the written "no". It corrects a statement to make it stronger, and in 〜か{否|いな}か it
means "whether or not".

これは{個人|こじん}の{問題|もんだい}ではない。{否|いな}、{社会|しゃかい}{全体|ぜんたい}の{問題|もんだい}である。 — This is not a personal problem. No: it is a problem for society as a whole.

{計画|けいかく}を{実行|じっこう}するか{否|いな}かは、{来月|らいげつ}{決|き}める。 — Whether or not to carry out the plan will be decided next month.

Lesson 1's 〜や{否|いな}や (no sooner than) has the same kanji.

### いわんや〜をや: let alone (to recognize)

いわんや is a classical "how much more (or less) so": A すら / でさえ…。いわんや B をや. The
sentence says that if even A is so, B certainly is. You will meet it in older essays and in
writers who like weight; recognize it, don't write it.

{専門家|せんもんか}ですら{判断|はんだん}に{迷|まよ}う。いわんや{素人|しろうと}をや。 — Even experts are unsure how to judge it, let alone amateurs.

The modern equivalents are まして (let alone, all the more) and 〜はおろか (lesson 9): {素人|しろうと}にはなおさら{難|むずか}しい ("all the more difficult for an amateur"; なおさら = all the more).

## "And" and "or" at two levels: laws, rules and forms

Laws, regulations and formal documents use four conjunctions with fixed meanings. Their kanji are
written in official text; in casual writing および and または are in kana.

| | Lower level (inner group) | Upper level (outer group) | One level only |
|---|---|---|---|
| and | {及|およ}び | {並|なら}びに | {及|およ}び |
| or | {若|も}しくは | {又|また}は | {又|また}は |

The two "and"s and the two "or"s work in opposite directions, so learn them as a pair of pairs:

- **And**: {及|およ}び joins the smaller group; {並|なら}びに joins that group to the next.
  「A{及|およ}びB{並|なら}びにC」 = (A and B) and C.
- **Or**: {若|も}しくは joins the smaller group; {又|また}は joins that group to the next.
  「A{若|も}しくはB{又|また}はC」 = (A or B) or C.
- With only one level, use {及|およ}び and {又|また}は.

{会員|かいいん}{及|およ}びその{家族|かぞく}{並|なら}びに{招待者|しょうたいしゃ}は、{入場料|にゅうじょうりょう}を{免除|めんじょ}する。 — Members and their families, as well as invited guests, are exempt from the entrance fee.

{本人|ほんにん}{若|も}しくはその{親族|しんぞく}{又|また}は{会社|かいしゃ}の{担当者|たんとうしゃ}が{申請|しんせい}することができる。 — The person concerned or a relative, or else the company's representative, may apply.

Everyday writing doesn't need the levels: {及|およ}び and {又|また}は on their own are the formal "and"
and "or" between nouns, and と, や, か or あるいは do the same in plain prose. Notices and forms
(lesson 29) use {及|およ}び and {又|また}は constantly.

## Hedged claims: how strong is the writer?

Academic Japanese rarely says "X is the case" without a hedge. The **[[hedge]]** tells you how much the
writer commits to the claim, and thematic comprehension questions often turn on it: "the writer
thinks X" is wrong if the text only says "it is said that X".

| Ending | Strength | Who holds the view |
|---|---|---|
| 〜である | asserted | the writer, as fact |
| 〜にほかならない | asserted, emphatically | the writer |
| 〜と{言|い}える / 〜と{言|い}えよう | a judgement the writer stands by | the writer |
| 〜と{考|かんが}えられる | a reasoned conclusion | the writer (on evidence) |
| 〜ものと{思|おも}われる | an inference, cautious | the writer |
| 〜のではないだろうか / なかろうか | a suggestion put to the reader | the writer, tentatively |
| 〜{可能性|かのうせい}がある / 〜{可能性|かのうせい}を{否定|ひてい}できない | a possibility | the writer, weakly |
| 〜とされる / 〜とされている | an accepted view | others (the field, officials) |
| 〜と{言|い}われている | a common view | people in general |
| 〜という{指摘|してき}がある / 〜とする{見方|みかた}もある | one view among others | some others |

{被害|ひがい}の{拡大|かくだい}は、{初動|しょどう}の{遅|おく}れによるものと{思|おも}われる。 — The spread of the damage appears to be due to the slow initial response.

{地球|ちきゅう}の{平均|へいきん}{気温|きおん}は{上昇|じょうしょう}を{続|つづ}けているとされる。 — The Earth's average temperature is regarded as continuing to rise.

- ものと{思|おも}われる uses the spontaneous 〜{思|おも}われる (lesson 16): the conclusion presents itself.
- 〜と{考|かんが}えられる can be the writer's own judgement; 〜とされる reports what is generally accepted.
  "According to the writer…" fits the first, not the second.
- When a writer reports a view with 〜という{指摘|してき}がある and then writes しかし, the writer's own
  claim usually comes after しかし.

## How a paper is built

A Japanese research paper ({論文|ろんぶん}) follows the international pattern, with these section
names. An N1 academic text is usually a cut-down version of the same shape.

| Section | Name | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Abstract | {要旨|ようし} | the whole paper in a few lines |
| Introduction | {序論|じょろん} / はじめに | the question, its background and the aim ({本稿|ほんこう}の{目的|もくてき}は〜) |
| Previous research | {先行研究|せんこうけんきゅう} | what is known; the gap this paper fills |
| Hypothesis | {仮説|かせつ} | what the paper expects to find |
| Method | {方法|ほうほう} | who or what was studied, and how |
| Results | {結果|けっか} | what was found, without interpretation |
| Discussion | {考察|こうさつ} | what the results mean; limitations ({限界|げんかい}) |
| Conclusion | {結論|けつろん} / おわりに | the answer to the question; next steps ({今後|こんご}の{課題|かだい}) |
| References | {参考文献|さんこうぶんけん} | the sources cited |

Fixed phrases mark each move: {本稿|ほんこう}では〜を{検討|けんとう}する (this paper examines…),
〜によれば (according to), 〜が{明|あき}らかになった (it became clear that), 〜を{示唆|しさ}している
(suggests), {今後|こんご}の{課題|かだい}としたい (we leave … for future work). {本稿|ほんこう} is "this
paper"; {筆者|ひっしゃ} is the writer referring to themselves.

**Citations.** Japanese papers cite by author and year in brackets: 「{山田|やまだ}（2020）によれば」 or
「…とされる（{山田|やまだ} 2020）」. The examples in this course are invented: no real study is
reported as real. When you read a citation in an exam text, the question is usually whether the
writer agrees with the cited view.

## Cohesion: how a text holds together

**[[Cohesion]]** is what ties sentences into a text. The text grammar questions test its four tools:

| Tool | Examples | What to check |
|---|---|---|
| Reference words | これ, それ, こうした, その{結果|けっか}, {前者|ぜんしゃ} / {後者|こうしゃ} | what exactly they point back to |
| Connectors | しかし, したがって, ただし, むしろ, ひいては, {一方|いっぽう}, つまり | the logical relation between the sentences |
| Repetition and paraphrase | a key word, or a kango for an earlier wago | the theme running through |
| Sentence endings | のである, にほかならない, と{考|かんが}えられる | the writer's stance |

For a gap: read the sentence before and after, decide the relation first (contrast, cause,
addition, example, restatement, condition), then choose the connector. For a long text: find the
sentences with the strongest endings; the writer's claim is in one of them, often after a turn
(しかし, むしろ, {否|いな}) and often repeated in the last paragraph. A **[[summary]]** of the claim in one
sentence of your own is the best check that you've found it.

- {要約|ようやく} (a summary) and ようやく (at last) sound the same.

[Note] The survey presented in this paper is a fictional one, set up to show the structure of a
paper.

Abstract. This paper examines the effect of handwriting and keyboard input on remembering kanji
through a comparative survey of university students. The group that practised by hand had a
significantly higher rate of correct answers. Handwriting appears to aid memory of the details of a
character's shape, but the subjects and the test method have limitations, and one must be cautious
about generalizing the conclusion.

1 Introduction. In recent years, with the spread of computers and smartphones, opportunities to
write by hand have fallen sharply. Along with this, people have begun to say, "I can read kanji but
can't write them." There is a view that handwriting is not merely a means of recording, but bears
on how firmly things are remembered and, by extension, on the quality of learning as a whole. The
aim of this paper is to examine which of handwriting and keyboard input makes kanji easier to
remember.

2 Previous research and hypothesis. It is regarded as having been pointed out by many researchers
that the action of writing letters aids memory. This is thought to be because moving the hand
processes visual and motor information at the same time. There is also a view that the stroke order used in writing serves as a cue for memory. On the other hand, there is also the
counter-argument that typing, too, directs attention to the shapes of characters, because one
compares several candidates when converting. This paper therefore set the hypothesis that "kanji
practised by hand are written correctly a week later at a higher rate than kanji practised by
typing".

3 Method. One hundred and twenty university students were divided at random into two groups of
sixty; one group practised the same thirty kanji by hand, the other by keyboard input. The kanji were chosen from ones that most participants, when checked beforehand, could read but not write. Practice time
was twenty minutes for both, and one week after practice (six to eight days, for reasons of
scheduling) a test was given in which they wrote kanji from their readings. As factors that could
affect memory, age, sex and everyday amount of reading were also examined.

4 Results. The average rate of correct answers was 68 per cent for the handwriting group and 52 per
cent for the input group, and a statistically significant difference between the two was found. In a check carried out immediately after practice, both groups had been able to write more than 90 per cent of the kanji correctly. No
differences by age or sex were seen, but in both groups, students who read more tended to score
higher. Looking at the wrong answers, the input group made many errors in which a radical or some of
the dots and strokes were missing.

5 Discussion. The above results support the hypothesis. Because handwriting requires reproducing a
character's shape down to the details, the memory appears to have been engraved more deeply. The
fact that the input group made many partial errors can be said to show that, while they remembered
the overall shape, they had left the details to the machine. Even native-speaker university
students could not write more than thirty per cent of the kanji a week later: how much more so
learners. This survey, however, has its limitations. The subjects were limited to students of
one university, so the results cannot be generalized to society as a whole. Nor can it be ruled out
that the test's being handwritten worked in the handwriting group's favour.

These results also hold some implications for schools. In recent years, learning with tablets has
been promoted in schools, but where acquiring kanji is concerned, one should be cautious about
replacing handwriting entirely with typing. That said, what this survey showed was a difference in
the ability to write, not in the ability to read or to understand texts. The very way the question
is put, whether handwriting or typing is better, may also need rethinking according to the purpose.

6 Conclusion. From the results of this paper, handwriting is thought to be effective, at least for
remembering kanji. Even today, when typing has become the norm, the act of writing has not lost its
value. No: is it not precisely now, when chances to write have dwindled, that we are called on to
set aside time to move our hands deliberately? As future work, we would like to confirm, with a wider
range of subjects and a different test method, whether similar results are obtained.
