## Common mistakes

- ひいては for a simple addition: {英語|えいご}、ひいては{数学|すうがく}も{得意|とくい}だ isn't used. B must be a wider
  consequence of A.
- Mixing the levels: in 「A{及|およ}びB{並|なら}びにC」, {並|なら}びに is the outer "and"; in
  「A{若|も}しくはB{又|また}はC」, {又|また}は is the outer "or". The two pairs run in opposite directions.
- Reading 〜とされる as the writer's own view. It reports an accepted view; the writer's claim may come
  after a しかし.
- Writing いわんや〜をや in a modern essay. Recognize it; write まして or はおろか.
- Asserting more than the data allow (the professor's point in the dialogue). Choose the ending
  that fits the evidence: と{考|かんが}えられる, ものと{思|おも}われる, {可能性|かのうせい}がある.
- Listing previous research without saying how it bears on your question.
- Reading {静脈|じょうみゃく} as せいみゃく, or {木綿|もめん} as きわた.

## Key points

- ひいては (and by extension), ないし (from … to; or), {否|いな} (no, rather; か{否|いな}か whether or not),
  いわんや〜をや (let alone: recognize); in modern writing まして.
- Legal "and": {及|およ}び (inner) / {並|なら}びに (outer). Legal "or": {若|も}しくは (inner) / {又|また}は (outer).
- Hedges show how much the writer commits: である > と{考|かんが}えられる > ものと{思|おも}われる >
  {可能性|かのうせい}がある; とされる and と{言|い}われている report others' views.
- A paper: {要旨|ようし}, {序論|じょろん}, {先行研究|せんこうけんきゅう}, {仮説|かせつ}, {方法|ほうほう}, {結果|けっか},
  {考察|こうさつ}, {結論|けつろん}, {参考文献|さんこうぶんけん}.
- Cohesion: reference words, connectors, repetition, endings. For text grammar, decide the
  relation before the connector; for thematic comprehension, find the strongest ending after a
  turn.
- New kanji: 推 仮 析 肯 旨 但 又 冒 序 符 羅 較 緯 脈 随 括 捉 彙 瞭 遡 礎 綿 寸 朴 垂 窒 髄 抹 蓋 挿 絞 伏.

The reference sheet "Literary and academic style" has the tables of connectors and hedges. The words
from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Reading and listening practice
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This lesson is a practice set in the shape of the N1: six reading texts, from a 300-character
notice to a 2,000-character essay, and five listening tasks at natural speed. Work through it like
a test the first time (time yourself, answer before you open the answers), then a second time
slowly, with the translations. The questions after the lesson practise the same task types.

No new grammar: everything is from this course and the earlier ones. The new words are those of
notices, letters, forms and the home, and most of the 32 kanji spell words you already know in
kana: {宛先|あてさき}, {添付|てんぷ}, {休憩|きゅうけい}, {封筒|ふうとう}, {廊下|ろうか}, {壁|かべ}, {雑巾|ぞうきん},
{拭|ふ}く, {餌|えさ}, {乾燥|かんそう}.

## Reading strategies for N1

The reading tasks of the N1 and what each one wants:

| Task | Length (roughly) | What to look for |
|---|---|---|
| Short passages | 200–400 characters | one point: the writer's purpose, a condition, what to do |
| Mid-size passages | 500–600 | reasons, the writer's view, what a reference word points to |
| Long passages | about 1,000 | the line of argument across paragraphs |
| Integrated comprehension | two texts of 400–600 | what A and B share and where they differ |
| Thematic comprehension | 1,500–2,500 | the writer's main claim, often after a turn |
| Information retrieval | about 1,000, with tables | the one condition that decides the answer |

(Lengths are this course's estimates from practice materials, not official figures.)

- **Read the questions first.** For information retrieval, read only the questions, then hunt in
  the text. For thematic comprehension, read the text first and the questions after.
- **Mark the turns.** しかし, むしろ, {否|いな}, ところが, だが and もっとも turn an argument. The
  writer's own view is usually after the last turn.
- **Watch the hedges** (lesson 28): とされる reports, と{考|かんが}えられる concludes.
- **In notices and rules, find the exceptions.** ただし, {除|のぞ}く, {限|かぎ}る, {以外|いがい},
  〜{以上|いじょう} / {未満|みまん} and ※ notes decide most answers.
- **Time.** The language knowledge and reading part is one 110-minute section. One workable plan:
  about 30 minutes for vocabulary and grammar, and the rest for reading, longest texts last.
  Practise your own split with a timer.

## Kanji

Thirty-two kanji for letters, forms, buildings and the home. Most of their words are carried.

### Letters, names and titles

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 宛 | address to | — | あ(てる) | 8 | {宛先|あてさき}, {宛名|あてな}, {宛|あ}てる |
| 添 | add, accompany | テン | そ(える), そ(う) | 11 | {添|そ}える, {添加物|てんかぶつ}, {添付|てんぷ} (carried) |
| 封 | seal | フウ, ホウ | — | 9 | {封|ふう}, {同封|どうふう}する, {開封|かいふう}する, {封筒|ふうとう} (carried) |
| 筒 | tube | トウ | つつ | 12 | {筒|つつ}, {水筒|すいとう}, {封筒|ふうとう} (carried) |
| 氏 | family name; Mr or Ms | シ | うじ | 4 | {氏|し}, {氏名|しめい} (carried) |
| 郎 | man (in names) | ロウ | — | 9 | {新郎|しんろう} (carried) |
| 称 | name, call; praise | ショウ | — | 10 | {名称|めいしょう}, {称|しょう}する |
| 賓 | guest | ヒン | — | 15 | {来賓|らいひん}, {賓客|ひんきゃく} |
| 頂 | top; receive | チョウ | いただ(く), いただき | 11 | {頂上|ちょうじょう}, {頂点|ちょうてん}, {頂戴|ちょうだい} (carried) |

- 郎 appears in men's given names ({太郎|たろう}, {一郎|いちろう}) and in {新郎|しんろう} (the groom). The
  rough insult やろう has it too.
- 頂 gives いただく, which this course always writes in kana, and {頂戴|ちょうだい}, written in kanji.
- 宛 has no on'yomi. In addresses, 〜{宛|あ}て means "addressed to": {人事部|じんじぶ}{宛|あ}て.
- 封 is ホウ only in old words for feudal lands ({封建|ほうけん}{的|てき}, feudal): fixed and rare.

```trace
宛添封筒氏郎称賓頂
```

### Rooms, buildings and grounds

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 房 | room; tuft | ボウ | ふさ | 8 | {冷房|れいぼう}, {暖房|だんぼう}, {冷暖房|れいだんぼう}, {文房具|ぶんぼうぐ} |
| 壁 | wall | ヘキ | かべ | 16 | {壁紙|かべがみ}, {障壁|しょうへき}, {壁画|へきが}, {壁|かべ} (carried) |
| 廊 | corridor | ロウ | — | 12 | {廊下|ろうか}, {画廊|がろう} |
| 敷 | spread; site | フ | し(く) | 15 | {敷|し}く, {敷地|しきち}, {敷金|しききん}, {屋敷|やしき}, {座敷|ざしき} |
| 軒 | eaves; houses (counter) | ケン | のき | 10 | {軒|のき}, {一軒家|いっけんや}, {軒並|のきな}み |
| 棟 | ridge; building | トウ | むね, むな | 12 | {棟|むね}, {病棟|びょうとう} |
| 荘 | villa; solemn | ソウ | — | 9 | {別荘|べっそう} |
| 壇 | platform | ダン, タン | — | 16 | {花壇|かだん}, {壇上|だんじょう} |

- 壁 (wall) has 土 (earth) at the bottom; 癖 (lesson 24's: {口癖|くちぐせ}) has the sickness radical.
  The on'yomi ヘキ is in both.
- 敷 is し in the verb {敷|し}く and しき (the noun form, "something spread") in {敷地|しきち}, {屋敷|やしき} and {座敷|ざしき}.
- 軒 counts houses and shops: {一軒|いっけん}, {二軒|にけん}, {三軒|さんげん} (げん after さん).
- 棟 counts buildings as トウ: {三棟|さんとう}. むな appears in a few compounds: {棟木|むなぎ} (the ridgepole).
- 荘 is common in the names of old apartment buildings ({〜荘|そう}).

```trace
房壁廊敷軒棟荘壇
```

### Handling, cleaning and gaps

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 扱 | handle | — | あつか(う) | 6 | {扱|あつか}う, {取|と}り{扱|あつか}い |
| 拭 | wipe | ショク | ふ(く), ぬぐ(う) | 9 | {拭|ぬぐ}う, {拭|ふ}く (carried) |
| 巾 | cloth | キン | — | 3 | {布巾|ふきん}, {雑巾|ぞうきん} (carried) |
| 潰 | crush | カイ | つぶ(す), つぶ(れる) | 15 | {潰|つぶ}す, {潰|つぶ}れる |
| 隙 | gap | ゲキ | すき | 13 | {隙|すき}, {隙間|すきま} |
| 臨 | face, attend | リン | のぞ(む) | 18 | {臨|のぞ}む, {臨場感|りんじょうかん}, {臨時|りんじ} (carried) |
| 沙 | sand | サ | — | 7 | {沙汰|さた}, {取|と}り{沙汰|ざた}, ご{無沙汰|ぶさた} |
| 汰 | sift | タ | — | 7 | {沙汰|さた}, {取|と}り{沙汰|ざた}, ご{無沙汰|ぶさた} |

- {拭|ふ}く (wipe a surface) and {拭|ぬぐ}う (wipe away sweat or tears; dispel a doubt) share one kanji.
  {拭|ふ}く is also a homophone of {吹|ふ}く (blow).
- 沙 and 汰 almost only occur together. ご{無沙汰|ぶさた} ("no news") is the standard apology for not
  having been in touch.
- 臨 (18 strokes) is the most complex kanji here; {臨|のぞ}む (face an occasion) and {望|のぞ}む (hope for)
  are homophones.

```trace
扱拭巾潰隙臨沙汰
```

### The garden, animals and the seasons

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 憩 | rest | ケイ | いこ(い), いこ(う) | 16 | {憩|いこ}い, {休憩|きゅうけい} (carried) |
| 餌 | feed, bait | ジ | えさ, え | 15 | {餌|えさ} (carried) |
| 飼 | keep (animals) | シ | か(う) | 13 | {飼育|しいく}する, {飼|か}う (carried), {飼|か}い{主|ぬし} (carried) |
| 刈 | cut, mow | — | か(る) | 4 | {刈|か}る |
| 燥 | dry | ソウ | — | 17 | {乾燥|かんそう} |
| 盆 | tray; Bon festival | ボン | — | 9 | {盆|ぼん}, お{盆|ぼん} (carried) |
| 鉢 | bowl, pot | ハチ, ハツ | — | 13 | {植木鉢|うえきばち}, {鉢植|はちう}え |

- {飼|か}う (keep an animal) and {買|か}う (buy) are homophones; {刈|か}る (mow) and {狩|か}る (hunt,
  lesson 3's kanji) too.
- 燥 has fire (火): drying by heat. Compare 操 (lesson 3's: {操|あやつ}る), with the hand.
- 鉢 is ハチ in {植木鉢|うえきばち} and {鉢植|はちう}え; ハツ is rare.

```trace
憩餌飼刈燥盆鉢
```

### Words you can now write in kanji

{拭|ふ}く, {飼|か}う, {飼|か}い{主|ぬし}, {餌|えさ}, {雑巾|ぞうきん}, {壁|かべ}, {封筒|ふうとう}, {添付|てんぷ}する, {休憩|きゅうけい},
{臨時|りんじ}, {氏名|しめい}, {新郎|しんろう}, お{盆|ぼん}, {御社|おんしゃ}, and {手拭|てぬぐ}い (written {手|て}ぬぐい until now).

## Text 1: a notice (short)

A notice on the board of a block of flats.

> {居住者|きょじゅうしゃ}{各位|かくい}
>
> **{共用|きょうよう}{廊下|ろうか}{床|ゆか}{改修|かいしゅう}{工事|こうじ}のお{知|し}らせ**
>
> {管理|かんり}{組合|くみあい}
>
> {日頃|ひごろ}より{管理|かんり}{運営|うんえい}にご{協力|きょうりょく}いただき、ありがとうございます。このたび、{老朽化|ろうきゅうか}した{共用|きょうよう}{廊下|ろうか}の{床|ゆか}を{張|は}り{替|か}える{工事|こうじ}を、{下記|かき}のとおり{行|おこな}います。{工事|こうじ}{期間|きかん}{中|ちゅう}は{騒音|そうおん}が{発生|はっせい}するほか、{一部|いちぶ}の{通路|つうろ}が{通行|つうこう}できなくなります。ご{不便|ふべん}をおかけしますが、ご{理解|りかい}のほどよろしくお{願|ねが}いいたします。
>
> 1　{期間|きかん}：{十二月|じゅうにがつ}{一日|ついたち}から{十日|とおか}まで（{土曜|どよう}・{日曜|にちよう}を{除|のぞ}く）、{午前|ごぜん}{九時|くじ}から{午後|ごご}{五時|ごじ}まで
>
> 2　{対象|たいしょう}：A{棟|とう}{及|およ}びB{棟|とう}の{二階|にかい}から{五階|ごかい}までの{廊下|ろうか}
>
> 3　お{願|ねが}い：{工事|こうじ}{期間|きかん}{中|ちゅう}は、{廊下|ろうか}に{植木鉢|うえきばち}や{自転車|じてんしゃ}などの{私物|しぶつ}を{置|お}かないでください。{期間|きかん}{中|ちゅう}に{残|のこ}っている{私物|しぶつ}は、{管理|かんり}{組合|くみあい}で{一時的|いちじてき}に{移動|いどう}させていただく{場合|ばあい}があります。
>
> ※ {一階|いっかい}の{廊下|ろうか}は、{来年度|らいねんど}{以降|いこう}に{実施|じっし}する{予定|よてい}です。

1. A resident of the third floor of block B keeps flowerpots in the corridor. What should they do,
   and by when?
2. Does the work affect the ground floor this time?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Take the flowerpots (private belongings, {私物|しぶつ}) out of the corridor before the work begins
   on 1 December; anything left may be moved by the residents' association.
2. No: the ground floor will be done next year or later (the ※ note); this time it's floors 2 to
   5 of blocks A and B.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

To all residents. Notice of renovation work on the floors of the shared corridors. The residents'
association. Thank you for your continued cooperation in the management of the building. We will be
replacing the worn floors of the shared corridors, as follows. During the work there will be noise,
and parts of the walkways will be closed. We apologize for the inconvenience and ask for your
understanding.

1. Period: 1 to 10 December (excluding Saturdays and Sundays), 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.
2. Area: the corridors of floors 2 to 5 of blocks A and B.
3. Request: during the work, please don't leave private belongings such as flowerpots or bicycles
in the corridors. Belongings left there during the work may be moved temporarily by the
association.

※ The ground-floor corridors are scheduled for the next financial year or later.

</details>

## Text 2: a business email (short)

> **{件名|けんめい}：{打|う}ち{合|あ}わせ{日程|にってい}{変更|へんこう}のお{願|ねが}い**
>
> {株式会社|かぶしきがいしゃ}{山中|やまなか}{商事|しょうじ}　{営業部|えいぎょうぶ}　{田村|たむら}{様|さま}
>
> いつも{大変|たいへん}お{世話|せわ}になっております。{東西|とうざい}{印刷|いんさつ}の{佐藤|さとう}でございます。{先日|せんじつ}は{新商品|しんしょうひん}のカタログ{制作|せいさく}の{件|けん}でお{時間|じかん}をいただき、ありがとうございました。
>
> さて、{来週|らいしゅう}{十八日|じゅうはちにち}{午後|ごご}{二時|にじ}からお{約束|やくそく}しておりました{打|う}ち{合|あ}わせですが、{弊社|へいしゃ}の{担当|たんとう}デザイナーに{急|きゅう}な{出張|しゅっちょう}が{入|はい}り、{同席|どうせき}できなくなってしまいました。{大変|たいへん}{恐縮|きょうしゅく}ではございますが、{二十日|はつか}{又|また}は{二十一日|にじゅういちにち}の{午後|ごご}に{変更|へんこう}していただくことは{可能|かのう}でしょうか。{田村|たむら}{様|さま}のご{都合|つごう}のよい{日時|にちじ}をお{知|し}らせいただけましたら{幸|さいわ}いです。
>
> なお、{前回|ぜんかい}いただいたご{意見|いけん}を{反映|はんえい}した{修正案|しゅうせいあん}を{添付|てんぷ}いたしましたので、{打|う}ち{合|あ}わせの{前|まえ}にご{査収|さしゅう}いただければと{存|ぞん}じます。
>
> こちらの{都合|つごう}で{誠|まこと}に{申|もう}し{訳|わけ}ございませんが、どうぞよろしくお{願|ねが}いいたします。

1. Why does Satō want to change the meeting?
2. What two things does Satō ask Tamura to do?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The designer in charge at Satō's company has had to go on a sudden business trip and can't
   attend on the 18th.
2. To say which time suits them, the afternoon of the 20th or the 21st; and to look over the
   attached revised draft before the meeting (ご{査収|さしゅう}いただければ).

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Subject: Request to reschedule our meeting. To Tamura, Sales Department, Yamanaka Shōji Co.,
Ltd. Thank you as always for your support. This is Satō from Tōzai Printing. Thank you for your time
the other day regarding the catalogue for your new product.

About the meeting we arranged for 2 p.m. on the 18th of next week: our designer in charge has had a
sudden business trip come up and will not be able to attend. I am very sorry to ask, but would it be
possible to change it to the afternoon of the 20th or the 21st? I would be grateful if you could let
me know a day and time that suits you.

I have also attached a revised draft reflecting the comments you gave us last time; I would
appreciate it if you could look it over before the meeting. My sincere apologies for the trouble
this causes you on our account.

</details>

## Text 3: a column (mid-size)

> {電車|でんしゃ}を{待|ま}つ{三分|さんぷん}、{会議|かいぎ}が{始|はじ}まるまでの{五分|ごふん}。こうした{隙間|すきま}の{時間|じかん}を、{私|わたし}は{長|なが}いことスマートフォンで{埋|う}めてきた。ニュースを{読|よ}み、メールに{返信|へんしん}し、それでも{余|あま}れば{動画|どうが}を{見|み}る。{電車|でんしゃ}の{中|なか}ではイヤホンで{語学|ごがく}の{講座|こうざ}を{聞|き}き、{歩|ある}きながら{予定表|よていひょう}を{確認|かくにん}する。{一分|いっぷん}たりとも{無駄|むだ}にしないことが、{有能|ゆうのう}な{大人|おとな}の{条件|じょうけん}だと{思|おも}い{込|こ}んでいたのである。
>
> ところが{先日|せんじつ}、{携帯|けいたい}を{家|いえ}に{忘|わす}れて{出|で}かけた{日|ひ}に、{奇妙|きみょう}なことが{起|お}きた。{駅|えき}のホームでぼんやり{線路|せんろ}を{眺|なが}めていると、{何週間|なんしゅうかん}も{解決|かいけつ}できずにいた{仕事|しごと}の{問題|もんだい}の{答|こた}えが、ふと{頭|あたま}に{浮|う}かんだのだ。{考|かんが}えようとしていたわけではない。むしろ、{何|なに}も{考|かんが}えていなかったからこそ{浮|う}かんだのだろう。
>
> {思|おも}えば、{子供|こども}の{頃|ころ}の{私|わたし}は{退屈|たいくつ}の{達人|たつじん}だった。{雨|あめ}の{日|ひ}には{窓|まど}の{外|そと}を{何時間|なんじかん}も{眺|なが}め、{天井|てんじょう}の{木目|もくめ}に{動物|どうぶつ}の{顔|かお}を{見|み}つけては、{一人|ひとり}で{物語|ものがたり}を{作|つく}っていた。{退屈|たいくつ}は{苦痛|くつう}であると{同時|どうじ}に、{想像|そうぞう}の{入|い}り{口|ぐち}でもあったのだ。{大人|おとな}になった{今|いま}、{私|わたし}たちは{退屈|たいくつ}する{暇|ひま}さえ、{自|みずか}ら{手放|てばな}しているのかもしれない。
>
> {日本|にほん}の{古|ふる}い{家|いえ}には、{縁側|えんがわ}や{軒下|のきした}のような、{内|うち}とも{外|そと}ともつかない{場所|ばしょ}があった。そこは{何|なに}かをするための{部屋|へや}ではない。だが、{人|ひと}はそこで{休|やす}み、{季節|きせつ}を{感|かん}じ、{通|とお}りがかった{近所|きんじょ}の{人|ひと}と{言葉|ことば}を{交|か}わした。{時間|じかん}にもまた、そうした{縁側|えんがわ}が{必要|ひつよう}なのではないか。{隙間|すきま}を{埋|う}めることばかり{考|かんが}えてきた{私|わたし}は、{隙間|すきま}が{生|う}み{出|だ}すものを{見落|みお}としていたのである。{明日|あした}からは{駅|えき}のホームで、{携帯|けいたい}をかばんにしまってみようと{思|おも}う。

1. What did the writer believe before, and what changed their mind?
2. What does the writer compare spare moments to, and why?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. That not wasting a single minute ({一分|いっぷん}たりとも{無駄|むだ}にしない) was the mark of a capable
   adult. One day without a phone, the answer to a work problem came to them while staring blankly at
   the tracks, precisely because they weren't thinking.
2. To the {縁側|えんがわ} and {軒下|のきした} of old houses: spaces that are neither inside nor outside
   and aren't for doing anything, yet where people rested and talked. Time, too, needs such spaces;
   gaps produce something.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

Three minutes waiting for a train; five minutes before a meeting begins. For a long time I filled
such spare moments with my smartphone: reading the news, answering emails and, if any time was left,
watching videos. On the train I listened to language lessons through earphones, and I checked my
schedule as I walked. I had convinced myself that not wasting a single minute was the mark of a capable
adult.

But the other day, when I went out having left my phone at home, something strange happened. As I
gazed absently at the tracks from the platform, the answer to a work problem I had been unable to
solve for weeks suddenly came to me. It wasn't that I was trying to think about it. Rather, it
probably came precisely because I wasn't thinking about anything.

Come to think of it, as a child I was a master of boredom. On rainy days I would gaze out of the
window for hours, find animal faces in the grain of the wooden ceiling and make up stories on my own.
Boredom was a torment, but at the same time it was the doorway to imagination. Now that we are
adults, perhaps we are giving up of our own accord even the time to be bored.

Old Japanese houses had places, like the veranda and the space under the eaves, that were neither
quite inside nor outside. They weren't rooms for doing something. Yet people rested there, felt the
seasons, and exchanged words with neighbours passing by. Doesn't time, too, need verandas of that
kind? Thinking only of filling the gaps, I had overlooked what gaps create. From tomorrow, I think I'll try putting my phone away in my bag on

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

The bench in front of the station has disappeared. That bench, a landmark for meeting people, had stood in the same place for decades. After the renovation work, flowerpots were lined
up in the square and there was nowhere left to sit. You can sit down if you go into the café nearby,
but only in exchange for the price of a cup of coffee. Before we knew it, the places in our towns
where one can sit down without paying have been dwindling, little by little.

This is not a story about one station square only. Benches in parks have been fitted with dividers
so that no one can lie down, and station waiting rooms have been moved inside the ticket gates. The
rest areas of shopping centres carry notices saying "for customers of this facility only". Each is a
small change, but piled together they alter the very character of a town. Towns are gradually
becoming places for people who spend money.

Those who remove benches have their reasons too. Some people stay for hours and there are
complaints; young people gather at night and make noise; upkeep and cleaning take effort. These are
all reasonable points, and when one thinks of the trouble taken by the people on the ground, one
can't criticize them lightly. Some also argue that, for crime prevention, benches and shrubbery
should be reduced to keep sight lines clear. The wish to prevent incidents at night is a pressing
one, and it goes without saying that residents' safety must come first.

But let us stop and think. Who was it who sat on that bench? Elderly people taking a break while
shopping, parents reading a book while their children played, teenagers with no place of their own
at school or at home. For them the bench was not just a seat. It was a place where they were allowed
to be without buying anything or doing anything.

An acquaintance of mine, an old man, made it his daily habit to read the newspaper on that bench
every morning. After losing his wife he had tended to stay shut up at home, but when he sat on the
bench someone would speak to him: a shopkeeper he knew by sight, a dog owner out for a walk,
schoolchildren on their way to school. Those brief greetings, piled up, were probably what kept him
connected to the town. Since the bench disappeared, I have not seen him.

The towns of Japan once had more such places. The veranda of a house was where neighbours sat down
for a while, and under a shop's eaves conversations arose between people sheltering from the rain
and the shopkeeper. Temple grounds and the stone steps of shrines were also gaps in the town,
belonging to everyone and to no one. The changing rooms of public baths and the shopfronts of
sweet shops for children were such places too. In the name of efficiency such gaps have been crushed one after
another, and now staying somewhere without a purpose is becoming something that arouses suspicion.

It is the same for children. Children used to play on vacant lots, in alleys and in shrine grounds,
keeping a distance where adults could just about, or just not quite, see them. Now many vacant lots
have become car parks, and alleys have become short cuts for cars. In after-school hours spent only
moving between lessons and cram school, there is hardly any time for doing nothing. Isn't it in
such gaps that children's ability to create their own play grows?

A place to be is a place where one is accepted without a role or a purpose. Public space is, by
rights, supposed to be a place anyone can use, whatever their purpose. Just as a
library is open to people who don't borrow books, a square must be open to people who don't buy
anything. People who have lost their place have no choice but to shut themselves up at home or move
to places they can pay for. The former deepens their isolation; the latter keeps people without
money in their pockets away from the town. The problem of a single bench is in fact nothing other
than the question of who is allowed to be in the town.

On the other hand, setting up and maintaining public space costs money. For local governments with
tight finances, keeping spaces that produce no profit is not easy. That is exactly why the idea
arises of bringing shops into squares and covering upkeep with the income. That in itself is not to
be rejected. The problem is that such spaces turn, before anyone notices, into places that welcome
only customers. Leave seats where people can sit without buying anything, even in a square with
shops: that alone should change the meaning of the space greatly.

Of course, putting the bench back won't solve everything. Dealing with complaints and the cost of
cleaning will still be needed. But these are not reasons to do away with places to be: they are
costs everyone should share to protect them. The cost of putting out one bench is surely not high
compared with how much connection is lost. I hear there are towns where residents take turns
tending the flower beds and cleaning the benches. Instead of leaving it all to the authorities,
residents themselves can surely take care of the gaps. Simply putting a small chair under the eaves
of one's own house can make it a place where someone rests. Left alone, the gaps in a town disappear. That is
exactly why we must consciously keep them and help them grow.

A town designed for efficiency is beautiful. But a town where people live needs margins that
efficiency cannot measure. I would like those who plan towns to look not only at how people move,
but at where they stop and where they rest. That someone who is doing nothing can be there: is that not the surest
proof of a town's richness?

</details>

## Listening strategies

N1 listening is at natural speed, with the fillers and contractions of real speech. Know them so they
don't slow you down:

| Spoken | Full form | | Spoken | Full form |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 〜ちゃう / 〜じゃう | 〜てしまう / 〜でしまう | | 〜とく | 〜ておく |
| 〜てる | 〜ている | | 〜てく | 〜ていく |
| 〜じゃん | 〜じゃないか | | 〜っけ | (checking a memory) |
| 〜って | 〜と / 〜というのは | | 〜んだ / 〜んです | 〜のだ / 〜のです |
| えっと, あのう, なんか, まあ | fillers: ignore | | 〜かなと{思|おも}って | soft "I was thinking…" |

- **[[Task-based]]**: listen for the final decision; plans change in the middle ("やっぱり…").
- **[[Key points]]**: the question is given first; listen for the reason, which often follows
  "{実|じつ}は" or "というのも".
- **[[General outline]]**: no question in advance; listen for what the speaker keeps coming back to.
- **[[Quick response]]**: one line, then three replies. N1 replies are indirect: an idiom, a hint, a
  polite refusal that never says no.
- **[[Integrated]]**: a long talk or a three-way discussion, then a question about two speakers or two
  options. Take notes in a table: option, for, against, who.

Choose the best reply to each line (answers below).

1. 「すっかりご{無沙汰|ぶさた}してしまって。」
   (a) いえいえ、こちらこそ。お{元気|げんき}そうで{何|なに}よりです。 (b) {沙汰|さた}はまだ{来|き}ていません。 (c) じゃあ、{連絡|れんらく}をお{待|ま}ちしています。
2. 「この{企画|きかく}、{部長|ぶちょう}は{首|くび}を{縦|たて}に{振|ふ}ってくれるかな。」
   (a) {首|くび}が{痛|いた}いなら{休|やす}んだほうがいいよ。 (b) {数字|すうじ}がそろえば、{大丈夫|だいじょうぶ}だと{思|おも}うけど。 (c) {横|よこ}に{振|ふ}ったら{困|こま}るね。
3. 「お{忙|いそが}しいところ{恐縮|きょうしゅく}ですが、{資料|しりょう}をご{査収|さしゅう}ください。」
   (a) はい、{確|たし}かに{拝受|はいじゅ}しました。 (b) いえ、{忙|いそが}しくないです。 (c) ご{査収|さしゅう}いたします。

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. (a): ご{無沙汰|ぶさた}している is an apology for not having been in touch; the reply returns the
   apology (こちらこそ). 2. (b): {首|くび}を{縦|たて}に{振|ふ}る is "to say yes"; the reply says it depends
   on the figures. (c) takes it literally. 3. (a): {拝受|はいじゅ}しました is the humble "received";
   (c) uses ご{査収|さしゅう}, which is for the other person's action, about oneself.

</details>

### Listening 5: integrated comprehension

Three former classmates plan a reunion. Which venue do they choose, and what does Yūki think of it?

```dialogue
# The reunion
はると: {同窓会|どうそうかい}の{会場|かいじょう}、{候補|こうほ}が{三|みっ}つあるんだ。{一|ひと}つ{目|め}は{駅前|えきまえ}のホテルの{宴会場|えんかいじょう}。{一人|ひとり}{八千円|はっせんえん}で、{料理|りょうり}もいいし{冷暖房|れいだんぼう}も{完備|かんび}。
= There are three candidates for the reunion venue. The first is the banquet room at the hotel by the station. Eight thousand yen each, good food, and full heating and air conditioning.
さき: {八千円|はっせんえん}はちょっと{高|たか}いなあ。{子供|こども}の{学費|がくひ}もあるし。
= Eight thousand is a bit steep. There are the kids' school fees too.
はると: {二|ふた}つ{目|め}は{川沿|かわぞ}いの{料亭|りょうてい}の{座敷|ざしき}。{六千円|ろくせんえん}で、{雰囲気|ふんいき}は{最高|さいこう}。ただ、{座敷|ざしき}だから{足|あし}の{悪|わる}い{人|ひと}にはきついかも。
= The second is the tatami room at the restaurant by the river. Six thousand, and the atmosphere is the best. But since it's a tatami room, it might be hard for anyone with bad legs.
ゆうき: {担任|たんにん}だった{先生|せんせい}、{去年|きょねん}{膝|ひざ}を{手術|しゅじゅつ}したって{聞|き}いたよ。
= I heard our old form teacher had a knee operation last year.
さき: じゃあ{座敷|ざしき}は{避|さ}けたほうがいいね。{三|みっ}つ{目|め}は？
= Then we'd better avoid the tatami room. And the third?
はると: {母校|ぼこう}の{近|ちか}くの{公民館|こうみんかん}。{会場|かいじょう}は{無料|むりょう}で、{料理|りょうり}は{仕出|しだ}しを{頼|たの}むから{一人|ひとり}{三千円|さんぜんえん}くらい。でも{片付|かたづ}けは{自分|じぶん}たちでやらないと。
= The community centre near our old school. The hall is free, and we'd order catering, so about three thousand each. But we'd have to clear up ourselves.
さき: {片付|かたづ}けぐらいなら{手伝|てつだ}うよ。{安|やす}いのが{一番|いちばん}。
= I'll help with clearing up. Cheap is best.
ゆうき: うーん、{公民館|こうみんかん}はちょっと{味気|あじけ}ない{気|き}もするけど…。まあ、{先生|せんせい}も{来|き}やすいし、{懐|なつ}かしい{場所|ばしょ}の{近|ちか}くだし、{悪|わる}くないか。
= Hmm, the community centre feels a bit dull, but… well, it's easy for our teacher to get to, and it's near the place we remember, so it's not bad.
はると: じゃあ、{公民館|こうみんかん}で{決|き}まりだね。
= Then the community centre it is.
```

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

The community centre (cheap, and easy for the teacher, who had a knee operation; the tatami room was
ruled out for that reason, the hotel for the price). Yūki finds it a little dull but accepts it as
"not bad", because it is easy for the teacher and near their old school.

</details>

## Words for notices, letters and the home

| Topic | Words |
|---|---|
| Addresses and titles | {宛先|あてさき}, {宛名|あてな}, {宛|あ}てる, {貴社|きしゃ}, {御社|おんしゃ}, {貴殿|きでん}, {殿|との} / どの, {各位|かくい}, {氏|し}, {名称|めいしょう}, {称|しょう}する |
| Letter phrases | {謹啓|きんけい}, {時下|じか}, ご{清栄|せいえい}, {平素|へいそ}, {格別|かくべつ}, ご{高配|こうはい}, ご{無沙汰|ぶさた}, ご{査収|さしゅう}, お{取|と}り{計|はか}らい, {拝受|はいじゅ}する, {末筆|まっぴつ}, ご{自愛|じあい} |
| Forms and procedures | {同封|どうふう}する, {開封|かいふう}する, {封|ふう}, {添|そ}える, {交付|こうふ}, {助成金|じょせいきん}, {払|はら}い{戻|もど}し, {先着順|せんちゃくじゅん}, {有効期限|ゆうこうきげん}, {取|と}り{扱|あつか}い, {扱|あつか}う |
| Ceremonies and events | {来賓|らいひん}, {賓客|ひんきゃく}, {壇上|だんじょう}, {臨|のぞ}む, {臨場感|りんじょうかん} |
| The building | {廊下|ろうか}, {敷地|しきち}, {敷|し}く, {敷金|しききん}, {屋敷|やしき}, {座敷|ざしき}, {軒|のき}, {一軒家|いっけんや}, {軒並|のきな}み, {棟|むね}, {病棟|びょうとう}, {別荘|べっそう}, {壁紙|かべがみ}, {障壁|しょうへき}, {壁画|へきが}, {画廊|がろう}, {冷房|れいぼう}, {暖房|だんぼう}, {冷暖房|れいだんぼう} |
| Housework and the garden | {布巾|ふきん}, {拭|ぬぐ}う, {潰|つぶ}す, {潰|つぶ}れる, {隙間|すきま}, {隙|すき}, {乾燥|かんそう}, {花壇|かだん}, {植木鉢|うえきばち}, {鉢植|はちう}え, {刈|か}る, {飼育|しいく}する, {憩|いこ}い, {盆|ぼん}, {筒|つつ}, {水筒|すいとう}, {文房具|ぶんぼうぐ}, {添加物|てんかぶつ} |
| Talk and rumour | {沙汰|さた}, {取|と}り{沙汰|ざた}, {頂点|ちょうてん}, {頂上|ちょうじょう} |

The reference sheet "Formal letters and notices" sets out the structure of a formal letter and the
language of notices.

## Say it

```speak
ご{無沙汰|ぶさた}しております。
= I'm sorry I've been out of touch for so long.
{資料|しりょう}を{添付|てんぷ}いたしましたので、ご{査収|さしゅう}ください。
= I have attached the materials; please look them over.
{確|たし}かに{拝受|はいじゅ}いたしました。
= I have duly received it.
{末筆|まっぴつ}ながら、{皆様|みなさま}のご{健康|けんこう}をお{祈|いの}り{申|もう}し{上|あ}げます。
= In closing, I wish you all good health.
{廊下|ろうか}に{私物|しぶつ}を{置|お}かないでください。
= Please don't leave personal belongings in the corridor.
```

## Key points

- Read the questions first for information retrieval; read the text first for thematic
  comprehension. Mark the turns and the hedges.
- In notices and rules, the answer is usually in an exception: ただし, {除|のぞ}く, {限|かぎ}る, ※.
- In integrated comprehension, note what A and B share before where they differ.
- Listening: learn the contractions; listen for the final decision and for indirect replies.
- Letters: ご{無沙汰|ぶさた}, ご{査収|さしゅう}, {拝受|はいじゅ}, {末筆|まっぴつ}ながら, ご{自愛|じあい}ください.
- New kanji: 宛 添 封 筒 氏 郎 称 賓 頂 房 壁 廊 敷 軒 棟 荘 壇 扱 拭 巾 潰 隙 臨 沙 汰 憩 餌 飼 刈 燥 盆 鉢.

lessons.title: The JLPT N1 and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the last core lesson of the course and of the series. It explains how the JLPT N1 is built
and scored, gives a plan for the last month and for the day itself, reviews the course's grammar by
what it does, and looks beyond N1. The facts about the test come from the official JLPT website
(jlpt.jp), checked for this course on 10 November 2026; the test can change, so check the site
again before you register. The descriptions are in this course's own words, except where a phrase
is marked as the official wording.

The last 32 kanji are those of the sea and fishing, farming and animals, and a handful that remain:
{漁師|りょうし}, {浅瀬|あさせ}, {穀物|こくもつ}, {家畜|かちく}, {竜巻|たつまき}, {猛暑|もうしょ}, {脂肪|しぼう},
{襟|えり}. With them, you have met 1,999 kanji since the kana course.

## The JLPT and the level N1

The Japanese-Language Proficiency Test has five levels, N5 (the easiest) to N1. It is usually held
twice a year, in July and December, in Japan and in many other countries; some cities outside Japan
hold it only once a year. It is multiple choice and machine-scored, with no speaking or writing.

The official summary of N1 says the examinee can read "writings with logical complexity and/or
abstract writings on a variety of topics, such as newspaper editorials and critiques" and can follow
"coherent conversations, news reports, and lectures, spoken at natural speed" (jlpt.jp, level
summary). In this course's words: at N1 you read the serious press and books of ideas, and you follow
lectures, meetings and the news, understanding not only what is said but how it is argued and how
the speakers relate to one another.

The JLPT has published no official lists of words, kanji or grammar since 2010. The scope of this
course (about 10,000 words, about 2,000 kanji) follows what learners' materials commonly describe;
it is an estimate, not a requirement.

## How the N1 test is built

The test has **two timed parts**:

| Part | Time |
|---|---|
| Language knowledge (vocabulary and grammar) and reading | 110 minutes |
| Listening | 55 minutes (it may vary slightly with the length of the recordings) |

The first part puts vocabulary, grammar and reading in one block: you decide how to divide the
time. The question types (jlpt.jp names them; the descriptions are ours):

### Vocabulary

- **Kanji reading**: the reading of an underlined word, bare kanji, four kana choices (lessons'
  kanji questions).
- **Contextually-defined expressions**: the word that fits a sentence.
- **Paraphrases**: the word or phrase closest in meaning.
- **Usage**: the one sentence of four that uses a word correctly.

Unlike N2, the N1 has no orthography (choosing the kanji) and no word-formation questions; the
course taught both for reading, not for the test.

### Grammar

- **Sentential grammar 1 (selecting grammar form)**: the form that fits the slot.
- **Sentential grammar 2 (sentence composition)**: four pieces to put in order, with one starred
  position to report. This course's build questions are the same task without the star: if you can
  build the sentence, you can find the star.
- **[[Text grammar]]**: gaps in a passage; connectors, reference words, endings (lesson 28).

### Reading

- **Comprehension** of short, mid-size and long passages.
- **[[Integrated comprehension]]**: two texts on one question, compared (lesson 29, Text 4).
- **[[Thematic comprehension (long passages)]]**: the writer's claim in a long editorial or essay
  (lesson 29, Text 5).
- **[[Information retrieval]]**: finding what you need in notices, rules or brochures (lesson 29,
  Text 6).

### Listening

- **[[Task-based comprehension]]**: what someone will do next.
- **[[Comprehension of key points]]**: a reason, a feeling, a point, with the question given first.
- **[[Comprehension of general outline]]**: what a talk is mainly about, with no question in advance.
- **[[Quick response]]**: one line, then the best of three replies.
- **[[Integrated comprehension]]**: a long talk or discussion, then a question comparing options or
  speakers.

jlpt.jp gives no fixed number of questions per type, and neither does this course.

## Scoring

The N1 has **three scoring sections** ({得点区分|とくてんくぶん}):

| Scoring section | Scaled score |
|---|---|
| Language knowledge (vocabulary and grammar) | 0–60 |
| Reading | 0–60 |
| Listening | 0–60 |
| **Total** ({総合得点|そうごうとくてん}) | **0–180** |

To pass you need **both**:

- a total of at least **100** (N2: 90), and
- at least **19** in each of the three sections (the sectional pass mark, {基準点|きじゅんてん}).

So a total of 120 fails if listening is 18. Missing any section of the test means failing, and the
score report then shows no section scores. Every examinee receives a score report; those who pass
also receive a certificate. Scores are scaled, not raw counts of correct answers, so you can't
convert "questions right" into points.

## Strategies

### In the last month

- **Do the official sample questions** (jlpt.jp has them for every level) and at least one full
  practice test under real timing. Note where the time goes.
- **Rotate the skills**: a long text every day (an editorial, an essay from this course), twenty
  minutes of listening at natural speed, a set of grammar questions.
- **Keep a mistakes notebook** of the questions you got wrong, why ({誤答|ごとう}の{理由|りゆう}), and
  the right form. Most N1 grammar mistakes are about restrictions: who the subject can be, what
  tense follows, whether it praises or criticizes.
- **Read the reference sheets** of this course once more: they are the course's grammar in tables.

### During the test

- **Vocabulary and grammar first, briskly.** Don't spend minutes on one item; mark it and move on.
  The reading needs the time.
- **Reading: longest texts with care.** Thematic comprehension rewards finding the turn and the
  strongest ending; information retrieval rewards reading the question first.
- **Use elimination** ({消去法|しょうきょほう}): in usage and paraphrase questions, rule out the choices
  with the wrong register or the wrong tone.
- **Listening: never stay behind.** Answer at once, guess if you must, and listen to the next item
  fresh. In quick response, prefer the indirect, idiomatic reply that fits the relationship.
- **Fill every answer.** There is no penalty for a wrong guess.

## The whole course by function

The grammar of this course, grouped by what it does. Lesson numbers are this course's.

| Function | Patterns | Lessons |
|---|---|---|
| As soon as | 〜が{早|はや}いか, 〜や{否|いな}や, 〜なり, 〜そばから | 1 |
| Starting and ending | 〜を{皮切|かわき}りに, 〜をもって, 〜を{限|かぎ}りに, 〜を{境|さかい}に, 〜を{経|へ}て | 2 |
| Alongside | 〜かたわら, 〜がてら, 〜かたがた | 3 |
| At the moment | 〜た{矢先|やさき}に, 〜{折|おり}から, 〜ところを, 〜にあって | 4 |
| Without, left undone | 〜なくして, 〜なしに, 〜ずじまい, 〜までだ | 5 |
| Even | 〜といえども, 〜たりとも, 〜とて, 〜たところで | 6 |
| If only, contrary to | 〜ものを, 〜と{思|おも}いきや, 〜にひきかえ, 〜ながらに | 7 |
| Whether A or B | 〜であれ, 〜といい〜といい, 〜といわず, 〜なり〜なり | 8 |
| Let alone, more than | 〜はおろか, 〜もさることながら, 〜にもまして, 〜ならいざしらず | 9 |
| It's not as if | 〜ではあるまいし, 〜ならまだしも, 〜ないまでも, 〜ともなく | 10 |
| Precisely because | 〜ばこそ, 〜ゆえ(に), 〜とあって, 〜こととて | 11 |
| In order to | 〜んがため, 〜べく, 〜べくもない, 〜をもって | 12 |
| Given that | 〜{手前|てまえ}, 〜とあれば, 〜ともなると, 〜あっての | 13 |
| Paying no heed | 〜をよそに, 〜をものともせず, 〜を{顧|かえり}みず, 〜にかこつけて, 〜をいいことに | 14 |
| In line with, depending on | 〜に{即|そく}して, 〜にのっとって, 〜を{踏|ふ}まえて, 〜に{鑑|かんが}みて, 〜いかんで, 〜いかんによらず | 15 |
| Can't help feeling | 〜を{禁|きん}じ{得|え}ない, 〜てやまない, 〜に{堪|た}えない, 〜ずにはおかない, 〜に{忍|しの}びない | 16 |
| Worth it or not | 〜に{足|た}る, 〜に{足|た}りない, 〜にかたくない, 〜かいがある | 17 |
| To the extreme | 〜{極|きわ}まりない, 〜の{至|いた}り, 〜の{極|きわ}み, 〜とは | 18 |
| Forced to | 〜を{余儀|よぎ}なくされる, 〜ないではすまない, 〜ずにはすまない | 19 |
| Must not | 〜まじき, 〜べからず, 〜べからざる, 〜てしかるべきだ | 20 |
| Only here | 〜ならでは, 〜をおいて, 〜にして, 〜に{至|いた}っては | 21 |
| Covered in | 〜ずくめ, 〜まみれ, 〜めく, 〜ぐるみ | 22 |
| Tendencies and likeness | 〜きらいがある, 〜ごとき / ごとく, 〜んばかり, 〜とばかりに | 23 |
| In its own way | 〜なりに, 〜たる, 〜と{相|あい}まって, 〜ともあろう | 24 |
| Once it happens | 〜が{最後|さいご} / たら{最後|さいご}, 〜(よ)うが〜まいが, 〜ずとも | 25 |
| Literary forms | 〜べし, 〜ごとし, 〜ざる, 〜をして〜しめる, なり | 26 |
| Academic connectors | ひいては, {並|なら}びに / {及|およ}び, ないし, {又|また}は / {若|も}しくは, いわんや〜をや, {否|いな} | 28 |

### Pairs to check

| Pair | The difference |
|---|---|
| 〜が{早|はや}いか / 〜や{否|いな}や / 〜なり / 〜たとたん | all "as soon as"; なり and が{早|はや}いか exclude the speaker as subject; たとたん is the neutral one |
| 〜ばこそ / 〜からこそ | ばこそ is written and stresses a reason that might seem unlikely; からこそ is everyday |
| 〜べく / 〜ために | べく is written and needs a verb of effort after it; ために is always right |
| 〜をよそに / 〜にもかかわらず | をよそに ignores others' worries or protests; にもかかわらず is any "despite" |
| 〜ならでは / 〜だけ | ならでは praises what only A can offer; だけ just limits |
| 〜ごとき / 〜ような | ごとき is written, and after a person it can show contempt or modesty |
| 〜ずくめ / 〜まみれ / 〜だらけ | ずくめ: all of one thing (often good); まみれ: covered in something messy; だらけ: full of (usually bad) |
| 〜まじき / 〜べきではない | まじき is written, before a noun, and condemns behaviour unworthy of a role |
| 〜とされる / 〜と{考|かんが}えられる | reports an accepted view / gives the writer's reasoned view |

## Kanji

The last thirty-two kanji: the sea and fishing, farming and food, fierce things, and a few that
remained. Carried words that take their kanji now: {漁業|ぎょぎょう}, {収穫|しゅうかく}, {読解|どっかい},
{聴解|ちょうかい}, {模擬試験|もぎしけん}.

### The sea, fishing and boats

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 漁 | fishing | ギョ, リョウ | — | 14 | {漁師|りょうし}, {漁|りょう}, {漁村|ぎょそん}, {漁港|ぎょこう}, {漁船|ぎょせん}, {豊漁|ほうりょう}, {不漁|ふりょう}, {漁業|ぎょぎょう} (carried) |
| 瀬 | rapids, shallows | — | せ | 19 | {浅瀬|あさせ}, {瀬戸際|せとぎわ}, {瀬戸物|せともの} |
| 舟 | boat | シュウ | ふね, ふな | 6 | {小舟|こぶね}, {舟|ふね} (= carried ふね, for small boats) |
| 帆 | sail | ハン | ほ | 6 | {帆|ほ}, {帆船|はんせん} |
| 桟 | jetty; scaffold | サン | — | 10 | {桟橋|さんばし}, {桟敷|さじき} |
| 隻 | ships (counter) | セキ | — | 10 | {隻|せき}, {一隻|いっせき} |
| 塚 | mound | — | つか | 12 | {塚|つか}, {貝塚|かいづか} |

- 漁 has two on'yomi: ギョ in most compounds ({漁業|ぎょぎょう}, {漁村|ぎょそん}) and リョウ in {漁師|りょうし},
  {漁|りょう} and {豊漁|ほうりょう} / {不漁|ふりょう}.
- {舟|ふね} (a small boat, rowing boat) and the carried {船|ふね} (a ship) are one word in two spellings.
- 瀬 (19 strokes) has water and 頼: rapids, shallows. {瀬戸際|せとぎわ} is the edge of a narrow strait: the
  brink.
- {桟敷|さじき} is a special reading: neither kanji has its usual reading.

```trace
漁瀬舟帆桟隻塚
```

### Farming, grain and fat

| Kanji | Meaning | On'yomi | Kun'yomi | Strokes | Words |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 穀 | grain | コク | — | 14 | {穀物|こくもつ}, {雑穀|ざっこく}, {穀倉地帯|こくそうちたい} |
| 穫 | harvest | カク | — | 18 | {収穫|しゅうかく} (carried) |
| 畜 | livestock | チク | — | 10 | {家畜|かちく}, {畜産|ちくさん} |

1. What surprised the writer about reading a whole book after passing N1?
2. What changed the writer's reading speed, and how does the writer contrast reading for a test with
   reading for pleasure?
3. What did reading columns and editorials teach the writer?
4. What does the writer say is more important than test scores?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Its length and difficulty: an exam text ends at about 2,000 characters, but the book had over 200
   pages; in the first week they read only 20, and looking up words made them lose the thread.
2. Stopping looking up every word: guessing from context and checking only words that came up three
   times and stayed unclear. Reading for the test means grasping every word precisely; reading for
   pleasure means carrying on while holding parts you don't understand.
3. That the same event is seen differently by different newspapers: one begins to see the
   standpoint behind the words. (Listening to debates and writing weekly responses taught them
   more: who stands where in a discussion, and the gap between reading and writing.)
4. The question of what you want to read and whom you want to talk to in Japanese: the test is only
   a key to a door, and N1 is an entrance, not a goal.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

When I passed the JLPT N1, I thought that was the end of my study of Japanese. Looking back now, it
was really where it began.

The month after I passed, I tried for the first time to read a Japanese paperback of non-fiction all
the way through. A long exam text ends at two thousand characters; but the book had more than two
hundred pages. In the first week I managed only twenty. There were far more words I didn't know
than in the test, and every time I looked one up, I lost the thread of the story. I must have learned nearly ten
thousand words studying for the test, yet the book's words spread endlessly beyond them.

The turning point was giving up the dictionary. Even when there was a word I didn't know, I guessed
from the context and moved on. Only when it had come up three times and was still unclear would I
look it up. Once I had decided this, my reading speed rose beyond recognition. Reading for the test
meant grasping each word precisely. Reading for pleasure means walking on while carrying the parts
you don't understand.

Newspapers are the same. Each morning I read one front-page column and summed up what the writer
wanted to say in a sentence. At first it took thirty minutes; half a year later, ten were enough.
Reading the editorials alongside, you notice that the same event is viewed differently by different
papers. It is thanks to that accumulation that the standpoint behind the words comes into view.

My listening, too, grew after the test. I made a habit of listening to radio debate programmes on
the train to work. In the test the audio plays only once, but a recording can be replayed as often
as you like. Discussions I couldn't even follow at first became clear with repeated listening: who
stood where, and where opinions divided. Even in the way people give back-channel responses, and in
the indirect phrasing before an objection, a very Japanese courtesy lies hidden.

Above all, what changed was writing. Every week I wrote a short response in Japanese to a book I'd
read and had a Japanese friend read it. Looking at the places corrected in red, I could see habits
of my own I'd never noticed in the test. Between being able to read and being able to write there
was a deeper gulf than I'd imagined.

For people who use Japanese at work there is also a test of business Japanese. But what matters
more than test scores is surely the question of what you want to read, and whom you want to talk
to, in Japanese. A novel by an author you like, or a magazine about your hobby, will do. People learn Japanese for all kinds of reasons, but when the test ends, the language does not. The test is
no more than a key that opens a door, and beyond the door countless words that never appear in a
test are waiting. N1 is not a goal. It is the entrance to the wide world of Japanese.

</details>

## After N1

- **Read for pleasure**: a 新書 on a subject you like, then a novel (Aozora Bunko has the
  public-domain classics: lessons 5h1, 10h1, 20h1, 25h1, 30h1).
- **Read the press**: a column every morning, an editorial once a week, summarized in one sentence.
- **Listen to the world**: news, documentaries, panel discussions, lectures.
- **Write and speak**: the JLPT tests neither; find a conversation partner and write short essays
  (N2's honors lesson on the {小論文|しょうろんぶん} is a start).
- **Business Japanese**: the BJT tests Japanese for work. Check its official site.

## Common mistakes

- Thinking a high total is enough. Each section needs 19 or more; a total of 120 with 18 in listening
  fails.
- Spending too long on vocabulary and grammar, then rushing the long reading texts.
- Reading {漁師|りょうし} as ぎょし, {猛者|もさ} as もうじゃ, {桟敷|さじき} as さんしき.
- {穫|かく} for prizes or {獲|かく} for crops: {獲得|かくとく} (win, gain), {収穫|しゅうかく} (harvest).
- Writing {舟|ふね} for a large ship. {船|ふね} is the general word; {舟|ふね} is for small boats.
- Treating N1 as the end. It is the entrance.

## Key points

- Two timed parts: language knowledge and reading (110 min), listening (55 min).
- Three scoring sections, 0–60 each; pass = total 100 or more **and** 19 or more in every section.
- Vocabulary: kanji reading, contextually-defined expressions, paraphrases, usage. Grammar: form,
  sentence composition, text grammar. Reading: short, mid, long, integrated, thematic, information
  retrieval. Listening: task, key points, outline, quick response, integrated.
- No orthography or word-formation questions at N1.
- New kanji: 漁 瀬 舟 帆 桟 隻 塚 穀 穫 畜 俵 桑 茎 茂 脂 肪 竜 猛 牙 砕 零 氾 雌 畿 斗 肖 椎 屯 孔 玩 尿 襟.

The reference sheets of this course ("Literary and academic style", "Formal letters and notices"
and the kanji list) are the best last review. The words from this lesson are listed below; they
join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson. お{疲|つか}れさまでした。

lessons.title: Nakajima Atsushi and "The Moon over the Mountain"
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

『{山月記|さんげつき}』 ("The Moon over the Mountain") is a short story you can read in one sitting, and one of the
most widely read works of modern Japanese literature: generations of Japanese high-school students
have met it in their textbooks, where it has become a staple ({定番|ていばん}). It tells of a gifted, proud
man who becomes a tiger. Its prose has the weight of **[[kanbun]]**, classical Chinese as Japanese
has read it for centuries, and this lesson uses it to show how that reading, **[[kundoku]]**, shaped
written Japanese. It brings together the literary forms of lesson 26 and the self-reflection of
the course's last reading texts.

## Nakajima Atsushi

{中島|なかじま}{敦|あつし} (1909–1942; the kanji of his given name is outside N1) was born in Tokyo on 5 May 1909. He suffered from
asthma from his school days. In 1941 he went to Palau, then a Japanese-governed territory in the
South Seas, as an official compiling Japanese textbooks for local schools; ill health brought him
back to Tokyo in March 1942, and he resolved to live as a writer. He died of his asthma in December
1942, at 33. Most of his fame came after his death: 『{李陵|りりょう}』 (its first kanji is outside N1), a novella about
a Han-dynasty general, appeared in 1943, and 『{光|ひかり}と{風|かぜ}と{夢|ゆめ}』 (1942) is a novel about
the last years of Robert Louis Stevenson.

『{山月記|さんげつき}』 was first published in February 1942 in the literary magazine 『{文學界|ぶんがくかい}』
(the magazine's title uses the old form of its second kanji), with 『{文字禍|もじか}』, under the joint title 『{古譚|こたん}』
("old tales"; its second kanji is outside N1). It is based on a Tang-dynasty Chinese tale known in Japan as
『{人虎伝|じんこでん}』 ("the man-tiger"), a classic {伝奇|でんき} (a tale of the strange). Nakajima kept the
frame of the old tale and added what makes it modern: the hero's long self-examination. Because he
died in 1942, his works are in the public domain.

## The story

{李徴|りちょう} (Li Zheng; the first kanji is outside N1), a young man of great learning, passes the imperial examination
early and receives an official post. Too proud to serve as a minor official, he resigns to become a
poet, hoping to leave a name for a hundred years. Fame doesn't come, his family grows poor, and he
takes a low post again, now serving under men he once looked down on. One night on a journey, he
goes mad, runs out into the dark and is never seen again.

The rest of the story, retold here in modern Japanese:

> {翌年|よくねん}、{李徴|りちょう}の{旧友|きゅうゆう}である{袁傪|えんさん}は、{役人|やくにん}として{旅|たび}をしていた。{夜明|よあ}け{前|まえ}、{人食|ひとく}い{虎|とら}が{出|で}るという{道|みち}を{進|すす}んでいると、{草|くさ}むらから{一匹|いっぴき}の{虎|とら}が{躍|おど}り{出|で}た。だが{虎|とら}は{袁傪|えんさん}に{襲|おそ}いかかる{寸前|すんぜん}で{身|み}を{翻|ひるがえ}し、{草|くさ}むらに{隠|かく}れた。そして{中|なか}から、「{危|あぶ}ないところだった」とつぶやく{人間|にんげん}の{声|こえ}が{聞|き}こえてきた。それは、{行方|ゆくえ}{知|し}れずになっていた{李徴|りちょう}の{声|こえ}であった。
>
> {李徴|りちょう}は{姿|すがた}を{見|み}せないまま、{自分|じぶん}が{虎|とら}になった{経緯|けいい}を{語|かた}った。{理由|りゆう}は{分|わ}からない。ただ、{一日|いちにち}のうちに{人間|にんげん}の{心|こころ}に{戻|もど}る{時間|じかん}が、{日|ひ}に{日|ひ}に{短|みじか}くなっている。やがて{自分|じぶん}は{完全|かんぜん}に{虎|とら}になり、{人間|にんげん}であったことさえ{忘|わす}れてしまうだろう。そうなる{前|まえ}に{頼|たの}みがある、と{李徴|りちょう}は{言|い}い、{今|いま}も{覚|おぼ}えている{自作|じさく}の{詩|し}を{書|か}き{留|と}めてほしいと{願|ねが}った。{袁傪|えんさん}は{部下|ぶか}に{書|か}き{取|と}らせながら、{詩|し}の{見事|みごと}さに{感心|かんしん}した。しかし{同時|どうじ}に、どこか{一流|いちりゅう}の{作品|さくひん}となるには{欠|か}けるものがある、とも{感|かん}じた。
>
> {詩|し}を{読|よ}み{終|お}えた{李徴|りちょう}は、なぜ{自分|じぶん}が{虎|とら}になったのかを、{自|みずか}ら{語|かた}り{始|はじ}めた。{自分|じぶん}は{詩人|しじん}として{名|な}を{成|な}したいと{望|のぞ}みながら、{師|し}に{就|つ}くことも、{仲間|なかま}と{互|たが}いに{磨|みが}き{合|あ}うこともしなかった。{才能|さいのう}がないと{分|わ}かるのが{怖|こわ}くて、{努力|どりょく}することもできず、かといって{自分|じぶん}には{才能|さいのう}があると{半|なか}ば{信|しん}じていたから、{凡人|ぼんじん}の{中|なか}に{交|ま}じって{生|い}きることもできなかった。その{臆病|おくびょう}な{自尊心|じそんしん}と{尊大|そんだい}な{羞恥心|しゅうちしん}こそが、{自分|じぶん}の{中|なか}の{猛獣|もうじゅう}であり、それがついに{自分|じぶん}を{虎|とら}の{姿|すがた}に{変|か}えたのだ、と。
>
> {別|わか}れ{際|ぎわ}、{李徴|りちょう}は{残|のこ}された{妻子|さいし}のことを{袁傪|えんさん}に{託|たく}した。そして、{本当|ほんとう}なら{詩|し}よりも{先|さき}に{家族|かぞく}のことを{頼|たの}むべきだった、そんな{男|おとこ}だから{獣|けもの}に{身|み}を{落|お}としたのだ、と{自分|じぶん}を{責|せ}めた。{袁傪|えんさん}の{一行|いっこう}が{丘|おか}の{上|うえ}から{振|ふ}り{返|かえ}ると、{一匹|いっぴき}の{虎|とら}が{草|くさ}むらから{現|あらわ}れ、{夜明|よあ}けの{空|そら}に{残|のこ}る{月|つき}を{仰|あお}いで{声|こえ}を{上|あ}げたかと{思|おも}うと、また{草|くさ}むらに{躍|おど}り{入|い}り、{二度|にど}とその{姿|すがた}を{見|み}せなかった。

{袁傪|えんさん} (Yuan Can; both kanji are outside N1) = Li Zheng's old friend; {身|み}を{翻|ひるがえ}す =
to turn away suddenly; {行方|ゆくえ}{知|し}れず = missing; {書|か}き{取|と}る = to take down in writing;
{妻子|さいし} = wife and children;
{託|たく}す = to entrust. The famous closing image
(the tiger crying out to the moon over the mountain) is the one most readers link with the title
(the mountain and the bright moon also appear in Li Zheng's improvised poem). This retelling simplifies the story and
leaves out the Chinese poem Li Zheng improvises after reciting his old ones.

## Nakajima's own words: two short passages

The quotations follow the text of Aozora Bunko ({青空文庫|あおぞらぶんこ}, the public-domain library), which uses
modern kana and shinjitai and is based on the Shinchō Bunko paperback 『{李陵|りりょう}・{山月記|さんげつき}』
(1969). The story first appeared in the spelling of its time, with historical kana usage; school
editions follow the modern spelling, as here. Kanji outside N1 are given furigana and listed after
each passage.

**The opening sentence:**

> {隴西|ろうさい}の{李徴|りちょう}は{博学|はくがく}{才穎|さいえい}、{天宝|てんぽう}の{末年|まつねん}、{若|わか}くして{名|な}を{虎榜|こぼう}に{連|つら}ね、ついで{江南尉|こうなんい}に{補|ほ}せられたが、{性|せい}、{狷介|けんかい}、{自|みずか}ら{恃|たの}むところ{頗|すこぶ}る{厚|あつ}く、{賤吏|せんり}に{甘|あま}んずるを{潔|いさぎよ}しとしなかった。

Outside N1: 隴, 李, 穎, 榜, 尉, 狷, 恃, 頗, 賤, 吏. In plain modern Japanese: {隴西|ろうさい} (a region of
western China) の{李徴|りちょう}は{学問|がくもん}が{広|ひろ}く{才能|さいのう}に{優|すぐ}れ、{天宝|てんぽう} (a Tang era name of
the mid-eighth century) の{終|お}わりごろ、{若|わか}くして{科挙|かきょ} (the imperial examination) に{合格|ごうかく}し、{次|つぎ}に
{江南|こうなん}の{役人|やくにん}に{任命|にんめい}されたが、{性格|せいかく}が{頑固|がんこ}で{人|ひと}と{打|う}ち{解|と}けず、
{自分|じぶん}の{才能|さいのう}を{固|かた}く{信|しん}じていたので、{身分|みぶん}の{低|ひく}い{役人|やくにん}でいることを
{良|よ}しとしなかった。

One sentence carries the whole man: learning, early success, pride and disdain. Notice how it is
built: noun phrases set side by side with commas ({博学|はくがく}{才穎|さいえい}、{性|せい}、{狷介|けんかい}) as
Chinese does; the classical passive {補|ほ}せられた (was appointed); 〜に{甘|あま}んずる (to content
oneself with), the classical form of {甘|あま}んじる; and the kundoku idiom 〜を{潔|いさぎよ}しとしない (to
think it beneath one). This is **[[kanbun-style]]** prose: Japanese that sounds as if it had been read
out of Chinese.

The Aozora text gives {隴西|ろうさい} the reading ろうさい; many school editions read it ろうせい.
Readings of old Chinese names vary between editions.

**The tiger within:**

> {人間|にんげん}は{誰|だれ}でも{猛獣使|もうじゅうつかい}であり、その{猛獣|もうじゅう}に{当|あた}るのが、{各人|かくじん}の{性情|せいじょう}だという。{己|おれ}の{場合|ばあい}、この{尊大|そんだい}な{羞恥心|しゅうちしん}が{猛獣|もうじゅう}だった。{虎|とら}だったのだ。

Outside N1: 羞. {己|おれ} is printed with the reading おれ (I, rough): Li Zheng's speech. {猛獣使|もうじゅうつかい}
is a tamer of wild beasts, written without the い that modern spelling adds ({猛獣使|もうじゅうつか}い);
{当|あた}る likewise without た ({当|あ}たる). Those are spellings of the text, not mistakes.

The phrase that sums up the story is Li Zheng's diagnosis of himself: 「{臆病|おくびょう}な{自尊心|じそんしん}と、
{尊大|そんだい}な{羞恥心|しゅうちしん}」, a cowardly self-respect and an arrogant sense of shame. Each half
turns a quality against itself: pride too timid to risk failure, shame so proud it refuses to
learn among others.

## Kanbun and kundoku

**[[Kanbun]]** ({漢文|かんぶん}) is classical Chinese. For over a thousand years Japanese readers did not
translate it; they read it directly as Japanese by **[[kundoku]]** ({訓読|くんどく}): keeping the Chinese
characters, adding Japanese endings and particles, and changing the order with small marks.

| Step | What is done | Example |
|---|---|---|
| The bare text ({白文|はくぶん}) | Chinese word order, no marks | {国|くに}{破|やぶ}{山河|さんが}{在|あ} |
| Add okurigana | Japanese endings in small kana | {国|くに}{破|やぶ}レテ{山河|さんが}{在|あ}リ |
| Add return marks ({返|かえ}り{点|てん}) | where Japanese order differs | {不|ず}{知|し} → {知|し}らず (read the second kanji first: a レ{点|てん}) |
| Write it out ({書|か}き{下|くだ}し{文|ぶん}) | the Japanese sentence | {国|くに}{破|やぶ}れて{山河|さんが}{在|あ}り |

The example is the first line of 『{春望|しゅんぼう}』 ("A spring view") by the Tang poet Du Fu, written after
the capital fell to rebels: "The country is broken, yet the mountains and rivers remain." In
kundoku it is 「{国|くに}{破|やぶ}れて{山河|さんが}{在|あ}り」, a line that every Japanese student meets.
Notice {在|あ}り: the classical あり, here written with its Chinese
character.

**Why it matters for N1.** Kundoku left its marks on written Japanese: the classical forms of lesson
26 (ず, べし, ごとし, しむ / しめる), set phrases such as 〜を{潔|いさぎよ}しとしない, 〜に{過|す}ぎない,
〜をもって, いわんや〜をや (lesson 28) and 〜ざるを{得|え}ない, and the habit of packing meaning into
compact kango. When an essay sounds weighty and terse, it is often kundoku you are hearing.

## Reading the story today

『{山月記|さんげつき}』 is read in schools less as a fantasy than as a story about the self. Li Zheng is not
punished by the gods; he is transformed by what he could not face in himself. Readers often take the
tiger as a figure for a talent that cut itself off from others out of fear of being judged, and the
question the story leaves is uncomfortable because it is ordinary: how many of us avoid trying, so
that we never have to find out what we are worth? (These are readers' interpretations; the story
never states a moral.)

## Grammar to notice

- Lesson 26: the classical forms {補|ほ}せられた (passive), {甘|あま}んずる, {潔|いさぎよ}しとしなかった; the
  perfective tone of the narration.
- Lesson 27: {刻苦|こっく}, {尊大|そんだい} and {性情|せいじょう}, kango with the weight of kanbun; the compound
  verb {書|か}き{取|と}る.
- Lesson 28: the reasoning of Li Zheng's confession: {才能|さいのう}がないと{分|わ}かるのが{怖|こわ}くて…かといって….

## Key points

- {中島|なかじま}{敦|あつし} (1909–1942); 『{山月記|さんげつき}』 (February 1942, in 『{文學界|ぶんがくかい}』 under 『{古譚|こたん}』),
  based on the Tang tale 『{人虎伝|じんこでん}』.
- The story: a proud poet who becomes a tiger; his diagnosis, 「{臆病|おくびょう}な{自尊心|じそんしん}と、{尊大|そんだい}な{羞恥心|しゅうちしん}」.
- Kanbun is classical Chinese; kundoku reads it as Japanese with okurigana and return marks:
  {国|くに}{破|やぶ}{山河|さんが}{在|あ} → {国|くに}{破|やぶ}れて{山河|さんが}{在|あ}り.
- Kanbun-style Japanese: compact kango, parallel phrases, classical forms and kundoku idioms
  (〜を{潔|いさぎよ}しとしない).

lessons.title: Japanese aesthetics
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Essays, museum labels, travel writing and advertisements love a handful of words for Japanese
beauty: もののあわれ, わび・さび, {幽玄|ゆうげん}, {間|ま}, {粋|いき}. N1 texts use them too, sometimes with
care, often as decoration. This lesson explains where each idea comes from and how it is used, and
ends with a critical essay of this course's own on how the words are overused. It links back to
noh and kabuki (10h2), the arts (21), haiku and waka (25h2) and 『{山月記|さんげつき}』 (30h1).

The facts below are checked (sources in the course notes); the interpretations are hedged, because
none of these words has one agreed definition.

## もののあわれ

もののあわれ (in older spelling もののあはれ) is the feeling of being moved by things: the deep,
quiet response to the beauty of nature and to the joys and sorrows of human life, coloured by the
sense that they pass. The phrase appears in Heian-period literature such as 『{源氏物語|げんじものがたり}』.

It became a theory through {本居宣長|もとおりのりなが} (1730–1801), the great scholar of **[[National Learning]]**
({国学|こくがく}) of the Edo period. Against readers who looked in literature for moral or Buddhist
lessons, he argued that the heart of 『{源氏物語|げんじものがたり}』 and of waka is もののあわれ: to know and
express how things move us. He developed the idea in 『{紫文要領|しぶんようりょう}』 (1763) and set it out
in his commentary on the Genji, completed in 1796 and published in 1799.

{桜|さくら}が{散|ち}るのを{見|み}て{胸|むね}が{痛|いた}むのは、もののあわれを{知|し}る{心|こころ}があるからだ。 — If seeing cherry blossoms fall hurts, it is because one has a heart that knows the pathos of things.

## わび and さび

Both words are written in kana in this course (one of their kanji is outside N1, and the other's
reading さび is best kept in kana here).

- **わび** is the beauty of poverty and simplicity accepted: a plain tea bowl, a small rough room,
  the quiet of having little. It is usually associated with the tea ceremony as shaped by
  {千利休|せんのりきゅう} in the sixteenth century, the ideal called わび{茶|ちゃ}.
- **さび** is the depth and richness felt in what is old, worn and still: moss on stone, weathered
  wood, a quiet that deepens with time. Dictionaries stress that it is not simply loneliness or
  age. It is usually associated with the haikai poetry of Bashō's school.

Together, わび・さび has become a single phrase in modern use, often vaguer than either word:
"rustic, aged, simple". Careful writers keep the two apart; advertising rarely does.

{簡素|かんそ}な{茶室|ちゃしつ}の{静寂|せいじゃく}に、わびの{心|こころ}を{感|かん}じた。 — In the stillness of the simple tea room, I felt the spirit of わび.

## {幽玄|ゆうげん}

{幽玄|ゆうげん} (幽: dim, hidden; 玄: dark, profound) is beauty that lies beyond what is shown: depth,
mystery, a meaning one feels but cannot state. Medieval poets used it as an ideal for waka, and in
noh it is linked above all with {世阿弥|ぜあみ} (its second kanji is outside N1; lesson 10h2), for whom it
was the grace a performer must reach. In modern prose it is used of noh, of misty landscapes and of
any art that suggests rather than says.

## {間|ま}

{間|ま} is the interval: the silence between notes, the pause in a speech, the empty space in a room
or on a scroll. The idea that the gap is part of the work, not its absence, runs through Japanese
music, theatre, architecture and conversation. {間|ま}が{悪|わる}い (badly timed, awkward) and
{間|ま}{抜|ぬ}け (a fool: someone who misses the timing) show how ordinary the word is; {間合|まあ}い is the
right distance or timing in martial arts and in storytelling. Lesson 29's texts on gaps and benches
are about {間|ま} in town planning.

## {粋|いき}

{粋|いき} (lesson 21) is the urban chic of Edo: stylish without showing off, worldly, a little
detached. Its opposite is {野暮|やぼ}, the boorish and tactless. The philosopher {九鬼周造|くきしゅうぞう}
(1888–1941; the second kanji of his surname is lesson 8's) analysed it in 『「いき」の{構造|こうぞう}』 ("the structure of
いき", 1930), which describes it as made of three things: allure, spirited pride and resignation
(this summary is the common one; the book itself is subtle).

## Reading: the trouble with "Japanese beauty"

An essay of this course's own (である style).

> 「{日本人|にほんじん}の{美意識|びいしき}」という{言葉|ことば}を{目|め}にする{機会|きかい}は{多|おお}い。{旅行|りょこう}{雑誌|ざっし}は{古|ふる}い{寺|てら}の{庭|にわ}を「わび・さびの{世界|せかい}」と{呼|よ}び、{家具|かぐ}の{広告|こうこく}は{白|しろ}い{壁|かべ}と{木|き}の{机|つくえ}を「{間|ま}の{美学|びがく}」と{説明|せつめい}する。{言葉|ことば}そのものに{罪|つみ}はない。だが、こうした{使|つか}い{方|かた}には{二|ふた}つの{危|あや}うさがある。
>
> {一|ひと}つは、{言葉|ことば}が{中身|なかみ}を{失|うしな}うことだ。わびもさびも、{本来|ほんらい}は{特定|とくてい}の{時代|じだい}と{場|ば}で、{具体的|ぐたいてき}な{物|もの}や{行|おこな}いを{通|とお}して{磨|みが}かれてきた{考|かんが}えである。それを「{素朴|そぼく}で{古|ふる}びたもの」{一般|いっぱん}に{当|あ}てはめれば、{便利|べんり}な{形容詞|けいようし}にはなっても、{何|なに}かを{見|み}る{目|め}は{育|そだ}たない。
>
> もう{一|ひと}つは、{美意識|びいしき}を{国民|こくみん}の{性質|せいしつ}であるかのように{語|かた}ることだ。もののあわれを{知|し}る{心|こころ}は、{日本人|にほんじん}{特有|とくゆう}のものだろうか。{散|ち}る{花|はな}に{胸|むね}を{痛|いた}める{人|ひと}は、どの{国|くに}にもいるはずである。{違|ちが}いがあるとすれば、それは{心|こころ}そのものではなく、その{心|こころ}を{表|あらわ}す{言葉|ことば}と{形|かたち}の{歴史|れきし}であろう。{本居宣長|もとおりのりなが}が{論|ろん}じたのも、{日本人|にほんじん}の{血|ち}ではなく、{物語|ものがたり}と{歌|うた}という{言葉|ことば}の{営|いとな}みであった。
>
> では、これらの{言葉|ことば}を{使|つか}うべきではないのか。そうではない。{使|つか}うなら、{具体|ぐたい}に{戻|もど}ればよいのである。どの{茶|ちゃ}わんの、どの{欠|か}けた{縁|ふち}に、なぜ{心|こころ}が{動|うご}いたのか。{幽玄|ゆうげん}を{語|かた}るなら、{能|のう}の{舞台|ぶたい}のどの{一瞬|いっしゅん}にそれを{感|かん}じたのか。{言葉|ことば}は、{見|み}たものを{確|たし}かめるための{道具|どうぐ}であって、{見|み}ることの{代|か}わりではない。{美|び}を{語|かた}る{言葉|ことば}が{豊|ゆた}かであるほど、{私|わたし}たちは{自分|じぶん}の{目|め}で{見|み}ることを{忘|わす}れてはならないのだ。

{危|あや}うさ = danger, precariousness; {古|ふる}びる = to grow old and worn; {特有|とくゆう} = peculiar to;
{営|いとな}み = workings, activity; {縁|ふち} = rim, edge.

1. What two dangers does the writer see in the popular use of these words?
2. Where, according to the writer, does any difference between cultures lie?
3. What does the writer recommend instead of giving up the words?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. That the words lose their content (turning into convenient adjectives for anything old and
   simple), and that a sense of beauty is talked about as if it were a national character.
2. Not in the heart itself (people everywhere are moved by falling blossoms) but in the history of
   the words and forms that express it; Norinaga, too, wrote about literature, not about "Japanese
   blood".
3. Going back to the concrete: saying which bowl, which chipped rim, which moment on the noh stage
   moved you. Words should confirm what you saw, not replace seeing.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Translation</summary>

We often come across the phrase "the Japanese sense of beauty". Travel magazines call the gardens
of old temples "the world of わび・さび", and furniture advertisements explain white walls and wooden
desks as "the aesthetics of {間|ま}". The words themselves are not to blame. But such uses carry two
dangers.

One is that the words lose their content. わび and さび were, by rights, ideas refined in
particular periods and places, through concrete objects and practices. Apply them to "anything
simple and old" in general, and they may become handy adjectives, but they won't train anyone's eye.

The other is talking about a sense of beauty as if it were a national trait. Is the heart that knows
the pathos of things peculiar to the Japanese? There must be people in every country whose hearts
ache at falling blossoms. If there is a difference, it lies surely not in the heart itself but in
the history of the words and forms that express it. What Motoori Norinaga discussed was not Japanese
blood, either, but the workings of language in tales and poems.

Then should we not use these words? Not so. If we use them, we need only return to the concrete.
Which tea bowl, which chipped rim, moved us, and why? If we speak of {幽玄|ゆうげん}, at which moment on the
noh stage did we feel it? Words are tools for confirming what we have seen, not a substitute for
seeing. The richer our words for beauty, the more we must not forget to look with our own eyes.

</details>

## Words for aesthetics

| Idea | Words |
|---|---|
| Feeling and atmosphere | もののあわれ, {情趣|じょうしゅ}, {風流|ふうりゅう}, {無常観|むじょうかん} |
| Simplicity and age | わび, さび, {簡素|かんそ}, {閑寂|かんじゃく}, {枯淡|こたん}, {静寂|せいじゃく} |
| Depth | {幽玄|ゆうげん}, {深遠|しんえん}, {奥|おく}ゆかしい |
| Timing and style | {間|ま}, {間合|まあ}い, {粋|いき}, {野暮|やぼ}, {通|つう} |
| Talking about it | {美意識|びいしき}, {美学|びがく}, {国学|こくがく} |

## Key points

- もののあわれ: being moved by things in their passing; made a theory by {本居宣長|もとおりのりなが}
  (1730–1801) in his writings on the Genji and waka.
- わび (simplicity accepted; the tea ceremony) and さび (depth in what is old and still; Bashō's school): two
  ideas, often merged as わび・さび.
- {幽玄|ゆうげん}: beauty beyond what is shown (waka, noh). {間|ま}: the meaningful interval.
- {粋|いき} and {野暮|やぼ}; {九鬼周造|くきしゅうぞう}'s 『「いき」の{構造|こうぞう}』 (1930).
- Write about these ideas concretely: what you saw, where, and why it moved you.

questions.stem: {電車|でんしゃ}のドアが{開|ひら}く（　）、{乗客|じょうきゃく}がホームに{飛|と}び{出|だ}した。
questions.explanation: {開|ひら}くが{早|はや}いか: "the instant the doors opened", a quick action that followed at once, as a past fact. とたん needs the た form ({開|ひら}いたとたん), ばかりに gives a cause of something bad ("only because"), and ついでに is "while you're at it", which makes no sense for a crowd rushing out.

questions.stem: {母|はは}は{手紙|てがみ}を{読|よ}む（　）、{黙|だま}って{泣|な}き{出|だ}した。 (As soon as my mother read the letter, she silently burst into tears.)
questions.explanation: {読|よ}むなり: one person (the mother) does A and at once does something unexpected, B, in the past: exactly what なり is for. そばから is for actions that keep being undone, うちに is "while (still)", and {以上|いじょう} is "since, now that", which needs a conclusion such as a duty after it.

questions.stem: いくら{掃除|そうじ}しても、{掃除|そうじ}する（　）{子供|こども}たちが{散|ち}らかしてしまう。
questions.explanation: {掃除|そうじ}するそばから: "no sooner have I cleaned than they make a mess", something that keeps happening and undoes A. いくら〜ても shows it's repeated. や{否|いな}や, なり and が{早|はや}いか describe a single past event, and なり would also need the same subject for both actions (here the speaker cleans and the children make the mess).

questions.stem: Which sentence is natural?
choices: {私|わたし}が{家|いえ}に{帰|かえ}るなり、{犬|いぬ}がほえた。
{一度|いちど}{説明|せつめい}したそばから、{彼|かれ}は{試験|しけん}に{合格|ごうかく}した。
{彼|かれ}は{席|せき}に{着|つ}くなり、{弁当|べんとう}を{食|た}べ{始|はじ}めた。
{駅|えき}に{着|つ}くが{早|はや}いか、{電話|でんわ}してください。
questions.explanation: {彼|かれ}は{席|せき}に{着|つ}くなり、{弁当|べんとう}を{食|た}べ{始|はじ}めた: one person, a past action done at once, slightly surprising: natural なり. が{早|はや}いか can't introduce a request (〜てください); なり needs the same subject for A and B ({私|わたし} and {犬|いぬ} differ); and そばから is for something repeatedly undone, not for a single happy result.

questions.stem: {日本|にほん}は（　）{諸国|しょこく}との{関係|かんけい}を{大切|たいせつ}にしてきた。
questions.explanation: {近隣|きんりん}{諸国|しょこく} = the neighbouring countries: {近隣|きんりん} is the formal word for the surrounding area, used before nouns such as {諸国|しょこく} and {住民|じゅうみん}. {隣人|りんじん} is a person next door, {両隣|りょうどなり} the neighbours on both sides, {隣家|りんか} the house next door: none of them combines with {諸国|しょこく}.

questions.stem: 「［{近頃|ちかごろ}］は、{手紙|てがみ}を{書|か}く{人|ひと}がめっきり{減|へ}った。」の［ ］に{意味|いみ}が{最|もっと}も{近|ちか}いものはどれか。
questions.explanation: {近頃|ちかごろ} means "these days, lately", close to N5's {最近|さいきん} (with a hint of comment on the times). いずれ is "some day", {一時|いちじ} "for a while (once)", and {昔|むかし} "long ago", the opposite.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses ［{手頃|てごろ}］ correctly?
choices: {彼|かれ}は{駅|えき}まで{手頃|てごろ}に{走|はし}っていった。
{今日|きょう}の{試験|しけん}は{手頃|てごろ}に{難|むずか}しかった。
{週末|しゅうまつ}は{手頃|てごろ}の{天気|てんき}が{続|つづ}くでしょう。
この{店|みせ}では、{手頃|てごろ}な{値段|ねだん}でおいしい{料理|りょうり}が{食|た}べられる。

questions.stem: {訪問先|ほうもんさき}でお{茶|ちゃ}を{出|だ}されて、「どうぞお（　）。」と{言|い}った。 (The guest is declining politely.)
questions.explanation: どうぞお{構|かま}いなく: "please don't go to any trouble", the guest's polite answer to a host's offer. お{世話様|せわさま} thanks someone for help, お{待|ま}ちどおさま apologizes for keeping someone waiting, and お{邪魔|じゃま}しました is said on leaving.

questions.stem: {震災|しんさい}から{十年|じゅうねん}、{町|まち}の復興はまだ{続|つづ}いている。
questions.explanation: 復興 is ふっこう: 復 (ふく) becomes ふっ before a k-sound, and 興 is コウ here, as in {興奮|こうふん} and {興行|こうぎょう}. 興 is キョウ in {興味|きょうみ} and {余興|よきょう}, but not in this word.

questions.stem: 叔父は{東京|とうきょう}で{小|ちい}さな{店|みせ}をやっている。
questions.explanation: 叔父 is a special reading, おじ (uncle: a parent's younger brother). The kanji aren't read one by one (×しゅくぶ; the rare formal reading しゅくふ isn't used in a sentence like this). おじい would be part of おじいさん (grandfather), and おば is 叔母 (aunt).

questions.stem: {彼|かれ}は{社長|しゃちょう}の{令|れい}（　）と{結婚|けっこん}した。 Which kanji goes in the blank?
questions.explanation: {令嬢|れいじょう}, someone else's daughter, is written with 嬢, which has the woman radical 女. 譲 (yield, with 言), 壌 (soil, with 土) and 醸 (brew, with 酉) share its right side and its sound ジョウ, so the left side is the clue.

questions.stem: Listen. What did the speaker's father do?

audio.text: ちちはいえにかえるなり、なにもいわずにへやにこもってしまった。

choices: He shut himself in his room without a word the moment he got home.
He came home and told the family something important.
He stayed in his room all day and didn't go out.
He came home late and went straight to sleep.

questions.stem: Listen. Which is the best reply?

audio.text: おいそがしいところ、きょうしゅくですが、しりょうをおおくりいただけますか。

choices: いえいえ、どうぞお{構|かま}いなく。
お{邪魔|じゃま}しました。
それは{恐縮|きょうしゅく}でしたね。

questions.stem: Listen. What is the speaker complaining about?

audio.text: せっかくかたづけたのに、かたづけるそばからこどもがちらかすんだから、いやになっちゃう。

choices: Every time the speaker tidies up, the children make a mess again straight away.
The children never help with the tidying.
The children made a mess once while the speaker was out.
The speaker has no time to tidy up.
questions.explanation: {片付|かたづ}けるそばから{子供|こども}が{散|ち}らかす: "no sooner do I tidy up than the children mess it up again", over and over. そばから is about a repeated pattern, not a single event, and the speaker does the tidying (せっかく{片付|かたづ}けた).

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: The moment the bell rang, the pupils rushed out of the classroom.
questions.explanation: ベルが{鳴|な}るが{早|はや}いか、{生徒|せいと}たちは{教室|きょうしつ}を{飛|と}び{出|だ}した. が{早|はや}いか follows the dictionary form {鳴|な}る; the subject of B and the object can come in either order, and the topic {生徒|せいと}たちは can also come first. そばから would describe something that keeps undoing A, which doesn't fit a single rush.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: As soon as he saw my face, he started laughing.
questions.explanation: {彼|かれ}は{私|わたし}の{顔|かお}を{見|み}るなり{笑|わら}い{出|だ}した. なり joins the dictionary form ({見|み}る, not {見|み}た), and one person, {彼|かれ}, does both actions. The topic {彼|かれ}は can also come after the なり clause.

Read the news item. What happened?

{昨夜|さくや}から{降|ふ}り{続|つづ}いた{大雪|おおゆき}の{影響|えいきょう}で、{県内|けんない}の{高速道路|こうそくどうろ}では、{今朝|けさ}までに{約|やく}{三百台|さんびゃくだい}の{車|くるま}が{立|た}ち{往生|おうじょう}した。{峠|とうげ}の{付近|ふきん}で{大型|おおがた}トラックが{動|うご}けなくなったのがきっかけで、{後|うし}ろの{車|くるま}も{次々|つぎつぎ}と{止|と}まったという。{県|けん}は{自衛隊|じえいたい}に{災害派遣|さいがいはけん}を{要請|ようせい}し、{車内|しゃない}に{残|のこ}された{人々|ひとびと}に{水|みず}や{毛布|もうふ}を{配|くば}った。{車内|しゃない}で{一晩|ひとばん}を{過|す}ごした{男性|だんせい}は「ガソリンが{減|へ}っていくのが{不安|ふあん}で、{夜明|よあ}けが{待|ま}ち{遠|どお}しかった」と{話|はな}した。{午前|ごぜん}{十時|じゅうじ}{現在|げんざい}、{通行止|つうこうど}めはまだ{解除|かいじょ}されていない。{道路|どうろ}を{管理|かんり}する{会社|かいしゃ}は「{予報|よほう}を{受|う}けて{早|はや}めに{通行止|つうこうど}めにすべきだった」と{述|の}べ、{対応|たいおう}の{遅|おく}れを{認|みと}めた。{気象台|きしょうだい}によると、{雪|ゆき}は{明日|あした}の{朝|あさ}にかけて{降|ふ}り{続|つづ}く{見込|みこ}みで、{再|ふたた}び{立|た}ち{往生|おうじょう}が{起|お}きるおそれもあるという。{県|けん}は、{不要不急|ふようふきゅう}の{外出|がいしゅつ}を{控|ひか}えるよう{呼|よ}びかけている。
choices: A lorry crashed and the road was closed for repairs.
The road company blamed the weather forecast for the delay.
The motorway was closed early, so no cars were stuck.
About 300 vehicles were stranded on the motorway after heavy snow.
questions.explanation: {約|やく}{三百台|さんびゃくだい}の{車|くるま}が{立|た}ち{往生|おうじょう}した: about 300 vehicles were stranded. It started when a lorry couldn't move near the pass (not a crash); the road wasn't closed early enough, and the company admitted it should have closed it sooner after the forecast, accepting the delay was its own. {峠|とうげ} (pass) is lesson 10's word; {災害派遣|さいがいはけん} = disaster deployment; {控|ひか}える = to refrain from (lesson 15's word).

questions.stem: Fill in the blank in hiragana: {新|あたら}しい{単語|たんご}を{覚|おぼ}えた___、{忘|わす}れてしまって、なかなか{増|ふ}えない。 (No sooner have I learned new words than I forget them, so my vocabulary hardly grows.)
questions.explanation: {覚|おぼ}えたそばから{忘|わす}れる: "forget as soon as I've learned", again and again. そばから joins the dictionary or た form and describes something that keeps undoing the first action. {覚|おぼ}えたとたん (the moment I learn them) is also natural here and is accepted; なり needs the dictionary form and a surprising action rather than a repeated loss.

questions.stem: {新作|しんさく}の{舞台|ぶたい}は、{来月|らいげつ}の{東京|とうきょう}{公演|こうえん}（　）、{全国|ぜんこく}{二十|にじゅう}{都市|とし}を{回|まわ}る。
questions.explanation: を{皮切|かわき}りに: the Tokyo performance is the first of a series that then spreads to twenty cities. を{境|さかい}に would need a change (before vs after), を{限|かぎ}りに would make Tokyo the last time something happens, and をもって marks a formal end or start date, not the first of a series.

questions.stem: 【お{知|し}らせ】{当店|とうてん}は、{三月|さんがつ}{三十一日|さんじゅういちにち}（　）{閉店|へいてん}いたします。{長年|ながねん}のご{愛顧|あいこ}、{誠|まこと}にありがとうございました。
questions.explanation: をもって marks the formal date on which something ends: {三月|さんがつ}{三十一日|さんじゅういちにち}をもって{閉店|へいてん} いたします, the language of notices. を{経|へ}て needs a stage passed through, を{皮切|かわき}りに a series after it, and を{境|さかい}に a change before and after, not the end itself.

questions.stem: {健康|けんこう}{診断|しんだん}の{結果|けっか}を{見|み}て、{今日|きょう}（　）たばこはやめると{決|き}めた。
questions.explanation: {今日|きょう}を{限|かぎ}りに: "with today as the last time", a personal decision to stop for good. を{皮切|かわき}りに would make today the first of a series, を{経|へ}て needs a stage passed through, and なくして (without) makes no sense after a day.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses ［を{境|さかい}に］ correctly?
choices: {雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}る{境|さかい}に、{傘|かさ}を{買|か}った。
{朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん}を{境|さかい}に、{駅|えき}まで{歩|ある}いた。
{入社|にゅうしゃ}したのを{境|さかい}に、{生活|せいかつ}のリズムががらりと{変|か}わった。
{週末|しゅうまつ}を{境|さかい}に、{旅行|りょこう}に{行|い}こう。
questions.explanation: を{境|さかい}に needs a turning point and a change after it: {入社|にゅうしゃ}したのを{境|さかい}に、{生活|せいかつ}のリズムが がらりと{変|か}わった (a verb clause takes の). Breakfast followed by a walk is just a sequence; {降|ふ}る{境|さかい}に lacks のを; and を{境|さかい}に reports a change that happened, not a plan (〜よう).

questions.stem: {法案|ほうあん}は、{委員会|いいんかい}での{審議|しんぎ}（　）、{本会議|ほんかいぎ}で{可決|かけつ}された。
questions.explanation: を{経|へ}て: "after going through" a stage, here the committee's deliberation, before the vote. を{限|かぎ}りに would end something for good, を{皮切|かわき}りに would start a series, and をもって would make the deliberation a formal date or a means ("by means of"), which doesn't fit "passed after".

questions.stem: {暖|あたた}かい{雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}った{後|あと}、{枯|か}れ{木|き}のように{見|み}えた{庭|にわ}の{木々|きぎ}が、{一斉|いっせい}に（　）{始|はじ}めた。
questions.explanation: {芽吹|めぶ}く: trees putting out new buds, the natural verb for bare-looking trees in spring. {巣立|すだ}つ (leave the nest) and {羽|は}ばたく (flap one's wings) are for birds, and {実|みの}る (bear fruit) comes at the end of the season, not straight after looking dead.

questions.stem: 「この{料理|りょうり}は［{季節感|きせつかん}］を{大切|たいせつ}にしている。」の［ ］に{意味|いみ}が{最|もっと}も{近|ちか}いものはどれか。
choices: {季節|きせつ}{外|はず}れの{材料|ざいりょう}
{季節|きせつ}ごとの{値段|ねだん}
{季節|きせつ}を{感|かん}じさせること
{季節|きせつ}に{関係|かんけい}なく{作|つく}れること
questions.explanation: {季節感|きせつかん} is "a sense of the season": a dish that values it makes you feel the time of year. The other choices describe the opposite (any season), out-of-season ingredients, or prices.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses ［{節目|ふしめ}］ correctly?
choices: {彼|かれ}の{話|はなし}には{節目|ふしめ}がない。
{節目|ふしめ}を{守|まも}ってお{酒|さけ}を{楽|たの}しもう。
{歌|うた}の{節目|ふしめ}を{覚|おぼ}えて{歌|うた}った。
{創立|そうりつ}{五十周年|ごじゅっしゅうねん}という{節目|ふしめ}の{年|とし}に、{記念|きねん}{式典|しきてん}が{開|ひら}かれた。
questions.explanation: {節目|ふしめ} is a milestone, a turning point worth marking: {五十周年|ごじゅっしゅうねん}という{節目|ふしめ}の{年|とし}. The tune of a song is its {節|ふし} (or メロディー), a story without a thread lacks {筋|すじ} (lesson 5), and drinking "in moderation" is {節度|せつど}を{守|まも}って.

questions.stem: {今朝|けさ}は{冷|ひ}え{込|こ}んで、{畑|はたけ}に霜が{降|お}りた。
questions.explanation: 霜 is しも (frost): {霜|しも}が{降|お}りる. つゆ is 露 (dew), きり is 霧 (fog) and あられ is hail; all three have the rain radical 雨 too, so read the part below it.

questions.stem: {公園|こうえん}の芝生の{上|うえ}で、{家族|かぞく}がお{弁当|べんとう}を{広|ひろ}げている。
questions.explanation: 芝生 is a special reading, しばふ (a lawn): 生 is read ふ only in this word. The other readings take 生 piece by piece (せい, う, なま) and don't exist.

questions.stem: {窓|まど}ガラスに{結|けつ}（　）がついて、{外|そと}が{見|み}えない。 Which kanji goes in the blank?
questions.explanation: {結露|けつろ}, condensation on cold glass, is written with 露 (dew). 霧 (fog), 霜 (frost) and 雷 (thunder) share the rain radical 雨, so read the part below it; {結露|けつろ} is the everyday word here.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker say?

audio.text: きょうをかぎりに、よふかしはやめることにしたよ。あしたからはやくねる。

choices: The speaker will stay up late only today.
The speaker stayed up late for the last time yesterday.
From today on, the speaker will stop staying up late.
The speaker can't stop staying up late.
questions.explanation: {今日|きょう}を{限|かぎ}りに{夜更|よふ}かしはやめる: "today is the last time; I'm giving up late nights". The second sentence confirms it: from tomorrow, early to bed.

questions.stem: Listen to the weather report. What happened?

audio.text: きのうのあめをさかいに、きせつふうがふきはじめ、いっきにふゆらしいさむさとなりました。

choices: It rained and was warm all day yesterday.
It will turn cold after tomorrow's rain.
Yesterday's rain stopped the seasonal wind.
After yesterday's rain, the seasonal wind began and it turned wintry all at once.
questions.explanation: {昨日|きのう}の{雨|あめ}を{境|さかい}に、{季節風|きせつふう}が{吹|ふ}き{始|はじ}め、{一気|いっき}に{冬|ふゆ}らしい{寒|さむ}さとなりました: the rain was the turning point; after it, the seasonal wind blew and it became wintry at once.

questions.stem: Listen. Which is the best reply?

audio.text: これをもちまして、ほんじつのかいをしゅうりょういたします。

choices: お{疲|つか}れさまでした。
questions.explanation: これをもちまして…{終了|しゅうりょう}いたします closes a meeting or event: "with this, we bring today's meeting to an end". The natural response is お{疲|つか}れさまでした. The others belong to leaving home, eating and letting someone go first.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: Starting with Kyushu, the cherry blossom front moves gradually north.
questions.explanation: {桜前線|さくらぜんせん}は{九州|きゅうしゅう}を{皮切|かわき}りに{少|すこ}しずつ{北|きた}へ{進|すす}んでいく. A series that spreads after its first point takes を{皮切|かわき}りに; を{境|さかい}に would need a change before and after. The topic and the adverb can move.

questions.stem: Build the sentence in Japanese.
questions.prompt: This flight goes to Sydney via Seoul.
questions.explanation: この{便|びん}は、ソウルを{経|へ}てシドニーへ{向|む}かう. を{経|へ}て gives the route ("via"); {経|へ}て is read へて. を{限|かぎ}りに would make Seoul a last time, which means nothing here.

questions.stem:
Read the column. What is the writer's main point?

「{小春日和|こはるびより}」という{言葉|ことば}を、{春|はる}の{暖|あたた}かい{日|ひ}のことだと{思|おも}っている{人|ひと}は{少|すく}なくない。{実際|じっさい}には、{晩秋|ばんしゅう}から{初冬|しょとう}にかけての、{穏|おだ}やかに{晴|は}れた{暖|あたた}かい{日|ひ}を{指|さ}す。「{小春|こはる}」は{旧暦|きゅうれき}の{十月|じゅうがつ}の{別名|べつめい}なのだ。{同|おな}じように、「{花冷|はなび}え」は{桜|さくら}の{咲|さ}く{頃|ころ}の{一時的|いちじてき}な{冷|ひ}え{込|こ}みを、「{春一番|はるいちばん}」は{立春|りっしゅん}を{過|す}ぎて{最初|さいしょ}に{吹|ふ}く{強|つよ}い{南風|みなみかぜ}を{言|い}う。こうした{言葉|ことば}は、{手紙|てがみ}の{書|か}き{出|だ}しや{天気予報|てんきよほう}で{今|いま}も{使|つか}われている。{気象台|きしょうだい}が「{春一番|はるいちばん}が{吹|ふ}いた」と{発表|はっぴょう}すると、ニュースでも{大|おお}きく{取|と}り{上|あ}げられる。{恥|は}ずかしながら、{私|わたし}も{長|なが}い{間|あいだ}、{小春日和|こはるびより}を{春|はる}の{言葉|ことば}だと{思|おも}い{込|こ}んでいた{一人|ひとり}である。{季節|きせつ}の{言葉|ことば}は、{自然|しぜん}の{小|ちい}さな{変化|へんか}に{気|き}づくための{手|て}がかりでもある。{意味|いみ}を{取|と}り{違|ちが}えたままでは、せっかくの{手|て}がかりも{役|やく}に{立|た}たない。{言葉|ことば}の{本来|ほんらい}の{意味|いみ}を{知|し}ってこそ、その{言葉|ことば}が{伝|つた}えてきた{季節|きせつ}も{見|み}えてくるのではないだろうか。
choices: The old calendar should be brought back.
Knowing what seasonal words really mean helps you notice the seasons.
Spring has become warmer than it used to be.
Seasonal words are no longer used in weather forecasts.
questions.explanation: The writer corrects a common mistake about {小春日和|こはるびより} and ends: only by knowing a word's original meaning ({本来|ほんらい}の{意味|いみ}を{知|し}ってこそ) can you see the season it has carried. The words are still used in forecasts ({今|いま}も{使|つか}われている); nothing is said about bringing back the old calendar or about warmer springs. {晩秋|ばんしゅう} = late autumn; {旧暦|きゅうれき} = the old lunar calendar; {立春|りっしゅん} = the first day of spring in the old calendar.

questions.stem:
Read the passage and choose what goes in the blank.
