Read the two opinions. What do A and B agree on?

A　お{礼|れい}の{気持|きも}ちを{伝|つた}えるなら、やはり{手書|てが}きの{手紙|てがみ}がいちばんだ。{字|じ}が{上手|じょうず}かどうかは{問題|もんだい}ではない。{相手|あいて}のことを{思|おも}いながら{一字|いちじ}ずつ{書|か}く{時間|じかん}そのものが、{感謝|かんしゃ}の{表|あらわ}れなのである。{手間|てま}を{惜|お}しまないことこそが、{相手|あいて}を{大切|たいせつ}にしている{証|あかし}になる。{受|う}け{取|と}った{側|がわ}も、{封|ふう}を{開|ひら}く{瞬間|しゅんかん}に{特別|とくべつ}なものを{感|かん}じるはずだ。メールでは、どうしても{用件|ようけん}を{伝|つた}えるだけになりやすい。

B　お{礼|れい}は、{何|なに}よりも{早|はや}く{伝|つた}えることが{大切|たいせつ}だ。{手紙|てがみ}を{書|か}こうと{思|おも}っているうちに{一週間|いっしゅうかん}が{過|す}ぎてしまっては、かえって{失礼|しつれい}になりかねない。{感謝|かんしゃ}の{気持|きも}ちがこもっていれば、メールでも{十分|じゅうぶん}{伝|つた}わる。{最近|さいきん}は、{手書|てが}きのカードを{写真|しゃしん}に{撮|と}ってメールに{添|そ}える{人|ひと}もいるが、それも{一|ひと}つの{工夫|くふう}だろう。もちろん、{目上|めうえ}の{方|かた}や{改|あらた}まった{場面|ばめん}では、{手紙|てがみ}がふさわしいこともあるだろう。{大切|たいせつ}なのは{手段|しゅだん}ではなく、{相手|あいて}を{思|おも}う{心|こころ}である。
choices: That thanks should be sent as quickly as possible.
That what really conveys thanks is thinking of the other person.
That email is unsuitable for thanking anyone.
That handwritten letters should be sent only to superiors.
questions.explanation: A says the time spent writing while thinking of the other person ({相手|あいて}のことを{思|おも}いながら) is the gratitude; B says what matters is the heart that thinks of the other person ({相手|あいて}を{思|おも}う{心|こころ}). Speed is only B's point; A doesn't rule email out entirely, and B only says letters suit some occasions.

questions.stem:
Read the rules. A group of 12 residents of the city wants to use Room A on a Saturday from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. How much will it cost?

{公民館|こうみんかん}{会議室|かいぎしつ}の{使用料|しようりょう}

・{使用料|しようりょう}は{午前|ごぜん}（{九時|くじ}〜{十二時|じゅうにじ}）、{午後|ごご}（{一時|いちじ}〜{五時|ごじ}）、{夜間|やかん}（{六時|ろくじ}〜{九時|くじ}）の{区分|くぶん}ごとに{定|さだ}めます。

・A{室|しつ}（{定員|ていいん}{二十名|にじゅうめい}）：{午前|ごぜん}{千二百円|せんにひゃくえん}、{午後|ごご}{千六百円|せんろっぴゃくえん}、{夜間|やかん}{千八百円|せんはっぴゃくえん}

・B{室|しつ}（{定員|ていいん}{五十名|ごじゅうめい}）：{各区分|かくくぶん}とも、A{室|しつ}の{二倍|にばい}とします。

・{土曜|どよう}・{日曜|にちよう}{及|およ}び{祝日|しゅくじつ}は、{上記|じょうき}の{料金|りょうきん}に{三割|さんわり}を{加算|かさん}します。

・{利用者|りようしゃ}の{半数|はんすう}{以上|いじょう}が{市外|しがい}{在住|ざいじゅう}の{団体|だんたい}は、{上記|じょうき}{料金|りょうきん}の{二倍|にばい}となります。

・{冷暖房|れいだんぼう}の{使用|しよう}は、{区分|くぶん}ごとに{三百円|さんびゃくえん}を{別途|べっと}いただきます。

・{予約|よやく}は{使用日|しようび}の{三か月前|さんかげつまえ}から{受|う}け{付|つ}けます。{営利|えいり}を{目的|もくてき}とする{使用|しよう}はお{断|ことわ}りします。{使用料|しようりょう}は、{予約|よやく}の{際|さい}に{窓口|まどぐち}でお{支払|しはら}いください。

・{使用後|しようご}は{机|つくえ}と{椅子|いす}を{元|もと}の{位置|いち}に{戻|もど}し、{窓|まど}を{閉|し}めてからお{帰|かえ}りください。
questions.explanation: The afternoon slot (1–5 p.m.) for Room A is 1,600 yen; Saturdays add 30 per cent: 1,600 × 1.3 = 2,080 yen. They are city residents, so the doubling doesn't apply. Heating or cooling would add 300 yen (2,380), but the question doesn't say they use it, and 1,900 adds the 300 without the weekend charge.

questions.stem:
Read the passage. What is the writer's main claim?

「{最近|さいきん}の{若者|わかもの}は{手紙|てがみ}を{書|か}かない」と{嘆|なげ}く{声|こえ}をよく{聞|き}く。{確|たし}かに{年賀状|ねんがじょう}を{出|だ}す{人|ひと}は{減|へ}っているし、{改|あらた}まった{手紙|てがみ}の{書|か}き{方|かた}を{知|し}らない{学生|がくせい}も{多|おお}い。{拝啓|はいけい}と{敬具|けいぐ}の{使|つか}い{方|かた}を{知|し}らずに{社会|しゃかい}に{出|で}て、{困|こま}る{人|ひと}もいるだろう。

しかし、{彼|かれ}らが{文章|ぶんしょう}を{書|か}かなくなったわけではない。むしろ、{一日|いちにち}に{書|か}く{文字|もじ}の{量|りょう}は、{昔|むかし}の{若者|わかもの}よりはるかに{多|おお}いかもしれない。{友人|ゆうじん}とのメッセージ、{日々|ひび}の{記録|きろく}、{趣味|しゅみ}の{感想|かんそう}。{形式|けいしき}が{変|か}わっただけで、{言葉|ことば}で{気持|きも}ちを{伝|つた}えたいという{欲求|よっきゅう}は{少|すこ}しも{衰|おとろ}えていないのである。

{問題|もんだい}があるとすれば、それは{書|か}く{量|りょう}ではなく、{相手|あいて}や{場面|ばめん}に{応|おう}じて{書|か}き{分|わ}ける{経験|けいけん}の{少|すく}なさだろう。{親|した}しい{友人|ゆうじん}への{言葉|ことば}と、{目上|めうえ}の{人|ひと}への{言葉|ことば}は{違|ちが}う。{若者|わかもの}を{嘆|なげ}く{前|まえ}に、{大人|おとな}がその{違|ちが}いを{見|み}せる{機会|きかい}を{作|つく}るべきではないか。
choices: Young people today write less than young people did in the past.
Young people should send more New Year cards.
The problem is young people's lack of experience in adapting writing to the reader, and adults should give them chances to learn.
Formal letters are no longer necessary in society.
questions.explanation: The writer grants the complaint (paragraph 1), then turns (しかし): young people write a great deal (むしろ…{多|おお}いかもしれない). The claim is in paragraph 3: the problem is a lack of experience in writing differently for different readers, and adults should create chances ({機会|きかい}を{作|つく}るべきではないか). The writer never says formal letters are unnecessary.

questions.stem:
Read the passage and choose the best expression for the blank.

{日本|にほん}の{手紙|てがみ}には、{季節|きせつ}のあいさつから{書|か}き{始|はじ}める{習慣|しゅうかん}がある。「{寒|さむ}さ{厳|きび}しき{折|おり}」「{新緑|しんりょく}の{候|こう}」といった{言葉|ことば}は、{手紙|てがみ}の{書|か}き{方|かた}の{本|ほん}に{例|れい}が{並|なら}んでおり、{一見|いっけん}{形式的|けいしきてき}で{中身|なかみ}のないものに{見|み}える。{実際|じっさい}、{何|なに}も{考|かんが}えずに{例文|れいぶん}を{書|か}き{写|うつ}すだけなら、そう{言|い}われても{仕方|しかた}がないだろう。（　）、{季節|きせつ}のあいさつには、{遠|とお}くにいる{相手|あいて}と{同|おな}じ{季節|きせつ}を{生|い}きていることを{確|たし}かめ{合|あ}う{働|はたら}きがある。{季節|きせつ}の{言葉|ことば}を{選|えら}ぶとき、{書|か}き{手|て}は{自然|しぜん}と、{相手|あいて}の{暮|く}らす{土地|とち}の{空|そら}や{風|かぜ}を{思|おも}い{浮|う}かべるだろう。{窓|まど}の{外|そと}の{景色|けしき}を{一言|ひとこと}{添|そ}えるだけで、{型|かた}どおりの{言葉|ことば}は{自分|じぶん}の{言葉|ことば}に{変|か}わる。メールの{時代|じだい}になってもこの{習慣|しゅうかん}が{消|き}えないのは、そのためではないか。{形式|けいしき}とは、{心|こころ}を{入|い}れるための{器|うつわ}なのかもしれない。{大切|たいせつ}なのは{型|かた}を{捨|す}てることではなく、そこに{何|なに}を{盛|も}るかである。
questions.explanation: The writer has just granted that copied phrases deserve the criticism; the next sentence defends seasonal greetings. とはいえ ("that said, even so") introduces such a counterpoint after a concession. したがって (therefore) and つまり (that is) would continue the criticism; なぜなら (because) would need a reason ending in から.

questions.stem: Listen. What will the listener do?

audio.text: すみません、さきほどいただいたしりょうですが、さいしょのページだけさしかえて、もういちどおくっていただけますか。ほかのページはそのままでけっこうです。

choices: Replace the first page and send the materials again.
Wait for new materials from the speaker.
questions.explanation: {最初|さいしょ}のページだけ{差|さ}し{替|か}えて、もう{一度|いちど}{送|おく}っていただけますか: replace only the first page and send it again; the other pages can stay as they are ({他|ほか}のページはそのままで{結構|けっこう}です).

questions.stem: Listen and choose the best reply.

audio.text: せっかくのおさそいですが、そのひはあいにく、ほかのよていがありまして。

choices: じゃあ、{何時|なんじ}に{来|き}られますか。
{予定|よてい}がないなら、ぜひ{来|き}てください。
お{誘|さそ}いくださって、ありがとうございます。
そうですか。では、またの{機会|きかい}にぜひ。
questions.explanation: せっかくのお{誘|さそ}いですが、あいにく… is a polite refusal that never says no. The natural reply accepts it and leaves the door open (またの{機会|きかい}に). Asking what time they'll come ignores the refusal; the second reply mishears it; thanking for the invitation is what the person invited would say.

questions.stem: Listen and choose the best reply.

audio.text: きょうのかいぎしつ、れいぼうがちょっときつくない？

choices: そうだね。{温度|おんど}を{少|すこ}し{上|あ}げようか。
うん、もっと{下|さ}げよう。
{会議|かいぎ}は{三時|さんじ}からだよ。
{暖房|だんぼう}は{冬|ふゆ}しか{使|つか}わないよ。
questions.explanation: {冷房|れいぼう}がきつい means the air conditioning is too strong (too cold). Raising the temperature answers it; lowering it would make it worse; the time of the meeting and the heating are beside the point.

questions.stem: Listen. Why were the benches removed?

audio.text: えきまえのベンチがなくなったのは、よるにさわぐひとがいて、きんじょからくじょうがでたかららしいよ。でも、おとしよりがすわるばしょがなくなって、こまってるひともいるんだって。

choices: Because the square was being rebuilt.
Because neighbours complained about people making noise at night.
Because old people didn't use them.
questions.explanation: {夜|よる}に{騒|さわ}ぐ{人|ひと}がいて、{近所|きんじょ}から{苦情|くじょう}が{出|で}たかららしい: neighbours complained about noise at night. The second sentence is the consequence (old people have nowhere to sit), not the reason.

questions.stem: Build the sentence.
questions.prompt: I have attached the materials, so please check them.
questions.explanation: {資料|しりょう}を{添付|てんぷ}いたしましたのでご{査収|さしゅう}ください. {添付|てんぷ}いたしました is the humble form of {添付|てんぷ}しました; ご{査収|さしゅう}ください asks the reader to receive and check. ご{自愛|じあい}ください (take care of yourself) belongs to a letter's closing.

questions.stem: Build the sentence (a notice).
questions.prompt: Please do not leave personal belongings in the corridor.
questions.explanation: {廊下|ろうか}に{私物|しぶつ}を{置|お}かないようお{願|ねが}いいたします. 〜ないようお{願|ねが}いいたします is the polite notice form of a request not to do something. The place phrase and the object can swap.

questions.stem: An examinee scores 45 in language knowledge, 40 in reading and 18 in listening. What is the result?
choices: Pass: two of the three sections are well above 19.
Fail: the total is 103, but listening is below the sectional pass mark of 19.
questions.explanation: The N1 needs a total of at least 100 out of 180 and at least 19 in each of the three scoring sections. 45 + 40 + 18 = 103 passes the total, but 18 in listening is below 19, so the result is a fail. There is no 110 pass mark.

questions.stem: Which question type is NOT part of the N1?
questions.explanation: The N1 vocabulary section has kanji reading, contextually-defined expressions, paraphrases and usage; unlike N2 it has no orthography and no word formation. Text grammar (grammar) and information retrieval (reading) are N1 question types.

questions.stem: How is the N1 timed?
choices: Three parts: vocabulary, grammar and reading, and listening, each timed separately.
Two parts: language knowledge (vocabulary and grammar) with reading, 110 minutes; listening, 55 minutes.
Two parts: language knowledge, 60 minutes; reading and listening, 105 minutes.
questions.explanation: Language knowledge and reading form one timed block of 110 minutes, so you divide the time yourself; listening takes 55 minutes (it can vary slightly with the recordings). There are three scoring sections but only two timed parts.

questions.stem: {彼|かれ}は{家族|かぞく}の{心配|しんぱい}を（　）、{毎晩|まいばん}{遅|おそ}くまで{遊|あそ}び{歩|ある}いている。
questions.explanation: 〜をよそに ignores other people's worries or protests: he goes out every night with no thought for his family's worry. 〜をものともせず is undaunted by an obstacle or danger, and it praises: it doesn't fit nights spent having fun; 〜をいいことに takes advantage of something; 〜にかこつけて uses something as a pretext (and needs に).

questions.stem: Which sentence is natural?
choices: {私|わたし}は{家|いえ}に{帰|かえ}るなり、{手|て}を{洗|あら}った。
{彼|かれ}は{部屋|へや}に{入|はい}るなり、{窓|まど}を{開|あ}け{放|はな}った。
{雨|あめ}が{止|や}むなり、{虹|にじ}が{出|で}た。
{明日|あした}{駅|えき}に{着|つ}くなり、{電話|でんわ}します。
questions.explanation: Dictionary form + なり ("as soon as… then") has the same subject in both clauses, describes a past event, and is not used of the speaker: he flung the window open the moment he came in. Not for the speaker (the first), not for natural events with different subjects (the third), and not for future plans (the fourth: 〜たらすぐに).

questions.stem: {教師|きょうし}にある（　）{発言|はつげん}だとして、{批判|ひはん}が{集|あつ}まっている。
questions.explanation: 〜にあるまじき + noun condemns behaviour unworthy of a role: a remark a teacher should never make. べからず ends notices and can't come before a noun; にあるべき would say the remark is fitting; ごとき (like) gives no sense here.

questions.stem: {山田|やまだ}さんの{実力|じつりょく}（　）、この{難|むずか}しい{交渉|こうしょう}もまとめられるだろう。
questions.explanation: 〜をもってすれば ("with A, if one uses A") introduces the means that makes something possible: with Yamada's ability, even this negotiation can be settled. をよそに ignores worries; ならでは needs の + noun after it; とあって gives a special reason for a past situation.

questions.stem: {会社|かいしゃ}は{倒産|とうさん}の（　）に{立|た}たされている。
questions.explanation: 〜の{瀬戸際|せとぎわ}に{立|た}つ is "to stand on the brink of": the company is on the brink of bankruptcy. {浅瀬|あさせ} (the shallows) and {桟橋|さんばし} (a pier) are literal places; {土俵|どひょう} is the sumo ring, figuratively the arena of a debate.

questions.stem: {台風|たいふう}は{猛烈|もうれつ}な{勢|いきお}いで{北上|ほくじょう}している。 Which is closest in meaning to 「{猛烈|もうれつ}な」?
choices: {非常|ひじょう}に{激|はげ}しい
questions.explanation: {猛烈|もうれつ} is "fierce, tremendous": {非常|ひじょう}に{激|はげ}しい. The typhoon is moving north with great force; nothing about speed being slow, unexpected or usual.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses 「{砕|くだ}けた」 correctly?
choices: {試験|しけん}に{砕|くだ}けて、{泣|な}いてしまった。
{長|なが}い{会議|かいぎ}で{時間|じかん}が{砕|くだ}けた。
{砕|くだ}けた{約束|やくそく}を{守|まも}った。
{先生|せんせい}の{砕|くだ}けた{話|はな}し{方|かた}のおかげで、{教室|きょうしつ}の{雰囲気|ふんいき}が{和|やわ}らいだ。
questions.explanation: {砕|くだ}けた{話|はな}し{方|かた} is a relaxed, informal way of speaking, a figurative use of {砕|くだ}ける (shatter). Failing an exam is {落|お}ちる, wasted time is {潰|つぶ}れた, and a broken promise is {破|やぶ}られた{約束|やくそく}.

questions.stem: {祖父|そふ}は{若|わか}い{頃|ころ}、漁師として{働|はたら}いていた。 How is 「漁師」 read?
questions.explanation: 漁師 (a fisher) is りょうし: here 漁 has its second on'yomi, リョウ, as in {漁|りょう}に{出|で}る and {豊漁|ほうりょう}. In most other compounds it is ギョ: {漁業|ぎょぎょう}, {漁村|ぎょそん}.

questions.stem: {大会|たいかい}には{全国|ぜんこく}から猛者が{集|あつ}まった。 How is 「猛者」 read?
questions.explanation: 猛者 (a tough veteran) is a special reading, もさ: 猛 is read も and 者 さ. The tempting もうじゃ follows the usual readings but isn't the word.

questions.stem: Which kanji completes 「{秋|あき}の{収|しゅう}（　）{祭|さい}」 (the autumn harvest festival)?
questions.explanation: {収穫|しゅうかく} (harvest) uses 穫, with the grain radical (禾): crops. 獲 (with the animal 犭) is for prey and prizes ({獲得|かくとく}); 護 is in {保護|ほご}; 穀 (grain) is in {穀物|こくもつ}, but not in this word.

questions.stem: Listen. What does the speaker recommend doing in the listening section?

audio.text: ちょうかいでは、わからないもんだいがあっても、そこでかんがえこまないでください。すぐにこたえをえらんで、つぎのもんだいにしゅうちゅうしましょう。

choices: Answer at once even when unsure, and concentrate on the next item.
Read all the choices before listening.
questions.explanation: {分|わ}からない{問題|もんだい}があっても{考|かんが}え{込|こ}まないで: don't brood over a question you don't know; choose an answer at once and focus on the next one ({次|つぎ}の{問題|もんだい}に{集中|しゅうちゅう}しましょう). Leaving blanks would lose points, since wrong guesses aren't penalized.

questions.stem: Listen and choose the best reply.

audio.text: しけん、おつかれさま。けっか、きになるね。

choices: うん、{一月|いちがつ}の{終|お}わりごろまでは{落|お}ち{着|つ}かないよ。
うん、{明日|あした}{受|う}けるんだ。
いいえ、{疲|つか}れていません。
そう、{結果|けっか}は{気|き}にならないって。
questions.explanation: The test is over and the speaker says the result is on their mind. Agreeing and saying one can't relax until the results (around late January for the December test) fits. The test isn't tomorrow; おつかれさま isn't a question about tiredness; the last reply contradicts the speaker oddly.

questions.stem: Listen. What is the announcement about?

audio.text: きしょうちょうによりますと、きょうはかくちでもうしょびとなるみこみです。こまめにすいぶんをとり、ひるまのがいしゅつはなるべくひかえてください。

choices: A very hot day, and how to stay safe.
A cold snap with temperatures below zero.
questions.explanation: {猛暑日|もうしょび} is a day of fierce heat; the advice is to drink water often and avoid going out in the daytime. Nothing about typhoons, {零下|れいか} temperatures or {氾濫|はんらん}.

questions.stem: Build the sentence.
tiles: {総合得点|そうごうとくてん}が
accept: {総合得点|そうごうとくてん}が
questions.prompt: Even if the total is high, you fail if one section is below the minimum.
questions.explanation: {総合得点|そうごうとくてん}が{高|たか}くても{一|ひと}つの{区分|くぶん}が{基準点|きじゅんてん}に{届|とど}かなければ{不合格|ふごうかく}だ. The concession (〜ても) and the condition (〜なければ) can come in either order before the conclusion.

questions.stem: Build the sentence.
questions.prompt: Only a master can make this taste.
questions.explanation: この{味|あじ}は{名人|めいじん}にして{初|はじ}めて{出|だ}せるものだ. N + にして{初|はじ}めて (lesson 21): only at the level of A is it possible. ならでは needs の + noun after it ({名人|めいじん}ならではの{味|あじ}).

questions.stem:
Read the passage. What does the writer mean by 「{試験|しけん}は{扉|とびら}を{開|ひら}ける{鍵|かぎ}にすぎない」?

N1に{合格|ごうかく}したとき、{私|わたし}はこれで{日本語|にほんご}の{勉強|べんきょう}は{終|お}わりだと{思|おも}った。だが{合格|ごうかく}の{翌月|よくげつ}、{初|はじ}めて{一冊|いっさつ}の{新書|しんしょ}を{読|よ}み{通|とお}そうとして、その{考|かんが}えが{甘|あま}かったことを{知|し}った。{試験|しけん}の{長文|ちょうぶん}は{二千字|にせんじ}で{終|お}わる。{本|ほん}は{二百|にひゃく}ページ{以上|いじょう}ある。{知|し}らない{言葉|ことば}は{試験|しけん}よりはるかに{多|おお}く、{一週間|いっしゅうかん}で{読|よ}めたのは、{僅|わず}か{二十|にじゅう}ページにすぎなかった。

それでも{読|よ}み{続|つづ}けるうちに、{少|すこ}しずつ{速|はや}く{読|よ}めるようになった。{新聞|しんぶん}のコラムを{毎朝|まいあさ}{読|よ}み、ラジオの{討論|とうろん}を{聞|き}き、{読|よ}んだ{本|ほん}の{感想|かんそう}を{書|か}く。そうした{日々|ひび}の{中|なか}で{出会|であ}った{言葉|ことば}の{多|おお}くは、{試験|しけん}には{一度|いちど}も{出|で}てこなかったものばかりだ。{試験|しけん}は{扉|とびら}を{開|ひら}ける{鍵|かぎ}にすぎない。{扉|とびら}の{向|む}こうには、{試験|しけん}に{出|で}ない{言葉|ことば}が{無数|むすう}に{待|ま}っているのである。
choices: The test is the most important goal of learning Japanese.
Passing the test gives access, but the real learning lies beyond it.
The test is too easy to measure real ability.
Only people who have passed can read books.
questions.explanation: The key opens the door; beyond it are countless words the test never asks about. Passing N1 is a start, not a goal: the writer found the real learning came afterwards, in books, papers, radio and writing. The writer doesn't call the test too easy, and the other two choices contradict the passage.

questions.stem: The N1 total score runs from 0 to 180. Type the minimum score needed in each scoring section (a number).
questions.explanation: Each of the three scoring sections (language knowledge, reading, listening; 0–60 each) has a sectional pass mark of 19, and the total must be at least 100.

questions.stem: Which statement about 『{山月記|さんげつき}』 is correct?
choices: It was first published in 1942 and is based on a Tang-dynasty tale.
It was written after Nakajima's return from Palau in 1943.
It is a translation of a Song-dynasty novel.
It was first published after Nakajima's death.
questions.explanation: It appeared in February 1942 in the magazine 『{文學界|ぶんがくかい}』, under the title 『{古譚|こたん}』, and is based on the Tang tale known in Japan as 『{人虎伝|じんこでん}』. Nakajima returned from Palau in March 1942 and died in December 1942; 『{李陵|りりょう}』, not this story, was published after his death. It is an adaptation ({翻案|ほんあん}), not a translation.

questions.stem: In the story, why did Li Zheng become a tiger, in his own account?
choices: He was cursed by a god for leaving his post.
He ate a poisonous plant in the mountains.
He wanted to escape his debts.
His fear of being shown to lack talent kept him from working with others, while his pride kept him from living among ordinary people.
questions.explanation: Li Zheng blames 「{臆病|おくびょう}な{自尊心|じそんしん}と、{尊大|そんだい}な{羞恥心|しゅうちしん}」 (one kanji of the last word is outside N1): afraid of finding he had no talent, he wouldn't study with others; half believing he had talent, he couldn't live among ordinary people. He himself says he doesn't know the outward cause; the story offers no curse or poison.

questions.stem: Before saying goodbye, Li Zheng reproaches himself. For what?
choices: For having asked his friend to write down his poems before asking him to look after his wife and children.
For not having finished his poems.
questions.explanation: He entrusts his family to Yuan Can and then says he should have asked that before asking about his poems: a man like that, he says, deserved to fall to the state of a beast. The self-reproach shows the same pride that made him a tiger.

questions.stem: What is kundoku ({訓読|くんどく})?
choices: Translating classical Chinese into modern Japanese prose.
Reading classical Chinese directly as Japanese, with added endings and marks that change the order.
Reading kanji with their native Japanese readings only.
questions.explanation: Kundoku keeps the Chinese characters and reads them as a Japanese sentence, adding okurigana and using return marks ({返|かえ}り{点|てん}) for the Japanese order: {国|くに}{破|やぶ}{山河|さんが}{在|あ} → {国|くに}{破|やぶ}れて{山河|さんが}{在|あ}り. Reading a kanji in kun'yomi is {訓読|くんよ}み, a different word.

questions.stem: With a レ{点|てん}, how is 「{不|ず}{知|し}」 read?
questions.explanation: The レ{点|てん} sends the reader back one character: {知|し} first, then {不|ず}, which becomes the negative ず: {知|し}らず (does not know). Reading in Chinese order or with on'yomi gives nonsense.

questions.stem: 「{賤吏|せんり}に{甘|あま}んずるを{潔|いさぎよ}しとしなかった」 (the first two kanji are outside N1). What does 「〜を{潔|いさぎよ}しとしない」 mean?
questions.explanation: 〜を{潔|いさぎよ}しとしない is a kundoku idiom: not to consider something honourable, so to refuse it as beneath one. Li Zheng would not content himself ({甘|あま}んずる) with being a lowly official. It has nothing to do with cleanliness.

questions.stem: {高校|こうこう}では古文のほかに漢文も{学|まな}ぶ。 How is 「漢文」 read?
questions.explanation: 漢文 (classical Chinese) is かんぶん, like {古文|こぶん} and {作文|さくぶん}: 文 is ブン. もん appears in other words ({文字|もじ}, {注文|ちゅうもん}).

questions.stem: {彼|かれ}の（　）な{態度|たいど}が、{周囲|しゅうい}の{人|ひと}を{遠|とお}ざけた。
questions.explanation: {尊大|そんだい} (haughty, self-important) describes an attitude that drives people away. {刻苦|こっく} is hard toil, {鬼才|きさい} a prodigy and {定番|ていばん} a staple: nouns that can't take な here.

questions.stem: Listen. What is the speaker explaining?

audio.text: さんげつきは、とうのじだいのじんこでんというはなしをもとにしています。なかじまあつしは、そのわくぐみをのこしながら、しゅじんこうのながいこくはくをくわえました。

choices: That Nakajima translated the Tang tale word for word.
That Nakajima kept the frame of a Tang tale and added the hero's long confession.
That the Tang tale was based on Nakajima's story.
That Nakajima wrote the story in Chinese.
questions.explanation: {人虎伝|じんこでん}を{基|もと}にしています: it is based on the Tang tale; {枠組|わくぐ}みを{残|のこ}しながら、{主人公|しゅじんこう}の{長|なが}い{告白|こくはく}を{加|くわ}えました: he kept its framework and added the hero's long confession.

questions.stem: Listen. According to the speaker, what do readers often take the tiger to stand for?

audio.text: とらは、ひとにひょうかされることをおそれて、たにんとのかかわりをたったさいのうのすがただと、よくよまれます。

choices: A talent that cut itself off from others for fear of being judged.
The power of nature over human beings.
The cruelty of the Tang government.
Li Zheng's love for his family.
questions.explanation: {人|ひと}に{評価|ひょうか}されることを{恐|おそ}れて、{他人|たにん}との{関|かか}わりを{断|た}った{才能|さいのう}の{姿|すがた}: a talent that cut off its ties with others for fear of being judged. よく{読|よ}まれます marks it as a common reading, not the story's stated moral.

questions.stem:
Read the passage from the story (in the spelling of the Aozora Bunko text). What does 「{猛獣|もうじゅう}」 stand for?

{人間|にんげん}は{誰|だれ}でも{猛獣使|もうじゅうつかい}であり、その{猛獣|もうじゅう}に{当|あた}るのが、{各人|かくじん}の{性情|せいじょう}だという。{己|おれ}の{場合|ばあい}、この{尊大|そんだい}な{羞恥心|しゅうちしん}が{猛獣|もうじゅう}だった。{虎|とら}だったのだ。

(One kanji of しゅうちしん is outside N1.)
choices: Each person's temperament, which they must tame.
The tigers of the mountains near the capital.
questions.explanation: Everyone is a tamer, and the wild beast is each person's nature ({性情|せいじょう}); in Li Zheng's case it was his arrogant sense of shame, and that beast became the tiger he is now. {猛獣使|もうじゅうつかい} and {当|あた}る are the text's spellings of {猛獣使|もうじゅうつか}い and {当|あ}たる.

questions.stem:
Read the opening sentence (Aozora Bunko text). Which description of Li Zheng is NOT given?

{隴西|ろうさい}の{李徴|りちょう}は{博学|はくがく}{才穎|さいえい}、{天宝|てんぽう}の{末年|まつねん}、{若|わか}くして{名|な}を{虎榜|こぼう}に{連|つら}ね、ついで{江南尉|こうなんい}に{補|ほ}せられたが、{性|せい}、{狷介|けんかい}、{自|みずか}ら{恃|たの}むところ{頗|すこぶ}る{厚|あつ}く、{賤吏|せんり}に{甘|あま}んずるを{潔|いさぎよ}しとしなかった。

(Ten of its kanji are outside N1: see the lesson.)
choices: He was kind and easy to get along with.
He had great confidence in himself.
questions.explanation: {博学|はくがく}{才穎|さいえい} (learned and gifted), {若|わか}くして{名|な}を{虎榜|こぼう}に{連|つら}ね (passed young), {自|みずか}ら{恃|たの}むところ{頗|すこぶ}る{厚|あつ}く (great self-confidence) are all there. {狷介|けんかい} says the opposite of easy-going: stubborn and unbending.

questions.stem: Who made もののあわれ into a theory of literature, and where?
choices: Kuki Shūzō, in a book of 1930.
Sen no Rikyū, in his writings on tea.
Zeami, in his treatises on noh.
Motoori Norinaga, in his writings on the Tale of Genji and waka.
questions.explanation: {本居宣長|もとおりのりなが} (1730–1801), the scholar of National Learning ({国学|こくがく}), argued that the heart of 『{源氏物語|げんじものがたり}』 and of waka is もののあわれ, first in 『{紫文要領|しぶんようりょう}』 (1763). Kuki analysed {粋|いき}, Rikyū is linked with わび, Zeami with {幽玄|ゆうげん}.

questions.stem: Which description fits わび rather than さび?
choices: The beauty of poverty and simplicity accepted, linked with the tea ceremony.
The depth felt in what is old and still, linked with Bashō's school.
questions.explanation: わび is simplicity and lack accepted as beautiful, usually associated with わび{茶|ちゃ}; さび is the depth felt in what is old, worn and still, associated with haikai. Urban chic is {粋|いき}; the interval is {間|ま}.

questions.stem: 「{間|ま}が{悪|わる}い」 means:
questions.explanation: {間|ま} is the interval or timing; {間|ま}が{悪|わる}い is "awkwardly timed, embarrassing" ({間|ま}の{悪|わる}いときに{来|き}た, came at a bad moment). It isn't about the size of a room.

questions.stem: {粋|いき}の{反対|はんたい}の{意味|いみ}を{表|あらわ}す{言葉|ことば}はどれか。
questions.explanation: {野暮|やぼ} (unsophisticated, tactless) is the opposite of {粋|いき}. {通|つう} (a connoisseur) and {風流|ふうりゅう} (refined taste) are close to it; {簡素|かんそ} (simple and plain) is about form, not style of manner.

questions.stem: {能|のう}の{舞台|ぶたい}では、（　）の{美|び}が{求|もと}められてきた。
questions.explanation: {幽玄|ゆうげん}, beauty beyond what is shown, is the ideal linked above all with noh and Zeami. {野暮|やぼ} is boorish, {通|つう} a connoisseur, and {閑散|かんさん} (lesson 25) describes a deserted, quiet place.

questions.stem: What does the essay "the trouble with Japanese beauty" recommend?
choices: Stop using words like わび・さび altogether.
Use the words only for temples.
Use the words, but go back to the concrete: what you saw, where, and why it moved you.
questions.explanation: The writer rejects giving up the words (そうではない) and asks writers to return to the concrete ({具体|ぐたい}に{戻|もど}ればよい): which bowl, which moment. Words confirm what one has seen; they don't replace seeing.

questions.stem: According to the essay, where does a difference between cultures in feeling for beauty lie?
choices: In the heart itself: only Japanese people are moved by falling blossoms.
In the history of the words and forms that express the feeling.
Nowhere: all cultures express beauty in the same way.
questions.explanation: The writer says people everywhere are moved by falling blossoms; any difference lies in the history of the words and forms that express the feeling ({言葉|ことば}と{形|かたち}の{歴史|れきし}), not in the heart or in "Japanese blood".

questions.stem: {能|のう}は幽玄の{美|び}を{追|お}い{求|もと}める。 How is 「幽玄」 read?
questions.explanation: 幽玄 is ゆうげん: 幽 is ユウ (as in {幽霊|ゆうれい}) and 玄 is ゲン (as in {玄関|げんかん}), not ケン.

questions.stem: Listen. What is the speaker saying about わび・さび?

audio.text: わびとさびは、もともとべつのかんがえでしたが、いまではひとつのことばのようにつかわれ、いみもあいまいになっています。

choices: They were originally different ideas but are now used as one, more vaguely.
They have always meant exactly the same thing.
questions.explanation: もともと{別|べつ}の{考|かんが}えでしたが: originally separate ideas; {一|ひと}つの{言葉|ことば}のように{使|つか}われ、{意味|いみ}も{曖昧|あいまい}に: now used like one word, and vaguer in meaning.

questions.stem: Listen. What did Kuki Shūzō write about?

audio.text: くきしゅうぞうは、いきのこうぞうというほんで、えどのまちのびいしきである、いきをぶんせきしました。

choices: The aesthetics of the tea ceremony.
The urban chic of Edo called いき.
questions.explanation: 『「いき」の{構造|こうぞう}』 (1930) analyses {粋|いき}, the sense of style of the townspeople of Edo ({江戸|えど}の{町|まち}の{美意識|びいしき}). (In speech the audio says いき without kanji.)

questions.stem:
Read the passage. What is the writer's first objection?

{旅行|りょこう}{雑誌|ざっし}は{古|ふる}い{寺|てら}の{庭|にわ}を「わび・さびの{世界|せかい}」と{呼|よ}び、{家具|かぐ}の{広告|こうこく}は{白|しろ}い{壁|かべ}と{木|き}の{机|つくえ}を「{間|ま}の{美学|びがく}」と{説明|せつめい}する。{言葉|ことば}そのものに{罪|つみ}はない。だが、こうした{使|つか}い{方|かた}には{二|ふた}つの{危|あや}うさがある。{一|ひと}つは、{言葉|ことば}が{中身|なかみ}を{失|うしな}うことだ。わびもさびも、{本来|ほんらい}は{特定|とくてい}の{時代|じだい}と{場|ば}で、{具体的|ぐたいてき}な{物|もの}や{行|おこな}いを{通|とお}して{磨|みが}かれてきた{考|かんが}えである。それを「{素朴|そぼく}で{古|ふる}びたもの」{一般|いっぱん}に{当|あ}てはめれば、{便利|べんり}な{形容詞|けいようし}にはなっても、{何|なに}かを{見|み}る{目|め}は{育|そだ}たない。
choices: That magazines use too many foreign words.
That applying the words to anything old and simple empties them and doesn't train the eye.
questions.explanation: The first danger: the words lose their content ({中身|なかみ}を{失|うしな}う). Ideas refined through particular objects and practices become handy adjectives for anything simple and old, and nobody learns to see. The writer says the words themselves are not to blame.

questions.stem:
Read the passage and choose the best expression for the blank.

もののあわれを{知|し}る{心|こころ}は、{日本人|にほんじん}{特有|とくゆう}のものだろうか。{散|ち}る{花|はな}に{胸|むね}を{痛|いた}める{人|ひと}は、どの{国|くに}にもいるはずである。（　）、{違|ちが}いがあるとすれば、それは{心|こころ}そのものではなく、その{心|こころ}を{表|あらわ}す{言葉|ことば}と{形|かたち}の{歴史|れきし}であろう。
questions.explanation: The conclusion follows from the point that people everywhere are moved: したがって (therefore), so any difference must lie elsewhere. しかも adds a further point, なぜなら needs a reason, ちなみに changes the subject.

glossary.definition: A short word in hiragana that follows a word or clause and shows its role: は (topic), が (subject), を (object), に, で, と, も, か, ね, よ… Much of what English does with word order and prepositions, Japanese does with particles.

A group of words that works as one particle, often a particle plus a verb form: について, に{対|たい}して, を{皮切|かわき}りに, にあって. Many belong to written style. The module 1 reference sheet lists which N1 patterns this course writes in kanji and which in kana.

Characters taken from Chinese that carry meaning as well as sound. Japanese writes most nouns and the stems of verbs and adjectives in kanji and the grammar in kana. This course writes a word in kanji when all its kanji are on its list of 1,999 (the 1,039 of N5–N2 and the 960 of N1).
Small kana printed over kanji to show how they are read: {隣人|りんじん}. This course puts furigana on every kanji except the one a question tests; you can switch them off.
A kanji reading that comes from the Chinese pronunciation borrowed with it, used mostly in words of two or more kanji: 隣 is リン in {隣人|りんじん}. Kanji tables write on'yomi in katakana.
A kanji reading that is a native Japanese word, often used for a kanji on its own or with okurigana: 隣 read となり, 匂 read にお in {匂|にお}う. Kanji tables write kun'yomi in hiragana.

The kana written after a kanji to spell the rest of a word, usually its changing ending: the う of {匂|にお}う, the える of {鍛|きた}える. In this course furigana go over the kanji only; okurigana stay outside: {憤|いきどお}る.
A reading of a kanji compound that can't be built from the readings of its kanji one by one: {叔父|おじ}, {玄人|くろうと}, {芝生|しばふ}, {梅雨|つゆ}. Learn each as a whole word. Many special readings are jukujikun.

A native Japanese word written with a compound of kanji chosen for its meaning, not its sound, so that the reading belongs to the whole compound and not to any single kanji: {今日|きょう}, {大人|おとな}, {梅雨|つゆ}, {叔母|おば}. A kind of special reading.

The unit of length in Japanese pronunciation, roughly one kana: か, き. A small ゃ, ゅ or ょ joins the kana before it (きょ is one mora), while っ, ん and the second half of a long vowel each count as one: がっこう has four morae. Pitch accent is counted in morae.

The pattern of high and low pitch on the morae of a word in standard Tokyo Japanese. The course marks it by the mora after which the pitch drops: 0 for flat words (no drop), 1 for a drop after the first mora, and so on. It tells apart words such as {箸|はし:1} (chopsticks), {橋|はし:2} (bridge) and {端|はし:0} (edge).
An adjective that ends in い in its dictionary form and changes its ending: {生臭|なまぐさ}い, {生臭|なまぐさ}くない, {生臭|なまぐさ}かった. It goes straight before a noun.
An adjective that takes な before a noun and です / だ at the end of a sentence: {頑丈|がんじょう}な{棚|たな}, {棚|たな}は{頑丈|がんじょう}だ. Vocabulary lists it without the な.
The basic plain non-past form of a verb, the one in dictionaries: {匂|にお}う, {鍛|きた}える, する, {来|く}る. Many N1 patterns join it: 〜が{早|はや}いか, 〜や{否|いな}や, 〜なり.
The part of a verb before ます: {釣|つ}り (from {釣|つ}ります), {見|み} (from {見|み}ます). Patterns such as 〜がてら and 〜つつ join it, and it can work as a noun.
The verb form ending in て or で: {煮|に}て, {嗅|か}いで. It links actions and clauses and builds many patterns: 〜ている, 〜てしまう, 〜てからというもの.
The plain past form, ending in た or だ: {酔|よ}った, {飽|あ}きた. Patterns such as 〜たとたん, 〜た{矢先|やさき}に and the second use of 〜までだ join it.
The plain negative of a verb, ending in ない: {蹴|け}らない, {飽|あ}きない. Its stem (the part before ない) also takes the written negative ず: {受|う}けず, {見|み}ず.
The written negative, formed from the ない stem + ず (する → せず, {来|く}る → こず): {受|う}けずに, {見|み}ずじまい. It descends from the classical auxiliary ず and is common in writing and set expressions.
The forms without です or ます: {行|い}く, {行|い}かない, {行|い}った, {行|い}かなかった. They are used in casual speech, in writing in だ / である style, and before most grammar patterns.
The forms with です and ます: {行|い}きます, {行|い}きません, {行|い}きました. Used with people you don't know well, at work, and in letters and notices.
A verb whose ending changes across a row of kana: {釣|つ}る → {釣|つ}らない, {釣|つ}ります, {釣|つ}って. Some end in -いる or -える and look like group 2 verbs but aren't: {蹴|け}る ({蹴|け}らない), {焦|あせ}る, {陥|おちい}る.
A verb that drops る and adds its endings to what is left: {鍛|きた}える → {鍛|きた}えない, {鍛|きた}えます, {鍛|きた}えて. All end in いる or える, though not every such verb is group 2.
The two irregular verbs する and {来|く}る, and the many する compounds: {隣接|りんせつ}する, {熟睡|じゅくすい}する.
The verb form that means "can": {釣|つ}れる, {鍛|きた}えられる, できる. Some verbs have no natural potential (stative and non-volitional verbs), so the course leaves it out of their drills.
The verb form for "let's" or "I'll": {挑|いど}もう, {鍛|きた}えよう. With とする it means "be about to": {出|で}かけようとした{矢先|やさき}に.
The ば form of a verb or adjective, "if": {眠|ねむ}れば, {暖|あたた}かければ. More broadly, any "if" form: 〜ば, 〜たら, 〜と, 〜なら.
The verb form for having something done to you, made with れる / られる on the ない stem: {叱|しか}られる, {見|み}られる. It also serves as an honorific and, with some verbs, for things that happen by themselves.
The verb form for making or letting someone do something, made with せる / させる on the ない stem: {酔|よ}わせる, {飽|あ}きさせる. Classical writing has しめる instead (lesson 26).
A verb that takes a direct object with を: {沸|わ}かす (boil water), {焦|こ}がす (scorch), {癒|いや}す (soothe). Many have an intransitive partner.
A verb without a direct object, often describing something that happens by itself: {沸|わ}く (boil), {焦|こ}げる (burn), {癒|い}える (heal up). Pairs such as {癒|い}える / {癒|いや}す are common.

A verb that follows another verb (usually its て form) and adds a meaning rather than an action: 〜ている, 〜てしまう, 〜ておく, 〜てくる. Auxiliaries are written in kana. In Japanese grammar books the word {助動詞|じょどうし} also covers endings such as れる, させる, ない and た.
A word that turns a clause into a noun phrase so it can take a particle: の and こと. {帰|かえ}るのを{待|ま}つ, {休|やす}むことなしに.
A noun with little meaning of its own that is used to build grammar: こと, もの, ところ, ため, わけ, はず, まま. Written in kana. ところ in 〜ところを (lesson 4) and そば in 〜そばから (lesson 1) work this way.

The form a word takes directly before a noun: plain verb forms ({飛|と}ぶ{鳥|とり}), い-adjectives ({淡|あわ}い{色|いろ}), な-adjectives with な ({頑丈|がんじょう}な{扉|とびら}) and nouns with の ({隣|となり}の{家|いえ}). Classical Japanese has a separate attributive form (lesson 5h2).
The language of newspapers, essays, reports and notices: plain だ / である endings, written conjunctions and patterns that speech seldom uses (〜や{否|いな}や, 〜かたわら, 〜なくして). Most N1 grammar lives in it.

The level of formality and the setting a word or pattern belongs to: casual speech, polite speech, formal speech, written style, literary or academic writing. N1 patterns are restricted in register: 〜かたがた belongs to formal letters, 〜がてら to everyday speech.

The system of respectful language: honorific forms that raise the person spoken about, humble forms that lower the speaker, and the polite です / ます style. お{忙|いそが}しいところを{恐縮|きょうしゅく}ですが is a typical keigo opening.
Keigo that raises the person who does the action: いらっしゃる, おっしゃる, {召|め}し{上|あ}がる, お〜になる, and the れる / られる form ({離|はな}れられる).
Keigo that lowers the speaker (or their side) in front of the listener: {伺|うかが}う, {申|もう}し{上|あ}げる, いたす, まいる, お〜する. {恐|おそ}れ{入|い}ります and {恐縮|きょうしゅく}です are humble set phrases.
Granting one thing while saying something that goes against it: "although, even though, even if". N2 taught ものの, とはいえ, にもかかわらず; module 2 adds といえども, たりとも and others.
Setting two things against each other: 〜{一方|いっぽう}で, 〜{反面|はんめん}, 〜にひきかえ (lesson 7). Lesson 1's 〜たかと{思|おも}うと often contrasts a sudden change with what came before.
A word or ending that softens a claim or makes it less certain: 〜と{言|い}われる, 〜と{考|かんが}えられている, 〜かもしれない, {必|かなら}ずしも〜ない. Academic and journalistic writing hedge what they can't prove.

The part of a sentence that shows the speaker's attitude to what they say (how certain, necessary or desirable it is) rather than the facts themselves: 〜はずだ, 〜べきだ, 〜かねない, 〜ざるを{得|え}ない. Module 4 adds the N1 expressions of feeling and judgement.

The order in which events happen and the patterns that express it: "before", "after", "as soon as", "ever since", "from … on". Module 1's patterns of sequence include 〜が{早|はや}いか, 〜を{皮切|かわき}りに, 〜を{境|さかい}に and 〜を{経|へ}て.
The meaning "A, and at once B": no time between two events. Lesson 1's 〜が{早|はや}いか, 〜や{否|いな}や and 〜なり, and N3's 〜たとたん, express it, each with its own limits on subject, tense and register.

The written language of Japanese literature from about the ninth to the nineteenth century, with its own verb endings and auxiliaries and written in historical kana usage. It survives in modern written style in forms such as ず, べし and ごとし. The course teaches it for reading only (lessons 5h2, 15h1, 26).

The kana spelling used before 1946, based on how words were pronounced around the Heian period. Read は-row kana inside a word as わ-row (いふ → いう), ゐ and ゑ as い and え, and vowel pairs by today's sounds (やうやう → ようよう, てふ → ちょう).

An ending of classical Japanese that adds a meaning to a verb: ず (not), けり (past told as a story; realization), なり (assertion), む / ん (will, conjecture), べし (should, must), ごとし (like). Each attaches to a particular verb form and has several forms of its own; the module 1 reference sheet tabulates them.

A negative made as strong as possible, usually by naming the smallest amount and saying that not even that is the case: {一円|いちえん}たりとも{無駄|むだ}にできない (not a single yen), {一人|ひとり}として{来|こ}なかった (not one person came), {少|すこ}しも / {全然|ぜんぜん}〜ない. At N1, 一 + counter + たりとも〜ない is the written form.

Describing what did not happen (or is not the case) as if it had: "if only you had told me", "it would have been better if…". Japanese marks it with 〜ば / 〜たら + よかった, often followed by のに (everyday) or ものを (written, reproachful): {言|い}ってくれればよかったものを.

Naming two or more cases or examples in a parallel pattern so that what follows applies to all of them. N1 patterns: 〜であれ〜であれ (whether A or B), 〜といい〜といい (A and B alike, in an evaluation), 〜といわず〜といわず (A, B, everywhere), 〜なり〜なり (A or B or something, in advice); earlier ones are 〜にせよ〜にせよ, 〜やら〜やら and 〜とか〜とか.

A question asked for effect rather than to get an answer: the speaker or writer already knows (or gives) the answer. Editorials use 〜のか / 〜だろうか to lead into their main point ({何|なに}ができるのか。{答|こた}えは{難|むずか}しくない。), and 〜ものか / 〜ではないか turn a question into a strong denial or claim (そんなことがあるものか: as if that could happen!).

The classical masked drama of Japan ({能|のう}), with chant, dance and the music of flute and drums. The main actor (シテ) often plays a ghost, god or spirit. It took its classic form in the 14th and 15th centuries under Kan'ami and his son Zeami; with kyōgen it makes up {能楽|のうがく}.

The comic theatre ({狂言|きょうげん}) performed on the noh stage, traditionally between two noh plays. Its characters are ordinary people (a master and his servant {太郎冠者|たろうかじゃ}, a husband and wife), it uses the everyday speech of its time and seldom uses masks. The word also means a sham: {狂言|きょうげん}{強盗|ごうとう}, a faked robbery.

Popular theatre of the Edo period and today ({歌舞伎|かぶき}), with music, dance and spectacular staging. It began in Kyoto in 1603; since bans on women (1629) and young men (1652), all roles are played by men, women's roles by {女形|おんながた}. Typical features: the {花道|はなみち} walkway, {見得|みえ} poses, くまどり make-up and {屋号|やごう} calls from the audience.

In the traditional arts, a fixed form of movement, posture or technique handed down from teacher to pupil ({型|かた}): the {見得|みえ} of kabuki, the steps and turns of noh, the forms of the tea ceremony or the martial arts. Learning begins by copying the kata exactly.

What a statement, a decision or an action rests on: the reason, motive, purpose, position or rule that justifies it. Module 3 of N1 covers reasons with a particular voice (〜ばこそ, 〜ゆえに, 〜とあって, 〜こととて, lesson 11), purposes (lesson 12), the position a situation puts you in (〜{手前|てまえ}, 〜とあれば, 〜ともなると, 〜あっての, lesson 13), what someone disregards or uses (lesson 14) and the facts and rules a decision follows (lesson 15).

A clause that says what an action is meant to achieve. Everyday Japanese uses 〜ために (a goal the subject can bring about) and 〜ように (a hoped-for state, often with potentials and negatives). Written Japanese adds 〜べく (dictionary form; する → すべく) and the dramatic 〜んがため (ない stem + ん; する → せんがため), lesson 12. Neither of the written ones can lead to a request or an order.

A pattern that says what a decision or an action follows as a standard: a law, a rule, a tradition or the facts. In N1: 〜にのっとって (in accordance with a norm such as a law or tradition), 〜に{即|そく}して (in line with the facts or the actual situation), alongside 〜を{踏|ふ}まえて (taking results into account) and 〜に{鑑|かんが}みて (in view of), lesson 15. N2's 〜に{基|もと}づいて is the general "based on".

A rule of classical Japanese ({係|かか}り{結|むす}び, "linking and binding"): when the particles ぞ, なむ, や or か appear in a sentence, the predicate at the end takes the attributive form ({連体形|れんたいけい}); with こそ it takes the realis form. Example: あやしうこそものぐるほしけれ (『{徒然草|つれづれぐさ}』), where こそ turns the conclusive ものぐるほし into ものぐるほしけれ. Modern Japanese keeps only traces in fixed patterns such as 〜こそすれ. Lesson 15h1.

The idea that a constitution is the supreme law and limits the power of the state ({立憲主義|りっけんしゅぎ}). The Constitution of Japan calls itself the supreme law ({最高法規|さいこうほうき}, chapter 10) and divides power among the Diet, the Cabinet and the courts ({三権分立|さんけんぶんりつ}). Lesson 15h2.

The られる form of a verb of thinking or feeling used to say that the thought or feeling arises by itself, without the speaker deciding to have it: {思|おも}われる (it seems to me), {感|かん}じられる (one senses), {悔|く}やまれる (I can't help regretting), {案|あん}じられる (I can't help worrying), {待|ま}たれる (is eagerly awaited). It looks like the passive, but nobody acts on anybody; the person who feels is the unstated subject and the thing felt takes が. Written Japanese uses it to report feelings in a measured way.

A pattern that passes judgement on how much something is worth rather than simply describing it: 〜に{足|た}る (worthy of: {信頼|しんらい}するに{足|た}る), 〜に{足|た}りない (not worth: {取|と}るに{足|た}りない), 〜に{値|あたい}する (deserves), 〜に{堪|た}える (stands up to: {鑑賞|かんしょう}に{堪|た}える), 〜かいがある (was worth the effort). Most are written style.

Saying that something must not be done. Everyday Japanese uses 〜てはいけない, 〜ないでください and 〜{禁止|きんし}; the classical べし gives the old-style 〜べからず of notices and sayings ({立|た}ち{入|い}るべからず, {初心忘|しょしんわす}るべからず), its noun-modifying form 〜べからざる ({欠|か}くべからざる, indispensable), and まじ gives 〜まじき (unworthy of: {教師|きょうし}にあるまじき{行為|こうい}). The classical forms aren't conjugation-drill forms.

A figure of speech that says one thing is like another, with an explicit word of comparison. In Japanese it is a {直喩|ちょくゆ}, made with ような / ように, まるで〜ようだ or, in writing, ごとく / ごとき: {雪|ゆき}のように{白|しろ}い (as white as snow).

A figure of speech that calls one thing another without a word such as "like": {人生|じんせい}は{旅|たび}だ (life is a journey). In Japanese it is a {隠喩|いんゆ} (also {暗喩|あんゆ}). {比喩|ひゆ} covers metaphors, similes and other figures.
A figure of speech that talks about a thing, an animal or an idea as if it were a person: {風|かぜ}が{歌|うた}う (the wind sings), {花|はな}が{笑|わら}う. In Japanese, {擬人化|ぎじんか} or {擬人法|ぎじんほう}.

Saying what something is like or seems like. Everyday Japanese uses ようだ, みたいだ and らしい; written Japanese adds ごとく / ごとき / ごとし ({夢|ゆめ}のごとき{日々|ひび}), んばかり (as if about to) and とばかりに (as if to say). Lesson 22's めく (with a touch of) is close.

A habit or leaning that shows up again and again. 〜がちだ (often, unwanted) and 〜{傾向|けいこう}がある (neutral, for facts and numbers) are everyday and neutral; 〜きらいがある is written and critical, for a person's or group's bad leaning: {物事|ものごと}を{大|おお}げさに{言|い}うきらいがある.

A classical Japanese poem of 5-7-5-7-7 morae (31 in all), in Japanese {和歌|わか}; today's name for the form is {短歌|たんか}. The 5-7-5 is the upper verse ({上|かみ}の{句|く}) and the 7-7 the lower verse ({下|しも}の{句|く}). 『{百人一首|ひゃくにんいっしゅ}』 is a famous anthology of a hundred waka.

A short poem of 5-7-5 morae (17 in all), in Japanese {俳句|はいく}, that usually contains a season word (kigo) and often a cutting word (kireji). It grew out of the opening verse ({発句|ほっく}) of linked verse ({連歌|れんが}); the great Edo-period masters are Bashō, Buson and Issa.

A season word in a haiku, in Japanese {季語|きご}: a word that places the poem in a season, such as {蝉|せみ} (summer) or {初霜|はつしも} (winter). Season words follow the old calendar, so spring begins in early February. They are collected in a {歳時記|さいじき}.

A "cutting word" in a haiku, in Japanese {切|き}れ{字|じ}: a word such as や, かな or けり that makes a pause or ends the poem and adds feeling. {古池|ふるいけ}や… : the や sets the old pond apart before the rest of the poem.

A piece of older Japanese that modern writing keeps for weight, rhythm or a touch of the past: ぬ, ざる, べし, ごとし, しめる, なり, まじき, たる and the like. Most are classical forms. N1 texts use them without warning; recognize them, and in your own writing use them sparingly.

An ending or auxiliary of classical Japanese (the written language before the twentieth century) that survives in modern writing, mostly in set phrases, proverbs, mottos and titles: べし (shall), ごとし (like), ざる (not, before a noun), the perfective ぬ ({風立|かぜた}ちぬ), しめる (causative), なり (is). None of them is a drill form.

In classical Japanese, an auxiliary showing that an action has happened or is complete, close to English "has done". The perfective ぬ survives in a few famous titles and lines: {風立|かぜた}ちぬ (the wind has risen). Don't confuse it with the negative ぬ of {知|し}らぬ (does not know), which follows a different form of the verb.

Classical Chinese as written and read in Japan ({漢文|かんぶん}). For centuries it was the language of scholarship and government, and Japanese students still read Chinese poems and Confucius in it. Prose with many two-kanji words, set phrases such as 〜を{潔|いさぎよ}しとしない and a terse rhythm is called kanbun-style: 『{山月記|さんげつき}』 is the classic example.

Reading classical Chinese directly as Japanese ({訓読|くんどく}): the characters stay, small marks show the Japanese word order, and okurigana add the endings, so the line {国|くに}{破|やぶ}{山河|さんが}{在|あ} of a Chinese poem is read {国|くに}{破|やぶ}れて{山河|さんが}{在|あ}り. Writing the result out in kana and kanji gives a kundoku sentence, the source of many literary phrases. Not the same as kun'yomi.

The style of research papers and reports: である style, no first person or a careful one ({筆者|ひっしゃ}, {本稿|ほんこう}), many kango, exact conjunctions and hedges, and a fixed order of sections (aim, previous research, method, results, discussion). It is the style of the longest reading texts in the JLPT.

What ties sentences into one text: conjunctions (しかし, つまり), words that point back (これ, その{点|てん}), repeated or paraphrased words, and the choice of what is left out. The JLPT's text grammar questions test cohesion; reading for it shows where an argument turns.

A statement of a text's claim in a sentence or two ({要旨|ようし}, {要約|ようやく}). In an essay, the writer's claim is usually in the last paragraph and after a turn (しかし, むしろ); in a paper, it is set out before the text as an abstract. Thematic comprehension questions ask for exactly this.

The JLPT task ({文章|ぶんしょう}の{文法|ぶんぽう}) that removes several words from a passage and asks for the one that fits each gap: a conjunction, a word pointing back, a sentence ending that suits the writer's view. The answer depends on the passage, not on the sentence alone.

The JLPT N1 task ({主張理解|しゅちょうりかい}) that gives a long essay or editorial and asks for the writer's claim or view. Find the counter-view the writer is answering, mark the turn and write the claim in one sentence before reading the choices.

A JLPT task ({統合理解|とうごうりかい}) that gives two or more texts or speakers on one topic and asks what they share or how they differ. In reading, two short opinions on the same question; in listening, a conversation that you must compare with what you have heard before.

The JLPT task ({情報検索|じょうほうけんさく}) that gives a notice, guide, timetable or form and asks a practical question about it: who may apply, how much it costs, what to do by when. Read the question first, then search the text for the conditions, the exceptions and the notes.

The first JLPT listening task ({課題理解|かだいりかい}): you hear a situation and a conversation and choose what the person must do next. The question is given before you listen; listen for the changes of plan.

A JLPT listening task ({ポイント理解|りかい}): the question and the choices come before you listen, and you listen for one point (the reason, the cause, what the speaker is most worried about) among many details.

A JLPT listening task ({概要理解|がいようりかい}) with no printed question or choices: you hear one speaker or a short conversation, then the question, then the choices, and must grasp the speaker's point or view as a whole.
A JLPT listening task ({即時応答|そくじおうとう}): you hear one short line and choose the natural reply from three spoken choices. Nothing is printed; decide quickly and move on.

Two verbs joined into one, the first in the ます stem: {踏|ふ}み{込|こ}む, {取|と}り{組|く}む, {見|み}{逃|のが}す. The second verb often adds a direction or a degree ({込|こ}む: into, thoroughly; {切|き}る: completely); the meaning of the whole is often more than the sum of its parts.

A word made of kanji read in on'yomi ({漢語|かんご}): {検討|けんとう}, {実施|じっし}, {困難|こんなん}. Kango are the core of written, formal and academic Japanese; speech often puts a native word in their place ({検討|けんとう}する → {考|かんが}える).

A native Japanese word ({和語|わご}), written with kun'yomi or in kana: {考|かんが}える, {話|はなし}, ゆっくり. Wago sound softer and more everyday than kango of the same meaning; literary prose often chooses them for that reason.

A set expression of four kanji ({四字熟語|よじじゅくご}), many of them from Chinese: {一石二鳥|いっせきにちょう}, {試行錯誤|しこうさくご}, {本末転倒|ほんまつてんとう}. They are frequent in editorials and speeches; learn them as words, with their usual sentence (〜は{本末転倒|ほんまつてんとう}だ).

A fixed phrase whose meaning isn't that of its words ({慣用句|かんようく}), very often built on a part of the body: {顔|かお}が{広|ひろ}い (to know many people), {骨|ほね}を{折|お}る (to take pains). Keep the words as they are: changing the particle or the verb usually breaks the idiom.

Words that always go together in the same form: an idiom, a four-character compound, a proverb or a formula of letters and notices ({時下|じか}ますますご{清栄|せいえい}のこととお{喜|よろこ}び{申|もう}し{上|あ}げます). Learn them whole, with the situation they belong to.

The Edo-period scholarly movement ({国学|こくがく}) that studied Japan's oldest texts, such as 『{古事記|こじき}』, 『{万葉集|まんようしゅう}』 and 『{源氏物語|げんじものがたり}』, to find a Japanese way of thinking before Chinese and Buddhist learning. {本居宣長|もとおりのりなが} (1730–1801) is its best-known scholar.

references.title: Classical Japanese (lessons 5h2, 15h1, 26)
references.body:
A reading guide to the classical Japanese ({古文|こぶん}) you meet in the honors lessons and in modern
written style: the old spelling, the auxiliaries, kakari-musubi and the classical forms that survive
in today's writing. All of it is for recognition: none of these forms is a conjugation drill form.

## Historical kana usage: how to read it

Classical texts (and most writing before 1946) are printed in historical kana usage
({歴史的仮名遣|れきしてきかなづか}い). Read them by today's pronunciation:

| Old spelling | Read as | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| は、ひ、ふ、へ、ほ inside a word | わ、い、う、え、お | {言|い}ふ → いう, {思|おも}ふ → おもう, かは → かわ, なほ → なお, こひ → こい ({恋|こい}) |
| ゐ、ゑ | い、え | ゐる → いる, こゑ → こえ, ゑむ → えむ |
| を (not the particle) | お | をかし → おかし, をとこ → おとこ |
| ぢ、づ | じ、ず | はぢ → はじ, みづ → みず |
| くわ、ぐわ | か、が | くわじ → かじ ({火事|かじ}), ぐわん → がん |
| あう、あふ | おう | やうやう → ようよう, あふぎ → おうぎ |
| いう、いふ | ゆう | いふ → いう (read ゆう), りう → りゅう |
| えう、えふ | よう | てふ → ちょう, けふ → きょう |
| む (in some endings) | ん | {行|ゆ}かむ → ゆかん |

Rules combine: てふ → てう → ちょう. The は-row rule applies inside words only; a particle は is
read わ as in modern Japanese.

## Verb forms named in the lessons

| Form | Japanese | What follows it | Modern counterpart |
|---|---|---|---|
| irrealis | {未然形|みぜんけい} | ず, む / ん, ば (if) | the stem before ない ({書|か}か-) |
| continuative | {連用形|れんようけい} | けり, たり, verbs | the ます stem ({書|か}き-) |
| conclusive | {終止形|しゅうしけい} | end of a sentence | the dictionary form |
| attributive | {連体形|れんたいけい} | a noun; ぞ / なむ / や / か endings | the dictionary form before a noun |
| realis | {已然形|いぜんけい} (已 is outside N1) | ば (because), ど / ども (though); こそ endings | the stem before ば ({書|か}け-) |

## Classical auxiliaries

| Auxiliary | Attaches to | Meaning | Main forms | Modern equivalent | In modern writing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ず | irrealis | not | ず, ぬ (attributive), ね (realis), ざる / ざれ (with あり) | ない | 〜ずに, 〜ずして, ずじまい (lesson 5), 〜ざるを{得|え}ない (N2), {知|し}られざる (lesson 26), {知|し}らぬ{顔|かお} |
| けり | continuative | past told as a story; sudden realization | けり, ける (attributive), けれ (realis) | 〜た, 〜たそうだ, 〜だなあ | rare; in haiku as a cutting word (lesson 25h2) |
| たり | continuative | completed action; a continuing state | たり, たる (attributive) | 〜た, 〜ている | {確固|かっこ}たる, {堂々|どうどう}たる (a different たり, after nouns) |
| なり | nouns, attributive | assertion: is | なり, なる (attributive), なれ (realis) | だ, である | 〜なる{人物|じんぶつ} (a person called…), {単|たん}なる |
| む / ん | irrealis | conjecture; will | む / ん, め (realis) | 〜だろう, 〜よう | んがため (lesson 12), んばかり (lesson 23); the modern 〜う / 〜よう comes from it |
| べし | conclusive | must, should; can; will surely | べし, べき (attributive), べから (irrealis) | 〜べきだ, 〜はずだ | 〜べきだ, 〜べからず, 〜べからざる (lesson 20), 〜べし (lesson 26) |
| ごとし | noun + の / が, attributive + が | like, as | ごとし, ごとき (attributive), ごとく (continuative) | 〜ようだ | {前述|ぜんじゅつ}のごとく, {私|わたし}ごとき (lesson 23), 〜ごとし (lesson 26) |
| ぬ (perfective) | continuative | has happened (completion) | ぬ, ぬる (attributive) | 〜てしまった, 〜た | 「{風立|かぜた}ちぬ」 (lesson 26); not the negative ぬ |
| しむ | irrealis | causative (make someone do) | しむ, しめる (modern) | 〜させる | をして〜しめる (lesson 26) |

Two ぬ: the negative ぬ is the attributive of ず ({知|し}らぬ{人|ひと}, a person one doesn't know); the
perfective ぬ is a separate auxiliary ({風立|かぜた}ちぬ, the wind has risen). The form before them
tells you which: ず and its ぬ take the irrealis ({知|し}ら-), the perfective ぬ the continuative
({立|た}ち-).

## Kakari-musubi (lesson 15h1)

A focus particle in the middle of a sentence changes the form of the verb that ends it:

| Particle | Function | Ending form |
|---|---|---|
| ぞ, なむ | emphasis | attributive ({連体形|れんたいけい}) |
| や, か | question, doubt | attributive |
| こそ | strong emphasis | realis ({已然形|いぜんけい}) |

Without a focus particle, the sentence ends in the conclusive form. Lesson 15h1 gives examples from
『{徒然草|つれづれぐさ}』 and 『{平家物語|へいけものがたり}』.

## Classical to modern: a quick table

| Classical | Modern | Classical | Modern |
|---|---|---|---|
| いと | とても | なし | ない |
| あり | ある | をり | いる |
| いふ | いう | す | する |
| をかし | おもしろい、{趣|おもむき}がある | あはれ | しみじみと{心|こころ}を{動|うご}かされる |
| つとめて | {早朝|そうちょう} | あけぼの | {夜明|よあ}け |
| さらなり | {言|い}うまでもない | ためし | {例|れい} |
| うたかた | {泡|あわ} | よどみ | {流|なが}れの{止|と}まったところ |
| 〜けれど | 〜けれども | 〜ずして | 〜ないで |

## Openings quoted in the course

- 『{枕草子|まくらのそうし}』 ({清少納言|せいしょうなごん}, around 1000): {春|はる}はあけぼの。やうやう{白|しろ}くなりゆく{山|やま}ぎは、
  すこしあかりて、{紫|むらさき}だちたる{雲|くも}のほそくたなびきたる。(lesson 5h2)
- 『{方丈記|ほうじょうき}』 ({鴨長明|かものちょうめい}, 1212; 鴨 is outside N1): ゆく{河|かは}の{流|なが}れは{絶|た}えずして、
  しかももとの{水|みづ}にあらず。(lesson 5h2)
- 『たけくらべ』 ({樋口一葉|ひぐちいちよう}, 1895–96; 樋 is outside N1): {廻|めぐ}れば{大門|おおもん}の{見返|みかえ}り{柳|やなぎ}
  いと{長|なが}けれど、(lesson 5h1; 廻 is outside N1)
- Lessons 15h1, 26 and 30h1 add their own.

references.title: Concession and condition
references.body:
Module 2 of Japanese N1 (lessons 06–10). Each row gives how the pattern joins, the meaning, an
example and where it lives. "Plain" is the plain form; "N" a noun. Speakers don't all draw the
lines between near-synonyms in the same place: the notes give the usual, safe choice.

## Even (lesson 6)

| Pattern | Joins | Meaning | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 〜といえども | N; plain | even (X, who you'd think an exception) | いかに{有名|ゆうめい}な{記者|きしゃ}といえども | very written; a judgment or rule follows |
| 一 + counter + たりとも〜ない | one of something | not a single one | {一円|いちえん}たりとも{無駄|むだ}にできない | emphatic negation; negative only |
| N + とて | N | even N, N too | {私|わたし}とて{同|おな}じだ | written; {私|わたし}とて in formal speech; 〜たとて = たところで (literary) |
| 〜たところで | た form | even if you do, it's no use | {今|いま}さら{謝|あやま}ったところで{遅|おそ}い | a dismissive judgment follows, usually non-past |
| 〜にしたって | N; plain | even for (casual にしても) | {部長|ぶちょう}にしたって{知|し}らなかった | spoken |

## If only, contrary to (lesson 7)

| Pattern | Joins | Meaning | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 〜ものを | plain (often 〜ばよかった) | if only (it didn't happen) | {言|い}ってくれればよかったものを | counterfactual; regret or reproach; everyday のに |
| 〜と{思|おも}いきや | plain (N / な-adj. ± だ; 〜かと) | I thought…, but | {雨|あめ}かと{思|おも}いきや{晴|は}れた | written, humorous; a narrated expectation overturned |
| 〜にひきかえ | N; plain + の | in contrast to | {兄|あに}にひきかえ{弟|おとうと}は… | one side praised, the other criticized |
| 〜ながらに / 〜ながらの | fixed nouns and stems | as it is, from | {涙|なみだ}ながらに, {昔|むかし}ながらの | fixed expressions only |

## Whether A or B (lesson 8)

| Pattern | Joins | Meaning | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 〜であれ (〜であれ〜であれ) | N; question word | whatever; whether A or B | {理由|りゆう}が{何|なん}であれ | written; a general rule follows |
| 〜といい〜といい | N (aspects or members of one whole) | A and B alike (it's…) | {味|あじ}といい{値段|ねだん}といい | ends in an evaluation |
| 〜といわず〜といわず | N (parts of a whole) | everywhere, all over | {顔|かお}といわず{手|て}といわず{泥|どろ}だらけ | vivid description |
| 〜なり〜なり | dictionary form; N | A or B or something | {電話|でんわ}なりメールなりで | advice and requests, not past facts |

## Let alone, more than (lesson 9)

| Pattern | Joins | Meaning | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 〜はおろか…も / さえ | N | let alone A, (not even) B | {漢字|かんじ}はおろか{平仮名|ひらがな}も{読|よ}めない | usually negative; not for requests |
| 〜もさることながら | N | A of course, but B even more | {内容|ないよう}もさることながら | praise; the weight is on B |
| 〜にもまして | N | even more than | {以前|いぜん}にもまして, {何|なに}にもまして | written |
| 〜ならいざしらず / 〜はいざしらず | N | A would be one thing, but B | {子供|こども}ならいざしらず | criticism or surprise follows |

## It's not as if (lesson 10)

| Pattern | Joins | Meaning | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 〜ではあるまいし / 〜じゃあるまいし | N; 〜わけ | it's not as if N, so | {子供|こども}じゃあるまいし | spoken; advice or criticism follows |
| 〜ならまだしも | N; plain + の | A would be tolerable, but B | {一度|いちど}ならまだしも | a complaint follows |
| 〜ないまでも | ない form | if not A, at least B | {毎日|まいにち}とは{言|い}わないまでも | せめて, 〜くらいは, 〜てほしい often follow |
| 〜ともなく / 〜ともなしに | dictionary form + same verb; question word | without meaning to; some… or other | {見|み}るともなく{見|み}る, どこからともなく | written, narrative |

## N1 and N2 concessions side by side

| Feel | N2 (and earlier) | N1 |
|---|---|---|
| even if (neutral) | 〜ても, 〜としても | 〜たところで (it's no use) |
| even X (no exception) | 〜でも, 〜だって | 〜といえども, N + とて |
| granted, but | 〜とはいえ, 〜ものの | 〜といえども (formal とはいえ) |
| not a single one | 〜も〜ない, {一|ひと}つも | 一 + counter + たりとも〜ない |
| whether A or B | 〜にせよ / にしろ, 〜ても〜ても | 〜であれ〜であれ, 〜なり〜なり (options) |
| if only, though | 〜のに, 〜くせに | 〜ものを |
| although (a fact) | 〜ながらも, 〜にもかかわらず | 〜にひきかえ (contrast with judgment) |
| let alone | 〜どころか, 〜はもとより | 〜はおろか, 〜もさることながら |
| A would be one thing | 〜ならともかく | 〜ならいざしらず, 〜ならまだしも |
| it's not as if | 〜わけではない | 〜ではあるまいし |
| if not A, at least B | せめて | 〜ないまでも |

references.title: Feelings, judgements and must not
references.body:
Module 4 of Japanese N1 (lessons 16–20). Each row gives how the pattern joins, the meaning, an
example and where it lives. "Stem" is the ます stem. Speakers don't all draw the lines between
near-synonyms in the same place: the notes give the usual, safe choice. The classical forms
(まじき, べからず, べからざる) aren't conjugation-drill forms.

## Feelings that rise up (lesson 16)

| Pattern | Joins | Meaning | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 〜を{禁|きん}じ{得|え}ない | noun of feeling ({怒|いか}り, {涙|なみだ}, {驚|おどろ}き, {同情|どうじょう}) | can't hold back | {涙|なみだ}を{禁|きん}じ{得|え}なかった | written, very formal; the speaker's own feeling |
| 〜てやまない | て form of {願|ねが}う, {祈|いの}る, {愛|あい}する, {期待|きたい}する | never stop (hoping, loving) | {成功|せいこう}を{願|ねが}ってやみません | speeches, letters; also {魅了|みりょう}してやまない |
| 〜に{堪|た}えない (1) | {見|み}る, {聞|き}く, {読|よ}む | too bad to bear | {見|み}るに{堪|た}えない{内容|ないよう} | critical |
| 〜に{堪|た}えない (2) | {感謝|かんしゃ}, {喜|よろこ}び, {感激|かんげき} | more than words can say | {感謝|かんしゃ}に{堪|た}えません | very formal |
| 〜に{堪|た}える | noun, {見|み}る / {読|よ}む | stands up to, worth | {鑑賞|かんしょう}に{堪|た}える | written |
| 〜ずにはおかない | ない stem (する → せず) | can't fail to cause; will see it done | {人|ひと}を{感動|かんどう}させずにはおかない | usually with a causative |
| 〜に{忍|しの}びない | dictionary form | can't bring oneself to (pity) | {捨|す}てるに{忍|しの}びない | formal |
| spontaneous form | られる form of {思|おも}う, {感|かん}じる, {悔|く}やむ… | a feeling arises by itself | {悔|く}やまれる, {案|あん}じられる | written; measured |

Everyday equivalents (N2): 〜てたまらない, 〜てならない, 〜ずにはいられない.

## Worth it or not (lesson 17)

| Pattern | Joins | Meaning | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 〜に{足|た}る | dictionary form, する noun | sufficient for, worthy of | {信頼|しんらい}するに{足|た}る{人物|じんぶつ} | written; before a noun |
| 〜に{足|た}りない / 〜に{足|た}らない | a few verbs | not even worth | {取|と}るに{足|た}りない, {恐|おそ}れるに{足|た}りない | set phrases |
| 〜に{値|あたい}する (N2) | noun, dictionary form | deserves | {称賛|しょうさん}に{値|あたい}する | written |
| 〜にかたくない | {想像|そうぞう}, {察|さっ}する | not hard to (imagine) | {想像|そうぞう}にかたくない | written; others' feelings |
| 〜かいがある / 〜かいもなく | た form, noun + の | was worth it / in vain | {練習|れんしゅう}したかいがあった | speech and writing |
| ます stem + がい | | worth doing | {生|い}きがい, やりがい | nouns |

## To the extreme (lesson 18)

| Pattern | Joins | Meaning | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 〜{極|きわ}まりない / 〜{極|きわ}まる | な-adjective | extremely | {失礼|しつれい}{極|きわ}まりない | written; criticism |
| 〜の{至|いた}り | {光栄|こうえい}, {感激|かんげき}, {恐縮|きょうしゅく}, {若気|わかげ} | the utmost | {光栄|こうえい}の{至|いた}りです | fixed list |
| 〜の{極|きわ}み | noun of feeling or state | the height of | {痛恨|つうこん}の{極|きわ}み | written |
| 〜とは | plain form | to think that…! | こんなところで{会|あ}うとは | casual: 〜なんて |
| 〜といったらない (N2) | adjective, noun | indescribably | {恥|は}ずかしいといったらない | spoken, emotional |
| 〜{限|かぎ}りだ (N2) | adjective | I feel so… | {心細|こころぼそ}い{限|かぎ}りだ | one's own feeling |

## Forced to (lesson 19)

| Pattern | Joins | Meaning | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 〜を{余儀|よぎ}なくされる | する noun | be forced (by circumstances) to | {中止|ちゅうし}を{余儀|よぎ}なくされた | news; cause with で / により |
| 〜を{余儀|よぎ}なくさせる | する noun | force (someone) to | {大雪|おおゆき}が{休業|きゅうぎょう}を{余儀|よぎ}なくさせた | the cause is the subject |
| 〜ないではすまない | ない form | won't get away without | {謝|あやま}らないではすまない | social or moral pressure |
| 〜ずにはすまない | ない stem (する → せず) | the same, more written | {弁償|べんしょう}せずにはすまない | |
| N + ではすまない | noun | won't end with just | {謝罪|しゃざい}だけではすまない | |
| 〜ざるを{得|え}ない (N2) | ない stem (する → せざる) | have no choice but to | {延期|えんき}せざるを{得|え}ない | the speaker's reluctant decision |

## Must not (lesson 20)

| Pattern | Joins | Meaning | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| N に / として あるまじき + N | ある | unworthy of | {教師|きょうし}にあるまじき{行為|こうい} | written; strong condemnation |
| 〜べからず | dictionary form (する → するべからず / すべからず) | must not | {立|た}ち{入|い}るべからず | notices, sayings, jokes |
| 〜べからざる + N | {欠|か}く, {許|ゆる}す, {侵|おか}す | that must not / cannot be | {欠|か}くべからざる{存在|そんざい} | written |
| 〜てしかるべきだ | て form | ought to (and hasn't) | {説明|せつめい}があってしかるべきだ | formal criticism |
| しかるべき + N | | proper, appropriate | しかるべき{措置|そち} | official, business |
| 〜べきだ / 〜べきではない (N3) | dictionary form | should / should not | {謝|あやま}るべきだ | both |
| 〜ものではない (N3) | dictionary form | one doesn't (as a rule) | {人|ひと}の{悪口|わるぐち}を{言|い}うものではない | advice |

## Obligation from N4 to N1

| Pattern | Pressure from | Register |
|---|---|---|
| 〜なければならない | neutral necessity | both |
| 〜べきだ | the speaker's judgement | both |
| 〜ないわけにはいかない | one's own sense of duty | both |
| 〜ほかない / 〜しかない | no other option | both |
| 〜ざるを{得|え}ない | circumstances, reluctantly | formal; also common in speech |
| 〜ないではすまない / 〜ずにはすまない | others or society | both / written |
| 〜を{余儀|よぎ}なくされる | outside forces | news, written |
| 〜てしかるべきだ | what would be proper | formal |

references.title: Formal letters, emails and notices (lessons 3, 4, 19, 29)
references.body:
Formal Japanese letters follow a fixed order with set phrases at each step, and notices follow a
fixed layout. N1 information retrieval and letter texts assume you know both: the phrases carry
little information, so the skill is to skip them quickly and find the part after さて. Business
emails keep the order but drop most of the ceremony. All the names and companies below are
invented.

## The parts of a formal letter

| Part | Name | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| Opening word | {頭語|とうご} | {拝啓|はいけい} and the like (paired with a closing word) |
| Seasonal greeting | {時候|じこう}の{挨拶|あいさつ} | a phrase for the month, or {時下|じか} in business |
| Wishing well | {安否|あんぴ}の{挨拶|あいさつ} | ご{清栄|せいえい}のこととお{喜|よろこ}び{申|もう}し{上|あ}げます |
| Thanks | {感謝|かんしゃ} | {平素|へいそ}は{格別|かくべつ}のご{高配|こうはい}をたまわり… |
| Main text | {主文|しゅぶん} | begins with さて (now, as for) |
| Closing lines | {末文|まつぶん} | good wishes; まずは〜まで |
| Closing word | {結語|けつご} | {敬具|けいぐ} and the like |
| After the letter | {後付|あとづ}け | date, sender, addressee |

## Opening and closing words

| Opening | Closing | When |
|---|---|---|
| {拝啓|はいけい} | {敬具|けいぐ} | an ordinary formal letter |
| {謹啓|きんけい} | {敬白|けいはく} | a very formal letter (to a superior, an important client) |
| {拝復|はいふく} | {敬具|けいぐ} | a reply |
| {前略|ぜんりゃく} | {草々|そうそう} | a short letter: no seasonal greeting, not for superiors |

かしこ is a closing used only by women in personal letters. An email uses none of these words.

## Seasonal greetings (〜の{候|こう}: "the season of …")

| Month | Phrase |
|---|---|
| 1 | {新春|しんしゅん}の{候|こう} / {厳寒|げんかん}の{候|こう} |
| 2 | {余寒|よかん}の{候|こう} |
| 3 | {早春|そうしゅん}の{候|こう} |
| 4 | {陽春|ようしゅん}の{候|こう} / {春暖|しゅんだん}の{候|こう} |
| 5 | {新緑|しんりょく}の{候|こう} |
| 6 | {梅雨|つゆ}の{候|こう} (read ばいう in this phrase) |
| 7 | {盛夏|せいか}の{候|こう} |
| 8 | {残暑|ざんしょ}の{候|こう} |
| 9 | {初秋|しょしゅう}の{候|こう} |
| 10 | {秋冷|しゅうれい}の{候|こう} |
| 11 | {晩秋|ばんしゅう}の{候|こう} |
| 12 | {初冬|しょとう}の{候|こう} |

Personal letters often use a sentence instead: {寒|さむ}さ{厳|きび}しき{折|おり}から (lesson 4:
at a time when the cold is severe), {桜|さくら}の{便|たよ}りが{聞|き}かれる{頃|ころ}となりました.
Business letters may use {時下|じか} (at this time) for any month.

## Set phrases of the opening

| Phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {時下|じか}ますますご{清栄|せいえい}のこととお{喜|よろこ}び{申|もう}し{上|あ}げます | I trust you are flourishing (to a person or company) |
| {貴社|きしゃ}ますますご{発展|はってん}のこととお{喜|よろこ}び{申|もう}し{上|あ}げます | I trust your company continues to prosper |
| {平素|へいそ}は{格別|かくべつ}のご{高配|こうはい}をたまわり、{厚|あつ}く{御礼|おんれい}{申|もう}し{上|あ}げます | thank you for your constant kind consideration |
| いつも{大変|たいへん}お{世話|せわ}になっております | thank you for your continued support (emails) |

## Linking the parts

| Word | Job | Example |
|---|---|---|
| さて | to the main point | さて、このたびは〜 |
| つきましては | as a consequence (a request follows) | つきましては、ご{出席|しゅっせき}いただきたく〜 |
| なお | one more point | なお、{資料|しりょう}を{添付|てんぷ}いたしました |
| 〜かたがた | combining two purposes (lesson 3) | お{礼|れい}かたがたご{報告|ほうこく}{申|もう}し{上|あ}げます |
| 〜{折|おり}から | at a time when (lesson 4) | {寒|さむ}さ{厳|きび}しき{折|おり}から |
| {末筆|まっぴつ}ながら | last but not least | {末筆|まっぴつ}ながら{皆様|みなさま}のご{健康|けんこう}をお{祈|いの}り{申|もう}し{上|あ}げます |

## Closing lines

| Phrase | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {今後|こんご}ともよろしくお{願|ねが}い{申|もう}し{上|あ}げます | I ask for your continued goodwill |
| {時節柄|じせつがら}ご{自愛|じあい}ください | take care of yourself in this season |
| まずは{略儀|りゃくぎ}ながら{書中|しょちゅう}にてご{挨拶|あいさつ}{申|もう}し{上|あ}げます | I send my greetings by letter, though it is an informal way |
| {取|と}り{急|いそ}ぎ、ご{連絡|れんらく}まで | just a quick note to let you know (emails) |
| ご{査収|さしゅう}のほど、よろしくお{願|ねが}いいたします | please check the attached / enclosed |
| お{取|と}り{計|はか}らいのほど、よろしくお{願|ねが}いいたします | I would be grateful if you could arrange it |

## Addressing people and organizations

| Word | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| {様|さま} | a person | {田村|たむら}{一郎|いちろう}{様|さま} |
| {御中|おんちゅう} | an organization or department, not a person | {株式会社|かぶしきがいしゃ}{山中|やまなか}{商事|しょうじ}{営業部|えいぎょうぶ}{御中|おんちゅう} |

{会社名|かいしゃめい}, the department and then the name with {様|さま}. Your own company is
{弊社|へいしゃ} (or {当社|とうしゃ}); the other company is {貴社|きしゃ} in writing and
{御社|おんしゃ} in speech.

## Notices (お{知|し}らせ, ご{案内|あんない})

| Part | What it holds |
|---|---|
| Top right | date; sender (organization, then the person in charge) |
| Top left | addressee: 〜{各位|かくい}, {住民|じゅうみん}の{皆様|みなさま} |
| Title | 〜のお{知|し}らせ, 〜のご{案内|あんない}, 〜{募集|ぼしゅう} |
| Body | the reason (〜につき, 〜のため) and a request |
| {記|き} … {以上|いじょう} | the details as a list: {日時|にちじ}, {場所|ばしょ}, {対象|たいしょう}, {内容|ないよう}, {費用|ひよう}, {申込方法|もうしこみほうほう}, {問|と}い{合|あ}わせ{先|さき} |

Words that decide an information retrieval answer:

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| {下記|かき}のとおり / {別紙|べっし} | as set out below / on a separate sheet |
| 〜に{限|かぎ}る / 〜を{除|のぞ}く | only … / except … |
| ただし、〜の{場合|ばあい}はこの{限|かぎ}りではない | however, this doesn't apply when … |
| {必着|ひっちゃく} | must arrive by (the date) |
| {消印有効|けしいんゆうこう} | the postmark date counts |
| {当日|とうじつ}{消印|けしいん}{有効|ゆうこう} | posted on the day is in time |
| {先着順|せんちゃくじゅん} / {抽選|ちゅうせん} | first come, first served / by lottery |
| {事前|じぜん}{申込制|もうしこみせい} | advance booking required |
| 〜{及|およ}び〜 / 〜{又|また}は〜 | and / or (the style sheet has the two-level rule) |

Find the conditions (who, when, how much), then read every ただし and なお: the answer is often
in them.

references.title: The N1 kanji
references.body:
The 960 kanji this course adds, in the order of the lessons that teach them. With the 102 kanji
of Japanese N5, the 177 of Japanese N4, the 370 of Japanese N3 and the 390 of Japanese N2 (each
listed in that course's kanji reference) they make 1,999: nearly every jōyō kanji in common use.
Any lesson in this course may use a kanji from any of the five lists, and a word is written with
kanji when all its kanji are on them.

On'yomi are in katakana; kun'yomi are in hiragana, with the okurigana in brackets: たず(ねる)
means the kanji is read たず in {尋|たず}ねる. Only the readings you meet at N1 are given. Stroke
counts are those of the tracing pads. 叱, 剥 and 頬 are printed in their common forms; the jōyō
table's official forms are 𠮟, 剝 and 頰.
